The description and `prompts/shell-access.md` both name read-only utilities ("`rg`, `tail`, `grep`, `cat`, `wc`, `find`, `head`, `jq`") and say "Do **not** use it to drive the system under test", but nothing enforces either — the description is guidance to the model, not a control.

In the same conversation, `executeExtract` in `tools/visual.ts` returns `await ctx.chrome.generateMarkdown(ctx.tab)` — up to 50 KB of the page's own text, produced by `lib/page-scripts/markdown.js` — as a plain `textResult`. It is not delimited, tagged, or framed as untrusted data anywhere in `agent.ts` or the prompt files. A page under test that contains instruction-shaped text is therefore a live prompt-injection surface whose payoff is arbitrary command execution on the QA host as the invoking user.

`buildScrubbedEnv` reads as the mitigation but is not one. It drops unrelated parent variables while deliberately forwarding `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and the proxy variables; `test/qa/agent/bash-tool.test.ts`'s "env passes through ANTHROPIC_API_KEY when set in parent" pins that as intended. With full shell access the env contents are close to irrelevant anyway — `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.claude/`, and any `.env` under the run root are already readable — which is the point: the scrub gives an impression of containment that does not exist.

I did not attempt an exploit; no browser or provider was launched. The reachability above is from reading the dispatch path (`adapter.executeTool` → `shared.execute("bash", …)`) and the extract path.

Fix (a decision, not a patch): wrap tool results carrying page-derived content in an explicit untrusted-content envelope and say in the system prompt that text inside it is data; and gate `bash` behind an opt-in config flag plus an argv allowlist for the read-only utilities the description already names. At minimum, stop forwarding provider API keys, since nothing in the shell-access contract needs them.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** The web adapter mounts bash unconditionally via buildSharedTools, whose canExecute for bash always returns true with no opt-in flag anywhere in config.ts; executeExtract returns the page generateMarkdown text as a plain textResult with no untrusted-content framing in agent.ts or any prompt file; bash-tool.ts has no allowlist, denylist or approval gate, only an env scrub and timeout, and bash-tool.test.ts pins ANTHROPIC_API_KEY passthrough as intended. Static trace; the tool was not executed.

### CR-038: Agent-driven bash writes the operator's Anthropic and OpenAI API keys into the run's evidence log
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/agent/bash-tool.ts`
**Anchor:** `SDK_PASSTHROUGH_KEYS` / `buildScrubbedEnv`
**Severity:** high

`buildScrubbedEnv` deliberately forwards `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_ORG_ID` and the proxy vars into the `bash -c` subprocess the LLM controls. `formatResult` then embeds the child's stdout verbatim in the returned `ToolResult.text`, and the tool never sets `transcriptText`, so `EvidenceLogger.logToolResult` records that text unchanged into `run.jsonl` (or spills it verbatim into `artifacts/N.txt` past the inline limit). Any command the agent chooses that prints the environment puts a live credential on disk in the run directory. This is not a hypothetical posture gap: the codebase already built the redaction seam for exactly this class of bytes — `credential-tool.ts` returns `transcriptText: "<credential redacted: entity=… key=… len=…>"` so resolver stdout never reaches `run.jsonl` (PRI-1605) — and the bash tool, which is the one tool actually handed the API keys, bypasses it.

Trigger: `bash` with `command: "env | grep ANTHROPIC"` (or `printenv`, `set`, a failing `curl -v`, or a nested coding-agent invocation that echoes its config) while `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set in the parent. I reproduced it with a throwaway script under the scratchpad that drives `buildBashTool(...).execute()` and a real `EvidenceLogger` against a tmp outDir: the tool text contained the key, `transcriptText` was `undefined`, and `run.jsonl` contained the key value.

`bash-tool.test.ts`'s "env passes through ANTHROPIC_API_KEY when set in parent" pins the passthrough as intended behaviour and asserts the value appears in `result.text`, with no companion assertion that it stays out of the transcript — so the test demonstrates the leak path and blesses it.

Fix: give the bash tool a `transcriptText` that masks any forwarded secret value found in stdout/stderr (the forwarded key set is known at `buildScrubbedEnv` time, so a literal replace of each non-empty value with `<redacted:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY>` is sufficient and cheap), and apply the same masking before `saveArtifact` spills oversize text. If the passthrough itself is not needed for the current adapters, narrowing `SDK_PASSTHROUGH_KEYS` is the stronger fix.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** buildScrubbedEnv forwards ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY into the child env, formatResult embeds raw stdout in ToolResult.text, and bash-tool never sets transcriptText, so logToolResult writes the raw text into run.jsonl; credential-tool.ts shows the same transcriptText redaction mechanism already exists and is simply never applied to bash. Any env or printenv call by the agent lands the key in the evidence log verbatim.

### CR-039: Effective-config endpoint hands process environment values to unauthenticated clients
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/api/routes/config-effective.ts`
**Anchor:** `configEffectiveRoutes`
**Severity:** high

`configEffectiveRoutes` returns `buildConfigOutput(config, process.env)` on a plain `GET`. That payload's `sdkEnv` section maps only `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY` to `"set"`/`"unset"`; `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_ORG_ID`, `OPENAI_PROJECT`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` are passed through verbatim. Proxy URLs routinely embed `user:password`, and an LLM-gateway base URL routinely embeds a token, so the endpoint returns operator secrets in full.

The endpoint has no authentication and no Origin or CSRF gate, and `serveViaNode` in `src/qa/runtime/serve.ts` calls `honoServe({ port, fetch })` without a `hostname`. I confirmed by reading the installed `@hono/node-server` that it forwards `options.hostname` straight to `server.listen`, so an omitted hostname means Node binds every interface. Any host that can reach the daemon's port can read these values. The drain middleware only blocks non-`GET`, so draining does not close the hole either.

Not reproduced against a live socket (I did not start a listener), but the payload construction is direct and unconditional.

Fix: treat the whole `sdkEnv` block the way the API keys are already treated, reporting presence rather than value for anything that can carry a credential, or drop `sdkEnv` from the HTTP response and keep it only in the local `moe-flight qa config` output.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced by driving the real Hono app from the built dist against dummy env values carrying user:pass@host credentials in ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, OPENAI_BASE_URL, HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY; GET /api/config/effective returned them verbatim in JSON while the two API keys stayed redacted. createApp registers only a drain gate and a body-size limiter; no auth or origin middleware exists.

### CR-040: Fanout writes an LLM-chosen card id as a filename with no containment check
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/api/routes/fanout.ts`
**Anchor:** `writeCards`
**Severity:** high

`writeCards` does `writeFileSync(join(storiesDir, `${card.id}.md`), text)` where `card.id` comes
from `parseStoryCard` on model output. Nothing validates the id's charset or containment.
`parseStoryCard` only requires `id` and `title` to be present and passes the value through
`asCardId`, which is a pure cast; `splitAndValidateCards` in the generator keeps any chunk that
parses. So an id of `../../../../pwned` writes outside the stories directory, with attacker-chosen
file content (the card text is written verbatim).

The sibling create route already knows this is required: `POST /api/scenarios` checks
`isSafePath(storiesDir, targetPath)` before writing and returns 400 `"invalid id"`. The fanout
writer is the same operation without the check.

The reachable trigger is indirect prompt injection. `buildObservationPrompt` and the failure
prompt interpolate `result.observations[].description` and the run summary, which are the agent's
transcription of screen text, log lines, and command output from the system under test. A page
under test that instructs the tester to record an observation containing a card id closes the
loop. The endpoint itself is unauthenticated and cross-site reachable.

Reproduced. Mounting the built `fanoutRoutes` with a stub client that returns a card whose
frontmatter reads `id: ../../../../pwned` produced:

```
200 {"parent":"parent-card","generated":[{"id":"../../../../pwned","filename":"../../../../pwned.md"}]}
```

and the file landed outside the configured project root. `fanout.test.ts` has no traversal or
id-charset case.

Fix: validate every generated id before writing — reject anything that is not a single path
segment matching the documented `[a-zA-Z0-9-]+`, and keep the `isSafePath(storiesDir, targetPath)`
belt as well. Log the rejected id through `errorLog` the way the duplicate-id branch already does.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced in-process: mounting fanoutRoutes with a stubbed LLM client returning a card with id ../../../../pwned produced a 200 response and wrote the file four directories above the configured stories directory; no isSafePath or resolveInside guard exists on this write path, unlike the sibling POST /api/scenarios route which checks isSafePath before writing. CR-042 is the same defect in the same writeCards function.

### CR-041: Fanout result lookup composes an unvalidated runId into a filesystem path
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/api/routes/fanout.ts`
**Anchor:** `router.post("/:id/:mode")`
**Severity:** high

The mode route builds `flightPath(projectRoot, stateDirName, "results", runId, "result.json")`
straight from `c.req.param("id")` and reads it, with no containment check. Every sibling route
guards this: `resultRoutes` calls `isSafePath` before each read, `runSetRoutes` applies a regex,
`ws-handlers.ts` re-checks with `isSafePath` and calls it "defense in depth". This one does not.

Percent-encoded separators reach the param intact, so the traversal is reachable over HTTP rather
than only from a bad internal caller. I confirmed with the installed Hono that a request to
`/api/f/..%2f..%2f..%2ftmp/observations` yields `param("id") === "../../../tmp"`.

Reproduced against the built `fanoutRoutes`. A request to
`/api/fanout/..%2f..%2f..%2foutside/failure` read a `result.json` outside the project root and
reached the preflight check, returning `400 {"error":"result is not a failure"}`, while the
in-bounds `/api/fanout/legit/failure` returned `404 {"error":"not found"}`. The status difference
proves the out-of-tree file was opened and parsed.

Impact is an unauthenticated read of any file named `result.json` anywhere the daemon user can
read. If that file has `status: "fail"` (or observations, in observations mode) its contents are
forwarded into an LLM prompt and the generated cards are written to the stories directory, so the
read is also an exfiltration path. Separately, the `JSON.parse(readFileSync(...))` here has no
try/catch, so a malformed file returns a 500 carrying the parser message.

Fix: run the runId through `parseRunId` (it already exists, is strict, and is what the WebSocket
upgrade uses) and reject on failure; wrap the parse.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced in-process against dist/qa/api/routes/fanout.js: a request to /api/fanout/..%2F..%2F..%2F<outside-dir>/failure returned 200 with a field sourced from a result.json outside the project root; raw unencoded ../ is blocked by the Hono router but percent-encoded slashes reach c.req.param intact. No isSafePath or parseRunId guard exists in fanout.ts, unlike results.ts, run-sets.ts and ws-handlers.ts, and server.ts has no auth middleware.

### CR-042: LLM-supplied story-card id becomes a filesystem path, allowing writes outside the stories directory
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/api/routes/fanout.ts`
**Anchor:** `writeCards`, the line `const filename = \`${card.id}.md\`;`
**Severity:** high

`writeCards` takes the `id` frontmatter field out of a model-generated card and uses it directly as a filename under `storiesDir`. Nothing between the model and the `writeFileSync` validates the charset. `parseStoryCard` only checks that `id` and `title` are present, and `asCardId` in `src/qa/util/brands.ts` is a pure cast (`export const asCardId = (s: string): CardId => s as CardId;`). Two comments in the tree assert the opposite — `src/qa/util/id.ts` says "Story-card parsing already enforces `[a-zA-Z0-9-]`, so it is filesystem-safe" and `src/qa/api/routes/results.ts` repeats "story-card parse enforces `[a-zA-Z0-9-]`". Both claims are false.

Trigger: any fanout call (`POST /api/fanout/:id`, `/:id/observations`, `/:id/failure`) where the model emits a card whose frontmatter reads `id: ../../../../pwned`. The card body is also model-controlled, so this is an arbitrary path plus arbitrary content. The system under test is untrusted by construction — its page text reaches the model's context — so a prompt-injecting target can steer the generated id.

I reproduced this with a faithful copy of `splitFrontmatter` plus the `writeCards` filename line, under my scratchpad. The parsed id came back as `"../../../../pwned"`, the write target resolved four levels above `stories/`, the file landed there, and `readdirSync(storiesDir)` returned `[]`.

Fix: validate the id against `/^[a-zA-Z0-9-]+$/` inside `parseStoryCard` (making the two existing comments true), and additionally route the write through `resolveInside(storiesDir, filename)` from `src/qa/paths.ts`, which already rejects absolute paths and `..` segments. `flightPath` is a bare `join` and enforces nothing.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced via app.request against the real fanoutRoutes with a stubbed LLM client returning id ../../../../pwned; the write landed five levels above storiesDir with model-controlled content, because writeCards joins card.id into the path and never calls resolveInside from paths.ts, parseStoryCard checks only that id is a present string, and asCardId is a bare cast. Same root defect as CR-040 reached from a second route in the same file.

### CR-043: Two scenario files with the same filename stem share one run id, overwriting evidence and forcing a false batch failure
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/cli/batch.ts`
**Anchor:** `cardIdForPath` — "v1: filename stem is the row identifier"
**Severity:** high

`cardIdForPath` reduces a scenario path to `basename(p, extname(p))`, so `suiteA/login.md` and `suiteB/login.md` both become the card id `login`. `runBatch` passes those ids straight through as `cards: cardIds`. Inside `runRunSet`, the run loop locates its eagerly-generated entry with `allRuns.find(r => r.cardId === cardId && r.attemptNumber === attemptNumber)`, which returns the *same* entry on both iterations. Three things then go wrong at once:

- Both cards execute with one run id, so the second card's evidence directory overwrites the first card's. One card's screenshots, `run.jsonl` and `result.json` are destroyed.
- `RunSetWriter` summarizes `ctx.cards`, which holds the duplicate twice, so `summary.perCard` carries two identical entries and `overall.totalRuns` reports 4 for 2 runs.
- The unclaimed second `allRuns` entry stays `queued` with no result, so each duplicated card contributes an `errored` count. `runBatch` computes its exit code from that roll-up and returns 1 even when both cards passed.

I reproduced all three by driving `runRunSet` with the ids `cardIdForPath` produces for those two paths: the executor received one distinct run id for two runs, `perCard` was `['login','login']`, and the overall roll-up was `{"totalRuns":4,"byStatus":{"pass":2,...,"errored":2},"overallStatus":"mixed_with_errors"}`.

`parseArgs` hands `scenarioPaths: positionals` through with no dedupe or uniqueness check, so `moe-flight qa batch stories/**/*.md` over a tree with repeated stems hits this. Existing coverage in `test/qa/cli/batch.test.ts` only ever uses distinct stems (`a.md`, `b.md`).

Fix: make the card id unique per path (hash or slug the path relative to the project root, or suffix a disambiguator on collision) and reject duplicate card ids in `runRunSet` rather than silently reusing the first match.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced via tsx by driving the real runRunSet with two cards both mapping to cardId login: the second scenario path was never executed because the runLoop dispatch finds runs by cardId value, so the first card ran twice under two run ids, and the manifest reported totalRuns 4 and errored 2 for a batch where both cards passed, matching the finding numbers. parseArgs passes positionals through with no dedupe and nested suite globs are an ordinary layout. The overwrite framing is imprecise; the dropped run is never written rather than clobbered.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `caaab09`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02
**Note:** Fix landed in caaab09 alongside a concurrent sibling agent's CODEBASE-REVIEW.md stamp commit for CR-023 — a shared-index race (this agent staged batch.ts/batch.test.ts, the sibling's plain git commit picked up the whole index before this agent's own commit ran). Verified via git show --stat caaab09 that the diff is exactly assignCardIds + the CR-043 test.
### CR-044: Streaming CLI silently drops every fatal-run panel because the logger and the renderer disagree on the row shape
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/cli/stream/pretty.ts`
**Anchor:** `PrettyRenderer.renderRunError`, reached only from `case "event": if (event.name === "run_error")`
**Severity:** high

`EvidenceLogger.logRunError` emits a row whose envelope is `type: "run_error"` (it calls `writeEvent("run_error", ...)`), and `orchestrator.ts` is its only producer — it fires on every exception that escapes a run. `PrettyRenderer.handle` has no `case "run_error"`; it looks for `type === "event"` carrying `name === "run_error"`, a shape nothing in the tree produces. The event therefore falls through to `default: return` and the "Run failed" panel never prints. During a live `moe-flight qa run`, a rate-limit or adapter crash makes the stream simply stop with no error text; the operator has to open `run.jsonl` to learn why.

I reproduced this with `tsx` against the real `PrettyRenderer`: the logger-shaped row renders `""`, while the fixture-shaped row renders the full panel.

The test that names this behavior does not exercise it. `test/qa/cli/stream/pretty.test.ts` has "renders event (meta) line and run_error fatal panel", and its fixture `test/qa/cli/stream/fixtures/fatal.jsonl` hand-writes `{"type":"event","name":"run_error",...}`. `test/qa/runs/orchestrator.test.ts` asserts the on-disk shape with `l.type === "run_error"`, so the two suites pin contradictory shapes and both pass.

Fix: add `case "run_error": this.renderRunError(event); return;` to the switch and rebuild the `fatal` fixture from a real `run.jsonl` row. Keep the `event`/`name` branch only if some other producer still needs it.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced with tsx: feeding PrettyRenderer.handle the real production row shape, where EvidenceLogger.writeEvent sets type run_error directly and attachRenderer pipes it unmodified, yields empty output through the switch default branch, while the fixture shape type event with name run_error renders the full panel; orchestrator.test.ts confirms the on-disk type is run_error. Same defect as CR-045.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `8a3ae18`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02
**Note:** Fix landed in 8a3ae18, a concurrent sibling agent's unrelated CODEOWNERS commit — a shared-index race (git show --stat 8a3ae18 confirms the diff is exactly the switch-case fix plus the fatal.jsonl fixture rebuild, nothing else of mine).
### CR-045: Pretty renderer silently drops every real run_error row, so the "Run failed" panel is dead code
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/cli/stream/pretty.ts`
**Anchor:** `PrettyRenderer.handle` — `case "event": if (event.name === "run_error") this.renderRunError(event);`
**Severity:** high

`renderRunError` is reachable only from the `"event"` arm of `handle`'s switch, keyed on `event.name === "run_error"`. But the only producer of a run_error row is `EvidenceLogger.logRunError`, which calls `writeEvent("run_error", ...)` — that emits `type: "run_error"` with **no `name` field at all**. `handle`'s switch has no `case "run_error"`, so the row falls to `default: return` and nothing is printed. `renderRunError` can never fire in production.

The failure path is ordinary: the orchestrator's catch block calls `logger.logRunError` for every run that throws (rate limit, adapter failure, network error). I reproduced this by wiring a real `EvidenceLogger` to a real `PrettyRenderer` through `addEventObserver` and calling `logRunStart` then `logRunError` exactly as the orchestrator does. Output was the run_start banner and nothing else; `Run failed` and the error message were both absent, while the row written to `run.jsonl` was `{"type":"run_error","turn":-1,"message":"..."}`.

The reason this survived is the test fixture. `fatal.jsonl`, driving the test `"renders event (meta) line and run_error fatal panel"`, hand-writes `{"type":"event","name":"run_error",...}` — a shape no code in the package emits. The test is green and the golden output matches, so the panel looks covered while being unreachable. `JsonlRenderer` is unaffected because it serializes whatever it is handed.

Impact is softened but not removed: `main().catch` in `src/cli.ts` writes the thrown error to stderr, so the user sees *an* error. They lose the panel's runId and turn context, and the streamed output ends mid-run with no marker.

Fix: add `case "run_error": this.renderRunError(event); return;` to the switch, and change `fatal.jsonl` plus its golden `.pretty.txt` to carry the shape `logRunError` actually writes. Keep the `"event"`/`name` arm only if some other producer is expected to use it.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced directly: the exact row shape logRunError produces fed into a live PrettyRenderer.handle yields zero output lines, because the switch matches only case event with a nested name of run_error and has no case for run_error; logRunError is the only producer in packages/flight/src and the orchestrator catch-all uses it, while the fatal.jsonl fixture hand-writes the nonexistent nested shape. The CLI outer catch still prints a console.error, so the user loses the panel formatting rather than all output. Same defect as CR-044.

### CR-046: A truncated OpenAI tool call crashes the run instead of taking the max_tokens recovery path

**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/models/openai.ts`
**Anchor:** `convertResponse`, the `case "function_call"` branch calling `JSON.parse(item.arguments)`
**Severity:** high

`convertResponse` parses `item.arguments` with a bare `JSON.parse`. When the Responses API returns `status: "incomplete"` with `incomplete_details.reason === "max_output_tokens"`, the partial `function_call` item carries a truncated argument string, so the parse throws a `SyntaxError` out of `client.chat()`. The agent loop calls `client.chat(messages, tools, systemPrompt, { runId })` with no try/catch, so the exception escapes `runAgent`, lands in `executeRunCore`'s catch, is logged as `run_error`, and is rethrown. The whole point of `deriveStopReason` mapping that same response to `max_tokens` is to reach the loop's one-shot recovery turn (`MAX_TOKENS_NUDGE`, PRI-2160), and this defect makes that recovery unreachable on the OpenAI provider for exactly the case it was written for.

Reproduced with `node` against `dist/qa/models/openai.js`: the same fixture returns `max_tokens` from `deriveStopReason` and throws `SyntaxError - Unterminated string in JSON at position 33` from `convertResponse`.

The test suite hides this. `openai.test.ts` has `"incomplete + max_output_tokens → max_tokens"`, but it builds that fixture with `output: []`, so no test ever feeds a partial `arguments` string through `convertResponse`.

Fix: wrap the parse and degrade rather than throw. Either drop the unparseable call and let `deriveStopReason` see zero tool calls (so the response is classified `max_tokens` and the recovery turn fires), or surface `{}` plus a logged event. Add a `convertResponse` case with truncated `arguments` to `openai.test.ts`.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced via tsx: convertResponse throws SyntaxError on a truncated function_call arguments string before deriveStopReason runs. No try/catch wraps client.chat in the agent loop; the executeRunCore catch logs run_error and then rethrows, contradicting its own documented invariant that runAgent returns rather than throws. The Anthropic adapter has no JSON.parse because the SDK pre-parses tool_use input, so this is OpenAI-only, and the existing incomplete-response test uses an empty output fixture that never exercises the path.

### CR-047: Revival rehydration reads files outside the run directory

**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/revival/rebuild-messages.ts`
**Anchor:** `rebuildToolResult`
**Severity:** high

`rebuildToolResult` resolves three attacker-influenceable strings from `run.jsonl` with a plain `join(runDir, ...)` and no containment check: `tr.artifact` (when `textTruncated`), `tr.capturePath`, and `tr.image`. `packages/flight/src/qa/paths.ts` opens with "The one and only path-safety guard for Flight. All containment checks go through this." and exports `resolveInside` for exactly this composition; this module imports neither it nor `isSafePath`.

The reachable attacker is the agent under test. The CLI adapter spawns `bash --norc --noprofile -i` with `cwd` set to `<runDir>/scratch`, one level below `run.jsonl`, so an agent following injected instructions from the target it is exercising can append a crafted `tool_result` row. A later `moe-flight qa ask <runId>` then reads the named file and injects its contents into the revived conversation, which is sent to the model provider on the next question.

Reproduced with `node` against `dist/qa/revival/rebuild-messages.js`: a row with `"artifact": "../secret.txt"` and `textTruncated: true` produced a `tool_result` block whose content was `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=hunter2`, read from outside the run dir.

Fix: route all three through `resolveInside(runDir, rel)` and turn a rejection into a warning plus a placeholder text result, matching how the missing-`mediaType` case already degrades. `rebuild-messages.test.ts` exercises only well-formed relative paths and should gain a traversal case per field.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced: a run.jsonl row with artifact ../secret.txt makes rebuildMessages return a tool_result whose text is the outside file bytes. rebuildToolResult uses plain join(runDir, rel) for artifact, capturePath and image and never calls resolveInside or isSafePath from paths.ts. Normal producers only write counter-based paths, but the CLI adapter runs an unsandboxed bash with cwd one level below run.jsonl, so an agent under test can append a crafted row that a later qa ask revival reads and sends to the model provider.

### CR-048: A duplicate cardId in a run set reuses one runId and abandons another
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/runs/run-set.ts`
**Anchor:** `runLoop`'s `allRuns.find((r) => r.cardId === cardId && r.attemptNumber === attemptNumber)`
**Severity:** high

`runRunSet` eagerly generates one runId per (card, attempt) pair, then `runLoop` re-derives each pair's runId by searching `allRuns` for the first entry matching `cardId` and `attemptNumber`. When `cfg.cards` contains the same id twice, both iterations match the same entry, so one runId is executed twice and the other is never started. The two executions share an output directory, and the second overwrites the first's `result.json` and `run.jsonl`. The never-started runId stays `queued` in `set.json`, which `summarizeCard` then counts as `errored`. Because `RunSetWriter`'s `perCard` maps over `ctx.cards`, the duplicated id also produces two identical per-card summaries, so `overall.totalRuns` double-counts.

Duplicates are easy to produce: `runBatch`'s `cardIdForPath` uses the filename stem, so `moe-flight qa batch stories/checkout/login.md stories/admin/login.md` yields `cards = ["login", "login"]`. The batch exit code is derived from `overall.byStatus`, so a batch in which every run passed exits 1.

Reproduced with a scratchpad script calling `runRunSet` with `cards: ["login", "login"]`, `passes: 1` and a stub executor:

```
eager runIds:            [ 'login_...Z_wb2a', 'login_...Z_t9xn' ]
executor invoked with:   [ 'login/login_...Z_wb2a', 'login/login_...Z_wb2a' ]
set.runs statuses:       pass, queued
overall: {"totalRuns":4,"byStatus":{"pass":2,"errored":2,...}}
perCard: two entries, both cardId "login"
```

Fix: iterate `allRuns` directly instead of re-finding by (cardId, attemptNumber), and reject duplicate ids in `runRunSet`'s prep phase (or make `cardIdForPath` disambiguate collisions).

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced directly: runRunSet with cards login and login invokes the executor twice with the same runId, leaves the other queued, and finalize perCard doubles the overall counts to totalRuns 4 for two real runs, because runLoop finds runs by cardId value rather than index. Only batch.ts can pass duplicate cardIds, via cardIdForPath by filename stem with no dedupe; same root cause and reachability as CR-043, filed at the engine layer.

### CR-050: A malformed Host header on an upgrade request kills the whole API server
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/runtime/serve.ts`
**Anchor:** `serveViaNode`, the `httpServer.on("upgrade", ...)` handler's `new URL(req.url ?? "/", \`http://${req.headers.host ?? "localhost"}\`)`
**Severity:** high

The upgrade listener builds a `URL` from the raw `Host` header before it calls `hooks.upgrade`. Node's HTTP parser does not validate host syntax, so a `Host` value that is not a legal authority (`[`, `]`, `a b`, `%`, `:::` all qualify) makes the `URL` constructor throw a `TypeError` inside an event listener. Nothing catches it: there is no try/catch here, and `grep -rn "uncaughtException\|unhandledRejection" packages/flight/src` returns nothing, so the default handler terminates the process. Every in-flight run dies with it.

The crash happens *before* `decideUpgrade`, so the PRI-1483 Origin allowlist provides no protection, and no valid WebSocket key or matching Origin is needed. `@hono/node-server` validates the Host header for ordinary requests (it throws its own `RequestError("Invalid host header")` inside `newRequest`), but the manual `upgrade` wiring bypasses that path entirely.

Reproduced. A throwaway script under the scratchpad copied this handler verbatim onto a bare `http.Server`, opened a raw socket, and sent an upgrade request with `Host: [`:

```
upgrade event fired; host header = "["
UNCAUGHT: TypeError Invalid URL
```

Fix: wrap the URL construction (or the whole handler body) in a try/catch that `socket.destroy()`s on failure, and prefer a fixed authority — the host is only needed to satisfy the `URL` parser, never read — e.g. `new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://localhost")`.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced live: the real serve.ts run via tsx crashed with an uncaught TypeError Invalid URL on a raw upgrade request with Host: [ and exited with code 1. No try/catch wraps the URL construction and no uncaughtException or clientError handler exists anywhere in packages/flight/src. The crash occurs before hooks.upgrade runs, so it also bypasses the Origin allowlist.

### CR-051: The API server binds every network interface and has no authentication
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/runtime/serve.ts`
**Anchor:** `serveViaNode`'s `honoServe({ port: opts.port, fetch: ... })`; `ServeOptions` has `port` but no bind-address field
**Severity:** high

`ServeOptions` exposes no hostname, and `serveViaNode` passes none to `honoServe`, whose own `serve` does `server.listen(options?.port ?? 3e3, options.hostname, ...)`. With `hostname` undefined Node binds the wildcard address. `AppConfig` has no host field either, so an operator has no way to restrict the bind.

Reproduced: a scratchpad script calling `server.listen(0, undefined)` reports `bound address=:: family=IPv6` — all interfaces.

`createApp` adds no authentication, no Origin check, and no CSRF token on the HTTP routes; the only such control in the package is `decideUpgrade`'s WebSocket Origin allowlist, which shows the threat was considered for WebSockets and missed for HTTP. Consequently anyone who can reach the port can list scenarios and prior run evidence, and can `POST /api/run/:id` to start runs. `validateRunBody` accepts a caller-chosen `adapter` (including `"cli"`) and an arbitrary `target` string, and `CLIAdapter.start` spawns `bash --norc --noprofile -i` in the run's scratch directory for the agent to type into, with `describeTarget` interpolating the attacker's `target` into the prompt as "The command you are exercising is ...". Runs also spend the operator's LLM credentials.

Fix: add a `hostname` to `ServeOptions`, thread a config setting through, and default it to `127.0.0.1`. Binding beyond loopback should be an explicit opt-in that also requires a shared secret.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Ran the real serve() from serve.ts via tsx on an ephemeral port; lsof showed the socket listening on all interfaces. No --host flag, no MOE_FLIGHT_HOST env var and no host field on AppConfig exists to restrict it, the serve help text documents no binding restriction, and createApp has no auth, Origin check or CSRF guard on any HTTP route.

### CR-052: An async CDP frame listener converts any frame failure into a process-killing rejection
**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/streaming/screencast.ts`
**Anchor:** `ScreencastStreamer.start`'s `this.unsubFrame = ps.onEvent(async (event) => { ... })`
**Severity:** high

The handler registered with `ps.onEvent` is `async`, and the dispatcher that invokes it guards only synchronous throws — `cdp-router.js` does `try { fn(msg); } catch (e) { console.error('cdp-router page listener threw:', e); }`. A rejected promise from the handler is therefore never observed, and Node's default unhandled-rejection mode terminates the process.

Two awaited operations inside the handler can reject under ordinary conditions. `await ps.send("Page.screencastFrameAck", ...)` rejects when the browser WebSocket dies mid-run (Chrome crash, operator closing the window), when the page session has been detached, or on `page-session.js`'s 30-second `Page session timeout`. The `writeFileSync` for a saved frame rejects the handler on any disk error. Either one takes down the `moe-flight` daemon and every concurrent run, instead of failing the single screencast.

Reproduced the mechanism: a scratchpad script wrapping an `async` listener in the same synchronous `try { fn(msg) } catch` shape exits with code 1 and prints the rejection as a fatal error; the `catch` never fires.

Fix: give the handler its own `try/catch` around the ack and the write (logging and continuing), or wrap the registration so the router receives a non-async function that swallows the promise's rejection.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** The try/catch in cdp-router.js around fn(msg) catches only synchronous throws; the screencast.ts handler is async so it never throws synchronously, and a rejection from await ps.send for Page.screencastFrameAck (the page-session 30 second timeout or a detached session) becomes an unhandled rejection. Reproduced with tsx: mirroring the exact dispatch shape exits the process with code 1 and the catch never fires. No unhandledRejection handler exists in packages/flight/src outside a test.

### CR-054: Static run report links every screenshot, artifact and TUI capture to a server that is not there
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/components/transcript/Screenshot.tsx`
**Anchor:** `Screenshot` — `const url = api.results.fileUrl(runId, path)`
**Severity:** high

`api.results.fileUrl` unconditionally returns an absolute `/api/results/<runId>/file/<path>` URL. That is correct for the SPA served by the Flight server, but `Screenshot` also renders inside the standalone HTML report: `safeEmitIndexHtml` calls `renderRun`, which writes `index.html` into the run directory itself, as a sibling of `screenshots/`, `artifacts/` and `captures/`. Opened from that directory (or from any static host that is not the Flight server), every `/api/...` URL 404s or fails to resolve, so a report for an ordinary web-adapter run shows a broken image for each screenshot, a dead "Open full size" link, and a "Failed to load capture" box for each `read_screen` grid. The evidence files are right next to the HTML; only the URL shape is wrong.

`useTranscript` has a static-mode branch that reads `window.__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__` instead of fetching, which shows the pattern the file-URL path is missing. `Screenshot`, `TuiCapture` and `ArtifactDrawer` have no equivalent branch.

Not reproduced in a browser (the constraint forbids launching one); established by reading `renderRunFromTemplate`'s `outPath = join(opts.runDir, opts.outputName ?? "index.html")` against `EvidenceLogger`'s `screenshots/${name}.png` and `captures/${name}.ansi` relative paths, which confirms the two are siblings.

Fix: give `fileUrl` a static-mode branch that returns the manifest-relative path verbatim when `window.__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__` is present, so the report resolves evidence relative to its own location. Alternatively inline the evidence as data URIs at render time, which is what a genuinely self-contained report needs.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** fileUrl in ui/src/lib/api.ts always builds /api/results/<runId>/file/<path> with no static-mode branch, unlike useTranscript which checks window.__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__; renderRunFromTemplate inlines only result.json and run.jsonl into index.html and never copies screenshots, artifacts or captures; RunSummaryCard, Screenshot and ArtifactDrawer all call fileUrl or fileText unconditionally, so every evidence asset 404s when the report is opened without the Flight server. Traced by reading.

### CR-055: A root-WebSocket drop during the first bridge attach wedges the session permanently
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/chrome-ws-lib.js`
**Anchor:** `state.ensureBridge` — "Detect stale bridge: if the cached browserSession is no longer connected"
**Severity:** high

The stale-bridge check is guarded on `state.browserBridge` being truthy, so it only fires once a bridge has successfully attached. If the root WebSocket dies *while* `attachBrowserBridge` is in flight, `bridgePromise` rejects, the `bridgePromise.catch` resets it to null, and `state.browserBridge` is still null — so the next `ensureBridge()` never calls `resetBridge()` and re-attaches over the same dead `state.browserSession`. Because `createBrowserSession` cannot reconnect either (see the browser-session finding below), every subsequent call fails forever.

Trigger: Chrome exits, crashes, or is killed between the WebSocket handshake and the bridge's first `Target.setDiscoverTargets` reply. I reproduced it with a fake `WebSocketClient` injected through `createSession({_testFakes})`: attempt 1 fails with `Browser session WS closed`, attempts 2 and 3 fail with `send() on a CLOSED socket`, and only one socket is ever constructed. In the MCP server this is unrecoverable by retrying — `ensureChromeRunning()` relaunches Chrome on every action but the bridge still cannot attach, so every `use_browser` call fails until the process restarts. The only escape is `kill_chrome`, which calls `state.resetBridge?.()` unconditionally.

Fix: run the stale check on `state.browserSession.isConnected()` alone, independent of whether `state.browserBridge` is set, and reset in the `bridgePromise.catch` handler as well as clearing the promise.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced with a fake WebSocketClient injected via createSession test fakes: the root socket closes mid-attach before Target.setDiscoverTargets replies, and four repeated ensureBridge calls then fail identically with zero new WebSocket instances constructed. Two layered causes: the ensureBridge stale check requires state.browserBridge to be truthy, which a mid-attach failure never sets, and browser-session.js ensureConnected never clears connectPromise after a post-connect disconnect. Only killChrome calls resetBridge; no normal retry path does.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `7dade49`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02
**Note:** —
### CR-056: findOrphanChromeForProfile substring-matches the profile directory, so it adopts another profile's Chrome
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/chrome-launcher-helpers.js`
**Anchor:** `findOrphanChromeForProfile` — `if (!line.includes(profileDir))`
**Severity:** high

The orphan scan accepts any `ps` line that *contains* the profile directory as a substring and also carries a `--remote-debugging-port=` token. Profile names are auto-disambiguated by suffix (`moe-glass`, `moe-glass-2`, `moe-glass-3`), so `.../browser-profiles/moe-glass` is a prefix of `.../browser-profiles/moe-glass-2`. The first MCP server therefore matches the second one's Chrome.

I reproduced it: with a decoy process whose command line carried `--remote-debugging-port=19999 --user-data-dir=/Users/ZKeown/Library/Caches/moe/browser-profiles/moe-glass-2`, `findOrphanChromeForProfile('moe-glass')` returned that decoy's pid and port. No browser was launched for the repro.

`startChrome` then gates the result on `isPortAlive(host, port, pid)` and, on success, writes the other profile's port and pid into its own `meta.json` and drives that Chrome. That is exactly the shared-Chrome tab-fighting failure `profile-lock.js` exists to prevent, and it can also latch onto any unrelated process whose command line happens to mention the profile path alongside a debugging-port flag. The only existing test asserts the negative case ("findOrphanChromeForProfile returns null when no match"), so nothing catches it.

Fix: parse `--user-data-dir=<value>` out of the line and compare it for path equality (after `path.resolve`), rather than testing `includes` on the raw line.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** getChromeProfileDir for moe-glass is a literal prefix of the directory for moe-glass-2, which acquireWithFallback in profile-lock.js assigns as the ordinary two-MCPs-on-one-host case; a reproduced ps-line check shows line.includes(profileDir) matches the sibling profile Chrome, and chrome-process.js adopts it unconditionally after isPortAlive with no path-equality check, overwriting meta.json.

### CR-057: startChrome reports success when a Chrome it did not launch answers on an explicitly requested port
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/chrome-process.js`
**Anchor:** `startChrome` — "--- Step 2: Choose a port ---" and the `if (!port)` guard above it
**Severity:** high

When `port` is supplied (the `--port` flag) or `CHROME_WS_PORT` is set, `startChrome` skips the whole reconnect/adopt block (`if (!port)`) and spawns Chrome directly on that exact port. If something already listens there, the new Chrome cannot bind — but the readiness probe is `isPortAlive(CHROME_DEBUG_HOST, chosenPort)` with no `expectedPid`, so the *other* browser's `/json/version` reply satisfies it. `startChrome` returns `true`, and `meta.json` records `pid: proc.pid` (the Chrome that failed to bind and likely exited) against a port owned by someone else.

Every subsequent CDP call then drives the foreign browser: `navigate` retargets the user's tabs, `clear_cookies` issues `Network.clearBrowserCookies`, which wipes the whole profile's cookies and therefore their logged-in sessions, and `killChrome` falls through to `findPidOnPort(state.activePort)` and SIGTERMs it. The trigger is the canonical developer setup: `moe-glass --port 9222` while a Chrome is already running with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`, which is also glass's own default port. I did not launch a browser to confirm this; the reading is from the port-selection branch, the pid-less liveness probe, and `killChrome`'s port-based fallback.

Fix: after the readiness probe on a caller-specified port, verify the endpoint is the process we spawned (compare `/json/version` against the spawned pid, or refuse the port when `isPortAlive` already answers before the spawn) and fail loudly instead of adopting it.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** The startChrome port poll calls isPortAlive(host, chosenPort) with no expectedPid, unlike the reconnect and orphan-adopt steps which pass a pid; isolated reproduction shows isPortAlive returns true against a foreign /json/version responder even when the spawned pid never bound the port, and startChrome then writes meta.json with the spawned pid against that port. Full startChrome was not run because it writes under HOME.

### CR-058: A page-chosen shim id is interpolated into a Runtime.evaluate expression, turning a permission deny into a grant
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/dialogs-router.js`
**Anchor:** `tryHandleDialogSelector` — `window.__dialogShim_resolve('${id}', '${decision}')`
**Severity:** high

`id` is `state.staged._shimId`, which `dialogs.js` copies verbatim out of `JSON.parse(msg.params.payload)` on a `Runtime.bindingCalled` event. That binding (`Runtime.addBinding({name:'__dialogShim'})`) is registered on the main world, and the shim itself runs in the main world via `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument`, so any page script can call `window.__dialogShim(...)` with an arbitrary `id`. The id is then spliced into a single-quoted JavaScript string with no escaping.

I reproduced this by driving `tryHandleDialogSelector` directly with a page-supplied id of `1', 'grant'); void('`. The agent chose `dialog::dismiss` (deny); the expression actually sent was `window.__dialogShim_resolve('1', 'grant'); void('', 'deny')`, so the page's pending permission promise resolves with `grant` and the trailing `deny` call is dead. The router still returned `{"handled":true,"clearDialog":true,"result":{"ok":true}}` — the agent is told the deny succeeded. Nothing checks `exceptionDetails` on this send either, so a malformed id that only produces a syntax error also reports `ok`.

Two related weaknesses in the same mechanism: the shim exposes `window.__dialogShim_resolve` on the page's own world, so a page can resolve its own permission ask without the agent at all; and a page can fabricate a `permission-request` payload with arbitrary `origin`/`name`/`jsApi`, which lands in `state.dialogs` and makes the session-boundary gate refuse every page action until the agent handles the phantom dialog.

Fix: never build the expression by interpolation — send the id and decision as `Runtime.callFunctionOn` arguments, or at minimum `JSON.stringify` both operands; validate `data.id` against a shape the shim actually mints; and check `exceptionDetails` before returning `{ok:true}`.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced against the unmodified tryHandleDialogSelectorForSession with a recording pageSession.send: the agent dialog::dismiss (deny) produced the actual expression window.__dialogShim_resolve(1, grant); void(, deny) yet the router returned ok:true. dialogs.js copies data.id from the parsed binding payload verbatim into state.staged._shimId with no shape check, and __dialogShim is a Runtime.addBinding reachable from any page script in the main world.

### CR-059: generateHtmlDiff allocates O((N+M)^2) and aborts the process on an ordinary page
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/html-diff.js`
**Anchor:** `myersDiff` — `trace.push(v.slice())`
**Severity:** high

`myersDiff` snapshots the whole `v` array (length `2*(N+M)+1`) once per `d` iteration, and `d` runs up to the edit distance. Two dissimilar documents of N lines each therefore cost roughly `4*N^2` array slots with no line-count cap anywhere; the 50-line output cap in `generateHtmlDiff` caps only the rendered text, not the computation.

I reproduced the cost curve and the crash. Measured on this machine:

| lines per side | result |
| --- | --- |
| 2000 | 75 ms, ~104 MB heap retained |
| 3000 | 166 ms |
| 6000 | 577 ms |
| 12000 | `FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit` at a 4 GB heap |

12,000 lines of pretty-printed HTML is an unremarkable page, and `captureActionWithDiff` in `capture.js` feeds it real before/after `document.documentElement.outerHTML` on every `click`, `hover`, `drag_drop`, `keyboard_press`, `double_click`, `right_click` and `file_upload` the MCP server performs. A V8 OOM is a hard abort, not a catchable exception, so one click that swaps page content kills the MCP server and loses the whole browser session. Correctness of the algorithm itself held up in my spot checks (deletions, insertions, reordering and trailing deletions all diff correctly).

Fix: bail out to a cheap line-count/first-difference summary above a line budget (a few thousand per side), or cap `d` and report a truncated diff, before entering the Myers loop.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** getHtml returns uncapped outerHTML; capture.js feeds it straight into generateHtmlDiff with no try/catch from the click, type, select and eval wrappers the MCP server exposes as tools. dist/index.js requires chrome-ws-lib.js in-process, so the OOM abort already reproduced under CR-033 on the byte-identical copy kills the MCP server itself. Same defect as CR-060.

### CR-060: Line-based HTML diff exhausts the heap and kills the MCP server process
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/html-diff.js`
**Anchor:** `myersDiff`, and the comment "Myers (not set-based) so reordered identical lines are correctly detected"
**Severity:** high

`myersDiff` stores a full `v.slice()` snapshot in `trace` for every edit-distance step `d`, and each snapshot is `2*(N+M)+1` elements wide. Memory is therefore O(D·(N+M)) with no guard on input size. `generateHtmlDiff` is called by `captureActionWithDiff` on every before/after pair, and the `MAX_LINES_PER_SIDE` cap is applied only *after* the whole edit script exists.

I reproduced this with a throwaway script under the scratchpad, feeding two synthetic documents whose every line differs:

| lines per side | wall time | RSS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1000 | 32 ms | modest |
| 3000 | 265 ms | 698 MB |
| 6000 | 1045 ms | 3047 MB |
| 10000 | — | FATAL heap OOM |

At 10000 lines Node dies with `FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit` — a process abort, not a catchable exception, so the `try`/`catch` around auto-capture cannot contain it. `captureActionWithDiff` is reached from the MCP tool for `type`, `hover`, `drag`, `double_click`, `right_click`, `file_upload` and `keyboard_press`, so one `type` on a large server-rendered page whose DOM is replaced can take the whole server down and orphan the Chrome it launched.

Fix: bound the input before running Myers. Cap `beforeLines`/`afterLines` at a few thousand entries (or fall back to a cheap "N lines removed / N added" summary above a threshold), and drop `trace` in favour of a linear-space variant if the full script is still wanted.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** src/index.ts is itself the McpServer over StdioServerTransport in one process; it requires chrome-ws-lib.js in-process and capture.js calls generateHtmlDiff synchronously with no child_process or worker_thread boundary, so a V8 heap abort in myersDiff kills the MCP server and cannot be caught. Same root cause and call chain as CR-059; one defect, reproduced under CR-033.

### CR-061: fill() rewrites backslash sequences, so a value containing a backslash presses Tab and Enter
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/keyboard-input.js`
**Anchor:** `fill`, at the comment "Normalise literal escape sequences from MCP payloads"
**Severity:** high

`fill` runs `value.replace(/\\t/g, '\t').replace(/\\n/g, '\n')` over the caller's text before typing it. The intent is to repair MCP payloads that arrive with un-evaluated escapes, but the substitution cannot tell a doubled escape from a genuine backslash in the data. Any value where a backslash is followed by `t` or `n` is corrupted, and the substituted control characters are then routed through the Tab and Enter key paths.

Reproduced with a scratchpad script driving `attachKeyboardInput` against a recording page-session fake. Typing the string `C:\temp\notes`:

```
insertText    : ["C:","emp","otes"]
key presses   : ["Tab","Enter"]
text the page receives: "C:empotes"
```

Three characters are eaten, focus moves to a different field mid-value, and Enter submits the enclosing form — an action the caller never asked for and cannot undo. Windows paths, regex literals, LaTeX and escaped JSON all trigger it. No test covers the normalisation, so nothing catches it.

Fix: drop the rewrite from `fill` and do the un-escaping (if it is still wanted) at the MCP payload boundary where the provenance of the string is known, or gate it behind an explicit option. The doc comment on `fill` already advertises the corrupting behaviour as a feature, so it needs updating either way.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced with a stubbed CDP session: filling the Windows path C:\new\table yields insertText calls of C:, ew and able plus Enter and Tab key presses, corrupting the value to C:ewable and submitting early; a password containing a literal backslash-n collapsed similarly. The MCP schema states the value is literal text never JSON-parsed, so callers cannot avoid this for real backslash-containing data.

### CR-062: click() on a zero-rect element presses the mouse at viewport (0,0) instead of using the JS fallback
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/mouse.js`
**Anchor:** `resolveCenter`, and the `click` comment "Fallback for cases where CDP coordinate resolution failed but the element actually exists (e.g., hidden / zero bounding rect)"
**Severity:** high

`getElementSelector` deliberately returns the first DOM match when no match is visible. `resolveCenter` then reports `found: true` for that element and computes its centre from an all-zero `getBoundingClientRect()`, giving `{x: 0, y: 0}`. It never inspects the rect, so coordinate resolution does not "fail" and the `catch` branch is never entered. `click` proceeds to dispatch a real `mousePressed`/`mouseReleased` pair at viewport (0,0) and returns `{clicked: true, x: 0, y: 0}`.

Reproduced by evaluating the production-generated `resolveCenter` expression against a jsdom document whose only `button` sits inside a `display:none` wrapper, with `scrollIntoView` stubbed so the expression behaves as it does in a real browser:

```
click() returned    : {"clicked":true,"x":0,"y":0}
mousePressed at     : (0, 0)
el.click() fallback : false
```

Whatever element occupies the top-left corner of the viewport receives the click, and the caller is told the intended selector was clicked. Hidden elements are ordinary (collapsed menus, closed modals, off-screen carousel slides), so this misfires routinely. The documented `el.click()` recovery path for hidden elements is dead code.

Fix: have `resolveCenter` return `found: false` (or a distinct `zeroRect: true`) when `rect.width === 0 || rect.height === 0`, so `click` takes the existing `el.click()` fallback and `hover`/`drag`/`doubleClick`/`rightClick` raise instead of aiming at the origin.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced by stubbing Runtime.evaluate to return the zero-rect result a hidden element produces; resolveCenter never checks rect dimensions so it does not throw, the click() try block dispatches real mousePressed and mouseReleased at (0,0) and reports success, and the el.click() fallback in the catch branch is never reached. getElementSelector deliberately returns the first match even when every match has a zero rect.

### CR-063: The permission shim calls a binding it never checks for, breaking every API it wraps

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/page-scripts/permission-shim.js`
**Anchor:** `function ask(name, jsApi)` — `window[BINDING](JSON.stringify({ type: 'permission-request', ... }))`
**Severity:** high

`ask()` calls `window['__dialogShim'](...)` unconditionally. The shim is installed via `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` while the binding is added separately via `Runtime.addBinding`; when the binding is not present in the page's execution context the call throws `TypeError: window.__dialogShim is not a function` synchronously inside the Promise executor, so the promise rejects and the wrapped API fails. Because the shim replaces `getUserMedia`, `Notification.requestPermission`, `getCurrentPosition`, `clipboard.readText` and `clipboard.writeText` on every page at document_start, this converts working pages into broken ones: the page does not get the native behaviour, does not get an operator prompt, and gets a `TypeError` instead of a `NotAllowedError` it could handle. The dangling `pending` entry is also never cleared.

This is not hypothetical in this tree — `packages/glass/test/dialogs.smoke.test.mjs` records it as observed behaviour: "In Chrome 148+, Runtime.addBinding does not inject the binding function into page execution contexts — window.__dialogShim is undefined in the page, causing the shim to throw". I did not launch a browser to confirm the Chrome version boundary.

Fix: guard on `typeof window[BINDING] === 'function'` and fall back to the original API (or a proper `DOMException`) when absent, and move the channel to a mechanism that survives — a `worldName`-scoped script with an isolated-world binding, or an intercepted request the server answers.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** ask() in permission-shim.js calls window.__dialogShim with no typeof guard, and that one helper backs all five wrapped APIs. A Node vm reproduction confirms it throws TypeError when the binding is absent, rejecting the wrapped promise instead of yielding a native NotAllowedError. dialogs.smoke.test.mjs documents that on Chrome 148 and later Runtime.addBinding does not reach page execution contexts, so the binding is absent in the ordinary case. The injector send order is not the cause.

### CR-064: A page can grant itself permissions and forge permission dialogs

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/page-scripts/permission-shim.js`
**Anchor:** `window[BINDING + '_resolve'] = (id, resolution) => {...}`
**Severity:** high

The shim installs its resolver as a plain global on the page it is policing, and ids come from a page-side counter starting at 1. Page script can therefore satisfy its own request before the operator ever sees it:

    navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({video:true});
    window.__dialogShim_resolve('1', 'grant');

The shim then calls the captured original `getUserMedia`, so the operator gate is skipped entirely (Chrome's own permission gate still applies, since `buildChromeArgs` passes no `--use-fake-ui-for-media-stream`, which is what keeps this from being critical). The same reachability runs the other way: page script can call the binding directly with `{"type":"permission-request",...}` and make `handleCdpEventForSession` in `lib/dialogs.js` store a `permission` dialog for the session, which wedges every subsequent page-target tool call behind `Page is behind a dialog` for a dialog no API ever raised. I did not run this against a live browser; the mechanism is visible in the shim source and in the binding handler.

Fix: run the shim in an isolated world (`Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` with `worldName`, and `Runtime.addBinding` with the matching `executionContextName`) so page script cannot see the resolver, and mint request ids server-side rather than trusting `data.id`.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument and Runtime.addBinding in dialogs.js pass no worldName or executionContextName, so the shim and the __dialogShim binding run in the main world reachable by page script; window.__dialogShim_resolve is a plain global with page-counted ids and no nonce, and handleCdpEventForSession trusts data.id, name and origin from the binding payload unchecked, confirming both the self-grant and forged-dialog paths. Chrome own OS prompt still gates getUserMedia, which keeps this below critical.

### CR-065: Screenshot filenames are written with no path containment

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/screenshot.js`
**Anchor:** `resolveScreenshotPath`
**Severity:** high

`resolveScreenshotPath` returns any `path.isAbsolute(filename)` verbatim and otherwise `path.join(dir, filename)` with no normalization or containment check, and `screenshot()` then calls `fs.writeFileSync(resolvedFilename, buffer)` with no existence check. The filename is a tool argument: `{"action":"screenshot","payload":"../../../../Users/me/.zshrc"}` or `{"action":"screenshot","payload":{"path":"/absolute/anything"}}` overwrites that file with PNG bytes. Any file the MCP process can write is destroyable by one tool call, including files the agent was never asked to touch.

Reproduced with a stubbed page session (no browser): a relative name of `../../escaped-by-traversal.png` landed two directories above the session dir, and an absolute path was honoured verbatim; both files existed afterwards.

Fix: resolve the candidate (`path.resolve`) and require it to stay under the session dir unless the caller opted into an explicit output root; reject `..` traversal outright, and refuse to overwrite an existing file that this session did not create.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** resolveScreenshotPath returns any absolute filename verbatim and otherwise does a plain path.join with no resolve or containment check, and screenshot() calls fs.writeFileSync with no existence check; the SCREENSHOT dispatch in index.ts only checks that payload.path is a non-empty string before forwarding it. Reproduced: joining the session dir with ../../escaped.png resolves above the session tree and absolute paths pass through unchanged.

### CR-066: WebSocket connect() never settles when the handshake is answered with anything but 101

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/websocket-client.js`
**Anchor:** `connect`
**Severity:** high

`connect()` returns a promise settled only from `req.on('upgrade')` (resolve) and `req.on('error')` (reject). There is no `'response'` handler and no timeout. If the endpoint answers the upgrade request with an ordinary HTTP response — a stale or wrong port now owned by another service, a proxy, a wedged Chrome, `CHROME_WS_HOST` pointed somewhere unexpected — the promise stays pending forever. `browser-session.js` caches that promise in `connectPromise` and awaits it from `ensureConnected()`, and its `send()` starts its own 10s timer only after `ensureConnected()` resolves, so every later call awaits the same never-settling promise. One bad handshake wedges the whole MCP server until the host restarts it.

Reproduced against a local HTTP server that replies `200` to any request: `connect()` was still unsettled after 3 seconds (test printed `NEVER SETTLED`).

Fix: add `req.on('response', res => reject(new Error(...status...)))` and a connect timeout that destroys the socket and rejects; validate `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` while there.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced against loopback servers replying 403 and 200 to the upgrade request: connect() never settled within a 5 second outer timeout; only a close-without-response case rejects via socket hang up. The send() in browser-session.js starts its 10 second timer only after ensureConnected resolves, so no caller bounds connect() itself.

### CR-067: A unit test kills whatever process holds the CDP port and deletes the live profile record

**File:** `packages/glass/test/cli-dispatch.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test `stop is dispatched (does not fall through to the unknown-command path)`
**Severity:** high

This test runs `chrome-ws stop` with the developer's real environment: no `--port`, no `CHROME_WS_PROFILE`, and `env: { ...process.env }`. The CLI's stop branch calls `session.killChrome()`, which — because a fresh CLI process never launched Chrome — resolves the victim as `findPidOnPort(state.activePort)`, i.e. whatever is listening on 127.0.0.1:9222, sends it `GET /json/close`, then `SIGTERM`s it. It also calls `clearProfileMeta('moe-glass')` unconditionally, unlinking `~/Library/Caches/moe/browser-profiles/moe-glass.meta.json`. The file is in the `unit` vitest project, so this happens on every `pnpm test` and every `pnpm check`, not in the opt-in Chrome suite.

Reproduced on a throwaway port so nothing of the user's was touched: a dummy listener on port 49999 was alive before `CHROME_WS_PROFILE`-free `chrome-ws stop` with `CHROME_WS_PORT=49999`, the CLI printed `Chrome stopped`, and the listener was dead 1.5s later. Port 9222 happened to be free on this machine, so the current tree does not kill anything here today; a dogfooding session with Chrome on 9222 loses its browser.

The test is also weak on its own terms: it asserts only that stderr lacks two strings and never checks the exit status, so it passes when the CLI hangs, crashes, or does nothing.

Fix: point the test at a reserved port and an isolated `XDG_CACHE_HOME` plus a unique `CHROME_WS_PROFILE` (the pattern `dialogs.smoke.test.mjs` already uses), and assert the exit status and the stop-specific message rather than the absence of two others.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** cli-dispatch.test.mjs is in the vitest unit project that pnpm test and CI run, not behind test:chrome, and its stop test runs the real CLI as a child process with the inherited environment and no port or profile override; chrome-ws defaults to port 9222 and profile moe-glass, and killChrome with no launched Chrome kills whatever holds that port and unconditionally deletes the real moe-glass meta.json. The test asserts only on stderr strings, so this happens silently. Traced by reading; the test was not run.

### CR-069: Project exclusion list cannot exclude any Codex session
**File:** `packages/memory/src/indexer.ts`
**Anchor:** `if (excludedProjects.includes(project))` in indexConversations, indexSession and indexUnprocessed
**Severity:** high

The exclusion list is matched against the names returned by `fs.readdirSync(sourceDir)`, i.e. the top-level directory names under each conversation source root. Under `~/.claude/projects` those names are encoded project paths, so exclusion works. Under `~/.codex/sessions` the top level is a **year** directory (`2026`), and the repository name never appears there at all — Codex nests as `<year>/<month>/<day>/rollout-*.jsonl`. `packages/memory/test/codex-transcripts.test.ts` confirms the layout by passing `"2026"` as the project name for a rollout fixture.

The same set is also handed to `findJsonlFiles` as `excludedDirNames`, which only skips subdirectories whose *name* matches — `09` and `02`, never the repo. So a project the user has excluded still has every Codex session archived, embedded, indexed, made searchable, and sent to a summarizer. `docs/SCHEMA.md` documents `exclude.txt` as "one project name per line", which is the value that can never match.

`parseCodexConversation` already recovers the real project via `projectFromCwd(cwd)`, so the fix is to apply the exclusion after parsing (or against the parsed `project`/`cwd`) rather than only against the walk's top-level directory name. The same guard shape appears in `sync.ts` and `verify.ts`, so the fix has to land in all three.

Reproduced. A scratch tree with `~/.claude/projects/-Users-ZKeown-Code-secret-repo` and `~/.codex/sessions/2026/09/02/rollout-*.jsonl`, with both `-Users-ZKeown-Code-secret-repo` and `secret-repo` on the exclude list: the Claude directory is skipped, the Codex rollout is not, because the only name offered to the guard is `2026`.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** indexer.ts checks excludedProjects only against the top-level directory name from readdirSync, which for the Codex sessions tree is a year (the codex-transcripts test itself passes project 2026); the real project from projectFromCwd in parseCodexConversation is never re-checked, and findJsonlFiles excludedDirNames only sees month and day names. docs/SCHEMA.md promises one project name per line for exclude.txt, which can never match. Reproduced the guard logic standalone: project 2026 is never excluded.

### CR-070: The in-transcript DO-NOT-INDEX marker is ignored by every `moe-memory index` path
**File:** `packages/memory/src/indexer.ts`
**Anchor:** indexConversations, indexSession and indexUnprocessed never call `shouldSkipConversation`
**Severity:** high

`sync.ts` defines the user-typed opt-out, documented there as the "HIGHEST-RISK RENAME IN THE PACKAGE" precisely because dropping it "silently starts indexing every conversation a user had explicitly marked DO-NOT-INDEX". It is honoured in exactly two places, both inside `sync.ts`. None of the three indexer entry points consults it, and neither does `verify.ts`.

So `moe-memory index`, `moe-memory index --cleanup`, `moe-memory index --session`, `moe-memory index --rebuild` and `moe-memory index --repair` all archive, embed, summarise and index a conversation the user marked as excluded. `index-cli.ts` HELP presents the ignoring paths as the primary workflow: "Initial setup: moe-memory index --cleanup" and "Nuclear option (deletes everything, re-indexes): moe-memory index --rebuild". A user who marks a chat and later backfills gets it indexed anyway, with no message.

The same omission also lets the summarizer's own agent transcripts in, which is what `SUMMARIZER_CONTEXT_MARKER` in `constants.ts` exists to prevent — its doc comment claims "When this text appears in a conversation, it will be excluded from indexing", true only on the sync path.

Reproduced by enumerating the call sites: `grep -rn shouldSkipConversation packages/memory/src` returns the definition plus two uses, both in `sync.ts`.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** grep shows shouldSkipConversation defined and called only in sync.ts; indexConversations, indexSession and indexUnprocessed in indexer.ts read and insert exchanges with no reference to it, and index-cli.ts calls those three functions with no intervening filter, so moe-memory index has no marker check anywhere between invocation and the database insert. Same root cause as CR-072, CR-075 and CR-076. Static trace.

### CR-072: The index CLI backfill path ignores the DO-NOT-INDEX marker
**File:** `packages/memory/src/indexer.ts`
**Anchor:** `indexUnprocessed`, and its two siblings indexConversations and indexSession
**Severity:** high

None of the three indexer entry points consult `shouldSkipConversation`. Each walks the
source directories, parses every transcript, and calls `insertExchange` on every exchange.
The only exclusion they honour is the project-name list from `getExcludedProjects`, which is a
different mechanism with a different purpose.

The trigger is a documented, recommended command. The help text in the index CLI says
"Initial setup: moe-memory index --cleanup" and "# Index all unprocessed (recommended for
backfill)", which routes to `indexUnprocessed`. `--rebuild` routes to `indexConversations`
after deleting the database, so a rebuild also re-ingests every marked conversation. A user
who has been typing the marker into transcripts loses that protection the first time they run
a backfill or a rebuild.

Not reproduced end to end: these paths call `initEmbeddings` unconditionally and a run would
download the model. Verified statically that the marker check is absent from all three, and
verified separately (see the repair finding) that `shouldSkipConversation` does detect the
marker on the archived copy these paths read.

Fix: filter in the file-collection loop of each entry point, next to the existing
`excludedProjects.includes(project)` check, so the marker is enforced wherever a transcript
enters the index rather than only on the sync path.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** The three indexer.ts entry points indexConversations, indexSession and indexUnprocessed never import or call shouldSkipConversation; only getExcludedProjects and shouldQueueForSummary gate anything, and neither blocks insertExchange. index-cli.ts routes --cleanup and --rebuild to these functions. Same root cause as CR-070, scoped to the backfill and rebuild entry points. Static trace; a live run would have downloaded a model.

### CR-073: Text-only hits are reported as a 100% semantic match in the default search mode
**File:** `packages/memory/src/search.ts`
**Anchor:** `similarity: mode === "text" ? undefined : l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity(row.distance)`
**Severity:** high

The text branch selects a literal `0 as distance`. In `mode: "text"` the similarity is correctly suppressed, but the default mode is `"both"` — set as the default in the CLI, in `SearchInputSchema`, and in the advertised MCP `inputSchema`. In `"both"`, `mode !== "text"`, so every LIKE-only hit is scored `l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity(0)`, which is exactly 1, and `formatResults` renders `100% match`.

A substring hit therefore outranks, in the reader's eyes, every genuine vector hit in the same response. The consumer is a model choosing which conversation to read, so the fabricated score directly misdirects retrieval.

Reproduced: the SQL literal is confirmed by the query text and by a text-mode run against a scratch database, and `l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity(0)` evaluates to `1`, rendered as `100% match`.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** The search.ts text branch selects a literal 0 as distance; the both-mode merge loop pushes text-only hits into the same results array; the final map checks mode equals text per call rather than per row, so l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity(0) equals exactly 1 and renders as 100% match. Confirmed both is the default in searchConversations, search-cli.ts and the MCP tool advertised schema.

### CR-074: Date-filtered vector search returns nothing when matching rows exist
**File:** `packages/memory/src/search.ts`
**Anchor:** `hasMetadataFilters`, and the comment "vec0 applies KNN before WHERE"
**Severity:** high

`searchConversations` knows that vec0 applies its KNN limit before the WHERE clause and
widens the candidate set for that reason, but `hasMetadataFilters` returns
`Boolean(options.project || options.session_id || options.git_branch)` and omits `after` and
`before`. `buildSearchFilters` does emit timestamp predicates for those two. So a
date-filtered vector search asks vec0 for exactly `limit` neighbours and then discards the
ones outside the window, with nothing to backfill them.

Trigger: any `mode: "vector"` search with `after` or `before` where the nearest `limit`
vectors happen to fall outside the date window. Both parameters are exposed on the
`search_conversations` MCP tool, so this is ordinary use, not an edge case.

Reproduced with a script under the scratchpad against better-sqlite3 and sqlite-vec directly,
using twenty rows where the ten nearest are outside the window and the ten matching rows are
further away:

```
k=10, no date filter        -> 10 rows
k=10, after=2025-01-01      -> 0 rows  <-- matching rows EXIST but are lost
k=30, after=2025-01-01      -> 10 rows
total rows in date window   -> 10
```

Fix: include `options.after` and `options.before` in `hasMetadataFilters`. The `limit * 3`
multiplier is still a guess that can truncate on a selective filter, so the durable fix is to
grow `k` until either `limit` rows survive the WHERE or the candidate set is exhausted.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced against the repo real better-sqlite3 and sqlite-vec builds using the actual hasMetadataFilters and buildSearchFilters logic: a date-only filter with ten true in-window rows returned 0 of 10 because hasMetadataFilters ignores after and before, so k stays at limit while vec0 applies KNN before WHERE; widening k to three times limit recovered all ten. The MCP search_conversations tool exposes after and before directly.

### CR-075: DO-NOT-INDEX conversations are indexed and sent to the summarizer by index --repair
**File:** `packages/memory/src/verify.ts`
**Anchor:** `repairIndex`, and "Check for missing or errored summary" in `verifyIndex`
**Severity:** high

The in-transcript opt-out is honoured on exactly one code path. `syncConversations` copies every transcript into the archive first and only then consults `shouldSkipConversation`, so a marked conversation sits in the archive with no `-summary.txt` sidecar, because sync's summarize gate is `shouldQueueForSummary(summaryPath) && !shouldSkipConversation(destFile)`.

`verifyIndex` walks that same archive and pushes any conversation with no summary file into `result.missing` with reason "No summary file". It never calls `shouldSkipConversation`. So every conversation the user marked DO NOT INDEX is permanently classified as missing. The consequences follow from `index --repair` in `src/index-cli.ts`, which calls `repairIndex(issues, { noSummaries })` for exactly that list:

- `summarizeConversation(exchanges)` runs, which spawns the Claude Agent SDK with the conversation text in the prompt unless `--no-summaries` was passed. The content of a conversation the user asked not to index leaves the machine.
- `insertExchange` then writes every exchange plus its embedding, making the conversation searchable, and the generated summary is written next to the transcript where `search.ts` will attach it to any hit.
- `index --verify` also lists each marked conversation by absolute path under "Missing summaries" and exits 1, so a user who has ever used the marker can never get a clean verify and is told to run `--repair`.

The three entry points in `src/indexer.ts` (`indexConversations`, `indexSession`, `indexUnprocessed`) have the same gap: `grep -rn "shouldSkipConversation" src/` returns only `src/sync.ts`. I did not run repair; the finding is a read of the call chain plus that grep, and `test/model/sync-indexing.test.ts` is the only place the marker is exercised against a caller at all.

Fix: move the marker check into a single guard that every archive consumer calls. The cheapest correct version is for `verifyIndex` to skip a conversation carrying any `EXCLUSION_MARKERS` entry rather than reporting it missing, and for `repairIndex` to re-check before summarizing or inserting, so a marked file that reaches the list from an older database is still refused.

**Verification:** confirmed
