**Verification evidence:** shouldSkipConversation is defined and called only in sync.ts; verifyIndex and repairIndex in verify.ts never call it, so a marked conversation that sync deliberately archived without a summary lands in missing with reason No summary file, and repairIndex then calls parseConversation, summarizeConversation (a Claude Agent SDK query carrying the full exchange text) and insertExchange unguarded. Same root cause as CR-076.

### CR-076: Index repair re-indexes and summarizes conversations the user marked DO-NOT-INDEX
**File:** `packages/memory/src/verify.ts`
**Anchor:** `repairIndex`, and verifyIndex's "No summary file" reason
**Severity:** high

The in-transcript opt-out is honoured in exactly one place. `shouldSkipConversation` is
called only from `syncConversations` (grep for EXCLUSION_MARKER across src confirms sync.ts
is the sole caller). That creates a chain that turns the opt-out into its opposite:

1. Sync copies a marked transcript into the archive but skips indexing it, and its summary
   guard is `shouldQueueForSummary(summaryPath) && !shouldSkipConversation(destFile)`, so no
   summary file is ever written.
2. `verifyIndex` walks the archive and reports every file without a summary under `missing`
   with reason "No summary file". The marked conversation lands there by construction.
3. `repairIndex` re-indexes every path in `missing` and `outdated` with no marker check, and
   unless `noSummaries` is set it also calls `summarizeConversation`, which sends the
   conversation text to the Claude Agent SDK.

So `moe-memory index --verify` followed by `moe-memory index --repair`, the recovery pair the
package's own help text recommends ("3. Health check ... 4. Recovery: moe-memory index
--repair (if issues found)"), indexes and externally summarizes precisely the conversations
the user excluded. The marker's own docstring calls this out as the failure it exists to
prevent: "it silently starts indexing every conversation a user had explicitly marked
DO-NOT-INDEX."

I reproduced steps 1 and 2 with a script under the scratchpad, using a marked transcript and
the built dist: `shouldSkipConversation` returns true on the archived copy, sync reports
copied 1 / indexed 0 / summarized 0 with no summary file, and `verifyIndex` returns that file
in `missing` with reason "No summary file". Step 3 needs the encoder, so I read it rather than
ran it.

Fix: call `shouldSkipConversation(conversationPath)` at the top of the `toReindex` loop and
skip. Better, have `verifyIndex` not classify a marked conversation as missing at all, so the
verify report stops describing a respected opt-out as an index defect.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** verify.ts has no reference to shouldSkipConversation or the exclusion marker and the repairIndex reindex loop has no marker check. Reproduced steps one and two against the compiled dist with scratch paths: a marked transcript with no summary file, which is exactly what sync.ts produces for a marked file, is classified missing with reason No summary file by verifyIndex, feeding the unconditional summarize-and-index loop in repairIndex. Same defect as CR-075.

### CR-077: Codex E2E copies the user's live auth.json into a temp tree that is never cleaned up
**File:** `packages/memory/test/manual/codex-e2e.js`
**Anchor:** `copyCodexAuth`
**Severity:** high

`copyCodexAuth` reads `auth.json` from the real Codex home, dies with a message telling the user to run `codex login` if it is absent, and then copies `auth.json`, `installation_id` and `models_cache.json` into `<tmpdir>/moe-memory-codex-e2e-XXXX/codex-home/`. `auth.json` holds the live Codex credential.

`main` never removes `root`. There is no try/finally, no cleanup on the failure path, and the success path prints `Codex E2E passed in ${root}` as though the tree is meant to be kept. Every run therefore leaves a permanent second copy of a live credential outside the credential store, in a location no revocation or rotation workflow knows about, alongside `seed.out`, `trigger.out` and `recall.out`.

I did not run the harness. What keeps this below critical is that `mkdtempSync` creates the root with mode 0700 and `copyFileSync` preserves the source mode, so there is no cross-user exposure on a normally configured machine; the exposure is duplication and unbounded retention, reachable by anything running as the user and by any backup or sync agent that indexes the temp directory.

Fix: register a cleanup that removes `root` on both success and failure, and prefer a symlink or a `CODEX_HOME`-relative auth reference over copying the credential if Codex permits it. At minimum, delete `auth.json` from the temp home as soon as the last Codex invocation returns, and say in the harness output that a credential copy existed.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** main() creates the root via mkdtempSync and copyCodexAuth copies auth.json, installation_id and models_cache.json into it, but no finally or exit handler ever removes the root on success or failure; the success path prints the retained path. The MODULE_NOT_FOUND premise from another shard does not apply: this file imports only Node builtins and passes node --check. mkdtempSync creates the directory at mode 0700, so exposure is same-user retention rather than cross-user.

### CR-078: Deep-tier checks truncate the invoking user's global OpenCode config and install into their live CLIs
**File:** `packages/mint/checks/run-checks.sh`
**Anchor:** `deep_opencode`, the line `printf '{"plugin":["%s"]}' "$WORK" > "$HOME/.config/opencode/opencode.json"`
**Severity:** high

The script's own header advertises a dev-host mode: "Set MOE_MINT_PLUGIN_ROOT to point at a different plugin root … it lets this script be unit-tested directly against a generated fixture without a container", and "A check whose CLI is absent from PATH emits `skip`, never `not ok`, so the script stays runnable on a dev host outside the container". Nothing in the script enforces the container. The deep tier then mutates the real `$HOME` of whoever runs it, and `deep_opencode` does so destructively: it `mkdir -p`s `$HOME/.config/opencode` and truncates `opencode.json` with `>`, unconditionally, with no existence check, no backup, and no prompt. The value it writes is a `mktemp -d` path that the `EXIT` trap deletes moments later, so the user is left with a config pointing at nothing.

I reproduced this, and it did real damage on this machine. Running `MOE_MINT_PLUGIN_NAME=kitchen-sink MOE_MINT_PLUGIN_ROOT=<scratch>/ks bash packages/mint/checks/run-checks.sh` against a scratchpad copy of the kitchen-sink fixture: overwrote `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (prior content unrecoverable), registered `kitchen-sink-market` in the live Claude Code and `kitchen-sink-dev` in the live Codex, and installed the fixture plugin into `~/.claude/plugins/cache/` and `~/.codex/plugins/cache/`. I reverted the two installs with each CLI's own uninstall/remove commands and deleted the orphaned cache directories; the OpenCode config could not be restored.

The vitest suite survives this only because `test/test-command.test.ts` neutralises the hazard from the outside, narrowing `PATH` to `sandboxBin()` and pointing `HOME` at `mkdtempSync` — its own comment names the risk ("which performs real, HOME-mutating installs when a harness CLI is present … instead of firing against this machine's own ~/.claude"). That knowledge lives in the caller, not in the script, so any other caller inherits the damage.

Fix: gate the whole deep tier behind an explicit opt-in that only `moe-mint test` sets inside the container (for example require `MOE_MINT_DEEP=1`, or refuse when `MOE_MINT_PLUGIN_ROOT` is set), and make `deep_opencode` write its config only after confirming the file is absent or backing it up.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** deep_opencode has no container, CI or opt-in guard and unconditionally truncates $HOME/.config/opencode/opencode.json with a temp path the EXIT trap then deletes; moe-mint test always wraps the script in docker, but the script header documents direct invocation and neither pnpm check nor .gitlab-ci.yml calls it, and the mint unit test sandboxes HOME and PATH itself, showing the authors knew the raw script is unsafe. Empirically established on this host by the reviewing shard; not re-run.

### CR-079: Generated marketplace descriptor omits the required owner, so any plugin without an author is rejected by Claude Code
**File:** `packages/mint/src/adapters/claude-code.ts`
**Anchor:** `marketplaceManifest`, the line `if (config.author) marketplace.owner = config.author`
**Severity:** high

`author` is optional in `moe-mint.yaml` (`config.ts`, `author: authorSchema.optional()`), and `moe-mint init` does not scaffold one. But Claude Code's marketplace descriptor requires `owner`, so omitting it makes `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` invalid and the plugin uninstallable through the very descriptor moe-mint emits for it. Copilot resolves through the same file, so both harnesses are affected.

Reproduced twice. A minimal config with no `author` generates a descriptor whose only top-level keys are `name`, `description`, `plugins`, and `claude plugin validate --strict` on it reports:

```
✘ Found 1 error:
  ❯ owner: Invalid input: expected object, received undefined
✘ Validation failed
```

Worse, the out-of-the-box scaffold hits it: `moe-mint init --dir <new>` writes a config with only `name`, `version`, `description`, `bootstrap`, and the resulting plugin fails `claude plugin validate --strict` with the same error. That is `check_claude_code` in `run-checks.sh` reporting `not ok` on a freshly scaffolded plugin. All five of this repo's own plugins set `author`, which is why the tree does not show it today.

No vendored schema catches it either: `schemas/claude-code-plugin-manifest.json` is the *plugin* manifest ("Manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json) for a Claude Code plugin"), and `SCHEMA_TARGETS` in `validate.ts` lists no marketplace descriptor, so `moe-mint validate` passes.

Fix: either require `author` whenever the claude-code adapter is active, or emit a derived `owner` (falling back to a name-only object) so the descriptor is always well-formed; and give `moe-mint init` an author placeholder.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced with claude plugin validate --strict on a synthetic marketplace.json matching the authorless scaffold from moe-mint init: owner Invalid input, expected object, received undefined; adding owner clears it. SCHEMA_TARGETS in validate.ts never checks marketplace.json, so moe-mint validate gives false confidence. All five of this repo own mint YAML files set author, which is why the shipped plugins tree never surfaces it.

### CR-080: A symlink at a generated path lets generate write outside the plugin root

**File:** `packages/mint/src/generate.ts`
**Anchor:** the conflict-detection loop guarding "refusing to overwrite existing file(s) not created by moe-mint"

`writeFileSet` enforces containment on the *path string* (`generated file path escapes plugin root`), then calls `mkdirSync` + `writeFileSync`, both of which follow symlinks. So a symlink planted anywhere in the plugin tree at a path an adapter emits redirects the write outside the root, and the containment check never sees it. The pre-existing-file guard in `generate` makes it worse rather than better: it uses `existsSync`, which returns `false` for a **dangling** symlink, so that case is not even reported as a conflict.

Reproduced with a script under my scratchpad against `dist/`, three cases:

- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` as a symlink to a **nonexistent** file outside the root: `generate(root)` with no flags succeeded and *created* the outside file with the generated manifest content. No warning, no `--force`.
- Same symlink pointing at an **existing** outside file holding `PRECIOUS USER DATA`: the no-force run correctly refused, then `generate(root, undefined, {force: true})` overwrote the victim through the link.
- `.claude-plugin` itself as a symlink to an outside **directory**: every file the adapter emits into it landed outside the root.

The `--force` variant is reachable on the documented happy path, because the `import` command's own closing message tells the user to do exactly that: "generate will report conflicts with your existing hand-maintained harness files (e.g. .claude-plugin/plugin.json); after reviewing, re-run with --force to let moe-mint own them." Importing a third-party Claude-format plugin is the advertised use of `import`, so the tree being converted is not necessarily trusted.

Fix: resolve containment against the real filesystem, not the path string. In `writeFileSet`, `lstat` each target (and each directory component it would create) and refuse when any component is a symlink, or open with `O_NOFOLLOW`. In `generate`, use `lstatSync`/`existsSync` with a symlink check rather than plain `existsSync` so a dangling link is a conflict instead of an absence. Note `test/generate.test.ts` covers the containment control only in the manifest-prune direction ("ignores manifest entries with unsafe paths and warns"); the write direction has no test.

**Severity:** high

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced against the compiled packages/mint/dist/fileset.js: a symlink at .claude-plugin/plugin.json pointing outside the plugin root caused writeFileSet to silently overwrite the outside file, because mkdirSync and writeFileSync follow symlinks and the only containment check is a lexical resolve().startsWith(), never lstat or realpath. The generate.ts conflict check uses existsSync, which returns false for a dangling symlink, so that case raises no conflict at all. The import workflow makes a third-party plugin tree an ordinary input.

### CR-081: Embedded cdylib is dlopened from a predictable shared-temp path without verifying its bytes
**File:** `packages/tab/bindings/go/tab/loader.go`
**Anchor:** `extractEmbedded`
**Severity:** high

`extractEmbedded` names its output directory after the content hash of the embedded library, then short-circuits with "if fileExists(target) { return target, nil }" — it never checks that the bytes already at `target` actually hash to that name. `openLibrary` then dlopens whatever is there. The directory is built from `cacheBases()`, whose second base is `os.TempDir()`, and the code comment shows that base is a designed-for path, not an exotic one ("persistent first then a noexec-resistant temp dir"): it is used whenever `os.UserCacheDir()` errors (no `HOME`/`XDG_CACHE_HOME`, which is the norm in containers, CI runners, systemd units and cron) or whenever extraction/dlopen from the user cache dir fails (a `noexec` cache mount, the exact case the comment anticipates).

On a shared host that yields local code execution. The hash is fully derivable from the published module's embedded bytes, which are public, so any local user can pre-create `/tmp/moe/tab-go/<hash>/libmoe_tab_ffi.so` containing arbitrary code; the next victim process that reaches the temp base loads it into its own address space. `os.MkdirAll(dir, 0o755)` does not fail on, or check the ownership of, an existing `/tmp/moe` the attacker created first, so the whole subtree can be attacker-controlled even without guessing the hash.

I did not reproduce this. `embeddedLib` is empty in this tree (the dev stub in `embed_stub.go`), so the branch is dead in-repo and live only in the published moe-tab-go module, whose generated embed files replace that stub. The reasoning is from the source and is not conditional on the embedded bytes.

Fix: re-hash the file at `target` and fall through to a rewrite when it does not match, refuse a `target` that is a symlink or is not owned by the current uid, create the tree with `0o700` under a uid-qualified path, and prefer a per-process `os.MkdirTemp` for the temp fallback rather than a shared predictable directory.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** extractEmbedded checks only os.Stat on the target before dlopen and never re-hashes the bytes; cacheBases falls back to the shared os.TempDir, which is world-writable /tmp on Linux, whenever UserCacheDir errors (no HOME, containers, CI, systemd), and the hash-named path is derivable offline from the shipped bytes, so a local attacker can pre-plant the file that gets dlopened. The embedded bytes are a stub in this tree, so the branch is live only in the published moe-tab-go module; source trace, no build.

### CR-083: OpenAI reasoning tokens are added to output_tokens that already contains them

**File:** `packages/tab/crates/moe-tab-core/src/transcript/provider/openai.rs`
**Anchor:** `normalize`, and the doc line "reasoning tokens fold into output"
**Severity:** high

`normalize` computes the output bucket as the sum of `output_tokens` and
`output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`. In the OpenAI Responses API those are
not disjoint: `reasoning_tokens` is a *subset* of `output_tokens` (reasoning is
billed as output), and the API's own invariant `total_tokens == input_tokens +
output_tokens` proves it — there is no room in the total for a separate
reasoning term. Adding them therefore bills the reasoning tokens twice.

The module header gets the analogous input rule right ("`input_tokens` is a
*total* that still includes cached tokens, so the uncached bucket is the
difference") and then treats the output side as if the provider had split it.

This is reachable in production, not only in tests: the `tab` house dialect
dispatches `provider: "openai"` rows straight into this function from
`parse_row` in `transcript/tab.rs`, and that dialect's contract is "the SDK's
usage object, verbatim". The overcharge scales with how much of the turn was
reasoning, so it is worst exactly where it matters — long Codex/o-series turns.

Reproduced (I mirrored `normalize` and `pricing::cost_for` in JavaScript,
because `cargo` is not on PATH in this environment, and priced the usage object
against the shipped `gpt-5.6-sol` entry in `prices/bundled.json`):

```
input_tokens 36, output_tokens 1252, reasoning_tokens 1152, total_tokens 1288
output tokens as written : 2404
output tokens correct    : 1252
usd as written           : 0.07230000
usd correct              : 0.03774000
overcharge factor        : 1.916
```

The script is at `/private/tmp/claude-503/-Users-ZKeown-Code-moe/4556b327-b63b-49d4-bbc6-78cd4f317e00/scratchpad/shard-036/repro-openai.js`.

Fix: set the output bucket to `g("output_tokens")` alone. `reasoning` is then
only useful as a diagnostic, so either drop the `nested("output_tokens_details",
"reasoning_tokens")` read or keep it for reporting. The unit test
`subtracts_cached_from_input_and_folds_reasoning_into_output` asserts the
double count (expects 25 for `output_tokens` 20 plus `reasoning_tokens` 5) and
must be updated with the fix; note the same code and the same test exist in the
`obol` snapshot under `.moe-references/`, so this is inherited, not introduced
here.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** openai.rs normalize() sums output_tokens with output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens into the output field and the unit test in the same file pins 20 plus 5 equals 25 as expected; tab.rs parse_row routes provider openai rows there unmodified and cost.rs cost_for multiplies output by the output rate directly, so reasoning tokens are billed twice for every OpenAI reasoning-model transcript. The API contract that reasoning_tokens is a breakdown inside output_tokens was confirmed from documentation knowledge, not fetched live.

### CR-084: Cross-language C ABI gate is invoked by nothing; only the Python binding is ever exercised
**File:** `packages/tab/scripts/validate-bindings.sh`
**Anchor:** the header comment "Consumers: Rust CLI, Python (ctypes), Go (purego), TypeScript under Node (koffi)" and its `check` function
**Severity:** high

AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and ARCHITECTURE.md all name `pnpm tab:test:bindings` as "the equivalence gate" and "the only check that the C ABI rename landed identically in the Rust FFI, the committed header and all three bindings". That guarantee does not hold. This script — the only thing that actually runs all consumers side by side — is invoked by no npm script, no turbo task, and no CI job.

Verified by grep across the tree (excluding `node_modules`, `.git`, `target`, `.venv`, `.moe`): every hit for `validate-bindings` is prose or a comment. Two are READMEs, one is the script's own usage line, one is a comment at the top of `bindings/typescript/src/total.ts` naming the script that never calls it. What `tab:test:bindings` actually expands to in the root `package.json` is:

```
pnpm tab:build && uv run --project packages/tab/bindings/python pytest packages/tab/bindings/python
```

That is the Python suite alone. The consequences, each verified:

- **Go binding: exercised by nothing.** `grep` for `go run`, `go build` and `go test` across `package.json`, `turbo.json`, `.gitlab-ci.yml` and `scripts/` returns no matches. `bindings/go/tab/tab_test.go`, `loader_embed_test.go` and `pricing_env_test.go` are never run.
- **TypeScript binding: FFI half exercised by nothing.** Its `test` script is `vitest run --project unit`, and the project that dlopens the library is the separate `test:ffi`. Grep finds no invoker for `test:ffi`, and turbo's `test` task runs only each package's `test` script. So `pnpm test` runs `test/unit/*`, which never touches the cdylib.
- **The committed header is not compared to anything here.** Header drift is caught by the Rust test `header_matches_source`, which runs under `pnpm tab:test` (`cargo test`), not under `tab:test:bindings`.

To answer the question directly: the script does not compare the header's symbol set against each binding, and it does not grep for a pattern either. It compares `total_usd` strings. Symbol-*name* drift is nonetheless caught for all four exports whenever a binding is executed, because every binding resolves eagerly — `bindings/python/moe_tab/_lib.py` touches all four `_lib.moe_tab_*` attributes at module import (ctypes raises `AttributeError` on a missing symbol), `loader.go`'s `ensureLoaded` calls `purego.RegisterLibFunc` for all four, and koffi's `lib.func` and bun's `dlopen` throw on a missing symbol. Since Python is the one binding that runs, a rename is caught. What is caught by nothing is *signature* drift: the argument lists in `_lib.py`'s `argtypes`, `ffi-node.ts`'s C-signature strings and `ffi-bun.ts`'s `FFIType` lists are hand-written and compared to `include/moe_tab.h` by no check in the repo.

Fix: add `packages/tab/scripts/validate-bindings.sh` to a root script and run it where the toolchain exists (it needs cargo, python3, go and node), or at minimum wire `pnpm --filter @tc/moe-tab test:ffi` and a `go test ./...` into `tab:test:bindings` so the claim in AGENTS.md becomes true. Per AGENTS.md's own rule that the tree wins, the three docs need correcting either way.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** grep confirms validate-bindings.sh is invoked nowhere outside its own header and a comment; tab:test:bindings resolves to Python pytest only; the CI tab job runs only cargo test; the turbo test task skips the TypeScript binding test:ffi project; no go test or go build exists outside the script itself. Broader parent of CR-082.

### CR-085: An eval name with no ASCII word characters makes `build` delete every other eval in the site
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/site.py`
**Anchor:** `build_eval`, the two statements "if eval_dir.exists(): shutil.rmtree(eval_dir)"
**Severity:** high

`slugify` in cli.py replaces every run of characters outside `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]` with a dash and
then strips leading and trailing dashes, so it returns the empty string for any name built
only from disallowed characters. A CJK, Cyrillic, or emoji eval name does this, and so does
`name: "!!!"`. `resolve_eval_slugs` hands that empty slug to `build_eval`, which computes
`eval_dir = site_dir / "evals" / slug`. Path treats an empty component as nothing, so
`eval_dir` becomes the site's `evals` directory itself, and the guard above rmtree's it.
Every previously built eval, including its copied run and grade artifacts, is deleted. The
command then reports success and exits zero.

Reproduced. I built an eval named `alpha` into a scratch site directory, confirmed
`evals/alpha/eval.json` present, then built a second eval named `!!!` into the same
directory. Afterwards the tree held only `evals/eval.json`, `index.html`, and `index.json`;
`evals/alpha/` was gone and the exit code was 0.

A name of exactly `..` or `.` survives slugify unchanged and is the same defect by another
route: `site_dir / "evals" / ".."` is `site_dir`, so rmtree walks the whole output directory.
The same empty slug also defeats `resolve_runs_root`, where `runs_dir / ""` is `runs_dir`, so
such an eval's runs land unnamespaced in a shared external runs directory and mix with other
evals' runs.

Fix: make `slugify` guarantee a single safe non-empty component. Fall back to a hash or the
directory name when the substitution empties the string, and reject or replace `.` and `..`.
Then assert in `build_eval` that the resolved `eval_dir` is a proper child of
`site_dir / "evals"` before removing anything.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced: slugify of punctuation-only and CJK names returns an empty string, making eval_dir in build_eval equal to site_dir/evals itself, so its rmtree guard deletes every prior eval artifact before writing; exit code stays 0. A name of two dots also survives slugify unchanged, resolving to site_dir. Eval names come from the eval.yaml name field or directory name, ordinary operator input, and neither resolve_eval_slugs nor build_eval guards an empty or dot-dot slug.

### CR-086: Provenance self-test is satisfied by a usage error, so the red fixture is never checked
**File:** `scripts/check-provenance.mjs`
**Anchor:** `main` argument guard, plus the CI line "if node scripts/check-provenance.mjs scripts/fixtures/provenance-red --min-readmes 1; then"
**Severity:** high

The provenance job's second script line is the only thing that proves the checker can fail. It invokes the checker with three arguments, but the entry point rejects anything past one argument: it prints the usage string and returns 2 before reading a single file. The shell test only asks for a non-zero status, so the self-test passes without the fixture ever being opened, and no assertion covers the flag name. I reproduced both halves: the three-argument form exits 2 with "usage: check-provenance.mjs [root]", and the corrected one-argument form does not report a problem either — it dies with an unhandled ENOENT on the fixture's missing NOTICE, exit 1. So the fixture directory (which holds only a PARITY.md and one README) cannot exercise any check the script actually performs; the checker no longer validates README "## Forked from" tables at all, which is what the job comment claims it guards. The fix is to make the checker accept the flags the self-test passes (or drop them), turn a missing NOTICE or PARITY.md into a reported problem rather than a crash, give the fixture the pair of files the register comparison needs, and assert on the specific problem text instead of merely on a non-zero exit.

**Verification:** confirmed
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced: the three-argument CI invocation exits 2 on the usage guard before opening any file; the corrected one-argument invocation against the fixture crashes with an uncaught ENOENT on the missing NOTICE inside checkAttributionRegister and never reaches the problems array. The checker has no exit code distinguishing a detected problem from a crash before checking, so no caller can write a working self-test against this fixture, a script-side defect distinct from the CI wiring in CR-005.

### CR-003: npm plugin sources pin a package name but no registry, so `@tc` falls back to public npm

**File:** `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`
**Anchor:** `"package": "@tc/moe-glass"`
**Severity:** medium

The `moe-memory` and `moe-glass` entries declare `{"source":"npm","package":"@tc/…","version":"0.0.0-tc.1"}`
and deliberately omit the source's `registry` field. `scripts/mint-plugins.mjs` states the
reasoning in its registry comment: "Registry and authentication stay in the consumer's existing
`@tc` scope configuration." The test named "pins npm sources to the exact canonical downstream
version" enforces the omission with `assert.equal(Object.hasOwn(entry.source, "registry"), false)`.

Claude Code's own schema for that field, read out of the installed binary at
`~/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.258`, says: "Custom NPM registry URL (defaults to using
system default, likely npmjs.org)". So the internal-only distribution of these two plugins is
enforced by nothing in the artifact itself. It depends entirely on every consumer having
`@tc:registry=https://proget.tcdevops.com/npm/tcnpm/` in their npm configuration. A consumer
without it, which is the ordinary state of a fresh laptop, a new hire, or a CI runner, resolves
`@tc/moe-memory` against the public registry instead.

I reproduced the exposure on the public registry side. Both package paths return HTTP 404 on
`registry.npmjs.org`, and `?text=scope:tc` returns `"total": 0`, so the `@tc` scope is
entirely unclaimed there. Today that fallback is a failed install, which is safe. The moment
anyone registers an npm org named `tc` and publishes `moe-memory@0.0.0-tc.1`, the exact pinned
version is satisfied by a stranger's tarball. The payload is not inert content: the composed
`@tc/moe-memory` tarball is required to carry a SessionStart hook, and
`plugins/moe-memory/hooks/moe-mint/hooks.json` runs
`node "${PLUGIN_ROOT:-${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}}/dist/cli.js" sync --background` on every startup,
resume and clear. Substituted code therefore executes on the consumer's machine at session
start. npm plugin sources have no integrity digest to fall back on, unlike archive sources
whose `sha256` field the same schema describes as refusing the install on mismatch, so
`registry` is the only available control.

I verified the schema text and the public-registry state. I did not exercise a real install
against a machine with no scope mapping, so the fallback step itself is read from the schema
sentence rather than observed.

Fix: give both npm sources an explicit
`"registry": "https://proget.tcdevops.com/npm/tcnpm/"`, and invert the test assertion to
require the field rather than forbid it. This leaks nothing new. That URL is already committed
in the root `.npmrc`, in the root `package.json` `publishConfig`, and as `PROGET_REGISTRY` in
`scripts/tc-release-validate.mjs`. Pinning the registry does not break authentication either,
since npm matches credentials by registry host independently of scope mapping. The identity-leak
scanner in `scripts/check-downstream-scope.mjs` only looks for upstream package names in this
file, so adding the field does not trip `pnpm scope:check`.

**Verification:** confirmed-lower
**Verification evidence:** marketplace.json and mint-plugins.mjs confirm the npm sources carry no registry and the omission is deliberate, leaving @tc resolution to the consumer npm config; standard scope-fallback semantics make public-npm fallback possible. The intended audience is a ~20-person team that already depends on @tc-scoped ProGet packages across many repos, so a missing scope mapping is an edge condition rather than the ordinary state; the challenger could not observe Claude Code install-time resolution directly.

**Disposition:** stale
**Commit:** —
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02
**Note:** Superseded by 9e31d3f, which introduced the current public @bubstack/moe-memory and @bubstack/moe-glass marketplace sources; the reviewed @tc package names are absent from this branch.
### CR-012: Eval fixtures encode a transcript envelope the hook never receives in production

**File:** `packages/core/test/latte/scenarios/24-created-component-need-styles.json`
**Anchor:** the transcript rows `{ "role": "assistant", "content": "..." }`
**Severity:** medium

Every row in every assigned scenario is a flat `{role, content:string}` object. That is not the shape
Claude Code writes to `transcript_path`. The authority is the sibling hook in the same package,
`packages/core/hooks/moe-completion-evidence`, which reads the same event field and discriminates on a
top-level `type` (`if (!entry || entry.type !== 'user') return false`) and then descends into
`entry.message.content` as an **array of content blocks** (`item.type === 'text'`,
`'tool_use'`, `'tool_result'`). Its fixture helpers in `packages/core/test/completion-evidence.test.ts`
build rows as `{ type: "assistant", message: { role: "assistant", content } }`.

So the two hooks in one package disagree about the format of the same file, and the eval corpus sides
with the one that is wrong. `claude-judge-continuation` never parses the rows — it interpolates the raw
`jq -s '.'` output into `EVALUATION_PROMPT` — so the mismatch does not crash. It silently changes the
judge's entire input. The fixtures feed clean prose; production feeds a nested envelope carrying
`tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks alongside `uuid`, `parentUuid`, `sessionId`, `cwd` and `timestamp`.

I reproduced both sides through the real pipeline (`jq -c '.transcript[]'` from `run-evals.sh`, then the
hook's `tail -n 4 | jq -s '.'`). Scenario 24 yields a two-element array of bare `role`/`content` pairs.
The same conversation in the production shape yields a four-element array in which a single file-write
round trip consumes three of the four rows the hook is willing to look at, and the assistant's prose is
buried under a `content` array.

The consequence is that a green run of this suite is not evidence about the deployed hook. The dominant
production failure mode — the stated next step sitting in an assistant row that tool traffic has pushed
outside the `tail -n 4` window — cannot be expressed by any fixture in this corpus, because no fixture
contains a tool row at all. I confirmed that suite-wide: `jq` over all 65 scenarios finds zero rows with
a top-level `type` and zero rows whose `content` is not a string.

Fix: regenerate the corpus in the real envelope, matching the `human()` / `assistant()` / `toolResult()`
helpers already written in `completion-evidence.test.ts`, and add fixtures where tool rows sit between
the assistant's stated intent and the end of the transcript. The corpus is imported work
(`double-shot-latte` at `dfe7567`, MIT, per `PARITY.md`), so reshaping it is permitted; no test guards
these files, only the opt-in `latte:evals` script consumes them.

**Verification:** confirmed-lower
**Verification evidence:** The cited authority, moe-completion-evidence, never consumes these fixtures; the actual consumer, claude-judge-continuation, does no structural parsing and interpolates raw JSON into a judge prompt, so there is no crash or silent-false path. The shape mismatch is real, confirmed against the production row shape in packages/memory/src/parser.ts, but the eval script is opt-in, not run by CI, and its own header documents an unestablished baseline.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `8f4db7e`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02
**Note:** —
### CR-013: Two surface cues let a classifier score 30/30 without reading the rubric

**File:** `packages/core/test/latte/scenarios/48-api-partially-implemented.json`
**Anchor:** `"[Implemented: POST /posts, GET /posts/:id]"`
**Severity:** medium

The fixtures leak their own labels through two lexical tells, so the suite cannot distinguish a judge
that understands the rubric from one that pattern-matches an artifact of how the fixtures were authored.

All 15 CONTINUE scenarios in this shard open the assistant message with a bracketed pseudo-summary of
tool work: `[Created: ...]`, `[Implemented: ...]`, `[Added: ...]`, `[Ran tests: ...]`. None of the 15
STOP scenarios do. That notation is also fabricated — Claude does not emit it, which is why it correlates
with nothing in production and everything here.

Separately, no CONTINUE scenario anywhere in the suite contains a question mark. I checked all 65: every
one of the 31 scenarios containing `?` is labelled STOP, and all 29 CONTINUE scenarios are `?`-free.

I reproduced the combined effect with a two-rule classifier that reads no rubric text at all — "contains
`?` then STOP, else starts with `[` then CONTINUE, else STOP". It scores **30/30 on this shard** and
**64/65 on the full suite**, missing only `04-work-complete.json`. No model call is involved.

This matters because the runner's headline output is a scenario pass count, and the script's own header
warns "Establish the baseline before reading anything into a number here." The number is weaker than
that warning implies: a 100% pass rate on this shard is achievable by a regex and therefore carries no
information about rubric comprehension. Combined with the envelope defect above, a judge could pass by
keying on a cue that does not exist in the transcripts it will actually be shown.

Fix: strip the bracketed prefixes so the CONTINUE cases read as ordinary assistant prose, and add
CONTINUE fixtures that contain a question mark plus STOP fixtures that do not, so neither cue is
predictive. The corpus already contains one such case (`04-work-complete.json`); it needs many more.

**Verification:** confirmed-lower
**Verification evidence:** Reproduced the two-rule classifier at 64 of 65 across all scenario files: 29 of 29 CONTINUE scenarios start with a bracket and 31 of 36 STOP scenarios contain a question mark. The affected script is opt-in, absent from pnpm test and CI, carries a header disclaiming its baseline, and the cue never appears in the real transcripts the production hook evaluates, so the harm is false confidence in a manual diagnostic rather than a break under ordinary use.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `893868b`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02

### CR-027: Launcher scripts resolve `tsx` against the caller's cwd and fail from the repo root
**File:** `packages/flight/examples/todo/run-tui.sh`
**Anchor:** `exec node --import tsx "$REPO_ROOT/examples/todo/tui.tsx"`
**Severity:** medium

Node resolves a bare `--import` specifier relative to the process cwd, not relative to the script. Both launchers compute an absolute `REPO_ROOT` for the entry file precisely because they cannot assume a cwd, then leave `tsx` cwd-relative. `tsx` is a dependency of `@tc/moe-flight` and pnpm does not hoist it, so it exists only in `packages/flight/node_modules`.

```

ok
```

Fix: point the loader at an absolute path, `exec node --import "file://$REPO_ROOT/node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs" …`, or `cd "$REPO_ROOT"` before the `exec`. Also rename `REPO_ROOT`, which actually holds the package root.

**Verification evidence:** Reproduced ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND when running the launcher by a repo-root-relative path, and confirmed tsx resolves from any cwd inside packages/flight because Node walks up to packages/flight/node_modules. The README literal command (cd to the git toplevel, then ./examples/todo/run-web.sh) fails earlier with No such file or directory in the monorepo layout and never reaches the tsx error, so the failure is not on the documented path; it hits a caller invoking the script by full path from outside packages/flight.

### CR-049: The run-input snapshot copies the credential context into a directory the API serves wholesale during a live run

**File:** `packages/flight/src/qa/runs/snapshot.ts`
**Anchor:** `snapshotRunInputs`
**Severity:** medium

`snapshotRunInputs` copies the entire source context root, `<projectRoot>/<stateDir>/context`, into `<runDir>/inputs/context` and again into `<runDir>/scratch`. That tree is where passkeys, cookies and credential material live: `src/qa/adapters/web/passkey.ts`, `src/qa/adapters/web/cookies.ts` and `src/qa/context/credential-tool.ts` all gate on `contextRootIsPopulated(contextRoot)`, and `snapshot.test.ts` itself seeds the fixture with `passkey.yaml` holding a `credentialId`.

The run directory is not a private location. The results route's per-file handler documents its own exception: "If the run is currently active (ActiveRunRegistry), we skip the manifest check and serve any file that exists under the run dir." `isSafePath(runDir, filePath)` only enforces containment, so for the duration of a live run any path under the run dir is fetchable, `inputs/context/<user>/passkey.yaml` included. The cheapest correct change is to exclude `inputs/context` and `scratch` from the live-run branch of the file route; binding the daemon to `127.0.0.1` by default is worth doing regardless. `snapshot.test.ts` asserts the copy is faithful and should also assert that the snapshot is not reachable through the file route.

**Severity:** medium

Every test in this file (and in `serve-errors.test.ts`) reaches the server over
`localhost`/`127.0.0.1`, so nothing in the suite observes which address
`serve()` actually binds. It binds all of them. `serveViaNode` calls
`honoServe({ port, fetch })` with no `hostname`, which is `server.listen(port)`,
i.e. the wildcard address. The production path is the same call: the `serve`
case in `src/qa/index.ts` passes `{ port, idleTimeout, wsIdleTimeoutSec, fetch,
websocket }` and never a hostname.

I reproduced this with the real `@hono/node-server` from
`packages/flight/node_modules`, using exactly those options. The listener
reported `{"address":"::","family":"IPv6","port":45997}` and answered `200`
both on `127.0.0.1` and on this machine's LAN address `192.168.50.239`.

The exposed surface is unauthenticated: there is no token, no session, and the
only gate anywhere in the stack is the `originAllowlist` in `decideUpgrade`,
which is opt-in and applies solely to WebSocket upgrades, not to HTTP. Anyone on
the same network segment can therefore `POST /api/run/:cardId` (which launches a
browser and spends model tokens), create, rewrite and delete story cards through
`/api/scenarios`, and read every file under the results directory through
`/api/results/:runId/file/*`.

Fix: pass `hostname: "127.0.0.1"` in `serveViaNode` (making the bind address an
explicit, overridable config value rather than a default), and add a test that
asserts the server does not answer on a non-loopback local address.

**Verification:** confirmed-lower
**Verification evidence:** The test asserts only response content via localhost fetch and WebSocket; it never reads server.address() or connects from a non-loopback address, so it passes identically whether serve binds loopback or the wildcard (reproduced: the same honoServe call with no hostname binds ::). It is a coverage gap on the bind dimension, not a false assertion, and CR-051 carries the production defect.

### CR-068: A smoke test documented as skipped is not skipped and is known to fail

**File:** `packages/glass/test/dialogs.smoke.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test `Notification.requestPermission goes through shim — accept yields granted`
**Severity:** medium

The comment block above it is headed "Test 4: Notification.requestPermission — skipped" and ends "Until the shim is updated to use a different IPC mechanism ... this test cannot reliably pass." The `it(...)` carries no `.skip` and no skip option, so on any machine where `detectChrome()` finds Chrome, `pnpm test:chrome` fails at `waitFor(() => session.dialogs.getOpen(wsUrl) !== null, 5000)`. The suite's whole point is to be runnable locally by contributors with Chrome; a permanently red test trains people to ignore the run. I did not execute the Chrome suite (the shard forbids launching a browser), so this rests on the comment's own account of the failure plus the missing skip.

Fix: mark it `it.skip` (or `it.fails`) with the same explanation, and file the shim's transport replacement as the unblocking work.

**Verification:** confirmed-lower
**Verification evidence:** The it() lacks .skip despite the comment above it saying skipped, and the comment describes a real unfixed Chrome 148 incompatibility that would fail the test if run; but vitest.config.ts lists this file only in the chrome project behind test:chrome, excluded from the unit project that pnpm test and CI run, and the describe self-skips without a Chrome binary. AGENTS.md already documents test:chrome as CI-excluded, so this cannot fail any default run.

### CR-087: The mint generate task omits every legal source it reads from its declared inputs
**File:** `turbo.json`
**Anchor:** the //#mint:generate task and its `inputs` array
**Severity:** medium

`inputs` lists the generator script, the marketplace, `skill-tiers.yaml`, and the per-package mint configs and component directories. `scripts/mint-plugins.mjs` reads five root files that are not on that list: `NOTICE` and `PARITY.md` (in `readAttributions` and `readDestinations`), `LICENSE-MIT` and `LICENSE` (in `writePluginLicense`), and root `package.json` (for the canonical version that `marketplaceProblems` enforces). The first four are the sole source of every `plugins/<name>/LICENSE` payload.

`outputs` is `plugins/**`, so a cache hit does not merely skip work, it restores the cached tree. Edit a copyright line in `NOTICE`, retarget a destination in `PARITY.md`, or bump the root version, then run the documented `pnpm mint` from repo law 1: no declared input changed, turbo replays the cached run, and it overwrites `plugins/**` with the pre-edit licence text while printing the success line. That is also the path that silently reverts a correct hand-regenerated tree.

I did not run `pnpm mint` because it writes into the tree. The gap is verified by reading `COMPONENTS` and `writePluginLicense` against the `inputs` globs; `COMPONENTS` matches the component globs exactly, and the five root reads match nothing.

CI is not exposed: the `plugins` job runs `pnpm mint:check`, which forces re-execution and then diffs, so drift fails the pipeline. The defect is that the documented local command produces a wrong tree and reports success, and the developer's only signal is a CI failure they cannot reproduce until the cache is cleared. Fix: add `NOTICE`, `PARITY.md`, `LICENSE`, `LICENSE-MIT` and `package.json` to `inputs`.

**Verification:** confirmed-lower
**Verification evidence:** The read gap is real: writePluginLicense reads NOTICE, PARITY.md, LICENSE and LICENSE-MIT and mint-plugins.mjs reads root package.json, none of which are in the mint:generate inputs globs, and the task is cacheable, so a warm local cache can replay a stale plugins tree on a bare pnpm mint. But mint:check runs turbo run mint:generate --force, which always bypasses the cache, and the CI plugins job runs exactly that, so the merge gate is unaffected.

### CR-088: The hooks branch of hook_targets discards relative targets that the MCP branch was deliberately fixed to catch
**File:** `.claude/skills/moe-dogfood/scripts/stage.py`
**Anchor:** `hook_targets`, `if "/" in candidate and candidate.startswith("/")`
**Severity:** medium

The MCP half of `hook_targets` carries an explicit comment about this hazard: "Resolve relative args against the plugin directory rather than skipping them. An unrepointed `./dist/cli.js` is exactly the failure this script exists to catch, and an absolute-only check walks straight past it." The hooks half was never given the same treatment. It keeps a candidate only when `candidate.startswith("/")`, so any hook command naming its target relatively contributes no target at all, and `verify()` reports success having checked nothing.

The `"/" in candidate` conjunct is also dead: `startswith("/")` already implies it.

I reproduced this with synthetic single-hook plugins. `node "./dist/cli.js" sync` and `node dist/emit-event.cjs` both yielded zero targets, while the identical relative path passed through `mcp.json` was caught and correctly reported as missing.

This is reachable through ordinary editing rather than an exotic input. Hook commands are hand-authored in `packages/<pkg>/hooks/hooks.json` and copied through by mint, so a new plugin that ships a compiled runtime and is added to the registry without a `REPOINTS` entry gets a clean bill of health from the verifier and takes down every hook it registers.

Fix: mirror the MCP branch. When a candidate looks like a filesystem target and is not absolute, resolve it against `staged` instead of dropping it.

### CR-089: Hook target expansion substitutes the plugin root for every shell variable, so any other variable produces a phantom verification failure
**File:** `.claude/skills/moe-dogfood/scripts/stage.py`
**Anchor:** `hook_targets` — "Collapse `${...}` innermost-first"
**Severity:** medium

The collapse loop runs `re.sub(r"\$\{[^{}]*\}", root, expanded)` up to five times, replacing every braced expansion with the staged plugin directory regardless of which variable it names. That is correct for `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` and, by luck of the substitution order, for the nested `${PLUGIN_ROOT:-${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}}` that `moe-memory` actually uses. It is wrong for anything else.

`${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` is a standard Claude Code hook variable, and a hook using it resolves to a path under the plugin root that cannot exist. I reproduced both cases: `node "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/scripts/lint.mjs"` produced `<plugin_root>/scripts/lint.mjs` and `"${HOME}/.local/bin/moe-hook"` produced `<plugin_root>/.local/bin/moe-hook`, each reported as missing.

The consequence is worse than a skipped check. The write phase has already completed by the time `verify()` runs, so `main` prints "FAILED verification — the install is broken as staged", lists a defect that does not exist, tells the operator to "Restore the backup above before starting a new session", and returns 1. A healthy stage is reported as a broken one, and the recommended remedy discards good work.

Fix: substitute only the plugin-root variable names, honour `:-` defaults rather than swallowing the whole expression, and expand the remaining variables from `os.environ`. A token still holding an unresolved `$` after expansion should be skipped explicitly with a note, not silently turned into a bogus absolute path.

### CR-090: The hand-rolled command tokeniser mis-parses shell quoting in both directions
**File:** `.claude/skills/moe-dogfood/scripts/stage.py`
**Anchor:** `hook_targets`, `re.findall(r'"([^"]+)"|(\S+)', expanded)`
**Severity:** medium

Hook commands are shell command lines, and several in this tree already carry `"shell": "bash"`. Splitting them with an alternation of "double-quoted run" and "non-whitespace run" gets the current inputs right by coincidence and fails on neighbouring shapes. I reproduced four:

| Command shape | Result |
|---|---|
| `sh -c "node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/emit-event.cjs"` | zero targets; the whole command matched as one quoted token that does not start with `/`, so nothing was checked |
| `sh -c 'node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/emit-event.cjs'` | target reported as `<root>/dist/emit-event.cjs'` with the closing single quote glued on; a file that exists is reported missing |
| `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/x.sh\|cat` | target reported as `<root>/hooks/x.sh\|cat`; same phantom failure |
| `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/emit-event.cjs 2>/dev/null` | correct, only because the redirect is whitespace-separated and does not begin with `/` |

The first row is the dangerous one: wrapping a command in `sh -c "..."` disables the check entirely while still reporting success. The second and third produce the same misleading "the install is broken as staged" verdict described in the previous finding.

Fix: tokenise with `shlex.split(expanded)`, which handles both quote styles and strips them, and drop tokens that are shell operators. Expansion must still happen before splitting, or after, against the unquoted tokens.

### CR-091: Retired plugin directories are deleted in the same run that prints the instruction to uninstall them first
**File:** `.claude/skills/moe-dogfood/scripts/stage.py`
**Anchor:** the printed note "`claude plugin uninstall <name>@moe` each of these FIRST"
**Severity:** medium

`main` prints that note, then, in the same process with no prompt and no abort, runs `for name in retired: shutil.rmtree(MARKETPLACE / "plugins" / name)`. The operator has no opportunity to act on "FIRST". The closing "Next:" block then emits `claude plugin uninstall <name>@moe` for each retired plugin, which is exactly the too-late ordering the skill document warns against: its "Retiring a plugin" section requires the uninstall "**before** its directory is removed", because uninstalling after "leaves the running session firing hooks at a path that no longer exists, and it reports `Plugin directory does not exist` on every event until you restart." Following the script's own printed sequence produces the documented failure.

A second problem shares the same code. `retired` is every directory under the marketplace's `plugins/` that is not in the registry, so an unrelated plugin staged into `~/.moe/local-marketplace` by any other means is deleted too, and the `--no-backup` path makes that permanent.

I reproduced both against a scratchpad marketplace seeded with `moe-retired-thing` and `somebody-elses-plugin`. The run printed the "FIRST" note, deleted both directories, exited 0 with "verified: every hook and MCP target resolves", and then listed the uninstall commands under "Next:".

Fix: when `retired` is non-empty and no explicit opt-in flag is given, print the uninstall commands and return without writing, so the documented order is achievable. Confine deletion to names the registry has previously owned, or require the flag to remove a directory the script did not stage.

### CR-092: No CI job runs scope:check, so the live package-map and identity scan depends on a human
**File:** `.gitlab-ci.yml`
**Anchor:** no pipeline job runs `pnpm scope:check`; compare the check script in package.json
**Severity:** medium

`pnpm check` is four gates plus `pnpm scope:check`. CI gives `lint`, `typecheck` and `test` their own jobs and drops `scope:check` entirely; grepping the pipeline for "scope" returns only prose in comments. AGENTS.md calls `pnpm scope:check` part of "the Node gate" and its "What CI runs, and what it does not" section does not list it among the deliberate omissions.

The script's unit test does not close the gap. `scripts/test/check-downstream-scope.test.mjs` calls `checkDownstreamScope` only on `mkdtempSync` fixture roots; it reads the real marketplace once to build a fixture and never evaluates the repository root. So `checkManifestIdentities` against the real manifests, and `scanUpstreamLeaks` over the real committed tree, run only when someone types the command.

Coverage is partial elsewhere: `tc-release-pack` asserts the eight-artifact path set and does run on merge-request pipelines, so an added or unprivated publishable package is caught there. What is caught nowhere is per-manifest identity beyond that path list, and the committed-surface scan.

Reproduced by grep and by reading the test. Fix: add a `check` stage job running `pnpm scope:check`, extending `.not-scheduled` like its siblings. It needs no install beyond the workspace the other jobs already build.

### CR-093: `tryExec` sets no timeout, so a wedged tool on PATH hangs the doctor and the installer forever
**File:** `bin/lib/probes.mjs`
**Anchor:** `tryExec`, whose options are only `encoding`, `stdio` and the caller's spread
**Severity:** medium

`execFileSync` defaults to `timeout: 0`, meaning no timeout. Every probe calls
`tryExec`, and `bin/moe-doctor` and `bin/moe-install`'s `runDoctor` call `allProbes()`
serially. One hung executable on PATH stalls the process indefinitely, with the report
already half-printed and nothing naming which probe is stuck.

Reproduced. I put a `#!/bin/sh` + `sleep 600` script named `npm` first on PATH and ran
`probeNpm` under a 5s watchdog; the child was still running at 5001ms and had to be
SIGKILLed. `stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "pipe"]` does close stdin, so a tool that prompts
gets EOF, but that does not help a tool blocked on a network mount, a stale credential
helper, or a lock.

This matters more than it would elsewhere: a diagnostic tool is reached for when the
machine is already misbehaving, so hanging is close to the worst available failure.

Fix: pass a bounded `timeout` (a few seconds) plus `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` in `tryExec`.
A timeout makes `execFileSync` throw, which the existing `catch` already maps to
undefined — the taxonomy is unchanged.

### CR-094: `moe proof` in a checkout without uv hands a Python project directory to node
**File:** `bin/moe.js`
**Anchor:** `resolve`, the `if (entry.runner === "uv")` block followed by `if (entry.workspace)`
**Severity:** medium

The uv branch is guarded on `uv && existsSync(project)`. When uv is absent it does not
return; control falls into the generic `entry.workspace` branch. For `proof`,
`entry.workspace` is `py/proof` — a directory, not a Node bundle — so `existsSync` is
true and `resolve` returns `{ command: process.execPath, args: [<root>/py/proof, ...] }`.

Reproduced with a synthetic checkout (pnpm-workspace.yaml plus `py/proof`, `PATH: ""`).
Three consequences, all observed:

- `resolve("proof", ["--foo"])` returns node as the command and the directory as argv[1].
  Running that for real gives `Error: Cannot find module '.../py/proof'`, not a usable message.
- `moe status` prints proof as `[present] ... (workspace)`. It is a false present.
- `missingMessage`'s proof-specific line, "From this checkout: `uv run --project py/proof
  moe-proof …` (needs uv)", is unreachable. It only prints when `resolve` returns
  `missing` and `root` is truthy, but in any checkout the `py/proof` directory exists, so
  `missing` is never returned. The one message written for this exact situation can never fire.

`probeUv` is deliberately soft ("Python is optional to Moe end-users"), so uv-absent is a
supported state, not an excluded one.

Fix: after the uv branch fails, `return { missing: true, entry, root }` for a
`runner`-bearing entry rather than falling through. Independently, the generic branch
should require the workspace path to be a file (see the directory finding below).

**Disposition:** stale
**Commit:** —
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02
**Note:** Superseded by bc27892: proof is runner-only in NAMESPACES and has no workspace directory, so resolve cannot fall through and hand py/proof to Node.
### CR-095: A directory on PATH or beside the dispatcher is accepted as the namespace executable
**File:** `bin/moe.js`
**Anchor:** `findInDir`, which decides with `if (existsSync(p)) return p`
**Severity:** medium

`findInDir` tests existence only — not that the entry is a regular file, and not that it
is executable. A directory named `moe-crew` beside `bin/moe.js`, or in any PATH element,
is returned as `{ source: "sibling" }` or `{ source: "path" }`. Because `resolve`
short-circuits on the first hit, the remaining links in the documented
sibling to PATH to workspace chain are never tried, and `spawnAndForward` fails with
EACCES and exits 127.

Reproduced. With a directory `moe-crew` in the injected `self` dir, `resolve("crew", [])`
returned `{"command":".../moe-crew","source":"sibling"}`. I separately confirmed
`spawnSync` on a non-executable path yields `EACCES`, which `spawnAndForward` turns into
"moe: could not spawn" and 127.

So a stray directory shadows a perfectly good installed binary and produces a spawn error
instead of falling through. Note this also fires for the workspace branch, where
`existsSync(cand)` on a directory is exactly the proof defect above.

Fix: replace `existsSync` with a `statSync(p).isFile()` check, and on POSIX also require
the executable bit via `accessSync(p, constants.X_OK)`, both inside try/catch.

### CR-096: Lifecycle tests recompute their expectations from the module under test
**File:** `bin/test/doctor.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "install invokes only fake npm/claude with sparse paths and exact versions"
**Severity:** medium

Every assertion in the "lifecycle action contract" and "clean-home lifecycle
acceptance" blocks builds its expected value by importing `MARKETPLACE`,
`NPM_CLI_PACKAGES` and `UMBRELLA_PACKAGE` from `config/distribution.mjs` — the
same module `bin/moe-install` reads. The comparison is therefore between a
value and itself, and no property of the distribution constants is verified.
Two test names assert counts that are never checked: "install persists the
exact running umbrella and all four namespace CLIs" and "upgrade updates
plugins before installing all five latest packages" contain no `4`, no `5`, and
no package literal.

Reproduced. Against the drift-injected copy described in the previous finding —
which also demoted `mint` to `npmCli: false` and rewrote `MARKETPLACE.repository`
to `https://example.invalid/typo/moe.git` — all three "lifecycle action
contract" assertions passed, while the generated plan read:

```
npm install --global @tc/moe@1.2.3-tc.4 @tc/moe-crew@1.2.3-tc.4 @tc/moe-glass@1.2.3-tc.4 @tc/moe-memory@1.2.3-tc.4
claude plugin marketplace add https://example.invalid/typo/moe.git --sparse .claude-plugin plugins
claude plugin install moe-ghost@moe
```

A typo in the repository URL, a silently dropped global CLI package, and an
install of a plugin that does not exist all ship green. Only one accidental
guard exists: emptying `sparsePaths` changes the recorded argument spacing and
so fails.

Fix: pin the load-bearing values as literals in the test rather than importing
them — the marketplace name, the repository URL, the two sparse paths, the
exact five plugin names, and the exact four npm CLI package names. `bin/test/moe.test.mjs`
already does this correctly in "namespace table has exactly the seven expected
keys", which is why the namespace set is genuinely protected and the
distribution constants are not.

### CR-097: The "packaging invariants" block guards `bin` but not `files`, and dropping either non-bin file breaks every published entry point
**File:** `bin/test/moe.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "root package.json publishes all three durable CLI bins"
**Severity:** medium

The `packaging invariants` describe block asserts `pkg.bin` maps `moe`, `moe-doctor` and
`moe-install`. Nothing anywhere asserts `pkg.files` still contains
`bin/lib/probes.mjs` and `config/distribution.mjs`. I grepped the whole repo: the only
mention of either path outside `bin/` is the `files` array itself, and no test in
`bin/test/` or `scripts/test/` reads `files`.

Reproduced. I assembled a directory holding only the three bin entries plus a
package.json, i.e. what ships if `config/distribution.mjs` leaves `files`, and ran each:
`moe` and `moe-install` both die at import time with
`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find module '.../config/distribution.mjs'`, on every
invocation, before parsing a single argument. `moe-doctor` survives because it only needs
`probes.mjs`. Drop the `probes.mjs` entry instead and `moe-doctor` and `moe-install` die
the same way.

Every test would stay green, because the tests import from the source tree where both
files always exist. A block named "packaging invariants" that guards the manifest's `bin`
half and not the payload half is the gap most likely to ship a wholly broken tarball.

Fix: extend that test to assert `pkg.files` is a superset of the transitive import set of
the three bins — at minimum `bin/lib/probes.mjs` and `config/distribution.mjs`.

### CR-098: The WSL test passes with no "microsoft" in the release string, and the guard it covers is a tautology
**File:** `bin/test/moe.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "under WSL (linux + microsoft-in-release) crew resolves normally"
**Severity:** medium

`isWSL(plat, rel)` in `bin/moe.js` returns `plat === "linux" && /microsoft/i.test(rel)`.
Its only call site is the crew guard, `ns === "crew" && plat === "win32" && !isWSL(plat, rel)`.
The second conjunct requires win32 and `isWSL` requires linux, so `isWSL` is false at
every reachable evaluation and `!isWSL(...)` is always true. `isWSL` is dead code, and the
`release` option threaded through `main` exists only to feed it.

Reproduced both halves. I enumerated the guard over win32 and linux release strings: the
guard fires for every win32 case regardless of the release text. Then I called
`main(["crew","list"])` with `platform: "linux"` and `release: "PLAIN-LINUX-NO-MICROSOFT"`
and got exit 0 with crew spawned — identical to the test's assertion. The test's name
claims the microsoft-in-release half is what makes crew resolve; in fact only
`platform: "linux"` matters, and the test would pass unchanged if `isWSL` were deleted.

The current behaviour is right by accident: WSL2 reports linux, so it never reaches the
win32 branch. The defect is a test asserting a claim it does not exercise, sitting on top
of a condition that cannot matter, which is how the tautology survived review.

Fix: either delete `isWSL` and the `release` plumbing from `bin/moe.js` and rename the
test to say it covers linux, or keep both and add a case that distinguishes them — the
only honest one being a native-Windows release string that contains "microsoft", which
must still be refused.

### CR-099: `proof` resolves to a directory when `uv` is absent
**File:** `config/distribution.mjs`
**Anchor:** `NAMESPACE_DISTRIBUTIONS.proof` — `workspace: "py/proof"` together with `runner: "uv"`
**Severity:** medium

`workspace` carries two incompatible meanings in this table. For six entries it
is a built file that `resolve()` in `bin/moe.js` hands to `process.execPath`.
For `proof` it is a uv project *directory*. `resolve()` guards the uv branch
with `if (uv && existsSync(project))`, then falls through to the generic
`if (entry.workspace)` branch, which only tests `existsSync(cand)` — and a
directory exists. `py/proof` is the only `workspace` value in the table that is
a directory; I checked all seven.

Trigger: a checkout with no `uv` on PATH. `INSTALL.md` grades `uv` as a **soft**
prereq gating `moe-proof`, and `bin/moe-doctor` warns rather than fails on it,
so this is a state the product explicitly supports.

Reproduced. `resolve("proof", ["--help"], { root: <repo>, env: { PATH: "" } })`
returns `{ command: <node>, args: ["<repo>/py/proof", "--help"], source:
"workspace" }`, and running that command prints:

```
Error: Cannot find module '/Users/ZKeown/Code/moe/py/proof'
    at Module._resolveFilename (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1517:15)
```

instead of `missingMessage()`'s purpose-written "From this checkout: `uv run
--project py/proof moe-proof …` (needs uv)." `namespaceStatuses()` is affected
the same way: with `PATH=""` it reports `[present] proof   moe-proof
(workspace)`, a false positive in the one table `USAGE` points users at ("Run
`moe status` to see which ones are present"). The existing test "proof workspace
fallback goes through `uv run --project py/proof`" always places `uv` on the
fixture PATH, so the uv-absent path is untested.

Fix: give the uv entry its own field so the two meanings stop sharing one key —
for example `project: "py/proof"` with `workspace` omitted — and make
`resolve()` skip the generic branch for any entry that declares a `runner`.
Either change alone closes it; the field split also removes the trap for the
next runner-based namespace.

**Disposition:** stale
**Commit:** —
**Resolved:** 2026-09-02
**Note:** Superseded by bc27892: the current proof namespace has runner uv and no workspace path, eliminating the only directory-valued workspace entry and the Node-directory fallback.
### CR-100: validate_skill.py rejects quoted and block-scalar YAML frontmatter
**File:** `packages/core/scripts/validate_skill.py`
**Anchor:** `parse_frontmatter`, `fm[key] = value` after `key, _, value = line.partition(":")`
**Severity:** medium

The hand-rolled parser stores the raw text after the first colon. It never strips quotes
and never recognises block scalars, so valid YAML produces false errors:

- `name: "my-skill"` keeps its quotes and fails `re.fullmatch(r"[a-zA-Z0-9-]+", name)`.
- `description: "Use when …"` fails the "Use when" test because the value starts with `"`.
- `description: >-` followed by an indented paragraph folds to `>- Use when …`, so the
  value starts with the block marker.

Reproduced all three with fixture files. The repo's own
`packages/core/skills/brainstorming/SKILL.md` hits the quoted case: the error text is
`starts with: '"You MUST use this before any '`, showing the retained quote.

Fix: parse with `yaml.safe_load` on the frontmatter block (`yaml` is already a
`devDependency` of the package, and the iterative-development tests run under plain
CPython, so `pyyaml` would be a new dependency — failing that, strip matching outer quotes
and handle the `>`/`>-`/`|` markers explicitly).

### CR-101: validate_skill.py's "Use when" rule is a hard error that nine of the repo's own skills fail
**File:** `packages/core/scripts/validate_skill.py`
**Anchor:** `errors.append(f"frontmatter 'description' should start with 'Use when' but starts with: {desc[:30]!r}")`
**Severity:** medium

The check is registered as an error, not a warning, yet the tree's convention does not
require the prefix. Running the validator over every `SKILL.md` under

before any creative work" as the reason it earns its place.

Reproduced by running the script over the 38 files. `test/iterative-development/test_skill_validator.py`
does not catch this because its three fixtures use plain unquoted scalars and a
purpose-built `description: Use when testing the skill validator …`.

Note the wording is already hedged — "should start with" — which is warning language on an
error path. Word count above 500 is correctly a warning; this should be too, or the rule
should be dropped.

Fix: move the prefix check into `warnings`, matching the treatment of the word-count
target.

### CR-102: The HTTP request handler has no error boundary, so a transient filesystem error kills the server
**File:** `packages/core/skills/brainstorming/scripts/server.cjs`
**Anchor:** `handleRequest`, and `getNewestScreen`'s `fs.readdirSync(CONTENT_DIR)`
**Severity:** medium

`http.createServer(handleRequest)` is installed with no `try`/`catch` inside
`handleRequest` and no `process.on('uncaughtException')` anywhere in the file. Several
synchronous filesystem calls on the `GET /` path can throw under ordinary conditions:
`fs.readdirSync(CONTENT_DIR)` if the content directory is removed after startup (a /tmp
reaper, a sibling `stop-server.sh`, manual cleanup), and `fs.readFileSync(screenFile)` /
`fs.statSync(fp)` in the window between the `isRegularFileInsideContentDir` check and the
read. `res.setHeader('Set-Cookie', ...)` throws `ERR_INVALID_CHAR` if `TOKEN` contains a
newline. The same class applies to `fs.appendFileSync(eventsFile, ...)` inside
`handleMessage`, which runs from a socket `data` listener.

Reproduced both halves separately: a throw from an `http` request listener terminates the
process with exit code 1 and no chance for the `server-stopped` marker to be written, and
`setHeader` with a newline in the value throws `ERR_INVALID_CHAR`. The user then sees the
`showTombstone` overlay from `helper.cjs`, which reads as "the agent paused the companion"
rather than "the server crashed".

Fix: wrap the body of `handleRequest` in `try`/`catch` that answers 500 with
`securityHeaders()`, and wrap the `appendFileSync` in `handleMessage`.

### CR-103: start-server.sh spins forever when an option is given without a value
**File:** `packages/core/skills/brainstorming/scripts/start-server.sh`
**Anchor:** the argument loop's `--project-dir) PROJECT_DIR="$2"; shift 2 ;;` arm
**Severity:** medium

The script does not set `-u` or `-e`. When an option that takes a value is the last
argument, `shift 2` fails with "shift count out of range" and shifts nothing, `$#` stays
1, and `case "$1"` matches the same arm again. The loop never terminates and never starts
a server. All four value-taking options are affected: `--project-dir`, `--host`,
`--url-host`, `--idle-timeout-minutes`.

Reproduced against the real script: `start-server.sh --host` was still running and burning
CPU three seconds later, having produced no output. The sibling
`finding-duplicate-functions/scripts/extract-functions.sh` has the same loop shape but
sets `set -euo pipefail`, so there the missing `$2` aborts cleanly — the difference is the
absent `-u`.

Fix: guard each arm with `[[ $# -ge 2 ]] || { echo '{"error":"'"$1"' needs a value"}'; exit 1; }`,
or add `set -u`.

### CR-104: start-server.sh's "Kill any existing server" block can never find a server
**File:** `packages/core/skills/brainstorming/scripts/start-server.sh`
**Anchor:** the comment "# Kill any existing server" and the `if [[ -f "$PID_FILE" ]]` block above `cd "$SCRIPT_DIR"`
**Severity:** medium

`PID_FILE` is `${SESSION_DIR}/state/server.pid`, and `SESSION_DIR` embeds
`SESSION_ID="$$-$(date +%s)"`, so it lives inside a directory created moments earlier in
this same invocation. The file cannot pre-exist unless a previous run had both the same pid
and the same wall-clock second. The block is unreachable, so a restart does not stop the
previous server.

The consequence is visible downstream. The old server holds the preferred port, so the new
one hits the `EADDRINUSE` path in `server.cjs`, binds a random port, and — because
`tokenSource === 'file'` — regenerates the token and deliberately does not persist either
value. The user's open tab keeps talking to the old server on the old port while the agent
writes screens into the new session directory, so the browser silently shows stale content.
The old server survives because `ownerAlive()` checks the harness pid, which is unchanged
across restarts within a session.

Not run (starting the server is out of scope for this pass); established by reading the
path construction and the `EADDRINUSE` handler together.

Fix: put the pid file at a per-project stable path next to `.last-port` and `.last-token`,
and verify the recorded pid carries a `--brainstorm-server-id` before signalling it, the
way `stop-server.sh`'s `is_brainstorm_server` already does.

### CR-105: The "only delete ephemeral /tmp" guard in stop-server.sh is bypassed by a parent reference
**File:** `packages/core/skills/brainstorming/scripts/stop-server.sh`
**Anchor:** `if [[ "$SESSION_DIR" == /tmp/* ]]; then rm -rf "$SESSION_DIR"; fi`, under the header comment "Only deletes session directory if it's under /tmp (ephemeral). Persistent directories (.moe/) are kept so mockups can be reviewed later."
**Severity:** medium

The guard is a string prefix test, not a path resolution. `[[ "/tmp/../home/zak/project" == /tmp/* ]]`
is true, so a session-dir argument containing `..` reaches `rm -rf` on a persistent tree —
exactly the case the comment says is protected. `[[ "/tmp/" == /tmp/* ]]` is also true,
which points `rm -rf` at the contents of `/tmp` itself.

Reproduced the matching: `/tmp/`, `/tmp/x` and `/tmp/../home/zak/proj` all match; `/tmp`
and `/tmpfoo/bar` do not. I did not run the delete. Reaching it also requires
`<dir>/state/server.pid` to name a live process carrying this session's
`--brainstorm-server-id`, so it is a guard weakness rather than a one-argument disaster.

Fix: resolve first, then compare — `SESSION_DIR="$(cd "$SESSION_DIR" && pwd -P)"` and test
the resolved value, rejecting `/tmp` itself.

### CR-106: The example plugin passes .sh filenames to run-hook.cmd, the one thing the polyglot reference forbids
**File:** `packages/core/skills/developing-claude-code-plugins/examples/full-featured-plugin/hooks/hooks.json`
**Anchor:** `"command": "\"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/run-hook.cmd\" session-init.sh"`
**Severity:** medium

`references/polyglot-hooks.md` in this same skill states the rule and the reason: "Hook
scripts are **extensionless** (`session-start`, not `session-start.sh`). This is
deliberate: it prevents Claude Code's Windows auto-detection from prepending `bash` to the
dispatcher command and breaking it", and its pitfall list names "Giving scripts a `.sh`
extension" plus "A command like `run-hook.cmd claude-judge-continuation.sh` can trigger
Claude Code's `.sh` auto-detection and bypass the intended CMD dispatcher path". The
example does exactly that for both of its hooks, and the scripts on disk carry the `.sh`
extension too.

`packages/core/hooks/hooks.json` follows the rule correctly (`run-hook.cmd plan-set-notice`),
and `run-hook.cmd`'s own header repeats it. So the shipped example is the only place in the
tree that teaches the anti-pattern, and it is the file a plugin author copies.

Not run — the failure is Windows-specific and WSL2 is the supported path here. The
contradiction with the skill's own reference is the defect.

Fix: rename to `hooks/session-init` and `hooks/post-write` and drop the extension from both
`hooks.json` commands. `references/plugin-structure.md` shows the same `format.sh` /
`init.sh` pattern and needs the same change.

### CR-107: The example MCP server writes prose to stdout, which breaks the stdio JSON-RPC transport
**File:** `packages/core/skills/developing-claude-code-plugins/examples/full-featured-plugin/mcp/server.js`
**Anchor:** `console.log("Example MCP server starting...")`
**Severity:** medium

The server is registered for real in the sibling `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` under
`mcpServers.example-server` with `"command": "node"`. MCP over stdio requires stdout to
carry only newline-delimited JSON-RPC, so these three `console.log` lines are parse errors
for the client, and `process.stdin.resume()` then holds the process open. A user who
installs the example to see what a full-featured plugin looks like gets a server that
reports an error every session and never exits on its own.

Not run (spawning it would be a long-lived process). The transport contract and the
`mcpServers` registration are both visible in the two files.

Fix: switch all three to `console.error`, which is the conventional channel for MCP server
diagnostics, and add a `process.on('SIGTERM', () => process.exit(0))`. The placeholder
comment can stay.

### CR-108: aggregate_stories.py silently discards every story after the first when titles are missing
**File:** `packages/core/skills/extracting-requirements/scripts/aggregate_stories.py`
**Anchor:** `dedup_stories`, `title = story.get("title", "").strip()`
**Severity:** medium

The dedup key is the title with an empty-string default, so every story whose extraction
omitted `title` collapses into a single entry keyed `""`. The survivor is then written as
`**Title:** Untitled` by `format_epic_file`, and the run reports success.

Reproduced: three distinct stories with no `title` field produced
`wrote ag/out/EPIC-001.md (1 stories)` and `OK: 1 epics, 1 stories`. Two stories were
silently lost with no warning on stderr.

Fix: treat a missing or empty title as un-dedupable — key on `id or title or index`, or
raise, since an untitled story cannot be back-referenced by `aggregate_scenarios.py`'s
`load_story_title_to_id` either.

### CR-109: Story and scenario IDs are positional, not stable, so a re-run renumbers already-cited findings
**File:** `packages/core/skills/extracting-requirements/scripts/aggregate_stories.py`
**Anchor:** `assign_ids`, docstring "Assign stable EPIC-NNN and STORY-NNNN IDs to all stories in place."
**Severity:** medium

IDs come from a counter walked over the dedup `OrderedDict`, whose order is the order of
the JSON files on the command line and of stories inside them. Nothing keys an ID to the
story's identity, so adding an input file or reordering the arguments reassigns every
