Nothing asserts it matches its sources. The ui package's `build` script runs both vite builds, and CI's `build` stage runs `pnpm build`, but no job compares the regenerated file against the commit. Compare `pnpm mint:check`, which does exactly that for `/plugins/` and is a named CI gate in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. `pnpm check`, the gate AGENTS.md tells contributors to run before opening an MR, does not include the static build at all.

The failure is silent and has already happened: a developer edits `ui/src`, passes lint, typecheck and test, and every static report emitted from that build ships the previous bundle's UI code. The commit message above is the evidence.

This file is assigned to no shard in this sweep, which is why I am reporting it here. Verified by `git ls-files packages/flight/ui/dist-static`, `grep -n dist .gitignore`, and reading the CI job list; I did not run a build.

Fix: add a `flight:static:check` gate that runs the static build and asserts the tree is byte-identical, wired into CI beside `plugins`. Or stop tracking the artifact and resolve the template from the build output, accepting a hard failure when the SPA has not been built, which `renderRun` already words an error for.

### CR-217: New-card form accepts ids that make the run's live stream permanently unreachable
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/components/NewCardForm.tsx`
**Anchor:** `handleSubmit` — `if (!id.trim() || !title.trim())`
**Severity:** medium

The only validation on the card id is non-emptiness. The rest of the system
depends on a much narrower character set: `src/qa/util/id.ts` states "Story-card
parsing already enforces `[a-zA-Z0-9-]`, so it is filesystem-safe and contains
no `_`, which makes the `_` separator unambiguous", and the results route repeats
the claim. `parseStoryCard` enforces neither; it only rejects a missing `id`, and
`asCardId` is a bare cast. Server-side, `POST /api/scenarios` checks
`isSafePath(storiesDir, targetPath)`, which stops `..` escapes but happily
accepts `login_v2`, `a b` and `foo.bar`.

So an ordinary id containing an underscore is accepted end to end and then
breaks the run. `makeRunId("login_v2")` yields `login_v2_<ts>_<nonce>`, which
`parseRunId` rejects, because its leading `[a-zA-Z0-9-]+` group cannot span the
extra underscore. `decideUpgrade` returns `null` for the `/api/ws` request, the
upgrade is refused, and `LiveRun` sits on "Connecting..." forever with no error
shown. I reproduced the id composition and the regex verdict with a copy of
`id.ts`'s own logic: `login_v2`, `a b`, `foo.bar` and `sub/dir` all produce
runIds that `parseRunId` rejects, and the last three also leave the
Chrome-profile character set.

Fix: validate the id against `/^[a-zA-Z0-9-]+$/` in this form with an inline
message, and enforce the same regex in `parseScenarioBody` so the API is not
relying on `isSafePath` to police an invariant about characters.

### CR-218: Static run report renders screenshots through an API URL that does not exist offline
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/components/RunSummaryCard.tsx`
**Anchor:** `src={api.results.fileUrl(result.runId, relPath)}` in the Screenshots block
**Severity:** medium

`RunSummaryCard` is documented as being used by both surfaces, "RunDetail (server
view...)" and "StaticRunPage (static HTML report, used directly)", and
`StaticRunPage` calls itself a "self-contained run report". But the screenshot
`src` is always built by `api.results.fileUrl`, which returns a root-relative
`/api/results/<runId>/file/<path>`. `renderRunFromTemplate` writes the report as
`index.html` inside the run directory, alongside `screenshots/`, and the template
has no `<base>` (a root-relative URL would ignore one anyway). Opened from disk
or served from anywhere but the API server, every screenshot resolves to a
nonexistent `/api/...` and renders broken.

The sibling data path was given a static branch, which shows the intent:
`useTranscript` checks `window.__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__` and parses the injected
`runJsonl` instead of fetching. Evidence images never got the equivalent. The gap
is untested because the one static-page test passes
`evidence: { screenshots: [] }`. `transcript/Screenshot.tsx` has the same bug on
the same static page.

Fix: resolve evidence URLs relative to the run directory when a static payload is
present (a helper next to `getStaticRunPayload`, used by both this component and
`Screenshot`), and give the static-page test a non-empty screenshot list.

### CR-219: Artifact drawer renders an unbounded file line-by-line and re-encodes it on every render
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/components/transcript/ArtifactDrawer.tsx`
**Anchor:** `LineNumberedPre` and `const bytes = text ? new TextEncoder().encode(text).length : 0`
**Severity:** medium

`LineNumberedPre` splits the file on newlines and emits a `LineRow` per line,
each of which renders a `<span>` plus a `<code>`, with no cap and no windowing.
The drawer only ever opens artifacts, and an artifact exists precisely because
the text was too large to inline: `logToolResult` spills to
`artifacts/NNN.txt` when the tool result exceeds `INLINE_TEXT_LIMIT` of 32 KB.
There is no ceiling on the other side. The web adapter's extraction path
evaluates `document.documentElement.outerHTML`, and the CLI adapter's
`read_output` returns the whole buffered terminal, so a multi-megabyte artifact
of tens of thousands of lines is an ordinary outcome, and it becomes twice as
many DOM nodes.

The byte counter compounds it. `new TextEncoder().encode(text).length` copies the
entire file to count bytes, and it runs on every render, not once per load. In
live mode the drawer is mounted inside the streaming view (`TranscriptView`
renders `ArtifactDrawer` in both branches), which re-renders on each incoming
event, so the copy repeats per event for as long as the drawer stays open.

I read this from the code and did not measure it in a browser. Fix: cap or
window the rendered lines with a "show the rest" affordance, and compute the byte
count once in the load effect (or use `text.length` and label it characters).

### CR-220: A failed TUI capture fetch is permanent, and a changed capture path is ignored
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/components/transcript/TuiCapture.tsx`
**Anchor:** `if (!expanded || capture || error) return;` inside `TuiCapture`'s effect
**Severity:** medium

The effect's own guard makes `error` a terminal state. Once a fetch fails, the guard short-circuits on every subsequent run, so collapsing and re-expanding via the "Hide/Show screen capture" button never retries. The user is left with `Failed to load capture: API error: 404` and no way to recover short of a full page reload.

That path is reachable on a completed run, not just a transient one. The file route consults the manifest for a run that is no longer in the active registry, and `shutdown-stub-writer` writes `evidence: { screenshots: [], log: "run.jsonl" }` with no `captures` key. So for any run interrupted by server shutdown, `collectManifestPaths` yields no capture entries, `captures/NNN.json` returns `{"error":"not in manifest"}` with 404, and every capture in that transcript is a dead box.

The same guard also drops a legitimate refetch: `runId` and `ansiPath` are in the dependency array but the guard returns before either is used, so if `ansiPath` changes on a mounted instance the stale grid keeps rendering under the new path in the toggle label. `ToolPairCard` keys on `pair.toolUseId`, and `applyEvent`'s `turn.tools[idx] = { ...existing, result: event }` replaces a result in place for a repeated `toolUseId`, which is the route to that state.

Not reproduced (needs the browser fetch path). Fix: clear `error` when `expanded` flips to true so the toggle retries, and reset both `capture` and `error` in a separate effect keyed on `[runId, ansiPath]` so a path change refetches.

### CR-221: `useCard` has no request cancellation, so a stale card can overwrite the one the URL names
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/hooks/useCard.ts`
**Anchor:** `refresh` — `const data = await api.cards.get(id); setCard(data);`
**Severity:** medium

`refresh` is recreated whenever `id` changes and the effect calls it, but nothing cancels the in-flight request from the previous `id`, and nothing checks on resolution whether `id` is still current. Two requests overlap on any quick navigation between cards in the sidebar (`/cards/:id` keeps `CardDetailPage` mounted across the id change), and last-resolved wins. If card A's response lands after card B's, `CardEditor` renders A's title, description and acceptance criteria while the address bar says B.

The first `finally` to run also sets `loading` false while the second request is still pending, so the spinner clears early and the stale content is what the user sees and edits.

Every other data hook in this shard already guards this: `useTranscript`, `useRunStream`, `useLiveTranscript` and `TuiCapture` all carry a `cancelled` flag. `useCard` and `useCards` do not, which reads as an omission rather than a decision.

Not reproduced (needs React and a server). Fix: capture `id` in a local, or use a `cancelled` flag in the effect cleanup, and ignore any response whose id no longer matches.

### CR-222: Neither WebSocket hook reconnects, so a live view freezes permanently after any close
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/hooks/useLiveTranscript.ts`
**Anchor:** `ws.onclose = () => { if (!cancelled) setConnected(false); }`
**Severity:** medium

Both `useLiveTranscript` and `useRunStream` open exactly one socket per `runId` and have no retry, no backoff, and no manual reconnect affordance. `onclose` and `onerror` only flip `connected` to false. Because the effect's only dependency is `runId`, nothing ever re-runs it, so the socket is never replaced.

The trigger is routine rather than exotic: `gracefulShutdown` calls `broadcaster.closeAll(1001, "shutting down")`, so every graceful server restart closes every live client's socket. A proxy idle timeout, a laptop sleep, or a network blip does the same. After that, `Container` renders `○ connecting` forever while the transcript sits at whatever event arrived last. The indicator actively misleads: it claims a connection attempt is in progress when none is.

The server side is already built for resumption. `handleWsOpen` replays `transcriptSnapshot` from `run.jsonl` on every new connection, and `applyEvent` drops any event whose `eventId <= model.maxEventId`, so a reconnect is idempotent and cheap by construction. Nothing on the client uses that.

Not reproduced (would need a live server). Fix: on an unexpected close while the run is not `gone`, schedule a reconnect with capped exponential backoff, keyed off a retry counter in the effect's dependencies, and distinguish `connecting` from `disconnected` in `Container`'s indicator.

### CR-223: `hasMore` and `loadMore` disagree, so "Load more runs" renders as a dead button while any run is in flight
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/hooks/useResults.ts`
**Anchor:** `const hasMore = results.length < total;` versus `if (nextOffset >= total) return;`
**Severity:** medium

The two guards use different quantities. `hasMore` compares rows received against `total`; `loadMore` compares the next offset against `total`. They only agree when the server returns exactly `limit` rows per page, and it does not: `GET /api/results` computes `total` from the count of run *directories*, then skips any directory whose `result.json` does not yet exist (`if (!existsSync(path)) continue;`). An in-progress run is a directory with no `result.json`.

So with one active run and no completed ones, the server answers `{ total: 1, results: [] }`. `hasMore` is `0 < 1`, true, so `RunsList` renders the `Load more runs` button; `loadMore` computes `nextOffset` of 50, sees `50 >= 1`, and returns immediately. The button is visible and inert for as long as the run is active, and the same mismatch appears on any page where some directories are unparseable.

Reproduced with `/private/tmp/claude-503/-Users-ZKeown-Code-moe/4556b327-b63b-49d4-bbc6-78cd4f317e00/scratchpad/shard-025/results-hasmore.mjs`:

```
{ total: 1, returned: 0, hasMore: true, nextOffset: 50, loadMoreIsNoop: true }
RunsList renders "Load more runs" and clicking it does nothing, forever.
```

Fix: derive both from the same quantity. Track pages consumed rather than rows, and set `hasMore = offset + limit < total`, matching `loadMore`'s guard. Separately, have the server report `total` as the count of results it would actually return so the two sides of the contract mean the same thing.

### CR-224: Window named access makes the static-payload null guard unreachable, turning a friendly message into a blank page
**File:** `packages/flight/ui/src/lib/api.ts`
**Anchor:** `declare global { interface Window { __MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__?: StaticRunPayload | undefined } }`
**Severity:** medium

The declared type says the global is a `StaticRunPayload` or `undefined`. At runtime it is neither when hydration does not run. The template gives the payload element `id="__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__"`, and every HTML element with an `id` becomes a supported property name on `Window`, so `window.__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__` resolves to the `HTMLScriptElement` unless the hydration block has assigned an own property over it. The hydration block deliberately skips the assignment when the payload is still the placeholder, and skips it on any JSON parse failure.

Consequence: `getStaticRunPayload`'s `return window.__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__ ?? null` returns a truthy element, `StaticRunPage`'s `if (!payload)` branch with "No run data available" is dead code, and `RunSummaryCard` is handed `undefined` for `result`, whose first statement is `formatRunTimestamp(result.runId)`. The designed error message is replaced by a TypeError and a blank report. `useTranscript` survives only by accident, because `staticPayload?.runJsonl` on an element is undefined and it falls through to the network fetch.

Reproduced with jsdom against the real `packages/flight/ui/static.html`, script at `/private/tmp/claude-503/-Users-ZKeown-Code-moe/4556b327-b63b-49d4-bbc6-78cd4f317e00/scratchpad/shard-025/repro-named-access.mjs`:

```
typeof window.__MOE_FLIGHT_RUN__ : object
constructor                      : HTMLScriptElement
Object.hasOwn(window, ...)       : false
getStaticRunPayload() -> null?   : false
payload.result                   : undefined
```

Fix: stop relying on the global's truthiness. Either read and parse the script element's `textContent` directly in `getStaticRunPayload`, or rename the hydration target so it cannot collide with an element id, and validate the shape (`typeof p === "object" && p !== null && "result" in p`) before returning it.

### CR-225: createBrowserSession can never reconnect after the WebSocket closes
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/browser-session.js`
**Anchor:** `ensureConnected` — "We do NOT null on success — leaving the resolved promise in place makes subsequent ensureConnected() awaits a no-op."
**Severity:** medium

`connectPromise` is cleared only in the `catch`. Once a connect succeeds it stays resolved forever, so when the socket later closes, `ensureConnected()` fails the `ws && ws.isConnected()` early return, hits `if (connectPromise) { await connectPromise; return; }`, and returns immediately holding the dead socket. `send()` then calls `ws.send(...)` on it. The `close` handler rejects pending requests but never nulls `ws` or `connectPromise`, so nothing restores the invariant.

I reproduced it with a fake `WebSocketClient`: after a simulated remote drop, `isConnected()` reports false and the next `send()` rejects with "send() on a CLOSED socket" while only one socket was ever constructed. The module's own contract advertises lazy connect plus `isConnected()`, and the existing suite only covers `close()` rejecting in-flight requests, never a reconnect. `chrome-ws-lib.js`'s stale-bridge check masks this for the normal path but not for the wedge case described above.

Fix: null `connectPromise` when the socket closes (and on success once `ws` is assigned), so a later `ensureConnected()` builds a fresh socket.

### CR-226: In-flight page-session commands are orphaned for 30 seconds when the browser WebSocket drops
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/browser-session.js`
**Anchor:** the `next.on('close', ...)` handler, "Browser session WS closed"
**Severity:** medium

The close handler clears and rejects `pendingRequests`, but that map holds only root-session correlations. Page-session commands are correlated in the cdp-router's per-session `pendingRequests`, and nothing tells the router the transport is gone: `close` emits no event, and neither `router.unregisterSession` nor `pageSession.detach` is called. `resetBridge` in `chrome-ws-lib.js` compounds it by calling `pageSessionResolver.releaseAll()`, which the helper documents as a cache clear "without calling detach".

Reproduced with a scratchpad script that opens a real `createBrowserSession` over a fake socket, builds a page session through `buildPageSessionFromAttached`, issues one `Runtime.evaluate`, and then closes the socket:

```
browser.isConnected() after drop : false
in-flight page-session send      : PENDING
```

The only thing that ever settles that promise is its own `timeoutMs = 30000` timer. So when Chrome is killed externally, every outstanding page action hangs for half a minute before failing with a timeout message that misattributes the cause, while the caller has no way to learn the transport already died.

Fix: give the router an explicit teardown (reject every registered session's pending requests) and invoke it from the browser-session `close` handler and from `resetBridge`, so a dropped socket fails page commands immediately with a transport error.

### CR-227: restoreFocus rebuilds a name-based selector and restores focus to the wrong element in a radio or checkbox group
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/capture.js`
**Anchor:** `restoreFocus`, the branch `focusInfo.type === 'name'`
**Severity:** medium

`saveFocus` records `{type: 'name', value: el.name, tag}` whenever the focused element has no `id`, and `restoreFocus` turns that into `document.querySelector(tag + '[name="' + value + '"]')`. `querySelector` returns the first document match, but a `name` is not unique: radio groups, checkbox groups and repeated `name="tags[]"` fields all share one. Reproduced against jsdom with a three-radio group where the third had focus:

```
element that had focus : blue
generated selector     : input[name="color"]
element focus restored to: red
same element?          : false
```

`captureActionWithDiff` calls `restoreFocus` immediately before running the user's action, so the action then lands on the wrong control — an arrow-key or space `keyboard_press` selects the first radio instead of the focused one, and the diff records a change the caller did not request.

The same concatenation also breaks outright when the `name` attribute contains a double quote, since only the surrounding JS string is escaped and not the CSS attribute value:

```
name with a quote      : "a\"b"
generated selector     : input[name="a"b"]
querySelector result   : DOMException: Invalid selector input[name="a"b"]
```

That throw reaches `throwIfExceptionDetails(restoreResult)` and aborts `captureActionWithDiff` before `actionFn()` runs, so a page can suppress the action entirely with one attribute value.

Fix: capture a stable handle rather than a rebuilt selector — save the sibling-index path unconditionally alongside the name, or resolve the focused node to a `RemoteObject`/`backendNodeId` and refocus that. If the name branch stays, escape the value with `CSS.escape` and disambiguate among matches.

### CR-228: Orphan-Chrome adoption matches profile directories by substring, so the default profile adopts a disambiguated one
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/chrome-launcher-helpers.js`
**Anchor:** `findOrphanChromeForProfile`, at "Must contain our profile dir"
**Severity:** medium

The scan accepts any `ps` line where `line.includes(profileDir)`. `getChromeProfileDir('moe-glass')` is a strict prefix of `getChromeProfileDir('moe-glass-2')`, and auto-disambiguation (`acquireWithFallback`) generates exactly those `-2`, `-3` names. Reproduced with a scratchpad script over a synthetic `ps` line for a `moe-glass-2` Chrome:

```
does the moe-glass-2 ps line satisfy the moe-glass matcher? -> true
port it would adopt       : 9333
pid it would adopt        : 4242
```

Consequence: a server that holds the `moe-glass` lock adopts the *other* server's browser, writes that port and pid into its own `meta.json`, and both servers then drive one Chrome — the exact tab-fighting the profile lock exists to prevent. A later `killChrome` from either one SIGTERMs a browser the other is using. Which server loses depends on `ps` ordering, so it is intermittent.

`findOrphanChromeForProfile` has one test, and it only asserts the no-match case, so nothing exercises the matcher.

Fix: match the flag boundary, not the substring — require `--user-data-dir=<profileDir>` followed by end-of-argument (whitespace or line end), rather than `includes`.

### CR-229: The console-message dedup discards legitimate same-millisecond repeats
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/console-logging.js`
**Anchor:** `enableConsoleLogging` — "Dedup: skip if the last entry has the same level+text at the same timestamp"
**Severity:** medium

The dedup key is `(timestamp, level, text)` where `timestamp` is `new Date().toISOString()`, i.e. millisecond resolution assigned at receipt. A page that logs the same string more than once inside one millisecond — a loop, a repeated warning, a retry counter that prints the same message — has all but the first occurrence dropped. I reproduced the predicate in isolation: three identical `console.log` calls sharing a timestamp are recorded as one entry.

This is silent loss of the exact data the caller asked for with `enable_console_logging`, and it is indistinguishable from the page not having logged. Fix: deduplicate on CDP identity rather than a synthesised timestamp — guard the listener registration so only one handler exists per session (see the next finding) and drop the content-based dedup entirely, or key it on `Runtime.consoleAPICalled`'s own `timestamp` plus `executionContextId`.

### CR-230: Permission dialog resolution ignores the evaluate result and interpolates a page-supplied id unquoted
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/dialogs-router.js`
**Anchor:** the permission branch, `window.__dialogShim_resolve('${id}', '${decision}')`
**Severity:** medium

`id` is `state.staged._shimId`, which `dialogs.js` copies from `data.id` in a `Runtime.bindingCalled` payload. That payload is a JSON string the page hands to `window.__dialogShim(...)`, so the value is page-controlled — the shim's own `String(nextId++)` is only what a cooperating page sends. It is then spliced into a single-quoted JS string literal with no escaping.

Two consequences, both from the same root cause: the router never inspects the `Runtime.evaluate` reply. It returns `{handled: true, clearDialog: true, result: {ok: true}}` unconditionally, so any failure is reported as a successful grant or deny. A crafted id containing a quote makes the expression a syntax error; so does the ordinary case where `window.__dialogShim_resolve` is absent, which happens whenever the page has navigated since the shim was installed or has deleted the property. In every one of those cases the agent is told the permission prompt was handled, the dialog state is cleared, and the page's `getUserMedia`/`Notification.requestPermission` promise is left pending forever.

There is no privilege boundary crossed by the injection itself — the expression runs in the page's own main world, which the page already controls — but the pattern is one quote away from mattering if the call is ever moved to an isolated world or the browser target. The router's permission tests only use ids like `42`, `9` and `SHIM-A`, so neither the escaping nor the unchecked result is covered.

Fix: pass the id as a parameter rather than by string splicing (`Runtime.callFunctionOn`, or `Runtime.evaluate` with a `JSON.stringify`-produced literal), call `throwIfExceptionDetails` on the reply, and only report `clearDialog` when the resolve actually landed.

### CR-231: attachToPageSession marks a session attached before its setup sends complete
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/dialogs.js`
**Anchor:** `attachToPageSession` — `state._dialogPageSessions.add(sid)`
**Severity:** medium

The sessionId is added to the guard set before the six awaited `send` calls (`Page.enable`, `DeviceAccess.enable`, `Fetch.enable`, `Runtime.enable`, `addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument`, `addBinding`) and before `pageSession.onEvent(...)` is registered last. If any send rejects — a 30-second page-session timeout under load, a target destroyed mid-attach, or `DeviceAccess` unavailable — the function throws with the sid already recorded, so every later call returns at the early `if (state._dialogPageSessions.has(sid)) return;` and no event listener is ever installed for that tab.

The consequence compounds with `Fetch.enable`: the command may well have taken effect in Chrome even when its reply was lost, in which case that tab has every request paused with no listener to continue it, and dialogs on it are never detected for the life of the session. `chrome-ws-lib.js`'s `onPageSession` hook swallows the failure with `console.error('onPageSession dialog attach failed:', e)`, so the only signal is a stderr line.

Fix: add the sid only after all sends succeed and the listener is registered, and register the listener first so a partial attach still sees events; on failure, disable `Fetch` for that session before rethrowing.

### CR-232: Fetch interception covers every request and continue failures are silently swallowed
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/dialogs.js`
**Anchor:** `handleCdpEventForSession` — `sendPageCmd('Fetch.continueRequest', { requestId: p.requestId }).catch(() => {})`
**Severity:** medium

`Fetch.enable` is issued with `patterns: [{ urlPattern: '*' }]`, so every single network request on every page is paused, round-tripped to the Node process, and re-issued. The continue call's rejection is discarded, so a dropped or timed-out `Fetch.continueRequest` leaves that request paused indefinitely with no error surfaced anywhere — the page just hangs, and the agent sees a navigate timeout with no indication of the cause. There is no `Fetch.disable` anywhere in the package, so the interception stays on for the session's life.

The auth-dialog feature genuinely needs `handleAuthRequests: true`, which forces a pattern list, so the interception itself is unavoidable. The unhandled rejection is not. Fix: log the continue failure and mark the tab as degraded (or fail the request explicitly with `Fetch.failRequest`) rather than dropping the error, and consider narrowing `requestStage` so sub-resource fetches are not all proxied.

### CR-233: fill() rewrites literal backslash escapes, dropping characters and pressing Enter mid-value
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/keyboard-input.js`
**Anchor:** `fill` — "Normalise literal escape sequences from MCP payloads."
**Severity:** medium

`value.replace(/\\t/g, '\t').replace(/\\n/g, '\n')` is applied unconditionally, and the loop below turns `\t` into a Tab keypress and `\n` into an Enter keypress. Any legitimate value containing a backslash followed by `t` or `n` is therefore corrupted, and `\n` submits the form.

Reproduced with a pure string script:

| input | typed as |
| --- | --- |
| `C:\temp\new` | `C:` Tab `emp` Enter `ew` |
| `regex: \n means newline` | `regex: ` Enter ` means newline` |
| `a\tb` | `a` Tab `b` |

So filling a search field with a Windows path presses Enter and submits the form partway through. The suite covers the intended `\t` and `\n` splitting but not the false-positive case. Fix: do the un-escaping in the MCP payload layer where the ambiguity actually arises (`src/payload.ts` already owns literal-versus-JSON decisions per action), or gate it behind an explicit option, and leave the library's `fill` byte-faithful.

### CR-234: await_element and await_text accept timeouts larger than the CDP send timeout
**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/navigation.js`
**Anchor:** `waitForElement` — `const t = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('waitForElement timeout: '`
**Severity:** medium

The wait predicate is a page-side promise whose deadline is the caller's `timeout`, delivered through `evaluate`, which uses `pageSession.send` with a default `timeoutMs` of 30000. The MCP schema admits `timeout: z.number().int().min(0).max(60000)`. So `{"action":"await_element","selector":"#x","timeout":60000}` cannot work: at 30 seconds the CDP send rejects with `Page session timeout: Runtime.evaluate` and the caller never gets the intended `waitForElement timeout: #x` message, nor the remaining 30 seconds of waiting. Anything above 30000 is silently truncated and misreported.

`timeout` is also interpolated raw into the generated page script, so a non-numeric value produces `setTimeout(..., NaN)`, which fires immediately and reports a timeout that never elapsed.

Fix: pass `{ timeoutMs: timeout + margin }` through `evaluate` to `pageSession.send`, and clamp or reject a `timeout` the transport cannot honour instead of letting the layers disagree.

### CR-235: An inline SVG with class "content" makes every auto-capture fail

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/page-scripts/dom-summary.js`
**Anchor:** `main.className.split(' ')[0]`
**Severity:** medium

The landmark query `document.querySelector('main, [role="main"], .main, #main, .content, #content')` can match an SVG element, whose `className` is an `SVGAnimatedString`, not a string. `.split` then throws. `generateDomSummary` in `lib/capture.js` calls `throwIfExceptionDetails(result)` on the evaluate, and the call sits inside the `Promise.all` of `capturePageArtifacts`, so the page-side `TypeError` fails the entire auto-capture — which means `navigate`, `click`, `type` and every other capturing action fail on such a page rather than degrading to a missing summary.

Reproduced with jsdom: `<svg class="content">…</svg>` before other candidates yields `TypeError: main.className.split is not a function` from the script as written.

Fix: read the class through `main.getAttribute('class')` (or guard on `typeof main.className === 'string'`), and make `generateDomSummary` degrade to an empty summary instead of failing the capture.

### CR-236: Markdown extraction emits nested content twice

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/page-scripts/markdown.js`
**Anchor:** `document.querySelectorAll('h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, p, a, li, pre, code, blockquote, table, img, figure')`
**Severity:** medium

The walk visits a flat query result and emits `el.textContent` for each match, so any matched element nested inside another matched element is emitted twice — once as part of the ancestor's text and once on its own. The idioms this hits are the common ones: `pre > code`, `blockquote > p`, `li > a`, `p > a`. The module's stated purpose is a "token-efficient Markdown" artifact written for every captured action, so the duplication is paid on every action, and the `.slice(0, 50000)` cap means the duplicate half also displaces real content on long pages.

Reproduced with jsdom on a three-element document: the blockquote paragraph appeared as both `> quoted paragraph` and a bare paragraph, the `pre > code` block was emitted as two identical fenced blocks, and the link text appeared inside the list item and again as a standalone link. The existing `test/lib/page-scripts/markdown.test.mjs` cases are all flat, so nothing pins the current output.

Fix: walk the tree and skip any element whose nearest matched ancestor already consumed it (or handle container tags by recursing into their children rather than by `textContent`).

### CR-237: Notification permission is reported as granted without ever granting it

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/page-scripts/permission-shim.js`
**Anchor:** `const orig = Notification.requestPermission.bind(Notification);`
**Severity:** medium

In the `Notification.requestPermission` branch, `orig` is captured and never called. On a `grant` decision the shim returns the string `'granted'` (and invokes the legacy callback with it) without asking Chrome for anything, so `Notification.permission` stays `'default'` and the page's subsequent `new Notification(...)` silently does nothing. The page is told it has a capability it does not have. Every other branch calls its captured original on grant; this one is the outlier, and because the shim is a template string no linter flags the unused binding.

Fix: `if (decision === 'grant') return orig(cb);` and let Chrome's own state be the source of truth, mirroring the geolocation and clipboard branches.

### CR-238: The permission gate covers five entry points and misses their siblings

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/page-scripts/permission-shim.js`
**Anchor:** `SHIM_SOURCE`
**Severity:** medium

The shim wraps `mediaDevices.getUserMedia`, `Notification.requestPermission`, `geolocation.getCurrentPosition`, `clipboard.readText` and `clipboard.writeText`. Unwrapped, and reachable from any page: `geolocation.watchPosition` (same data, no prompt), `clipboard.read` and `clipboard.write` (the non-Text variants, so clipboard-read is gated only for plain text), `mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia` (screen capture), and the legacy `navigator.getUserMedia`. `navigator.permissions.query` is also unwrapped, which `dialogs.smoke.test.mjs` pins as intentional in its test `navigator.permissions.query completes normally — not hijacked by shim`. A gate that a page bypasses by calling the adjacent method is not a gate; it mainly creates the impression that these capabilities are supervised. Not reproduced against a browser — this is a coverage reading of the wrapped set.

Fix: enumerate the intended capability surface once and wrap every entry point that reaches it, or document in the skill that the shim is best-effort observation rather than enforcement.

### CR-239: Two MCP instances can both claim the same profile lock

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/profile-lock.js`
**Anchor:** "File creation uses `wx` flag for atomicity — two MCPs starting at the same millisecond can't both win."
**Severity:** medium

`fs.writeFileSync(lockPath, ..., {flag:'wx'})` is two operations: an exclusive create, then a write. In the window between them the file exists and is empty. A second acquirer in that window gets `EEXIST`, calls `readLockFile`, gets `null` from the failed `JSON.parse`, treats the lock as stale, unlinks it and claims it. Both processes then believe they hold the lock and drive the same Chrome with the same `activeTab` pointer — exactly the tab-stomping the module was written to prevent, and the header's atomicity claim does not hold. The same path makes any truncated or corrupt lock permanently stale, and `release()` unlinks when `readLockFile` returns `null`, so the racer's release removes the other holder's lock.

Reproduced with `XDG_CACHE_HOME` pointed at a scratch dir: with holder A's descriptor open from `openSync(lockPath, 'wx')` and the body not yet written, `acquire('repro-profile')` returned the lock path rather than `null`.

Fix: write the payload to a temp file and `link`/`rename` it into place so the lock never exists empty, or claim with `wx`, write, then re-read and verify the pid is ours before returning success.

### CR-240: closeTab compares a rewritten WebSocket URL against the raw target list

**File:** `packages/glass/skills/browsing/lib/tabs.js`
**Anchor:** `closeTab`
**Severity:** medium

`closeTab` calls `resolveWsUrl(tabIndexOrWsUrl)`, whose `ws://` branch returns `rewriteWsUrl(...)`, then matches it against `tabs.find(t => t.webSocketDebuggerUrl === wsUrl)` on the *unrewritten* `/json` listing. With a host override active (`CHROME_WS_HOST` / `CHROME_WS_PORT`, the documented way to drive a Chrome that is not at 127.0.0.1:9222), the two strings differ, `find` returns undefined, and `closeTab` returns silently having closed nothing — while `close_tab` in `src/index.ts` reports `Closed tab N`. The mirror-image inconsistency is in the same file: `resolveWsUrl`'s index branch returns `pageTabs[index].webSocketDebuggerUrl` raw, skipping the rewrite that `getTabs` and `newTab` apply to that exact field, so an index resolves to a URL the caller may not be able to reach. Not reproduced — it needs a remapped host.

Fix: match on `tab.id` (resolve the index or URL to a target id once) instead of on URL string equality, and apply `rewriteWsUrl` consistently in `resolveWsUrl`'s index branch.

### CR-241: The documented numeric payload form is rejected by the tool schema

**File:** `packages/glass/src/index.ts`
**Anchor:** `payload: z.union([z.string(), z.record(z.any())])`
**Severity:** medium

The schema accepts only a string or an object, but three places promise a bare number. The help text shows `switch_tab: {"action": "switch_tab", "payload": 1}`; the action enum comment says `get_console_messages` payload is "also accepted as a bare epoch-ms number/string"; and the tool description says "get_console_messages={since:epochMs} or a bare epoch-ms timestamp". A number payload never reaches `parsePayload` — Zod rejects the call first, and the model gets `Error: Invalid input` for the exact form the tool told it to use. `resolveConsoleSince`'s `typeof value === 'number'` branch and `PAYLOAD_SPECS.get_console_messages.numericDefaultKey` are consequently only reachable via a numeric *string*.

Reproduced with the package's own Zod: `1` and `1716000000000` are rejected, `"1"` and `{tab:1}` accepted. Nothing guards this — `payload-normalization.test.mjs` calls `parsePayload` directly and never crosses the schema.

Fix: add `z.number()` to the union (both `parsePayload` and `resolveConsoleSince` already handle numbers), or delete the numeric form from the help text, the enum comments and the tool description.

### CR-242: Page content is returned as tool output with no provenance marking

**File:** `packages/glass/src/index.ts`
**Anchor:** `return await chromeLib.evaluate(tabIndex, 'document.body.innerText');`
**Severity:** medium

`extract` returns raw page text as the entire tool result, and `formatActionResponse` / `formatCaptureResponse` splice page-derived `domSummary` and console text into their responses. Nothing marks any of it as untrusted third-party content, so text a visited site chose is indistinguishable to the model from the server's own output — the standard indirect-injection setup, on a tool annotated `openWorldHint: true` whose description actively steers the model to read captured page artifacts. It matters more here than usual because the same tool exposes `file_upload`, which hands `DOM.setFileInputFiles` any absolute path (`~/.ssh/id_rsa`) with no allow-list or confirmation, giving injected instructions a ready exfiltration path.

Fix: wrap page-derived text in an explicit untrusted-content envelope naming the origin URL, and keep the model's instructions outside it.

### CR-243: The tool declares itself non-destructive while it overwrites files and kills processes

**File:** `packages/glass/src/index.ts`
**Anchor:** `destructiveHint: false`
**Severity:** medium

`use_browser` is registered with `destructiveHint: false`. The same tool overwrites any writable path via `screenshot` (see the containment finding above), terminates processes via `kill_chrome` and `restart_chrome`, and mutates remote state through `click`, `type` and `eval`. MCP clients use this annotation to decide what can run without asking, so the hint suppresses exactly the confirmation the destructive actions warrant.

Fix: set `destructiveHint: true` for the tool as registered, or split the destructive actions into a separately annotated tool.

### CR-244: The array-guard tests assert source text rather than behaviour

**File:** `packages/glass/test/array-guards.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test `resolveWsUrl() guards against non-array chromeHttp response`
**Severity:** medium

All three tests read `lib/tabs.js` as a string, slice out a function body with a brace counter, and assert the body `includes('Array.isArray')`. They pass if the substring appears anywhere in the body — in a comment, or in a guard whose branch does nothing — and they fail on a correct refactor that validates the response before dispatch or renames the helper. The behaviour is cheaply testable and the seam already exists: `attachTabs({ state, _chromeHttp })` takes an injected HTTP client, so a test can hand `getTabs` a `{message: '...'}` object and assert `[]`, and hand `resolveWsUrl` the same and assert the thrown message. As written, the suite documents an implementation detail and calls it a regression check.

Fix: rewrite the three cases against `_chromeHttp` returning a non-array, asserting the documented outcomes (`getTabs` returns `[]`, `resolveWsUrl` throws "invalid response", `closeTab` returns without calling close).

### CR-245: The dialog-refusal test never stages a dialog or calls a gated action

**File:** `packages/glass/test/dialogs-wiring.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test `returns refused result when a dialog is open and a page-target action is attempted`
**Severity:** medium

The body asserts `session.dialogs.getOpen(wsUrl) === null` for two URLs that were never touched, and stops. No dialog is staged, no page-target action runs, and no refusal is checked, so the test passes on any build where the gate is entirely absent. Its own comments admit it ("We can't stage a dialog without a live CDP connection, so we verify the refusal path through a different approach"), but the name is what a reader trusts, and the gate is a safety mechanism whose failure mode is a 30s CDP hang.

The pieces for a real test are present in the same file: `stageAlertDialog` builds an `attachDialogs` over an injectable `state` and injects `Page.javascriptDialogOpening` directly. What is missing is constructing the session over that same state so a wrapped method can be called and its rejection asserted.

Fix: let `createSession` accept an injected `state` (or export the gate wrapper), then stage a dialog and assert the wrapped call rejects with `refused === true`. Failing that, rename the test to what it checks.

### CR-246: awaitPromise regression test greps module source text instead of exercising the call
**File:** `packages/glass/test/evaluate-await-promise.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** `extractFunction`, and the assertion "evaluate() must include awaitPromise: true in its Runtime.evaluate call"
**Severity:** medium

The whole file reads `evaluation.js` with `readFileSync`, slices out a function body by counting braces, and asserts the literal substring `awaitPromise: true` appears. No production code runs. The test passes if the string appears only in a comment, in dead code, or in a differently-named sibling that the brace scanner happens to swallow; it fails if someone writes `awaitPromise : true` or hoists the params into a shared object. The brace counter also ignores braces inside strings and template literals, so it survives only because `evaluateJson`'s embedded page script happens to balance.

`packages/glass/test/lib/evaluation.test.mjs` already asserts the same property behaviourally — "evaluate passes returnByValue and awaitPromise" reads `call.params.awaitPromise` off a page-session fake — and covers `evaluateRaw` too. This file is a strictly weaker duplicate, and asserting that a past edit stayed present in the source text is the scaffolding-test shape `AGENTS.md` steers away from.

Fix: delete the file and add the missing `evaluateJson` param assertion to `evaluation.test.mjs`.

### CR-247: Bug 1a regression test reimplements the production exit listener instead of invoking it
**File:** `packages/glass/test/lib/chrome-process.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** describe "chrome-process: Bug 1a — exit listener clears owned proc, ignores stale procs"
**Severity:** medium

Both tests under that heading build a fake `ChildProcess` and then attach their own copy of the guard:

```
state.chromeProcess = proc;
proc.on('exit', () => {
  if (state.chromeProcess === proc) state.chromeProcess = null;
});
proc._die();
```

`chrome-process.js` is never called. The assertions verify the listener the test just wrote, so they hold no matter what `startChrome` does — delete the `proc.on('exit', ...)` block from production and both tests still pass. The file's own comment concedes the approach ("(a) is tested via a direct logic test of the listener's identity guard"), but the describe name claims the production listener is covered, which a reader will take at face value.

Fix: drive the real `startChrome` with the `require.cache` seam the rest of the file already uses (see the `captureSpawnPath` helper), return the fake proc from the stubbed `spawn`, then emit `exit` on it and assert `state.chromeProcess === null`.

### CR-248: Bug 1b regression test self-skips on every machine without Chrome, including CI, for a reason that no longer holds
**File:** `packages/glass/test/lib/chrome-process.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "state.chromeProcess is null after startChrome fails to bind port"
**Severity:** medium

The test opens with `if (!chromeInstalled) return;` and its comment justifies this by asserting that "the `require.cache['child_process']` patch below cannot intercept a builtin, so the module gets the real spawn". That premise is false on this toolchain. I verified it with a two-file scratchpad script: a consumer module doing `require('child_process')` after `require.cache['child_process']` was replaced receives the stub.

```
node v24.19.0
cache patch intercepted builtin: true
```

So the stubbed `spawn` is in effect and no real Chrome is ever launched; the 15-second cost comes from the `isPortAlive: async () => false` readiness poll, not from a browser. The guard is nonetheless still load-bearing for a *different* reason — `chrome-process.js` does its own inline binary scan that `fakeHelpers` does not cover — but the two sibling tests in this file already solve that by setting `CHROME_WS_BROWSER = process.execPath`. Because the guard is a bare `return`, the test reports as passing while asserting nothing, so the readiness-timeout handle-clearing fix is unverified in CI (`node:24`, no Chrome) and on any contributor machine without Chrome.

Fix: set `process.env.CHROME_WS_BROWSER = process.execPath` inside the test and drop the `chromeInstalled` early return, matching "startChrome rejects when the spawned proc emits error".

### CR-249: A unit test shells out to the CLI and closes a tab in the developer's live Chrome
**File:** `packages/glass/test/lib/cli-close-numeric.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "close 0 does not reject with \"Invalid WebSocket URL\""
**Severity:** medium

The test spawns the real `chrome-ws` CLI with `close 0`. Nothing stubs the transport and no port override is set, so the CLI's `resolveWsUrl` issues `GET /json` against `127.0.0.1:9222` — the default `PORT_RANGE_START` and precisely the port a dogfooded moe-glass Chrome binds. When a debug-enabled Chrome is listening there, the command resolves the first page tab and issues `/json/close/<id>`, closing a tab the developer is using. When no tab exists, `resolveWsUrl` first *creates* one (`/json/new`) and closes that.

This test is in the CI-safe `unit` project, so `pnpm test` triggers it on every local run. The sibling test in the same file correctly aims at the unbound port 19999.

Both assertions are also purely negative — they only check that stderr lacks the string `Invalid WebSocket URL`. The test passes if the `close` command is deleted outright, or if the CLI exits before printing anything.

Fix: set `CHROME_WS_PORT` to an unbound high port in the spawn env (as the second test does via its URL), and assert positively on the expected connection-failure message rather than on the absence of the old one.

### CR-250: Console double-write regression test asserts nothing about the scenario in its name
**File:** `packages/glass/test/lib/console-logging.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "double-write scenario: two onEvent listeners on the same session produce exactly N entries for N events (Bug 1 regression)"
**Severity:** medium

The test builds the two-writer scenario on session `S-dedup`, adds a second listener that pushes to the same buffer, injects three console events, then calls `await getConsoleMessages(0)` and discards the result without asserting on it. Its inline commentary works through the arithmetic and concludes "Since the simulated second listener IS present in this test, we get 6" — so the named condition produces six entries, and the test declines to check that. It then constructs a *second*, single-writer session and asserts three entries there.

The surviving assertion duplicates the plain single-writer behaviour already covered by "Runtime.consoleAPICalled string arg is captured into sessionId buffer", and the entire first half is dead setup. A reader scanning names will believe the two-listener case is pinned when nothing about it is.

Fix: split it. Keep the single-writer count assertion under an honest name, and either assert the two-writer count explicitly (documenting that the dedup does not defend against a second writer) or delete that half.

### CR-251: mouse fallback test stubs a Runtime.evaluate shape resolveCenter never returns
**File:** `packages/glass/test/lib/mouse.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "still runs the fallback when no dialog is open (preserves not-found path)"
**Severity:** medium

The fake returns `{result: {value: {x: 0, y: 0, width: 0, height: 0}}}` for the bounding-box lookup, with the comment "bbox lookup returns a zero-size rect to force resolveCenter to fail". `resolveCenter`'s generated expression never returns `width`/`height`; it returns `{x, y, found}`. So the value the fake supplies makes `resolveCenter` throw because `found` is `undefined`, i.e. because the element was reported *missing* — not because the rect was empty.

That matters because the shape production actually returns for a zero-rect element is `{x: 0, y: 0, found: true}`, which does not throw at all (see the separate `mouse.js` finding above). The test therefore certifies the hidden-element fallback while covering only the not-found path, and it is the reason the real hidden-element bug survived. The sibling test "click falls back to el.click() when CDP coord resolution throws but element exists" has the same problem: its comment says "return found:false so it throws", which is again the missing-element path.

Fix: stub the two shapes production really produces — `{x, y, found: true}` for a zero-rect element and `null` for a miss — and assert what `click` does with each. That will fail until `resolveCenter` distinguishes them.

### CR-252: The replace-semantics test cannot detect the clearing loop being removed
**File:** `packages/glass/test/lib/select-option.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "replace semantics: previous selections are cleared"
**Severity:** medium

The test primes a multi-select with `['a','b','c']`, calls `selectOption` again
with `['b']`, then asserts `r.matched.length === 1` and
`r.matched[0].value === 'b'`. But `matched` in the returned payload is the list of
options resolved from the *requested* values, not the select's resulting state.
It is `['b']` whether or not the page-side code cleared the previous selections.
Playwright-style replace semantics are the documented contract of this action, and
nothing tests them.

Reproduced. I copied `select-option.js` to scratch, deleted the
`for (const o of options) o.selected = false;` line, and ran the test's exact two
assertions against jsdom. They passed, while the page's actual selected set was
`["a","b","c"]` instead of `["b"]`. Against the unmodified module the same probe
reports `["b"]`.

Fix: read the resulting state back after the call, for example asserting on
`Array.from(el.selectedOptions).map(o => o.value)` through a `Runtime.evaluate`,
rather than on the `matched` echo.

### CR-253: Every file under test/manual fails at load with MODULE_NOT_FOUND
**File:** `packages/glass/test/manual/test-harness.js`
**Anchor:** the shared literal `require('./skills/browsing/chrome-ws-lib.js')`
**Severity:** medium

All seven files in `test/manual/` require the library with a path relative to the
manual directory, so Node resolves
`packages/glass/test/manual/skills/browsing/chrome-ws-lib.js`, which does not
exist. The library lives two levels up, at
`packages/glass/skills/browsing/chrome-ws-lib.js`. The require is the first
statement in each file, so none of them can run at all — not the harness, not
`test-headless-toggle.cjs`, `test-issue-18-pid.cjs`,
`test-issue-19-fullpage.cjs`, `test-issue-20-hidpi.cjs`, `test-profiles.cjs`, or
`test-xdg-cache.cjs`.

Reproduced. Running the require from the manual directory yields
`MODULE_NOT_FOUND Cannot find module './skills/browsing/chrome-ws-lib.js'`, and a
resolver sweep over all seven files reports the same path MISSING in every one.

These are excluded from the vitest run (`exclude: [... "test/manual/**" ...]`) and
are documented as run-by-hand, which is why the rot went unnoticed. Fix: change
the specifier to `../../skills/browsing/chrome-ws-lib.js` in all seven.
`test-issue-19-fullpage.cjs` additionally reads
`'./skills/browsing/chrome-ws'` through `fs.readFileSync`, which is CWD-relative
rather than file-relative, so that one needs a `__dirname`-anchored path too or it
only works when invoked from the package root.

### CR-254: The manual harness drives an API chrome-ws-lib has not exported since it became a factory
**File:** `packages/glass/test/manual/test-harness.js`
**Anchor:** `chromeWs.initializeSession`, `chromeWs.click`, `chromeWs.fill`, `chromeWs.eval`
**Severity:** medium

Fixing the require path is not enough to revive this file. It treats the module as
a flat namespace (`chromeWs.click(...)`, `chromeWs.fill(...)`,
`chromeWs.eval(...)`, `chromeWs.navigate(...)`,
`chromeWs.initializeSession()`), but `chrome-ws-lib.js` exports only
`createSession`, `PAGE_TARGET_SESSION_METHODS` and `DialogRefusedError`. The six
sibling `.cjs` files all call `.createSession()` first; the harness never does, so
every call would be `TypeError: chromeWs.click is not a function`. `eval` is worse
than stale — the session API has no `eval` under any casing; the method is
`evaluate`.

Reproduced. Enumerating the module's exports prints exactly
`createSession, PAGE_TARGET_SESSION_METHODS, DialogRefusedError`, and probing the
session object shows `click`, `fill`, `navigate` and `initializeSession` present
but `eval` undefined.

Two further dead edges in the same file: `DEFAULT_TEST_URL` points at
`test-react-inputs.html` in `__dirname`, and no file by that name exists anywhere
in the package, so the default run navigates to a dead `file://` URL;
`testTypeAndEnter` and `testXPathClick` are never called, and both use `'\\n'`
(an escaped backslash followed by n) where a newline was clearly meant, as does
the `line1\\nline2` textarea case in `runIteration`. Fix: port the harness to
`createSession()` and `evaluate`, or delete it — it has not been runnable through
either defect for a long time.

### CR-255: The startChrome boolean-contract tests are satisfied by any return false anywhere in the file
**File:** `packages/glass/test/mcp-postel-fixes.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "startChrome returns false when reconnecting to existing Chrome"
**Severity:** medium

Both tests in the final describe read `chrome-process.js` as text and assert

against the whole file. The file is 400+ lines with many functions. The assertion

Reproduced. I rewrote a scratch copy of `chrome-process.js` so that all three of

Three more tests in the same file have the same shape and the same problem.

consumed to set chromeWasRestarted" accepts `srcContent.includes('spawned')`,
which matches four places. Fix: assert on behaviour — `startChrome` is reachable
with a stubbed `child_process`, which the neighbouring

### CR-256: The whole MCP schema test file is file-wide substring grep over an 800KB bundle
**File:** `packages/glass/test/mcp-schema.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "schema has selector parameter", and "switch_tab handler searches by url or title substring"
**Severity:** medium

Every test in this file asserts only that some short string appears somewhere in

### CR-257: The parsePayload tests exercise a copy defined in the test file, not production code
**File:** `packages/glass/test/schema-collapse.test.mjs`
**Anchor:** test "parsePayload coercion logic", opening with the comment "Mirror the helper logic for white-box testing"
**Severity:** medium

The describe block defines its own three-line `parsePayload` and then runs six
tests against that local function. No production module is imported. The six
tests cannot fail on any change to `src/payload.ts`, and the mirrored copy is no

Reproduced. Comparing the mirrored copy against the real `parsePayload` imported

### CR-258: The env allowlist in the memory MCP config reaches no consumer
**File:** `packages/memory/.mcp.json`
**Anchor:** the `env_vars` array in the moe-memory server entry
**Severity:** medium

`env_vars` is a Codex convention inherited from the pinned upstream
`episodic-memory` snapshot. In this repo nothing honours it:

- Claude Code's MCP server config has no `env_vars` key; additional environment
  is declared under `env` as an object. The array is unrecognised there.
- The generated `plugins/moe-memory/.mcp.json` is a byte-for-byte copy of this
  file, so the key survives but stays inert.
- mint's Agent Plugins translation (`translateMcpServer` in
  `packages/mint/src/adapters/agent-plugins.ts`) reads `command`, `args`,
  `env` as an object, and `cwd`. It never looks at `env_vars` and emits no
  warning for the unknown key, so `plugins/moe-memory/mcp.json` drops the whole
  list silently.
- mint's Codex adapter — the one harness whose convention this is — declares
  `mcp: 'none'` and warns "mcp servers are not emitted for codex in v1", so the
  Codex plugin carries no MCP server block at all.

Verified by reading the four artifacts and the adapter source, not by running a
harness. `packages/memory/test/codex-plugin.test.ts` pins the list and its
docstring calls the allowlist "the classic silent failure", which makes the key
read as enforced when it is currently dead in every direction. Fix: either
translate `env_vars` in the adapters that need it and add the missing-key warning
to `translateMcpServer`, or drop the key and record in `PARITY.md` that the
upstream Codex allowlist is not carried forward.

### CR-259: The env allowlist omits the two variables that choose which transcript tree is indexed
**File:** `packages/memory/.mcp.json`
**Anchor:** the `env_vars` array, which lists `MOE_MEMORY_CONFIG_DIR` through `CONVERSATION_SEARCH_EXCLUDE_PROJECTS`
**Severity:** medium

`src/paths.ts` resolves the conversation corpus through `getClaudeDir()` and
`getCodexDir()`, which read `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `CODEX_HOME` respectively;
`getConversationSourceDirs()` joins them into the three scanned roots
(`<claude>/projects`, `<claude>/transcripts`, `<codex>/sessions`). Neither
variable is on the allowlist. Wherever `env_vars` is honoured as an allowlist —
which is its stated purpose — a user who has relocated their Claude Code config
directory or Codex home gets an MCP server that reads and searches the default
`~/.claude` and `~/.codex` instead, while the CLI (which inherits the full
environment) resolves them correctly. The two then disagree about what the corpus
is, with nothing reporting it: exactly the divergence the guard test says it
exists to prevent.

The guard cannot catch this. `codex-plugin.test.ts`'s check "passes through every
path-resolving env var src/paths.ts actually reads" collects names with
`/\bMOE_[A-Z0-9]+(?:_[A-Z0-9]+)*\b/g` and then hardcodes exactly two extras,
`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` and `CONVERSATION_SEARCH_EXCLUDE_PROJECTS`. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`
and `CODEX_HOME` match neither arm.

Verified by reading `src/paths.ts` and the guard test. Fix: add both names to
`env_vars`, and widen the guard to scan for every `process.env.X` read in
`paths.ts` minus an explicit `TEST_`-prefixed exemption list, so the next
path-resolving variable is caught rather than depending on the `MOE_` prefix.

### CR-260: Filter and injection assertions live only in the test project that no gate runs
**File:** `packages/memory/package.json`
**Anchor:** the scripts named test and test:model
**Severity:** medium

`test` is `vitest run --project unit` and `test:model` is a separate script. Nothing invokes
`test:model`: the root CI file runs `pnpm test`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm build`,
`pnpm mint:check` and `pnpm provenance`, and turbo's `test` task maps to the package script.
So the nine suites under `test/model/` never execute automatically anywhere.

That set is not peripheral. It holds the only coverage of `indexUnprocessed`, of
`searchConversations` end to end, of every metadata filter, of both DO-NOT-INDEX markers on
the sync path, and of `repairIndex`. It also holds the one security regression test in the
package, "rejects a single-quote in a filter value (no string-interpolation injection)", which
asserts that filter values reach SQLite as bound parameters. A change that reintroduced string
interpolation in `buildSearchFilters` would pass every gate.

Most of those assertions do not need a real encoder. `search-metadata-filters.test.ts` checks
exact-match filtering, and `sync-indexing.test.ts` checks marker handling; neither depends on
semantic quality. They sit in the model project only because `indexUnprocessed` and
`searchConversations` call `initEmbeddings` with no injection seam, even though
`test/test-utils.ts` already ships `fakeEmbed` for exactly this purpose and documents it as
letting "the offline project exercise retrieval end to end".

Fix: thread an optional embed function through `indexUnprocessed` and `searchConversations`,
then move the filter, injection, and marker suites into the `unit` project on `fakeEmbed`.
Leave only the genuinely encoder-dependent assertions behind.

### CR-261: Schema migrations print to stdout, which is the MCP JSON-RPC channel
**File:** `packages/memory/src/db.ts`
**Anchor:** `console.log("Migration complete.")` and the surrounding migration logging in migrateSchema, migrateToolCallsCascade and migrateJournalRoot
**Severity:** medium

`initDatabase()` writes its migration progress with `console.log`, i.e. to file descriptor 1. Every other diagnostic on the server path deliberately uses `console.error` — `mcp-server.ts` does, `install-check.ts` does, `journal/store.ts` does, and `embeddings.ts` carries the comment "In MCP, stdout is reserved for JSON-RPC communication". The migration path is the one exception, and `runMemoryMcpServer` calls `initDatabase()` on the transport's own stdout, as do five of the seven tool handlers (`process_thoughts`, `search_journal`, `read_journal_entry`, `list_recent_entries`, `read_recent_entries`).

The trigger is an existing database that predates any of the sixteen guarded columns, the `ON DELETE CASCADE` rebuild, or `journal_entries.root` — i.e. the first server start after an upgrade. The reference SDK client survives it (`processReadBuffer` catches the parse failure, reports it through `onerror` and continues), so this is protocol noise rather than a hang there, but a stricter client that treats a transport error as fatal loses the session, and `createMemoryMcpServer` is exported for embedders that do not run the startup `initDatabase()` first — in that case the migration lands mid-stream inside a live tool call. Route all three functions through `console.error`.

Reproduced. A database built with the pre-migration schema, then opened with the shipped `initDatabase()`: twenty non-JSON lines on stdout, nothing on stderr.

### CR-262: insertExchange is not atomic, and an exchange that loses its vector row is invisible to semantic search forever
**File:** `packages/memory/src/db.ts`
**Anchor:** `insertExchange`
**Severity:** medium

`insertExchange` issues the `exchanges` upsert, then a `DELETE FROM vec_exchanges`, then the `vec_exchanges` insert, then the tool-call inserts, each as its own autocommitted statement with no surrounding transaction. Callers do not add one either: `syncConversations` and both indexer loops call it directly per exchange.

If the process dies between the row write and the vector write, which is ordinary for a detached background sync across a sleep, reboot or kill, the result is durable and self-concealing:

- `searchConversations` in vector mode selects `FROM vec_exchanges AS vec JOIN exchanges AS e`, so the exchange can never be returned by semantic search.
- `getFileLastIndexed` returns a non-null stamp, so `verifyIndex` reports the conversation healthy and `--repair` never revisits it.
- `pickStaleBatch` filters on `embedding_version < EMBEDDING_VERSION`, and `insertExchange` already stamped the current version, so the embedding migration will not repair it either.

The `DELETE` then `INSERT` pair is also a window in which a concurrent reader sees the row with no vector, which WAL does not close because the two statements are separate transactions. Note that `runMigrationBatch` gets this right and wraps its batch in `db.transaction`, so the pattern is already established in the package.

I did not stage a crash; this is a read of the statement sequence plus the three recovery paths, and I confirmed with a scratch better-sqlite3 script that `SELECT MAX(last_indexed) ... WHERE archive_path = ?` returns `{lastIndexed: null}` for a file with no rows and a real number as soon as any row exists.

Fix: wrap the whole of `insertExchange` in `db.transaction`, and prefer one transaction per file at the sync and indexer call sites.

### CR-263: Embedding migration re-embeds from different text than the indexer wrote
**File:** `packages/memory/src/embedding-migration.ts`
**Anchor:** `GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT tc.tool_name) AS tools` in pickStaleBatch
**Severity:** medium

The doc comment says the tool names are joined "so the caller can reproduce the production exchange-text format". They do not. `indexer.ts` passes `exchange.toolCalls?.map((tc) => tc.toolName)` — every call, with duplicates, in transcript order — into `generateExchangeEmbedding`, which appends `\n\nTools: <joined>`. The migration's `DISTINCT` collapses repeats, and `GROUP_CONCAT` has no defined ordering, so a migrated row's vector is computed from a different string than a freshly indexed row's.

That is precisely the condition `EMBEDDING_VERSION` exists to rule out: after a version bump the corpus is a mix of two text formats, both stamped at the current version, with no error and no log line. The constant's own comment warns that a mixed corpus "ranks wrongly with no error". Select the tool names in insertion order without `DISTINCT` (order by `tool_calls.timestamp`, or by rowid).

Reproduced. An exchange whose tool calls are `Read, Bash, Read, Read`: the indexer embeds `…Tools: Read, Bash, Read, Read`, `pickStaleBatch` yields `…Tools: Read, Bash`.

### CR-264: Journal entry filenames collide about one time in a thousand, silently overwriting an entry
**File:** `packages/memory/src/journal/markdown.ts`
**Anchor:** `formatEntryBasename`
**Severity:** medium

The sub-millisecond component of an entry filename is `date.getMilliseconds() * 1000 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000)`, so two entries written in the same millisecond into the same directory collide with probability 1/1000, and `writeToLocation` uses a plain `fs.writeFile` with no existence check, so the loser is destroyed with no error.

The collapsed-roots configuration makes this a guaranteed exposure rather than a rare race. `writeThoughts` takes a single `new Date()` and uses it for both the project and the user write; when `MOE_MEMORY_JOURNAL_PATH` points both roots at one directory, which `test/journal-store.test.ts` documents as "the documented containerised configuration", the two files differ only in that random suffix. Every `process_thoughts` call carrying both `project_notes` and any user category then has a 1/1000 chance of losing one of the two entries, and the index ends up with two rows (the ids differ by scope) one of which points at the other's content.

I measured the rate with a scratch script over 200,000 trials calling the function twice with one shared `Date`: 204 collisions, 0.102 percent. The paired test in my shard, "produces distinct filenames for rapid successive writes", is the same coin flip and will flake at that rate whenever both writes land in one millisecond.

Fix: derive the suffix from a monotonic counter, or retry with a fresh suffix while the target path exists, or write with the `wx` flag and retry on EEXIST.

### CR-265: `read_conversation` reads any path with no containment and bypasses both exclusion controls
**File:** `packages/memory/src/mcp-server.ts`
**Anchor:** `const jsonlContent = fs.readFileSync(params.path, "utf-8");` in the read_conversation handler
**Severity:** medium

The handler validates only that the string is non-empty and that the file exists, then reads it and renders it. There is no restriction to the archive directory or the transcript source roots, and no realpath check. Contrast `read_journal_entry`, which routes through `JournalSearchService.readEntry` and its deliberate two-stage containment guard (extension check, containment in the roots, realpath, containment in the realpath'd roots) — the module comment explains why that guard has two stages and asks that it not be simplified. The conversation half has no equivalent.

Two consequences beyond generic file reading. First, a conversation carrying the DO-NOT-INDEX marker, or belonging to an excluded project, is kept out of the index but can still be read in full through this tool by supplying its source path. Second, MCP tool results are not path-gated by the host the way a native read tool is, so this reaches files the harness would otherwise prompt about.

The blast radius on non-transcript files is limited by accident rather than design: `formatConversationAsMarkdown` parses every line with `JSON.parse` and throws on the first non-JSON line, and filters anything that is not a `user`/`assistant` message, so an arbitrary text file yields an error and an arbitrary JSON-lines file yields `""`. Any Claude- or Codex-shaped transcript anywhere on disk is returned verbatim. Confine the path to `getArchiveDir()` plus `getConversationSourceDirs()` using the journal guard's shape.

### CR-266: `process_thoughts` reports success when every category is an empty string
**File:** `packages/memory/src/mcp-server.ts`
**Anchor:** `const hasAnyContent = Object.values(thoughts).some((value) => value !== undefined);`
**Severity:** medium

The handler's guard tests only for `undefined`, while `JournalStore.writeThoughts` routes through `hasContent`, which requires `value !== undefined && value !== ""`. An argument such as `{"reflections": ""}` passes the handler guard, writes nothing, and returns `Thoughts recorded successfully.` with an empty path list. The model is told its journal entry was recorded when no file exists and no row was indexed — the one failure mode the store's own module comment says the redesign exists to eliminate ("a failed encode wrote an entry that no read path could ever see again"), reintroduced at the boundary above it.

Align the handler's predicate with `hasContent`, or have `writeThoughts` report that it wrote nothing.

Reproduced. `writeThoughts({reflections: ""}, db)` returns `[]`, the journal root stays empty, and the handler's guard evaluates to `true`.

### CR-267: Journal indexing, and the model load it triggers, blocks the MCP handshake
**File:** `packages/memory/src/mcp-server.ts`
**Anchor:** `const result = await store.indexJournal(db);` before `await server.connect(transport)` in runMemoryMcpServer
**Severity:** medium

The startup index runs to completion before the transport is connected, so the server cannot answer `initialize` until it finishes. `JournalStore`'s default encoder is `generateEntryEmbedding`, which calls `initEmbeddings()`; a single edited entry, a new entry, or a bumped `EMBEDDING_VERSION` is enough to reach it. On a cold cache that is a ~35 MB ONNX download whose own timeout is 180 seconds (`DEFAULT_INIT_TIMEOUT_MS`), and on a large journal it is one forward pass per entry after that.

Typical MCP client startup timeouts are far shorter, so the observable failure is "the server never connected", with the real cause visible only as the `Loading embedding model` line on stderr. The comment above the block reasons carefully about *failure* being non-fatal, which it is, but not about *latency*, which is the mode that actually bites. Connect the transport first and index in the background, or skip the index when nothing needs re-embedding without instantiating the encoder.

### CR-268: `both` mode returns up to twice the requested limit, in non-monotonic score order
**File:** `packages/memory/src/search.ts`
**Anchor:** `if (results.length > limit) { results = results.slice(0, limit); }` in searchConversations
**Severity:** medium

The trim to `limit` and the `ORDER BY vec.distance ASC` both happen inside the vector branch. The text branch then appends every deduplicated LIKE hit — itself capped at `limit` — to the already-trimmed array, with no second trim and no re-sort. So `both` yields up to `2 * limit` results, and the tail is ordered by timestamp rather than by score.

The MCP schema documents `limit` as "Maximum number of results to return (default: 10)" with `maximum: 50`, so a caller asking for 50 can get 100 exchanges back, which is a context-budget problem as well as a contract violation. `formatResults` then reports the inflated count as "Found N relevant conversations". Trim and re-sort after the merge.

### CR-269: `--before` silently discards the whole named day
**File:** `packages/memory/src/search.ts`
**Anchor:** `parts.push("e.timestamp <= ?")` in buildSearchFilters
**Severity:** medium

`e.timestamp` holds full ISO-8601 strings; the filter binds a bare `YYYY-MM-DD`. String comparison makes `2025-10-01T00:00:00.000Z <= 2025-10-01` false, so `--before 2025-10-01` excludes every exchange on 1 October, including one recorded at midnight UTC. `--after` has the mirror-image behaviour and includes the whole day, so the two flags are asymmetric and `--after D --before D` returns nothing at all — the obvious way to ask for a single day.

No test covers the date filters; there is no `test/search.test.ts`. Fix by appending a day-end suffix to `before` (or comparing on `date(e.timestamp)`).

Reproduced. Three rows at `2025-09-30T12:00:00Z`, `2025-10-01T00:00:00Z` and `2025-10-01T23:59:59Z`: no filter returns three, `before: "2025-10-01"` returns only the September row, `after: "2025-10-01"` returns both October rows.

### CR-270: The sidechain predicate consumes the KNN budget, so plain vector search under-returns
**File:** `packages/memory/src/search.ts`
**Anchor:** the clause "AND e.is_sidechain = 0" in searchConversations
**Severity:** medium

The vector query always filters `e.is_sidechain = 0`, and that predicate is applied after
vec0 has already cut to `k`. Nothing widens `k` for it: with no options at all,
`k = limit`. Sidechain exchanges are genuinely present in the table, because
`parseClaudeConversation` copies `isSidechain: parsed.isSidechain` onto every exchange and
`insertExchange` persists it. So whenever a sidechain row is among the `limit` nearest
vectors, the caller silently gets fewer results than it asked for, and the missing slots are
never refilled from the next-nearest non-sidechain rows.

Reproduced in the same scratchpad script: with the three nearest rows flagged as sidechain and
no filter options set, a `k=10` query returns 7 rows where 10 were expected.

Fix: either widen `k` for the sidechain predicate the way the metadata filters are meant to
be widened, or stop indexing sidechain exchanges so the predicate is unnecessary.

### CR-271: Text-only matches are reported as a 100% similarity match in the default search mode
**File:** `packages/memory/src/search.ts`
**Anchor:** the expression `similarity: mode === "text" ? undefined : l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity(row.distance)`
**Severity:** medium

The text branch selects a literal `0 as distance` so its rows share a shape with the vector
rows. The similarity is then suppressed only when `mode` is exactly `"text"`. In `"both"`
mode the text rows keep their placeholder distance of zero and go through the conversion, and
`l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity(0)` is 1. `formatResults` renders that as "100% match".

`"both"` is the default for both `searchConversations` and the `search_conversations` MCP
tool, so on the ordinary path every substring hit is presented to the model as a perfect
match, scored above real semantic neighbours that can never reach 1.0. The merge appends text
results after vector results without re-sorting, so the displayed ordering and the displayed
scores disagree.

Reproduced the conversion against the built dist: distance 0 yields similarity 1, which
`formatResults` prints as "100% match". I did not run a full `"both"` search, which needs the
encoder.

Fix: leave `similarity` undefined for rows that came from the text branch regardless of mode.
Tracking provenance per row rather than per query is the small change that makes this
expressible.

### CR-272: One truncated line makes a whole transcript unreadable
**File:** `packages/memory/src/show.ts`
**Anchor:** `const allMessages: ConversationMessage[] = lines.map((line) => JSON.parse(line));`
**Severity:** medium

Neither `formatConversationAsMarkdown` nor `formatConversationAsHTML` guards the per-line parse, so a single malformed line aborts the entire render. `parser.ts` wraps each line in `try {} catch {}` for exactly this reason, and `isCodexRollout` also tolerates unparseable lines.

The ordinary trigger is the live transcript: Claude Code appends to the session JSONL continuously, so reading the current session's file catches a partial final line and the tool fails outright instead of returning the complete turns that precede it. The same happens on any transcript truncated by a crash or a disk-full write. `read_conversation` surfaces it as `Error: Unterminated string in JSON at position …`, and `moe-memory show` exits 1. Skip unparseable lines the way the parser does.

Reproduced. A two-turn transcript renders (149 chars); the identical file with one truncated trailing line throws `SyntaxError: Unterminated string in JSON`.

### CR-273: One truncated line makes read_conversation fail on the whole transcript
**File:** `packages/memory/src/show.ts`
**Anchor:** `formatConversationAsMarkdown`, at "const allMessages: ConversationMessage[] = lines.map((line) => JSON.parse(line))"
**Severity:** medium

Both markdown and HTML formatters map an unguarded `JSON.parse` over every non-blank line, so
a single unparseable line throws a SyntaxError that abandons the entire file. Transcript
JSONL files are appended to by a live session, so a half-written trailing line is the normal
state of any transcript belonging to a session that is still running, which is exactly the
conversation a user is most likely to ask to read.
