`parser.ts` treats the same input correctly: its read loop wraps each line in a try/catch and
skips the bad ones. So the index can contain an exchange that `read_conversation` then refuses
to display. Through the MCP server the failure surfaces as an `isError` result carrying a raw
"Unterminated string in JSON at position 57" and no content; through `moe-memory show` it is
"Error reading file" and exit 1.

Reproduced against the built dist: a two-message transcript renders, and the same transcript
with one truncated trailing line throws SyntaxError.

Fix: parse per line inside a try/catch and drop unparseable lines, matching `parser.ts`. The
same change is needed at the two other unguarded `JSON.parse` map sites in this file, in the
HTML formatter and in the Codex entry path.

### CR-274: The HTML report escapes raw markup but emits live javascript: links
**File:** `packages/memory/src/show.ts`
**Anchor:** `renderMarkdownSafely`
**Severity:** medium

`renderMarkdownSafely` overrides `renderer.html` so raw HTML in a message becomes escaped
text, which shows the author intended the generated report to be safe to open. Link
destinations are not covered. Current marked does no scheme filtering, so a markdown link in
a transcript renders as an anchor with whatever scheme the text supplied.

The exposure path is the documented one: the show CLI help says
`moe-memory show --format html conversation.jsonl > output.html`, described as "Generate HTML
for browser viewing". Transcript content is not author-controlled. An assistant turn that
quotes a fetched page, a file, or a tool result can carry the link, and `isMarkdown` only
needs two markdown patterns present to route the text through the renderer.

Reproduced against the installed marked with the same renderer override the source uses.
Block and inline HTML are escaped as intended; the link case is not:

```
input:  **b** see [click](javascript:alert(document.domain)) and `c`
output: <p><strong>b</strong> see <a href="javascript:alert(document.domain)">click</a> and <code>c</code></p>
```

Fix: also override `renderer.link` and drop or neutralise any href whose scheme is not http,
https, or mailto. The suite's escaping test covers only the raw-markup half, and only on the
Codex path, so a link case should be added for both harnesses.

### CR-275: A dangling or vanished project entry aborts the whole sync walk before any project is synced
**File:** `packages/memory/src/sync.ts`
**Anchor:** `const stat = fs.statSync(projectPath);` in `syncConversations`
**Severity:** medium

The per-project loop stats each `readdirSync` entry with no guard, while the per-file loop inside it is carefully wrapped in try/catch. `fs.statSync` follows symlinks, so a dangling symlink under `~/.claude/projects` throws ENOENT and takes down the entire call. The same is true of a directory entry that disappears between the `readdirSync` and the `statSync`, which is a live race because sync runs from a SessionStart hook while harnesses are writing into that tree.

I reproduced the abort with a throwaway script under the scratchpad: a source directory containing `dangling -> /nonexistent-target` and `real-project/a.jsonl` aborts at the first entry with `ENOENT: no such file or directory, stat '.../dangling'`, and `real-project` is never reached. Because `readdirSync` returns entries in directory order, one bad entry can starve every real project.

The error propagates out of `syncConversations`, past `runSync`'s finally (the lock is released correctly), into `main`'s catch in `src/cli.ts`, which prints `Error: ENOENT...` and returns 1. Under `sync --background` that text goes only into the log file, so the user sees nothing and sync stays broken on every subsequent session start.

`verifyIndex` in `src/verify.ts` repeats the identical unguarded `statSync` on the archive walk.

Fix: use `readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` and test the entry type, or wrap the stat in try/catch and `continue`, matching the defensiveness the inner loop already has.

### CR-276: Typing the exclusion marker mid-conversation never removes what is already indexed
**File:** `packages/memory/src/sync.ts`
**Anchor:** `shouldSkipConversation` and "Skip indexing but file is already copied"
**Severity:** medium

Transcripts are append-only and sync re-copies them as they grow, so a long conversation is indexed incrementally across several sync runs. If the user types the marker partway through, the next run sees the marker and stops indexing, but every exchange already written to `exchanges`, `tool_calls` and `vec_exchanges` stays there and stays searchable forever.

There is no removal path: `grep -rn "deleteExchange" src/` shows the only caller is orphan pruning in `repairIndex`, keyed on the archive file being gone, and `DELETE FROM exchanges` appears once, inside `deleteExchange`. No CLI surface removes a conversation by path or session id.

The marker's own docblock frames it as a privacy control whose failure mode is silent, which is exactly what this is. Mid-conversation is the natural way to use a marker you only decide you need once the conversation has gone somewhere private, so a reader would not expect that case to be excluded.

Fix: when sync detects the marker on a file, delete the rows whose `archive_path` is that file (and optionally the archive copy) rather than only declining to add more.

### CR-277: verifyIndex reports a conversation with zero indexed exchanges as healthy
**File:** `packages/memory/src/verify.ts`
**Anchor:** `if (lastIndexed !== null) {` in `verifyIndex`
**Severity:** medium

`result.missing` means only "no summary file, or an error sentinel". The one check that looks at the index is guarded by `lastIndexed !== null`, and `getFileLastIndexed` returns null both when the file has never been indexed and when its rows carry no timestamp. So a conversation that was copied and summarized but whose indexing failed falls through every bucket: not missing, not outdated, not corrupted, not orphaned.

This is reachable through the ordinary error handling in `syncConversations`: the per-file catch inside the indexing loop records the error and moves on, while the summary loop later writes a real summary for the same file. From then on the conversation looks healthy to `--verify` and `--repair` skips it, so its exchanges are permanently absent from search with no diagnostic anywhere. The command whose entire job is finding index gaps cannot see the most basic one.

I confirmed the SQL semantics with a scratch better-sqlite3 script: no matching rows and rows with a NULL stamp both yield `{lastIndexed: null}`, indistinguishable from each other.

Fix: treat `lastIndexed === null` as its own finding ("conversation not indexed") and add it to `missing`, or add a not-indexed bucket. `repairIndex` already re-indexes everything in `missing`, so the repair side needs no change.

### CR-278: Verify reports an excluded project's existing files as orphaned, and repair deletes them
**File:** `packages/memory/src/verify.ts`
**Anchor:** `verifyIndex`, its foundFiles set and the orphan loop
**Severity:** medium

`verifyIndex` builds `foundFiles` only from projects that survive the exclusion check, then
reports every database row whose `archive_path` is not in that set as orphaned. Excluding a
project therefore reclassifies all of its already-indexed exchanges as orphans even though
their archive files are present and readable. `repairIndex` calls `deleteExchange` on every
orphan, so the follow-up repair silently drops that project's rows from both `exchanges` and
`vec_exchanges`.

Trigger: add a project to `CONVERSATION_SEARCH_EXCLUDE_PROJECTS` or to `exclude.txt`, then run
verify and repair. The same applies to the nested-directory exclusion, so excluding
`subagents` marks every previously indexed subagent exchange as orphaned. The verify report
gives no hint that the files exist, and re-indexing after removing the exclusion is a full
rebuild.

Reproduced with a script under the scratchpad: one archived conversation with a real summary
and one matching row yields zero orphans unexplained, and the same tree with the project
excluded yields one orphan whose path still exists on disk.

Fix: gather `foundFiles` from the whole archive and apply the exclusion only to the
summary, outdated, and corruption checks. If dropping an excluded project's rows is wanted,
it should be its own reported category with its own wording, not folded into orphan cleanup.

### CR-279: The exclusion-marker suite guards the predicate but no caller, so the marker can stop being enforced without a test failing
**File:** `packages/memory/test/exclusion-markers.test.ts`
**Anchor:** "This suite pins both forms offline, where they cannot be skipped."
**Severity:** medium

The docblock states the risk precisely: dropping the marker "does not fail loudly — it silently starts indexing every conversation someone had explicitly marked DO-NOT-INDEX". Every assertion in the file then tests only the two constants and `shouldSkipConversation` itself. Nothing asserts that any archive-writing or index-writing path consults the predicate.

That is the gap that lets the live defect above pass green: `repairIndex` and all three `src/indexer.ts` entry points already ignore the marker at this base SHA, and the unit project is entirely silent about it. The only caller-level coverage is `test/model/sync-indexing.test.ts`, which is in the opt-in `model` project that CI does not run.

Fix: add a caller-level test in the unit project. It does not need the encoder: build an archive containing one marked and one ordinary conversation, run `verifyIndex`, and assert the marked one is absent from `missing`. That single assertion fails today and would have caught the repair path.

### CR-280: The only test of the sync mutex passes even if every concurrent acquirer holds the lock at once
**File:** `packages/memory/test/file-lock.test.ts`
**Anchor:** "at most one of many concurrent acquirers ends up holding the lock"
**Severity:** medium

Eight subprocesses each print `HELD` or `SKIP`, and the assertions are that `heldCount` is at least one and that `heldCount + skipCount` equals N. Both hold if all eight children acquire simultaneously: heldCount would be 8, skipCount 0, the sum 8. The children report no timing, so overlap is unobservable and the mutual-exclusion property named in the title is not asserted at all.

This matters more than a normal weak assertion because the whole point of #97 was replacing a hand-rolled lock that could not guarantee mutual exclusion, and this is the only test that exercises real cross-process contention. The suite's other stale-recovery tests are genuinely good, so a regression in the mtime protocol would be caught; a regression in exclusion would not.

Fix: have each child write its acquire and release timestamps (or create and then remove a witness file whose prior existence it reports), then assert no two held intervals overlap.

### CR-281: Date-filter tests pass unchanged when the filter returns nothing
**File:** `packages/memory/test/model/integration.test.ts`
**Anchor:** the three tests under describe "Date Filtering"
**Severity:** medium

All three follow the shape `results.forEach((r) => { expect(...) })` with no assertion that
`results` is non-empty. A `forEach` over an empty array runs zero callbacks, so each test
passes when the filter returns nothing. The suite therefore asserts only "no returned row
violates the filter", never "rows that satisfy the filter are returned".

That is the exact blind spot the KNN-budget defect reported above occupies: a date-filtered
vector search that drops every matching row satisfies all three tests. The tests pass today
only because the fixture's exchange count stays under the default limit of 10, so the KNN cut
happens not to bite; growing the fixture or lowering the limit would make the production
defect real while the tests stayed green.

Fix: add `expect(results.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)` to each, and index exchanges on both
sides of a boundary so the filter has something to exclude and something to keep.

### CR-282: The unit test project is not offline: the single-instance suite downloads the embedding model
**File:** `packages/memory/vitest.config.ts`
**Anchor:** the comment "`pnpm test` is the CI-safe set: no network, no model, no Claude auth"
**Severity:** medium

`test/sync-cli-single-instance.test.ts` lives in the `unit` project and spawns the real
`dist/cli.js sync` four times. `runSync` calls `syncConversations(sourceDir, destDir)` with no
options, so `skipIndex` is falsy. The suite stages a transcript that gets copied, which makes
`filesToIndex` non-empty, which enters the indexing block and calls `initEmbeddings`. Each
test gets a fresh `MOE_MEMORY_CONFIG_DIR` from `mkdtempSync`, so `getModelCacheDir` resolves
to a new empty directory every time and the cache is always cold.

The result is that the project documented as needing no network fetches
`Xenova/bge-small-en-v1.5` on all four tests, and fails outright where the network is
unavailable, since "Sync complete" is never printed and the process exits 1.

Reproduced by driving the built CLI exactly as the suite does, with
`MOE_MEMORY_MODEL_INIT_TIMEOUT_MS=1` so the probe aborted before transferring anything (the
cache directory measured 0 bytes afterwards). On a fresh tree the run reaches "Loading
embedding model", never prints "Sync complete", and exits 1. A second run over the same tree
succeeds only because the file is already archived, so `filesToIndex` is empty and the encoder
is never reached, which is why this is easy to miss when re-running by hand.

Fix: pass `skipIndex: true` from the test by pointing it at a run that has nothing to index,
or give `runSync` a flag the test can set. The broader fix is the one the shard's other
findings also want: let `syncConversations` and `searchConversations` accept an injected
embed function so `fakeEmbed` from `test/test-utils.ts` can serve them.

### CR-283: MCP translation copies cwd, argument items, env values and headers through unvalidated, emitting schema-invalid output with no warning
**File:** `packages/mint/src/adapters/agent-plugins.ts`
**Anchor:** `translateMcpServer`, the line `if (typeof source.cwd === 'string') entry.cwd = source.cwd === '.' ? './' : source.cwd`
**Severity:** medium

The adapter validates some fields and not others. `command` gets `isValidStdioCommand` plus a warn-and-skip; reserved `env` keys get a warn-and-drop. But `cwd` is passed through verbatim apart from one special case, and `args` items, `env` values and `headers` values are copied with no type check at all. The vendored `schemas/agent-plugins-mcp.schema.json` anchors `cwd` on `^(?:\./|\$\{PLUGIN_ROOT\}(?:/|$)|\$\{PLUGIN_DATA\}(?:/|$))` and requires strings for `args` items, `env` values and `headers` values, so ordinary Claude Code input produces `mcp.json` that moe-mint's own `validate` rejects.

The adjacent comment shows this exact class was already hit once and fixed only for the single literal `"."`: "Passing it through verbatim meant valid input produced output that mint's own `validate` then rejected — caught by wiring packages/memory, whose .mcp.json says `\"cwd\": \".\"`". Every sibling case remains.

Reproduced. A `.mcp.json` with `"cwd": "servers/thing"`, `"cwd": "/opt/thing"`, `"cwd": "../../etc"`, `"args": ["--port", 8080]` and `"env": {"PORT": 8080}` generates cleanly, emitting all five verbatim with no warning mentioning any of them; `moe-mint validate` then exits 2 with `mcp.json/mcpServers/relative-cwd/cwd: must match pattern …` and the equivalent for each other server. Fix: normalise a bare relative `cwd` to `./`-prefixed form and warn-and-skip anything else, and apply the existing warn-and-skip treatment to non-string args, env values and headers.

### CR-284: Cursor, Codex and Kimi manifests point at a skills directory that does not exist when the plugin ships no skills
**File:** `packages/mint/src/adapters/cursor.ts`
**Anchor:** `pluginManifest`, the unconditional `manifest.skills = \`./${config.components.skills}/\``
**Severity:** medium

Three adapters write the skills pointer unconditionally: cursor's `pluginManifest`, and the same unguarded assignment in `codex.ts` and `kimi.ts`. The claude-code adapter guards it (`if (model.skills.length && config.components.skills !== 'skills')`), so the asymmetry is clearly unintended. A commands-only, hooks-only or MCP-only plugin therefore ships three manifests naming a directory that was never created, and `check_manifest_harness` correctly flags all three.

Reproduced with a config carrying only `name`, `version`, `description`, `bootstrap: none`. `generate` succeeds with no warning, no `skills/` directory is created, and the shallow tier fails:

```
not ok codex: .codex-plugin/plugin.json references missing path(s): ./skills/
not ok cursor: .cursor-plugin/plugin.json references missing path(s): ./skills/
not ok kimi: .kimi-plugin/plugin.json references missing path(s): ./skills/
EXIT=3
```

The deep tier already contemplates zero-skill plugins ("plugin has no skills to verify"), so this is a supported shape that fails its own gate. Fix: guard the assignment on `model.skills.length` in all three adapters.

### CR-285: Bump reserialises the whole JSON file, reformatting hand-maintained release files
**File:** `packages/mint/src/field-edit.ts`
**Anchor:** `writeField`, the JSON branch `writeFileSync(filePath, JSON.stringify(data, null, 2) + '\n')`
**Severity:** medium

The YAML branch below it goes to real trouble to edit surgically, using `parseDocument` and `doc.setIn` so comments and layout survive; the kitchen-sink fixture exists partly to pin that ("comment here guards bump's comment-preservation"). The JSON branch does the opposite: it parses, mutates, and reserialises at two-space indent, rewriting the entire file. `release.files` names non-generated files the plugin author maintains by hand, so every `moe-mint bump` produces a large spurious diff in them.

Reproduced. A `version.json` written at four-space indent with an inline `"keep": [1, 2, 3]`, declared as a `release.files` entry, came back after `moe-mint bump 0.2.0` reindented to two spaces with the array exploded one element per line. The reported change was only `0.1.0 -> 0.2.0`.

Fix: edit the JSON text surgically the way the YAML path does, or at minimum detect and preserve the file's existing indentation.

### CR-286: Generated-file containment is checked lexically, so a symlinked directory writes output outside the plugin root
**File:** `packages/mint/src/fileset.ts`
**Anchor:** `writeFileSet`, the guard `if (!abs.startsWith(rootAbs + sep))` and its message "generated file path escapes plugin root"
**Severity:** medium

`writeFileSet` resolves each path with `path.resolve` and compares strings. `resolve` is purely lexical: it normalises `..` but never consults the filesystem, so it cannot see a symlink. `writeFileSync` and `mkdirSync` both follow symlinks, so a symlinked directory anywhere inside the plugin root defeats the stated invariant.

Reproduced. With `<scratch>/symlink/.claude-plugin` symlinked to `<scratch>/outside`, `moe-mint generate --dir <scratch>/symlink` reported "Generated 19 files for 8 harness(es)" and wrote `plugin.json` and `marketplace.json` into `<scratch>/outside`, outside the plugin root, with no error. The prune loop in `generate.ts` applies the identical lexical test before `rmSync`, so deletion follows symlinks too.

The blast radius is bounded because reaching it needs pre-existing write access to the plugin tree, and the mint pipeline wipes each staging root before copying (`mint-plugins.mjs`, `fs.rmSync(dest, …)` then `copyInto`, whose `statSync` dereferences rather than reproducing links). But the guard exists precisely to make containment true, and it is not. Fix: compare `fs.realpathSync` of the parent directory against `realpathSync(root)`, or open with `O_NOFOLLOW`.

### CR-287: A UTF-8 BOM silently discards a component's whole frontmatter

**File:** `packages/mint/src/frontmatter.ts`
**Anchor:** `parseFrontmatter`

The delimiter regex is anchored with `^---`, so a leading U+FEFF makes it fail to match. `parseFrontmatter` then returns `data: {}` and a body that still contains the raw fence. Nothing warns; every downstream field degrades to a default.

Reproduced end-to-end through `generate`, with a BOM-prefixed `SKILL.md` and a BOM-prefixed command file:

- The generated `hooks/moe-mint/bootstrap.md` bullet came out as `- **alpha**: ` with an empty description. The description is the entire trigger signal the bootstrap exists to deliver, so the skill silently stops being invocable.
- The generated `.opencode/command/go.md` contained moe-mint's own frontmatter block followed by the source's BOM and a second, stray `---` block in the body, with `description` dropped from the real frontmatter.

BOMs are what several Windows editors and PowerShell redirections emit, and `AGENTS.md` routes Windows contributors through WSL2 while `.gitattributes` pins LF, so cross-platform authoring is expected. Fix: strip a leading BOM before matching (`src.replace(/^﻿/, '')`). A degenerate empty block (`---\n---\n`) also fails to match and leaks its fences into the body; the same relaxation is worth applying there.

**Severity:** medium

### CR-288: Exec-bit drift is asserted by checkDrift but never repaired by generate

**File:** `packages/mint/src/manifest.ts`
**Anchor:** `isExecutable`, used in `checkDrift`'s `checkExecBit && isExecutable(filePath) !== Boolean(entry.executable)`

`checkDrift` treats a mode mismatch as `modified`, but nothing enforces the mode in the false direction: `writeFileSet` chmods `0o755` only when `file.executable` is set, and `writeFileSync` over an existing file preserves its mode. So an exec bit that gets set out of band on a non-executable generated file is permanent drift that the tool advertises as fixable and cannot fix.

Reproduced against `dist/`: after `generate`, `validate.ok` was `true`; after `chmod 755 .claude-plugin/plugin.json`, drift reported that path as modified; a fresh `generate` produced no warnings, left the mode at 755, and `validate` still reported the same path as modified. The CLI's advice for that state is "regenerate, or move the change into harnesses.<name>.manifest", neither of which works, and the message never mentions the mode.

The environment where this bites without any `chmod` is the one AGENTS.md documents: `checkExecBit` defaults off only for `process.platform !== 'win32'`, but under WSL2 the platform is `linux`, and a repo kept on a DrvFs mount (`/mnt/c`) without metadata reports every file as mode 0777, so every manifest-tracked non-executable file reads as drifted. I reproduced the `chmod` path only, not the DrvFs mount.

Fix: have `writeFileSet` set the mode in both directions (`chmodSync(abs, file.executable ? 0o755 : 0o644)`), and distinguish content drift from mode drift in the reported reason so the CLI advice matches the cause.

**Severity:** medium

### CR-289: Component ordering uses locale collation, so generated output differs by machine

**File:** `packages/mint/src/model.ts`
**Anchor:** `readSkills`, `readMarkdownComponents` and `buildModel`'s agent sort, all `.sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))`

`localeCompare` with no locale argument resolves against the process's default locale, which comes from the environment. `readdirSync` order is not stable across filesystems, so this sort is the only thing making the emitted component order deterministic, and it is not machine-independent. AGENTS.md makes `/plugins/` byte-identity a CI gate (`pnpm mint:check` runs `pnpm mint` then `git diff --exit-code -- plugins`), so a mint run on an affected machine produces a reordered, non-reproducible tree.

Reproduced on this repo's live skill set (`ls packages/core/skills`, 37 entries, all ASCII): sorting under `lt-LT` swaps `subagent-driven-development` and `systematic-debugging` relative to `en-US`, because Lithuanian collation orders `y` right after `i`. Also confirmed that Node's default collator follows `LANG`/`LC_ALL` (`LANG=lt_LT.UTF-8` resolves to `lt-LT`), so no code change is needed to hit it.

Fix: compare code points (`a.name < b.name ? -1 : a.name > b.name ? 1 : 0`) or pin the collator (`localeCompare(b.name, 'en')`). A code-point sort produces the identical order to today's `en-US` result for the current skill set, so the fix is a no-op on committed output.

**Severity:** medium

### CR-290: validate schema-checks files by name whether or not moe-mint generated them

**File:** `packages/mint/src/validate.ts`
**Anchor:** `SCHEMA_TARGETS`

Each entry is matched by path and validated whenever the file merely exists (`if (!existsSync(filePath)) continue`), with no check that the path is one moe-mint actually emitted. `validate` already has that information: `checkDrift` loads the generation manifest immediately above. Two supported configurations therefore fail the documented CI gate on files the tool does not own and cannot fix.

Both reproduced against `dist/`:

- `components.mcp: mcp.json` (an explicitly supported setting; `test/generate.test.ts` has "does not warn about a stray root mcp.json when components.mcp is explicitly set to mcp.json", and the agent-plugins adapter deliberately skips emitting `mcp.json` in this case). With an ordinary Claude-shaped source config there, `generate` succeeded and drift was clean, while `validate` returned twelve schema errors against the user's own source file, including `mcp.json: must have required property '$schema'` and the `cwd` pattern error. The CLI exits 2. Renaming the source is the only way out.
- `harnesses.exclude: [agent-plugins-1.0]` plus a hand-written root `plugin.json` for an unrelated purpose: drift clean, and three schema errors against the Agent Plugins 1.0 plugin schema on a file no active adapter emitted.

Fix: skip a `SCHEMA_TARGETS` entry whose path is absent from the loaded manifest's `files`, so only moe-mint's own output is schema-checked.

**Severity:** medium

### CR-291: sandboxBin() omits two tools the checks script invokes, so the whole-script suites silently exercise a degraded script
**File:** `packages/mint/test/test-command.test.ts`
**Anchor:** `sandboxBin`
**Severity:** medium

`sandboxBin()` builds a PATH from an explicit tool list and is documented as making the checks suite "deterministic on any host". `checks/run-checks.sh` invokes `cut` (inside `oneline()`) and `mv` (inside `rewrite_market_source_local()`), and neither is in that list. The suite asserts only on `result.stdout` and `result.status`, never `result.stderr`, so the resulting failures are invisible.

Reproduced. I generated a kitchen-sink copy under the scratchpad with the committed `dist/cli.js`, then ran the real checks script twice with `env -i`, once with exactly the tools `sandboxBin()` symlinks and once with `cut` and `mv` added:

```
A exit: 0    B exit: 0
diff of stdout: (identical)
stderr A: run-checks.sh: line 88: mv: command not found
```

Every assertion in the suite passes either way. Two concrete consequences. First, `rewrite_market_source_local()` sets `MARKET_REWRITE_OK=1` in a statement separate from the failed `mv`, so the descriptor is never rewritten while the script reports the rewrite succeeded — the "skip, not a silent pass" contract this suite documents does not hold under its own PATH. Second, with `cut` absent `oneline()` emits nothing, so every check's detail text is blank, including the one the corrupted-manifest test exists to surface:

```
without cut: not ok codex: .codex-plugin/plugin.json is not valid JSON:
with cut:    not ok codex: .codex-plugin/plugin.json is not valid JSON: jq: parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 5
```

The test "exits 3 when a generated manifest is corrupted, with a matching not ok line" asserts only the `not ok codex:` prefix and the exit status, so it passes with the diagnostic gone.

Fix: add `cut` and `mv` to the tool list, make `sandboxBin()` throw when a listed tool cannot be found in the parent PATH instead of skipping it, and assert `result.stderr` is empty in the whole-script cases.

### CR-292: Symbol-resolution failure panics instead of returning an error, and the diagnostic is lost on the second call
**File:** `packages/tab/bindings/go/tab/loader.go`
**Anchor:** `ensureLoaded`
**Severity:** medium

`ensureLoaded` treats `purego.RegisterLibFunc` as fallible-by-return, but it is not: purego's `RegisterLibFunc` does `sym, err := loadSymbol(...); if err != nil { panic(err) }`. So a cdylib that is loadable but missing a symbol — exactly what a C ABI rename produces — panics out of `EstimatePath` rather than returning the `(*CostEstimate, error)` the package's whole error model promises. `loadErr` is never assigned on that path.

Worse, `sync.Once` records itself as done even when the function panics, so the second call gets `loadErr == nil` and immediately dereferences a nil function value. The first call at least carries purego's message; every call after that reports a bare nil-pointer dereference with no hint that the library failed to bind.

Reproduced with a standalone Go program that mirrors the structure (`purego.RegisterLibFunc`'s panic is confirmed by reading purego v0.10.1's `func.go`):

```
call 1 panicked: purego: symbol not found: moe_tab_estimate_path
call 2: ensureLoaded returned nil, invoking cFn (nil? true)
call 2 panicked: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
```

Fix: wrap each `RegisterLibFunc` in a `func() (err error) { defer func(){ if r := recover(); r != nil { err = fmt.Errorf(...) } }(); ... }()` helper and assign the result to `loadErr`, so a missing symbol becomes the documented error on every call.

### CR-293: pricing_source is dropped by the Go and Python result types, so callers cannot tell a bundled price sheet from a refreshed one
**File:** `packages/tab/bindings/go/tab/tab.go`
**Anchor:** `CostEstimate`
**Severity:** medium

The Rust core serializes `pricing_source` on every estimate (`moe-tab-core`'s `CostEstimate` carries it, and its own test asserts `v["pricing_source"] == "bundled"`). The TypeScript binding declares it and its comment records exactly why that matters: without it "TS consumers could not tell a bundled (possibly stale) price sheet from a refreshed one". The Go `CostEstimate` struct has no `PricingSource` field and `moe_tab/__init__.py`'s `CostEstimate.from_json` does not read one, so both silently discard it.

This is not a cosmetic omission. The core falls back to the compiled-in snapshot whenever no on-disk snapshot is present, and that fallback is the only signal that a cost figure came from prices baked in at build time. A Go or Python consumer reporting spend has no way to detect it.

Nothing catches the divergence: `scripts/validate-bindings.sh`, the only cross-language check, compares `total_usd` alone, and no Go or Python test asserts the field.

Fix: add `PricingSource string` with tag `json:"pricing_source"` to the Go struct and a `pricing_source: str` field to the Python dataclass, reading it in `from_json`.

### CR-294: An unresolvable MOE_TAB_LIB is silently ignored and a different library is loaded instead
**File:** `packages/tab/bindings/python/moe_tab/_lib.py`
**Anchor:** `_candidates`
**Severity:** medium

`_candidates()` yields the `MOE_TAB_LIB` path first, and `_load()` skips any candidate that fails `p.exists()`. An operator who sets the override to a path with a typo, or to a build that has since been cleaned, gets no error: the loader falls through to the package-local copy or to the in-tree `target/release` or `target/debug` build and loads that instead. Every subsequent estimate then comes from a library the operator did not select, and `moe_tab.version()` is the only visible clue.

The Go loader shows the intended contract for the same variable — `openLibrary` does `return dlopen(env)` with the comment "explicit override: no fallback". An explicit override that resolves to something else is the specific failure mode that makes an ABI-mismatch investigation intractable, which is why it matters here more than in most loaders. The TypeScript twin of this bug is in `lib-path.ts`, outside this shard.

Fix: when `MOE_TAB_LIB` is set, attempt only that path and raise the `OSError` naming it if it does not exist or does not load.

### CR-295: The Bun FFI backend has neither compile-time signature checking nor any test that runs it
**File:** `packages/tab/bindings/typescript/src/bun-ffi.d.ts`
**Anchor:** `BoundSymbol`
**Severity:** medium

`BoundSymbol` is declared as `(...args: FfiArg[]) => number`, so the `args` tuple each symbol declares is decorative — TypeScript derives no arity and no per-argument type from it. Real `bun-types` maps the `args` array onto the call signature, which is the only compile-time check that a Bun FFI call matches the C prototype.

Reproduced: I copied this file verbatim into a scratch project and compiled a caller against it under `strict`.

```
const a = symbols.moe_tab_estimate_path(new Uint8Array([120,0]));   // 1 of 3 args
const b = symbols.moe_tab_estimate_path(0, 0, 0, 0);                // 4 args, wrong types
$ tsc -p tsconfig.json ; echo $?
0
```

Both calls typecheck cleanly. That would be tolerable if something executed `ffi-bun.ts`, but nothing does: the vitest `unit` project excludes the FFI suite, the `ffi` project runs under Node and therefore takes the koffi branch (`ffi.ts` picks the backend from `typeof globalThis.Bun`), and `scripts/validate-bindings.sh` skips its bun leg when `bun` is not on PATH — which it is not in the pnpm/Node toolchain this repo pins. So a wrong-arity or wrong-type Bun call has no gate at all.

I separately verified with a probe under Bun 1.4 on darwin-arm64 that the mechanics `ffi-bun.ts` relies on are correct today: a `cstring` argument fed a `Buffer`, a `cstring` argument fed `null`, a `BigUint64Array(1)` out-parameter passed via `ptr()`, the `Number()` narrowing of the resulting bigint, and passing that plain number back as a pointer to the free. All behaved as the code assumes, and a non-ASCII UTF-8 payload round-tripped through `CString` intact. The defect is the missing enforcement, not the current call sites.

Fix: type `dlopen`'s return so each symbol's signature is derived from its `args`/`returns` tuple (a mapped type over `T[K]["args"]`), and add the bun leg of `validate-bindings.sh` to a gate that actually runs, or drop the Bun backend.

### CR-296: The TypeScript FFI suite is unreachable from every repo script and CI job

**File:** `packages/tab/bindings/typescript/vitest.config.ts`
**Anchor:** the comment sentence "`pnpm test:ffi` is opt-in and needs the cdylib built"
**Severity:** medium

The config splits the package into a toolchain-free `unit` project and an `ffi`
project that dlopens the cdylib, and the package's `test` script runs only
`--project unit`. Nothing then runs the `ffi` project. I grepped the tree
(excluding `node_modules`, `dist` and `.git`): `test:ffi` appears only in this
comment, in the package's own `package.json`, in the binding's README, and in
`packages/flight`. There is no turbo task for it, and the root script that
AGENTS.md credits with this coverage, `tab:test:bindings`, expands to
`pnpm tab:build && uv run --project packages/tab/bindings/python pytest packages/tab/bindings/python`
— the Python binding only. `scripts/validate-bindings.sh`, the script that
actually compares `total_usd` across the Rust CLI, Python, Go, Node and Bun, is
referenced only from prose (`docs/history/README.md`, the binding README, and
the header comment of `src/total.ts`) and is invoked by nothing. The CI `tab`
job runs `cargo test` and nothing else.

So the seam this shard is supposed to be guarding is unguarded on the
TypeScript side. If a C ABI symbol were renamed, the hand-written prototype
strings in `src/ffi-node.ts` and the `dlopen` symbol map in `src/ffi-bun.ts`
would still compile and typecheck, and no test that anyone runs would fail. The
Rust-side `header_matches_source` test keeps the committed header honest, and
the Python binding keeps one consumer honest; the other three consumers are on
the honour system. That directly contradicts the AGENTS.md claim that
`pnpm tab:test:bindings` "is the only check that the C ABI rename landed
identically in the Rust FFI, the committed header and all three bindings".

Fix: have `tab:test:bindings` also run `pnpm --filter @tc/moe-tab test:ffi`
after `pnpm tab:build`, or invoke `packages/tab/scripts/validate-bindings.sh`
and let it gate the consumers it already knows how to compare. Either way the
AGENTS.md sentence and the reality need to be brought back into agreement.

### CR-297: Untrusted token counts accumulate into u64 with no overflow guard

**File:** `packages/tab/crates/moe-tab-core/src/cost.rs`
**Anchor:** `estimate`, the accumulation "totals.input += u.input_uncached"
**Severity:** medium

`estimate` accumulates five `u64` buckets across every record with plain `+=`,
and both `per_model` entries do the same. The values come straight from
transcript JSON via `Value::as_u64`, which happily yields `u64::MAX`. The
workspace manifest declares no `[profile]` overrides, so `overflow-checks` is
on in debug and off in release. Debug therefore panics with "attempt to add
with overflow" and release wraps silently.

The first overflow point is even easier to reach: `step_usage` in
`transcript/atif.rs` computes `request_input_tokens: input_uncached +
cache_read + cache_write` per record, so a two-key trajectory step with
`"prompt_tokens": 18446744073709551615` and `"cached_tokens": 1` is enough. The
release-mode result is `request_input_tokens` wrapping to 0, which silently
flips tier selection in `cost_for` to the cheaper below-boundary rates, and
reported token totals that bear no relation to the input.

Through the FFI the panic is contained — `moe_tab_estimate_path` wraps
everything in `catch_unwind` and returns status 8 — so debug builds degrade
loudly. The CLI has no such net and aborts with a panic message instead of its
`error: ...` line. Release builds are the real problem, because they answer
wrongly and quietly.

Not reproduced: this needs a built binary and `cargo` is unavailable here. The
claim rests on the `+=` on `u64` fields declared in `model.rs`, the absence of
any `[profile]` section in `packages/tab/Cargo.toml`, and serde_json accepting
`u64::MAX` as `N::PosInt`.

Fix: use `saturating_add` for the accumulators (a saturated total is visibly
absurd rather than invisibly small), or validate each bucket against a sane
ceiling in the dialect parsers and reject with `TabError::MalformedTranscript`.

### CR-298: The 1h cache-write rate ignores the tier boundary, halving the charge above it

**File:** `packages/tab/crates/moe-tab-core/src/pricing/mod.rs`
**Anchor:** `cost_for`, the binding of r_cw1 from price.cache_write_1h.unwrap_or(price.cache_write)
**Severity:** medium

Every other rate in `cost_for` goes through the `pick` closure, which switches
to the `_above` rate when `request_input_tokens` exceeds `tier_boundary`. The
1h cache-write rate does not: it falls back to the *base* `cache_write` rate
even above the boundary, ignoring `cache_write_above`. The result is that the
same tokens are cheaper in the 1h bucket than in the 5m bucket, which inverts
the real price relationship — a 1h cache write is never cheaper than a 5m one.

The shipped snapshot makes this live. In `prices/bundled.json` there are 24
entries that carry a `tier_boundary`, a `cache_write_above` different from
`cache_write`, and a null `cache_write_1h`. Several are Anthropic models with a
200k boundary, which are precisely the models that can emit
`cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` and so populate `cache_write_1h`
through `provider::anthropic::normalize`.

Reproduced against the shipped rates for `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6`
(again mirroring `cost_for` in JavaScript; script at
`/private/tmp/claude-503/-Users-ZKeown-Code-moe/4556b327-b63b-49d4-bbc6-78cd4f317e00/scratchpad/shard-036/repro-1h-tier.js`):

```
1M 1h-cache-write tokens, 300k billed input (above the 200k boundary)
  as written (base 5m rate)         usd: 3.7500
  with the tier applied to the fallback usd: 7.5000
  identical tokens in the 5m bucket  usd: 7.5000
```

Fix: make the fallback tier-aware, `price.cache_write_1h.unwrap_or(pick(price.cache_write, price.cache_write_above))`.

A related shortfall is not fixable from the LiteLLM sheet and should just be
recorded: `ModelPrice` has no `cache_write_1h_above` field, so for a model that
*does* publish a 1h rate (`claude-sonnet-4-5` has `cache_write_1h` 6.0 with
`cache_write_above` 7.5) the 1h rate stays flat across the boundary. LiteLLM
publishes no combined "1hr above 200k" key, so a comment saying so belongs next
to `r_cw1`.

### CR-299: Neither price-sheet fetch sets a read timeout, so a refresh can hang forever

**File:** `packages/tab/crates/moe-tab-core/src/pricing/refresh.rs`
**Anchor:** `fetch_litellm` and fetch_openrouter, both ureq::get(...).call()
**Severity:** medium

Both fetches use the bare `ureq::get` shortcut, which runs on ureq's default
agent. I read the pinned crate source (`Cargo.lock` pins ureq 2.12.1; the
vendored copy is in the local cargo registry) and its default config is
`timeout_connect: Some(Duration::from_secs(30))` with `timeout_read: None`.
There is no overall `timeout` either. So a server or middlebox that completes
the TCP and TLS handshake and then stalls leaves the call blocked with no
deadline.

This is worse than a slow CLI. `moe_tab_refresh_pricing` is a synchronous C ABI
entry point, so the hang happens on the caller's thread: under the TypeScript
binding, `refresh()` in `bindings/typescript/src/index.ts` blocks the Node or
Bun event loop for as long as the peer holds the socket open, with no cancel
path. A captive-portal or hijacked-DNS network is enough to trigger it; no
malice is required.

Verified by reading the pinned crate's `src/agent.rs` defaults rather than by
running anything.

Fix: build one `ureq::AgentBuilder` with explicit `timeout_connect`,
`timeout_read` and an overall `timeout`, reuse it for both fetches, and map an
elapsed deadline to `TabError::Network`. While there, note that
`Response::into_string` caps a body at `INTO_STRING_LIMIT` (10 MiB in this
version) and errors above it; the LiteLLM sheet is the input most likely to
cross that line eventually, and today the failure would surface as an opaque
`Network` error.

### CR-300: A non-integer token count in an ATIF step silently becomes zero and drops the step

**File:** `packages/tab/crates/moe-tab-core/src/transcript/atif.rs`
**Anchor:** `step_usage`, the m closure over Value::as_u64
**Severity:** medium

`step_usage` reads every token bucket with `.and_then(Value::as_u64).unwrap_or(0)`.
I confirmed from the vendored serde_json 1.0.151 source that `Number::as_u64`
returns `None` for `N::Float` and `N::NegInt`, so a metric serialized as a JSON
float — `"prompt_tokens": 12.0`, which is what any Python normalizer that
divides, averages, or passes through numpy will emit — is read as zero. Strings
such as `"12"` behave the same way.

The consequence is not a small undercount. When every bucket reads zero and the
step has no `cost_usd`, the guard "No tokens AND no cost -> nothing to price for
this step" drops the step entirely. A whole trajectory of float-valued metrics
therefore yields no records at all, and `estimate` returns `total_usd` 0.0 with
an empty `unpriced_models` and an empty `approximations` list. There is no
error, no approximation, and nothing for a consumer to branch on: the answer is
a confident zero.

That is inconsistent with the rest of the parser's stance. `non_object_document_is_a_loud_error`
covers a bad document, and `transcript/tab.rs` calls an unrecognized schema
version "a loud error, not a silent mis-parse". A malformed number deserves the
same treatment.

I did not run this (no `cargo`); the claim rests on the serde_json source I
read plus the `unwrap_or(0)` and the early-return guard in this function.

Fix: read each metric through a helper that accepts an integral `Number` and
returns `Err(TabError::MalformedTranscript)` for a non-integral or negative one,
rather than folding every unparseable value into 0. The same closure shape
appears in `provider/anthropic.rs` and `provider/openai.rs` (the `g` and
`nested` closures) and in `transcript/tab.rs`; there the record survives with
zero tokens, so the model at least stays visible in `per_model`, but the silent
zero is the same.

### CR-301: Bundled price snapshot is overwritten before the guard that rejects it runs
**File:** `packages/tab/scripts/update-bundled-prices.sh`
**Anchor:** `cp "$TMPD/current.json" "$DEST"` preceding the heredoc that exits with "ERROR: openrouter namespace missing or empty"
**Severity:** medium

The script copies the freshly refreshed snapshot over the committed asset first, then validates it. When validation fails, the script exits 1 with the tree already mutated: `crates/moe-tab-core/prices/bundled.json` now holds the snapshot the script itself just declared invalid. The guard is defeated on exactly the path it exists for.

Reproduced. I copied the script into the scratchpad, put a stub `cargo` on PATH that writes a `current.json` with an empty `openrouter` namespace (the upstream-table-changed case the guard targets), and pointed the destination at a throwaway tree. Nothing in the repo was touched. The committed file went from a good snapshot to:

```
{"as_of":"2026-09-02","namespaces":{"litellm":{"m":1},"openrouter":{}}}
```

while the script printed `ERROR: openrouter namespace missing or empty` and exited 1.

Why it matters beyond a dirty tree: the bundled snapshot is the out-of-the-box pricing source, and `cost::estimate` in `crates/moe-tab-core/src/cost.rs` charges 0.0 for any model it cannot find, recording it in `unpriced_models`. Committing an empty-openrouter bundle silently zero-prices every OpenRouter model for every consumer that has not run a refresh. The same window is open for a schema change, since `d["namespaces"]` raises `KeyError` after the copy too.

Fix: validate `$TMPD/current.json` and only `cp` on success. The Python block already takes the path as `sys.argv[1]`, so it is a two-line reorder.

### CR-302: Gate exports MOE_TAB_LIB without asserting it exists, and two of three bindings silently load a different library
**File:** `packages/tab/scripts/validate-bindings.sh`
**Anchor:** `export MOE_TAB_LIB="$LIBDIR/$LIBNAME"`
**Severity:** medium

The script pins every consumer to one library by exporting `MOE_TAB_LIB`, then never checks the file is there. The three bindings disagree on what a set-but-broken override means, so the gate can compare consumers that loaded different builds.

- `bindings/go/tab/loader.go`'s `openLibrary` does `return dlopen(env)` with the comment "explicit override: no fallback" — a broken override is a hard error. Correct.
- `bindings/python/moe_tab/_lib.py`'s `_candidates` yields the override but only takes it `if p.exists()`, then falls through to `target/release` and `target/debug`.
- `bindings/typescript/src/lib-path.ts`'s `resolveLibPath` does `if (existsSync(env)) return env;` and otherwise falls through to `native/<platform>-<arch>`, then `target/release`, then `target/debug`.

Reproduced on this checkout at the base SHA: with `MOE_TAB_LIB=/nonexistent/libmoe_tab_ffi.dylib`, I executed the module-level portion of `_lib.py` and printed the candidate walk. It skips the override, skips the package-local copy, and resolves to `packages/tab/target/release/libmoe_tab_ffi.dylib`, which exists here while `target/debug/libmoe_tab_ffi.dylib` does not. So Python would silently price against a stale release build.

The trigger is a `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` in the environment or a `[build] target-dir` in a user or system `.cargo/config.toml`, both common on machines with a shared cargo cache. `cargo build` then writes elsewhere, `$ROOT/target/debug/...` never appears, and the script proceeds: Go fails loudly with a dlopen error while Python and TypeScript quietly load whatever is left in `target/`. The reported mismatch points at Go, when the fault is that the other two loaded the wrong file. Note the Rust CLI leg is immune either way, because `cargo run -p moe-tab-cli` links `moe-tab-core` statically and never opens the cdylib — so the reference value in the comparison is always fresh while the binding values may not be.

Fix: `[ -f "$MOE_TAB_LIB" ] || { echo "MOE_TAB_LIB not built: $MOE_TAB_LIB" >&2; exit 1; }` right after the export. Separately, Python and TypeScript should adopt Go's semantics and fail on a set-but-missing override rather than substituting a different library.

### CR-303: The moe-proof distribution carries no MIT license text or upstream copyright notice
**File:** `py/proof/pyproject.toml`
**Anchor:** the two adjacent keys "license = MIT" and `license-files = []`
**Severity:** medium

PARITY.md records `py/proof` as derived from `smevals` at `0c28dc6` under MIT, and NOTICE
carries "Copyright (c) 2026 Prime Radiant, Inc.; authored by Simon Willison". MIT requires
that the copyright notice and permission notice travel with all copies and substantial
portions. A wheel or sdist built from this pyproject carries the `MIT` metadata expression
and nothing else: `license-files = []` explicitly opts out of the default license-file globs,
and there is no LICENSE or COPYING file anywhere under `py/proof` for those globs to have
found. AGENTS.md repo law states that "generated distributions carry applicable license terms"
and that `pnpm provenance` checks their completeness, but neither
`scripts/check-provenance.mjs` nor `scripts/check-downstream-scope.mjs` mentions `py/proof` or
any `py/` path, so no gate covers this artifact.

Verified by grep, not by building a wheel: neither script contains the string `proof` or
`py/`, and `find py -iname 'LICENSE*' -o -iname 'COPYING*'` returns only paths inside the
gitignored `.venv`.

Fix: add the MIT text with the upstream copyright line to `py/proof/LICENSE` and drop the
`license-files = []` override so the default globs pick it up, or list the file explicitly.
Extend `pnpm provenance` to cover `py/proof` so the omission cannot recur silently.

### CR-304: Two task files sharing one task name silently execute only one of them
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/cli.py`
**Anchor:** the scheduling dict in `run`, keyed as "remaining[(task['name'], model)]"
**Severity:** medium

`run` selects tasks by file stem (`-t` matches `p.stem`) but schedules them by the `name`
field inside the YAML. `remaining` is keyed on `(task["name"], model)`, so two task files
whose documents carry the same `name` collapse to one entry. The scheduling loop iterates
`task_docs`, decrements the shared counter for the first file, and then hits `if not
remaining[...]: continue` for the second, skipping it entirely. Nothing validates that task
names are unique, and the run directory layout would collide for them anyway.

Reproduced. An eval with `tasks/easy.yaml` and `tasks/hard.yaml` both declaring
`name: shared` produced exactly one run directory; the recorded `task.prompt` was
`easy variant` and the `hard variant` task was never executed. The command printed one `ok`
line and exited zero.

Fix: reject duplicate task names when `task_docs` is loaded, naming both files, the same way
`resolve_eval_slugs` already rejects duplicate eval slugs. Alternatively key `remaining` on
the task file path and slugify the name for the directory, but the duplicate-name check is
what a reader needs, because the two tasks cannot have distinct run directories.

### CR-305: Distinct model identifiers that share a slug share a run directory, so `-n` counts the wrong model's runs
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/cli.py`
**Anchor:** `count_existing_runs`, "parent = runs_root / task_name / config_name / slugify(model)"
**Severity:** medium

`slugify` is not injective. Both `openai/gpt-4` and `openai:gpt-4` map to `openai-gpt-4`, as
do `gpt 4` and `gpt-4`. `execute_run` and `count_existing_runs` both address the run
directory by the slug, so runs for one model identifier are counted as runs for the other.
Under `-n` the shortfall for a model that has never been run is computed as zero, and the
command reports the target already met.

Reproduced. `run EVAL -m openai/gpt-4 -n 2` created two runs under `openai-gpt-4/`. The
follow-up `run EVAL -m openai:gpt-4 -n 2` printed
`t / default / openai:gpt-4: already have 2 run(s)` and executed nothing. Both `run.yaml`
files record `openai/gpt-4`, so `report` shows a leaderboard row for `openai/gpt-4` with two
runs and no row at all for `openai:gpt-4`, which the operator asked to evaluate.

Fix: `count_existing_runs` must confirm the model, not the directory. Read each candidate
`run.yaml` and compare its `config.model` against the requested model, or append a short
digest of the exact model string to the slugged directory name so distinct identifiers get
distinct directories.

### CR-306: A task name is used raw as a path component, so a run can be written outside the runs root
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/cli.py`
**Anchor:** `execute_run`, "parent = runs_root / task['name'] / config_name / slugify(model)"
**Severity:** medium

The model name is slugified before it becomes a directory and the eval name is slugified
before it becomes an external runs namespace, but the task name is interpolated verbatim.
`run_dir.mkdir(parents=True)` then creates whatever that resolves to. A task name containing
a path separator creates unintended nesting, and one containing `..` escapes `runs_root`
altogether. The escaped run is not a containment breach of anything the operator did not
already control, but it is silent evidence loss: `grade`, `report`, and `site.collect_eval`
all enumerate `runs_root.rglob("run.yaml")` and will never see it. reference.md documents
only that "The model name is slugified for the path", so a grader author has no reason to
expect the task name to be treated differently.

Reproduced. A task declaring `name: "../../escaped"` produced
`... ok (0.1s) -> wk2/escaped/default/m/2026-09-02T15-33-56Z`, two levels above the eval
directory, and reported success. A later `grade` on that eval finds no runs.

Fix: slugify the task name for the directory component exactly as the model name is
slugified, keeping the exact name in `run.yaml` where it already lives, and assert the
resolved `run_dir` is under `runs_root` before creating it.

### CR-307: The `contains` built-in raises FileNotFoundError instead of failing the check when output.txt is absent
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/cli.py`
**Anchor:** `check_contains`, "if value in (run_dir / 'output.txt').read_text()"
**Severity:** medium

`check_contains` reads output.txt with no existence check. Its sibling `check_xml_valid`
handles the same situation cleanly and returns `{"notes": "no such file: ..."}`. Runs that
lack output.txt are an anticipated shape, not a hypothetical: `run_failed` carries the
comment "Missing exit_code (e.g. imported runs) is treated as success", `grade_run` notes
that "Older run.yaml files recorded just the task name", and `site.collect_eval` reads an
`imported_from` key. Such a run is graded, reaches `contains`, and takes down the whole
`grade` invocation.

Reproduced. I hand-wrote a run directory containing only a `run.yaml` with `imported_from`
set and no `exit_code`, then ran `grade`. It exited 1 with an uncaught
`FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: .../output.txt` rather than
recording a failed check, so the remaining runs in the tree were never graded.

Fix: return `False, {"notes": "no such file: output.txt"}` when the file is missing, matching
`check_xml_valid`.

### CR-308: A list-valued `creates` never reaches the checker's environment
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/cli.py`
**Anchor:** `scalar_env_vars`, docstring "Scalar mapping values as env vars"
**Severity:** medium

`grade_run` accepts `creates` as either a string or a list, via
`names = [promised] if isinstance(promised, str) else promised`, and reference.md documents
it as "a filename, or list of filenames" followed by "All other keys are configuration for
the Checker, passed through via environment variables." But `scalar_env_vars` keeps only
`str`, `int`, `float`, and `bool` values, so a list-valued `creates` is dropped and
`MOE_PROOF_CHECK_CREATES` is never set. The core still asserts the promised files exist,
which is why the gap is invisible in the suite: `test_creates_missing_file_fails_check`
passes a list but drives the checker through a separate `write:` key.

This is not theoretical for the shipped examples. `examples/pelican-riding-a-bicycle/checkers/render-svg`
runs under `set -euo pipefail` and writes to `"$MOE_PROOF_CHECK_CREATES"`, and
`examples/pelican-riding-a-bicycle/checkers/extract-svg` reads
`MOE_PROOF_CHECK_CREATES` with a hardcoded default. Both silently depend on `creates` being
scalar.

Reproduced. With a checker shaped like `render-svg`, `creates: a.txt` graded ok. Changing
only that key to `creates: [a.txt, b.txt]` failed the check with
`MOE_PROOF_CHECK_CREATES: unbound variable`.

Fix: serialize list values for the env pass-through, or state in reference.md that a
list-valued `creates` is not exposed to the checker environment and have `grade_run` reject
the combination.

### CR-309: A checker emitting a non-numeric score or metric crashes the run instead of failing the check
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/cli.py`
**Anchor:** `normalize_check_info`, "out['score'] = float(info['score'])"
**Severity:** medium

`normalize_check_info` is the documented trust boundary for checker output. Its docstring
says "Anything else is folded into details rather than trusted at the top level, so
core-owned keys can never be clobbered", and `test_core_keys_cannot_be_clobbered` covers the
key-clobbering half. The value half is not covered: `score` is passed straight to `float()`,
and `metrics` is accepted as any dict whose values are never checked despite the docstring
promising "metrics (dict of name -> number|bool)".

Reproduced by calling the function directly. `{"score": "high"}` raises
`ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'high'` and `{"score": [1]}` raises
`TypeError`. Both propagate out of `grade_run` and abort the whole `grade` invocation, losing
grades for every run after the offending one. A string metric survives normalization and then
detonates later instead: `render_model_blocks` does `mean_stderr([float(v) for v in values])`,
so the bad value crashes `report` rather than `grade`.

Fix: coerce inside a try block in `normalize_check_info`. On failure, drop the key and record
the raw value under `details` with a note, which is the treatment every other malformed field
already gets. Filter `metrics` to `int`, `float`, and `bool` values in the same pass.

### CR-310: A checker score is never range-checked, so an unnormalized judge score clears every threshold
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/cli.py`
**Anchor:** `normalize_check_info`, docstring "score (float 0-1)"
**Severity:** medium

The check result contract fixes scores at 0.0 to 1.0. The pelican grader restates it in a
comment: "Scores are normalized 0.0-1.0 per the check result contract." Nothing enforces it.
`normalize_check_info` coerces to float and stores whatever it gets, `grade_run` compares it
against `pass_threshold` with `score >= threshold`, and `render_leaderboard` averages it.

Reproduced by calling the function directly: `{"score": 10}` yields `{"score": 10.0}` and
`{"score": -5}` yields `{"score": -5.0}`, both accepted without complaint. The realistic
trigger is a judge checker that forgets to divide: both shipped LLM judges ask the model for
an integer 0 to 10 and normalize with `judged["score"] / 10`. Drop that division and every
grade passes any threshold and the leaderboard mean is inflated tenfold, with no error
anywhere. For an eval harness, a silently wrong score is the worst failure mode available.

Fix: reject or clamp out-of-range scores in `normalize_check_info`, and record the raw value
under `details` plus a note so the grade shows what the checker actually emitted.

### CR-311: The live server hands model-authored HTML artifacts to the browser as text/html
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/site.py`
**Anchor:** `serve_eval`, "ctype = mimetypes.guess_type(target.name)[0] or 'text/plain; charset=utf-8'"
**Severity:** medium

Run and grade artifacts are produced by the model under evaluation and by checkers, which is
exactly the untrusted side of an eval harness. `serve_eval` guesses a Content-Type from the
filename and sends the bytes with no `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, no
`Content-Disposition`, and no CSP. A `.html` artifact is therefore served as `text/html` from
the same origin as the report app, where script in it can read `/index.json` and every
`/evals/<slug>/eval.json` and any file under any served eval's runs tree, then post them
elsewhere. A run artifact named `page.html` is ordinary output for a task that asks a model
for a web page, and the app's own "open raw" link navigates to it.

Reproduced. I served a fabricated eval whose run directory held a `page.html` containing a
script tag, and requested it. The response was `200` with `Content-Type: text/html` and the
script body intact.

Fix: send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on every artifact response, and restrict the
guessed type to an allowlist of types that cannot execute (text, images, PDF), falling back
to `text/plain` or `application/octet-stream` with
`Content-Disposition: attachment` for everything else. Keeping the default bind at 127.0.0.1
limits the blast radius but does not close it, since `--host` widens it.

### CR-312: The live server never percent-decodes the request path, so artifacts under a name with a space are unreachable
**File:** `py/proof/src/moe_proof/site.py`
**Anchor:** `do_GET`, "path = self.path.split('?')[0]"
**Severity:** medium

The request target is treated as a filesystem path with no percent-decoding anywhere. That is
what makes the traversal guard hold against encoded dot segments, but it also means any run
path containing a character the browser must encode can never be fetched. Task names are used
verbatim as directory components and are never slugified, so a task named `sonnet 18` is
enough. `app.html` compounds it: `runURL` and `gradeURL` interpolate the run path and filename
without `encodeURIComponent`, so the app emits a URL the browser then encodes on its behalf.

Reproduced. Serving an eval with a task named `sonnet 18`, `collect_eval` reported the run
path as `sonnet 18/default/m/2026-01-01T00-00-00Z`. The unencoded form cannot even be sent
(`http.client` rejects the space), and the form a browser actually sends,
`/evals/demo/runs/sonnet%2018/default/m/2026-01-01T00-00-00Z/output.txt`, returned `404 not
found`. Every artifact for that task is invisible in the file viewer. `%`, `#`, `+`, and any
non-ASCII character in a task name or checker-written filename fail the same way. The suite
does not catch it because `write_run` only ever uses ASCII-safe names.

Fix: `urllib.parse.unquote` the path once in `do_GET` before splitting it, keeping the
existing `is_relative_to` containment check, which is what actually stops traversal. Encode
each path segment in `runURL` and `gradeURL` on the client side.

### CR-313: Attribution register comparison ignores revision and license, checking only the name column
**File:** `scripts/check-provenance.mjs`
**Anchor:** `checkAttributionRegister`
**Severity:** medium

Both tables carry four columns; PARITY.md's Map has upstream repo, pinned revision, date, license status and destination, and NOTICE's imported works has project, revision, license and copyright. `tableNames` extracts the first cell only, and the checker compares the two name sets in both directions and nothing else. AGENTS.md says a changed pinned revision belongs in PARITY.md and NOTICE, and calls `pnpm provenance` the check on their completeness, so revision divergence between the two surfaces is exactly the failure this gate reads as covered. I reproduced it: with PARITY.md and NOTICE copied to a temp root and NOTICE's superpowers row rewritten from MIT at b36e082 to Apache-2.0 at deadbee, the checker prints "provenance: legal metadata and generated payloads are complete" and exits 0. This also matters downstream, because the mint generator reads the NOTICE license column to decide which license text a plugin ships. Compare the revision and license cells for every shared name, not just membership.

### CR-314: A plugin config with no license line disables both license-terms checks silently
**File:** `scripts/check-provenance.mjs`
**Anchor:** `checkPluginLicenses`
**Severity:** medium

The expression comes from a single regex over the mint config and falls back to the empty string when no top-level license line matches; both content assertions are then guarded by `expression.includes(...)` and neither runs. So the only check that a generated plugin's LICENSE payload matches its declared SPDX expression evaporates without a word. The trigger is reachable rather than theoretical: mint's own config schema declares the field optional, so a new plugin can be minted with no license at all, and an indented or otherwise non-anchored license line has the same effect. Any expression outside MIT and Apache-2.0 is equally unverified. I reproduced it by adding a plugin directory whose config contains only a name and whose LICENSE contains the word "hello"; the checker counted two plugin licenses and reported the payloads complete. Fail when no expression is found, and fail for an expression with no corresponding terms assertion.

### CR-315: The mint task does not declare the legal files its license generator reads
**File:** `scripts/mint-plugins.mjs`
**Anchor:** `writePluginLicense`, which reads NOTICE, PARITY.md, LICENSE and LICENSE-MIT
**Severity:** medium

Generating a plugin's LICENSE reads four repository-root files: NOTICE for the attribution rows, PARITY.md for destinations, and LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE for the terms text. The turbo task that runs this script declares an explicit input list covering the script itself, the marketplace descriptor, the skill tiers file, the per-package mint configs and the staged component trees, and none of those four files appear in it, while the task declares the whole plugins tree as its output. So after a NOTICE edit the cache key is unchanged: `pnpm mint` reports a hit and restores the previous generated tree, overwriting a correct LICENSE with a stale one. The CI gate forces execution, so it regenerates and fails with "plugins/ is not reproducible from source", a message that blames a hand edit and directs the developer to run the command that just restored the stale bytes. I did not run this, because doing so would write into the tracked plugins tree. Add NOTICE, PARITY.md, LICENSE and LICENSE-MIT to the task's inputs.

### CR-316: Linux native payloads receive header-only validation, with no ABI export or build-path check
**File:** `scripts/tab-native.mjs`
**Anchor:** `inspectTabNativeBytes`, the else branch that only reads the ELF class, type and machine
**Severity:** medium

For darwin targets the inspector calls `inspectDarwinReleaseBytes`, which requires exactly one relocatable install name, scans for `FORBIDDEN_DARWIN_PATHS`, and requires all four symbols in `TAB_NATIVE_ABI_EXPORTS`. For linux targets it verifies the ELF magic, 64-bit little-endian class, shared-object type and machine, and stops. Since `assertPackedTabPayload` reaches the shipped bytes only through this function, the four C ABI exports are never verified in either Linux artifact that goes to the registry, and AGENTS.md calls the C ABI rename the load-bearing one. The linux-dir default is a repo-root `.tc-tab-native`, which is exactly the sort of leftover that survives a branch switch, and pack accepts whatever ELF files it finds there. The mitigation is out of band: the CI build script links a smoke program against both stripped libraries, and that program references all four symbols, so a same-pipeline build would fail earlier. Nothing links the pack-time check to that job's output, and the Linux build sets no path-remapping flags, so the embedded cargo registry path that the darwin scan forbids is present in the Linux libraries and unexamined. Apply the export scan to both families, and apply a path scan appropriate to the Linux build.

### CR-317: Unparseable tar mode output makes the executable-bit assertion self-fulfilling
**File:** `scripts/tc-release-compose.mjs`
**Anchor:** `inspectPluginTarball`, at the comment "Injected command runners in release-policy tests return the historical path-only listing"
**Severity:** medium

When the verbose listing yields no parseable mode for any entry, the inspector fabricates a mode table: 0644 for every file, then 0755 for every path in `REQUIRED_EXECUTABLE_PLUGIN_FILES` that the archive happens to contain. `assertExecutableFiles` then checks the fabricated table against the same list it was derived from, so it can only pass. The branch exists to accommodate test doubles, but it lives in the production path used to verify the final tarball, and the executable bit on the hook launcher and the browsing helpers is the thing it guards. The trigger is any tar whose first verbose column is not a ten-character symbolic mode; parsing is all-or-nothing, so a per-entry failure fails shut while a wholesale one fails open. I reproduced it against a real gzipped tarball: with the honest runner the inspector reports mode 420 for a 0644 run-hook.cmd, and with a runner that prefixes each listing line (making the mode column unparseable) the same file is reported as 493. Model the historical path-only listing in the test doubles instead, and treat an unparseable listing as an error.

### CR-318: The two composed plugin artifacts are exempt from every license assertion in the release train
**File:** `scripts/tc-release-pack.mjs`
**Anchor:** `EXPECTED_RELEASE_PACKAGES` entries for @tc/moe-glass and @tc/moe-memory
**Severity:** medium

Six of the eight release entries carry a `directLicense` or `license` field; the glass and memory entries carry neither. Two consequences follow. `assertPackedManifest` computes its expected license from those fields and skips the comparison when both are absent, so the packed manifest's declared license is never checked for these two packages. And `assertDirectLegalPayload` only runs under `directLicense`, so their LICENSE bytes are never compared to a canonical root file. What remains is the existence check in `REQUIRED_PLUGIN_FILES`, which lists LICENSE among the common plugin files. That is precisely the assertion an inherited license satisfies: the comment opening `scripts/tc-release-legal.mjs` records that packing in this monorepo makes a package silently inherit the repository's Apache license, and the seed tarball for these two is packed the same way. Today the overlay copies the mint-generated MIT text over it and the committed payloads are correct (I checked both begin "MIT License"), so this is a missing gate rather than a live mislicensing. Nothing in the suite covers it either: the compose fixtures write the literal string "fixture" as the LICENSE body. Give both entries an expected license expression and compare their LICENSE bytes against the generated plugin payload.

### CR-319: Three publishable packages have no files allowlist, so build-cache logs ship and packed bytes vary per job
**File:** `scripts/tc-release-pack.mjs`
**Anchor:** `assertPackedEntrypoints`, which verifies entrypoint existence but never an expected file set
**Severity:** medium

The pack pipeline verifies the shape of every archive path and that each declared entrypoint exists, but never asserts an expected file set. Core, crew and backstory declare no `files` array, so their tarball is whatever the packing job's working tree holds minus the packer's built-in exclusions, and the repository-root gitignore does not apply inside a package directory. I reproduced the effect with a dry-run pack of the core package: 362 files, including `.turbo/turbo-test.log` and `.turbo/turbo-typecheck.log`, plus 134 files under the test directory, for 2.52 MB unpacked. In the release job the build step runs immediately before packing, so the published artifact carries that job's turbo task log. The operational consequence is worse than bloat. The publisher hashes each local tarball and compares it to the registry's recorded integrity, and hard-fails with "registry integrity mismatch" when an existing exact version has different bytes; immutable versions make that unrecoverable without a new tcRelease. So a pipeline retry that re-packs, with a different set of turbo tasks having run, can permanently block the resume path the publisher was written to support. The two composed plugin tarballs are canonicalised into byte-stable form precisely to avoid this; the directly packed ones are not. Give each package an explicit files allowlist and assert the packed file set.

### CR-320: The build task's declared outputs miss the second directory flight-ui emits, so a cache hit yields an incomplete build
**File:** `turbo.json`
**Anchor:** the build task, outputs declared as `dist/**`
**Severity:** medium

`outputs` is a single repo-wide `dist/**`. `packages/flight/ui` has `build` set to two vite invocations, and `vite.static.config.ts` sets `outDir: "dist-static"` with `emptyOutDir: true`. That directory is not covered by `dist/**`, so turbo neither saves nor restores it. `packages/flight/tsconfig.json` records why it matters: flight "consumes its BUILD OUTPUT by file path (`ui/dist`, `ui/dist-static/static.html`), never its types".

Remove the static output and rebuild with a warm cache and turbo replays a hit, restores `dist/**`, and leaves the static bundle absent. The compensating check lives downstream in flight's own copy step, not here.

The same directory is also missing from `.gitignore`, which ignores `dist/` and enumerates seven tab-specific exceptions but not this one. I confirmed with `git check-ignore` that `packages/flight/ui/dist-static` is not ignored. Turbo's default inputs enumerate tracked plus untracked-and-unignored files, so building once changes the ui package's own input hash and the next `build` misses; and a `git add -A` after a build stages the bundle.

I did not reproduce by building, which the shard constraints forbid. CI is unaffected today because no remote cache is configured and the GitLab cache carries only `.pnpm-store`, so every job starts cold. Fix: add `dist-static/**` to `build.outputs` and add the directory to `.gitignore`.

### CR-321: The typecheck task emits into the build task's output directory with no ordering edge between them
**File:** `turbo.json`
**Anchor:** the typecheck task, dependsOn of ^build with empty `outputs`
**Severity:** medium

Seven packages set `typecheck` to `tsc -b --pretty` against a composite config that inherits `composite`, `declaration` and `declarationMap` from `tsconfig.base.json` and sets `outDir: dist`. So `typecheck` emits JavaScript, declarations and a `.tsbuildinfo` into exactly the tree `build` claims as its output, while declaring no outputs of its own.

`typecheck` depends on `^build`, meaning its dependencies' builds, not its own package's build. There is therefore no edge between a package's `typecheck` and its own `build`. AGENTS.md documents `turbo run typecheck test --filter=@tc/moe-crew` for scoping a package; in that single invocation crew's `test` pulls in crew's `build` (which is `tsc -b && tsup`) while crew's `typecheck` is free to start immediately. Two `tsc -b` processes then compile one project concurrently with no locking, interleaving writes to the same emitted files and the same `.tsbuildinfo`. A `.tsbuildinfo` that is newer than the sources but describes a partial build makes the following `tsc -b` skip work it should have done.

I did not reproduce this; running builds writes into the tree. It follows from the task graph and the package scripts. Fix: give `typecheck` `dependsOn: ["build"]` so it follows its own package's build, or point the package `typecheck` scripts at non-emitting companion configs the way `packages/core` and `packages/flight/ui` already do.

## Low

### CR-071: Exchanges are indexed against a never-refreshed archive, so cited line ranges point past its end
**File:** `packages/memory/src/indexer.ts`
**Anchor:** `if (!fs.existsSync(archivePath))` guarding the copyFileSync in indexConversations
**Severity:** low

`indexConversations` copies a transcript into the archive only when the archive does not yet exist, then parses the **live source** and stores `lineStart`/`lineEnd` from that parse against `archive_path`. Transcripts are appended to for the life of a session, so every exchange added after the archive was first taken is recorded with line numbers that do not exist in the file the row points at.

`read_conversation` is the tool whose stated purpose is fetching the full context behind a search hit, and it is handed exactly that path and range by `formatResults` ("Lines 3-4 in <archive>"). It returns an empty string.

`--rebuild` makes this the steady state rather than a transient: it deletes the database and the summary sentinels but never the archives, so the next index pass sees an existing archive for every conversation. `indexUnprocessed` has a partial guard, `if (!fs.existsSync(archivePath) || maxIndexedLine > 0)`, which does not fire either in that situation — the database is empty, so `maxIndexedLine` is 0 and the archive exists.

Reproduced. Source archived at 2 lines, four more lines appended, second pass replayed with the shipped guard and `parseConversation`: rows recorded as lines 3-4 and 5-6 against a 2-line archive, and `formatConversationAsMarkdown(archive, 5, 6)` returns `""`.

**Verification:** confirmed-lower
**Verification evidence:** The live SessionStart path (syncConversations in sync.ts, via copyIfNewer then parseConversation with the archive as both source and archive) always refreshes the archive before citing it and never reproduces this. Only the manual --rebuild sequence with the DB wiped and archives kept hits the mismatch, and it self-heals on the next indexUnprocessed or sync pass because maxIndexedLine greater than zero then forces a refresh.

### CR-322: The moe-glass catalog description claims zero dependencies, but the published package has two

**File:** `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`
**Anchor:** `"Direct Chrome DevTools Protocol access. Skill mode plus MCP mode, zero dependencies."`
**Severity:** low

The claim is inherited from upstream and was true there, but is false in this fork. I confirmed
the upstream reference snapshot `../.moe-references/superpowers-chrome/package.json` declares
`dependencies: {}`, while `packages/glass/package.json` declares
`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and `zod`. Both are genuinely required at runtime, not stray
devDependencies: `packages/glass/src/index.ts`, which is the package `main` and `bin`, imports
`McpServer`, `StdioServerTransport` and `z` from them.

This matters more than ordinary stale copy because the entry it sits on is npm-sourced. A
consumer reading the catalog concludes that installing `moe-glass` needs no registry access
beyond the one package, when `npm install @tc/moe-glass` will in fact resolve two more. I
reproduced the dependency read directly from both manifests. The staged
