## Checked and found sound

I ran the script end to end against the real repository with `MARKETPLACE` redirected into the scratchpad, confirming afterwards that the working tree is still clean at `a01dcd5ffd06fefba341c2480fdae2c4777151f7` and that `~/.moe/local-marketplace` and its existing backup were untouched. The happy path staged all five registry plugins, applied five repoints, collected twenty-one hook and MCP targets, found every one of them on disk, and returned 0.

The repoint table matches the tree. Grepping `plugins/` for `dist/cli.js` returns exactly the four files the skill document names, `hooks/hooks.json`, `hooks/moe-mint/hooks.json`, `mcp.json` and `.mcp.json`, and all four are covered by the `hooks/**/hooks.json` walk plus the two-filename MCP loop. `emit-event` appears only in `moe-crew/hooks/hooks.json`, and all five of its events resolved to the copied `dist/`.

The dedup invariant that the mint adapter depends on survives staging. After the rewrite, the two `moe-memory` SessionStart entries still carry byte-identical matchers and commands, so Claude Code's exact-duplicate deduplication still collapses them and the hook does not double-fire. Scoping both walks to `staged/hooks/` correctly excludes the nested example plugin at `plugins/moe/skills/developing-claude-code-plugins/examples/full-featured-plugin/hooks/hooks.json`, which must not be verified. The nested `${PLUGIN_ROOT:-${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}}` form does collapse correctly within the five-pass budget, taking two passes.

Plugins with no `hooks/` directory return no targets rather than raising, since `Path.rglob` on a missing directory yields nothing. Backup directories are created as siblings of the marketplace root, not inside it, so they neither nest nor grow with each run. The source rewrite to `./plugins/<name>` correctly flattens the npm source objects that `moe-memory` and `moe-glass` carry in the committed registry.

I chased the absence of any MCP config in `plugins/moe-glass` and it is deliberate, not a staging gap: `packages/glass/mint/moe-glass.yaml` records "no .mcp.json in the package: glass's MCP server is registered by the consumer". The live `moe-glass` MCP tools come from consumer-side registration, so wholesale replacement of that directory loses nothing.

On security, the file holds no credentials or tokens. `npm root -g` is invoked through `subprocess.run` with a list argv and no shell, so the resolved path cannot inject a command. There are no symlinks anywhere under `plugins/`, so the symlink-dereferencing default of `shutil.copytree` is not currently exercised, and every path the script writes is rooted at `MARKETPLACE` or a plugin directory beneath it.

One gap worth recording without calling it a defect: nothing in the repository tests this script. Grepping the tree for `stage.py` and `moe-dogfood` outside the file itself returns nothing, and it sits under `.claude/` where no package test surface reaches it. Every behaviour above had to be established by running it.

The file is valid JSON, 1636 bytes, LF-only per `git ls-files --eol`, with a trailing newline
and no BOM. It holds no credentials; `owner.email` is the maintainer's own address and is the
appropriate value for that field.

The npm source shape is correct for this Claude Code version. The installed binary's schema
lists `npm` among the supported plugin source types, in the sentence "Plugins in a
settings-sourced marketplace must use remote sources (github, git-subdir, npm, url, archive,
command)", and documents `package`, `version` and `registry` as its fields. That same sentence
confirms the three relative `./plugins/<name>` sources are valid here, because this marketplace
is repository-sourced rather than settings-sourced, which matches the rationale recorded in
`.gitignore` for tracking generated `/plugins/` output.

`strict: true` on all five entries is both correct and the safer choice. The schema defines it
as "Require the plugin manifest to be present in the plugin folder. If false, the marketplace
entry provides the manifest," and I confirmed each of the five generated plugins ships a real
`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` with a matching `name` and `version`.

Both directions of the registry agreement hold on the live tree: the five listed names are
exactly the five entries in the `PLUGINS` registry, and `ls plugins/` shows exactly those five
directories with no orphan left behind by the `moe-core` and `moe-everything` consolidation in
commit `15aa668`. That consolidation delisted two plugin names without a marketplace-level
auto-uninstall flag, but it is covered by a deliberate operator runbook, the "Retiring a plugin"
section of `.claude/skills/moe-dogfood/SKILL.md`, so I am not treating it as a defect.

I also traced the npm-source install target end to end and found it sound. `EXPECTED_RELEASE_PACKAGES`
in `scripts/tc-release-pack.mjs` composes the `@tc/moe-memory` and `@tc/moe-glass` tarballs from
`pluginRoot: "plugins/moe-<name>"`, and `REQUIRED_PLUGIN_FILES` requires
`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` in the payload, so the published packages really are installable
plugin roots rather than bare library packages. `assertRequiredPluginPayload` additionally
proves the memory manifest points its hooks at `./hooks/moe-mint/hooks.json` and that the
background sync and bootstrap session-start commands are present.

The security surface is clean. Nothing in these four files invokes a shell: `tryExec` uses
`execFileSync`, `spawnAndForward` uses `spawn`, and neither passes `shell: true`, so
argument content cannot become shell syntax. Command names are never attacker-derived —
`resolve` looks `ns` up in the frozen `NAMESPACE_DISTRIBUTIONS` table and uses
`entry.bin`, so an arbitrary `ns` can only produce `{ unknown: true }`, never a path. No
credentials, tokens or hostnames are committed; the only embedded URL is the internal
GitLab marketplace remote in `config/distribution.mjs`. `workspaceRootFrom` is bounded at
16 iterations and also terminates on the filesystem-root fixpoint. `selfDir` resolves
through `realpathSync`, so a symlinked npm shim yields the real package directory rather
than the link's parent.

The flag-smuggling path I expected to find does not exist. `bin/moe.js` strips `--apply`,
`--upgrade` and `--uninstall` from forwarded lifecycle arguments, and `bin/moe-install`'s
`parseArgs` matches flags by exact string, so `moe install --uninstall=1` cannot reach
uninstall mode — the token becomes the distinct flag `--uninstall=1` and
`flags.has("--uninstall")` stays false.

`cmpVersion` is correct, including the `2.9.0` versus `2.10.0` case its comment calls out,
and the `parseInt(...) || 0` guard means a malformed segment degrades to 0 rather than
NaN-poisoning the comparison. `extractVersion` handles every real three-part output I
collected from this host: `git version 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155)`, `npm 11.17.0`,
`uv 0.12.8 (Homebrew 2026-08-31 aarch64-apple-darwin)`, `Docker version 29.5.3, build d1c06ef`,
`Python 3.9.6`, `2.1.258 (Claude Code)`. `probeNode` correctly reads `process.version`
rather than PATH, which is the version actually in use. `overallExit`'s hard-versus-soft
split matches the two-tier taxonomy in the file header and the exit contract in
`bin/moe-doctor`.

The clean-home acceptance tests in `doctor.test.mjs` are the strongest work in the shard.
Replacing PATH with a directory of three recorder scripts, redirecting HOME into the
fixture, and asserting `readdirSync(run.home)` is empty genuinely proves the installer
touches nothing outside its own action list — not merely that the plan text looks right.
The recorders answer `--version` without logging, so the doctor's own probe calls do not
pollute the assertion. `lifecycleActions` ordering is verified where it matters: umbrella
last on uninstall, marketplace update without `--scope` on upgrade, exact versions on
install. `resolve`'s purity is real, and every branch except proof-without-uv and the
directory cases above is covered.

Two process notes. First, `main` in `bin/moe.js` never calls `process.exit` itself and the

are in no shard's file list (the sharding glob appears to require a file extension, and

finding I noticed `bin/moe-doctor` prints "3 optional capabilitys unavailable" — its

that file.

I looked specifically for a licence gap in `sparsePaths` and did not find one. My
hypothesis was that a `--sparse .claude-plugin plugins` clone would omit the
root `NOTICE` that `AGENTS.md` calls Apache-2.0-required, since no generated
plugin carries a NOTICE and `checkCanonicalLegalFiles()` forbids per-package
copies. I disproved it by cloning this repo into the scratchpad and running
`git sparse-checkout set .claude-plugin plugins`: cone mode writes `/*` plus
`!/*/`, so every root-level file arrives, and `NOTICE`, `LICENSE`, `LICENSE-MIT`
and `PARITY.md` were all present in the sparse worktree. Each generated plugin
also carries its own `LICENSE`, which `scripts/check-provenance.mjs` verifies
for MIT and Apache-2.0 terms against its `moe-mint.yaml` expression.

No credentials, tokens, or secrets appear in the file. The repository URL is the
plain internal HTTPS form of `origin`, with no embedded userinfo. Every value is
a compile-time constant, so there is no injection or traversal surface here; the
only path construction happens in `resolve()`, which joins onto a `root` derived
from the module's own realpath rather than from `cwd` or the environment.

The brainstorm companion's authentication is careful and holds up under the checks I could
make without running it. `isAuthorized` compares both the `?key=` parameter and the cookie
with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` behind a length guard; `securityHeaders` sets `no-referrer`,
`no-store`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `frame-ancestors 'none'` and
`Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` on every response including the 403 and the 404s; the cookie
is `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` and its name is keyed on the actually-bound port in
`onListen`, which is the right fix for the fact that browsers do not scope cookies by port.
The DNS-rebinding claim in the comment checks out: a rebound page is a different origin, so
it carries neither the cookie nor the key and gets the 403. `isRegularFileInsideContentDir`
rejects symlinks, non-regular files and hardlinks (`stat.nlink !== 1`) and then compares
`realpath` against `realContentDir + path.sep`, which is the correct containment test.
`maybeOpenBrowser` uses `execFile` with the URL as an argv element and only shells out for
the explicitly operator-supplied `BRAINSTORM_OPEN_CMD`, so a hostile `--url-host` cannot
inject a command. `MAX_FRAME_PAYLOAD_BYTES` is checked on both the 16-bit and 64-bit
extended-length paths before any allocation, and unmasked client frames are rejected.
`decodeFrame`'s partial-frame handling correctly returns null and leaves the buffer intact.
The `EADDRINUSE` path refuses to fall back when `BRAINSTORM_TOKEN` was set explicitly, which
is the right call. `shutdown` destroys upgraded sockets so `server.close` can complete.

`stop-server.sh` is the most careful script in the shard: `is_brainstorm_server` requires a
live pid *and* a `state/server-instance-id` matching `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{32,64}$` *and* that
exact `--brainstorm-server-id=` argument in the process command line, and it fails closed
on ambiguity. The id charset validation is what makes the `case " $command_line " in *" $expected_arg "*)`
pattern safe from glob metacharacters, and a `-1` in the pid file is caught because
`command_has_server_id` cannot resolve it. `start-server.sh` sets `umask 077` before
creating anything, generates the instance id from `/dev/urandom` with a validated fallback,
validates `--idle-timeout-minutes` as `^[0-9]+$`, and correctly resolves the harness pid as
the grandparent with a documented WSL/MSYS escape hatch.

`stamp-disposition.mjs` is otherwise sound: the `--id` regex closes the obvious injection
into `new RegExp`, the double-stamp refusal works, the tally is recomputed from the body
rather than incremented, and its `/^\s+total:\s*(\d+)/m` matches the two-space-indented
`total:` that `review-merge.mjs` actually emits under `findings:` — I checked the producer.
The `#{2,3}` block terminator lines up with the merge script's `## <Severity>` sections and
`### CR-###: title` headings.

`packages/core/hooks/hooks.json` dispatches bash hooks through `run-hook.cmd` and Node
hooks through `node` directly, which is coherent rather than inconsistent, and it uses the
extensionless filenames that `run-hook.cmd`'s header and `references/polyglot-hooks.md`
both require. `run-hook.cmd` itself is a correct polyglot: `: << 'CMDBLOCK'` is a no-op
heredoc under bash and a label under cmd.exe, and the no-bash branch's decision to report
loudly and still `exit /b 0` is argued explicitly.

`helper.cjs` keeps its reconnect logic pure and testable (`nextReconnectDelay` is exported
for exactly that), lets `onclose` own reconnection so the backoff is not scheduled twice,
queues events while disconnected and flushes on open, and distinguishes a brief blip from a
tombstoned outage by elapsed time rather than attempt count.

`validate_requirements_index.py`'s section-boundary logic is correct, including the
interaction between `\s*$` under `re.MULTILINE` and the following `^## ` search.
`chunk_spec.py`'s heading regex correctly declines to match `#### Foo` at level two.
`generate-report.sh` uses a brace group rather than a subshell, so its counters survive to
the stderr summary. `aggregate_scenarios.py`'s `dedup_scenarios` merge, ugly as the
`existing.get(...)`/`setdefault(...)` pairing is, does mutate the right list.

`packages/core/package.json`, `packages/backstory/package.json`,
`packages/backstory/mint/moe-backstory.yaml`, the two example `plugin.json` files and the
example `marketplace.json` are internally consistent, and the mint configs' `marketplace.name: moe`
override is correct for the reason its comment gives — the generated install command would
otherwise name a `<plugin>-dev` marketplace that does not exist. A grep for credential
patterns across all 30 files found nothing but the local `TOKEN = generateToken()`
assignment. `brandMarkup` HTML-escapes the version it interpolates, and the removal of
upstream's remote `<img>` beacon is documented where it happened.

Several things I expected to be defects turned out to hold, and I confirmed them rather than reporting them. `tmux-wrapper.sh` does not re-parse its arguments through a shell on the multi-argument path: tmux 3.7 execs argv directly, verified by passing a single argv element containing `; touch <path>` and confirming no separate command ran, and by confirming `sh -c` received its script as one element. `browser-launcher.test.cjs` can safely `require()` `server.cjs` because the listener is behind `if (require.main === module)`; the module-scope work is three reads and no writes, so the unit test neither starts a server nor hangs. Its claim that Windows launching avoids a command interpreter also holds at the call site, where `maybeOpenBrowser` uses `execFile` with an argv array, though the test pins only the descriptor and not the spawn options, and the `BRAINSTORM_OPEN_CMD` shell path is untested by design as trusted operator input. The `exit_code: 0` expectation in `keeps current Claude skill expansions inside the active human turn` looked like an invented value; the hook documents the inference, "Preserve explicit codes when present; infer", so the test asserts intended behaviour. `MOE_EVIDENCE_DISABLED` is covered, in `metadata.test.ts`. `.audit/` is genuinely in the repository `.gitignore`, not a global exclude. `http_check` in the Windows suite indexes `process.argv` correctly for `node -` with trailing arguments, which I verified on Node 24. The fixed ports across the brainstorm suites are safe from cross-file collision because `test:brainstorm` chains with `&&`, and safe from silent fallback because every fixture sets `BRAINSTORM_TOKEN`, which makes the server refuse an `EADDRINUSE` fallback rather than bind elsewhere. The two committed governance fixtures contain no credential: `restricted/secret.txt` holds the string "restricted fixture placeholder" and `.ai-privacy.yml` is a privacy-level map, so the `ALWAYS` pattern in `review-scope.mjs` that pulled them into this shard fired on the filename, correctly and harmlessly. `condition-based-waiting-example.ts` is excluded from the type-check by `tsconfig.tests.json`, so its unresolvable `~/threads/...` imports are illustrative rather than broken, and its only real weakness is that a throw from `getEvents` inside the polling `setTimeout` leaves the promise unsettled instead of rejecting. On the review scripts themselves, the parts I tried hardest to break held: shard assignment is a clean partition, the manifest is byte-identical across reruns, the dirty-tree and HEAD-drift refusals both fire, the shallow-depth narrowing genuinely preserves credential-bearing paths, `lstat` does keep a tracked source symlink out of the denominator, the verification ledger rejects duplicates, unexpected ids, missing verdicts, empty evidence and a `confirmed-lower` severity that is not actually lower, and the "Checked and found sound" section survives the merge, which the file's comments say it once did not.

All thirty assigned files were read in full: the six Python test modules, `run-evals.sh`,
and scenarios 01 through 23 (whose complete content I enumerated, confirming the per-row
key union is exactly `content,role` and the top-level key set is exactly `description,
expected_decision, name, transcript`).

I ran the Python suite with `TMPDIR` pointed at scratch: 37 tests, all passing, no writes
into the tree. The validator negative fixtures are substantive rather than vacuous, which
I checked by running each validator against its `.invalid.md` fixture:
`iteration-log.invalid.md` fails on five missing required fields,
`roadmap.invalid.md` on the missing `## Iteration list` section plus four fields, and
`requirements-index.invalid.md` on the malformed `STORY-` header. So each
`test_invalid_example_fails` fails for the reason its fixture name implies.
`test_missing_story_id_is_flagged` and `test_missing_walking_skeleton_is_flagged` both
assert on stderr text rather than exit code alone, and both messages match.
`test_story_ids_are_sequential` is sound: `assign_ids` increments the epic and story
counters in the same insertion order, so lower story IDs always land in the
lexicographically earlier epic file that the test's sorted glob reads first.

I found no committed credential in any assigned file; a scan for key, token, password,
bearer, `sk-`, `AKIA`, and PEM-header patterns across the latte directory and the Python
tests returned nothing. `run-evals.sh` has no injection surface: every interpolation is
double-quoted, `jq -n --arg` is used to build the hook event, there is no `eval`, and the
only `echo -e` lines interpolate the loop counter and the hook's own `decision` value.
Temporary state lives in a `mktemp -d` directory with a trap-installed `rm -rf`, and the
`MOE_LATTE_FAKE_CLAUDE` stub is created inside that 0700 directory, so the `PATH` prepend
is not locally hijackable and shadows nothing but `claude`. The header's arithmetic checks
out: there are exactly 65 scenario files, all with a boolean `expected_decision`, split 36
false to 29 true. The `latte:evals` script is wired as
`bash test/latte/run-evals.sh` and is absent from `test`, matching the header's claim and
the CI exclusions in `AGENTS.md`. Both `run-evals.sh` and the scenario JSON are LF per
`git ls-files --eol`, and the shell script carries mode 100755.

Every scenario's `expected_decision` is consistent with the judge prompt in
`claude-judge-continuation`: the twelve CONTINUE labels all rest on an explicit statement
of the next action ("Next I need to...", "Now I'll implement the controller"), and the
eleven STOP labels all rest on a question put to the user or a completion summary. Scenario
07 is correctly labelled STOP despite the prompt's mid-task carve-out, because no work has
begun. I found no mislabelled scenario.

Schema and self-consistency across all 30 assigned files hold up. I validated each with `jq`: all parse,
all carry exactly the four keys `name`, `description`, `expected_decision`, `transcript` in that order,
`expected_decision` is a JSON boolean in every file (so `jq -r` yields the literal `true`/`false` string
that `run-evals.sh` compares against `hook_should_continue`), and every transcript ends on an `assistant`
row as the runner's decision logic requires. I cross-checked each `description`'s trailing "should
CONTINUE" / "should STOP" claim against its `expected_decision` and found no mismatch in any of the 30, so
the human-readable line the runner prints never contradicts the assertion. `name` values are unique across
the full 65-scenario corpus, so no two scenarios are ambiguous in the runner's output.

The runner's serialization of these fixtures is also sound. `jq -c '.transcript[]'` produces one row per
line with embedded newlines correctly escaped as `\n` inside JSON strings, so multi-line assistant messages
and the fenced ```yaml and ```typescript blocks in `25` and `32` do not corrupt the NDJSON. I confirmed by
running the transform and re-parsing the output. The per-run `session_id` that `run-evals.sh` derives as
`moe-latte-eval-$total_scenarios-$run` keeps each scenario on its own throttle file, so the hook's
three-continuations-per-300s limiter cannot bleed one scenario's result into the next.

I found no security defects in these files. They contain no credentials, tokens, hostnames, or paths
outside the fixture's own invented examples, and nothing that reaches a shell. The scenario content does
flow untrusted-style text into the judge prompt with no delimiting, but none of the 30 files attempts an
injection, and the fixtures themselves are authored data rather than an attack surface.

The 15 CONTINUE labels are individually correct against the rubric's "explicitly states what it will do
next" test. Each closes on an unambiguous forward commitment: "Now I need to add the CSS styling",
"Let me fix these test failures one by one", "I'll add message pagination", or an explicit "Still need
to:" list in `38`, `42` and `48`. The 15 STOP labels are likewise individually correct, each ending on a
question that hands the decision back to the user. My findings above concern what the corpus as a whole
fails to discriminate, not the individual judgements.

The remaining nine scenarios in this shard label consistently against the judge prompt in `claude-judge-continuation`: the four CONTINUE fixtures each pair a completion confirmation with an explicit next-step statement matching the prompt's "Now I'll..." trigger, and the prompt's "ONLY IF ... in ALL other cases" phrasing resolves that overlap as an if/else rather than leaving it ambiguous. The three question fixtures and the four completion fixtures land squarely in the prompt's STOP branches, including the "Offering optional actions" clause that scenario 65 is built around.

`metadata.test.ts` holds up well beyond the parser issue. The execute-bit pair is genuinely bidirectional, and the `discovered.length >= X_BIT_ALLOWLIST.length` floor combined with the empty-`unlisted` assertion pins it to equality rather than a subset. The script-parse router covers the three extensionless Node hooks and the five extensionless bash scripts by name, so a regression in the shebang read cannot hide behind the `.sh` count. The two-map completeness and disjointness assertions correctly test the raw parse (`tiers.authored`) rather than the coalesced local, and separate the null and undefined cases as the comment claims. I counted the pinned imported literal: 14 + 4 + 6 + 1 + 2 + 4 = 31, matching the assertion. The test name "accounts for every skill the six upstream sources shipped" now covers seven sources, but the comment directly above it names mattpocock-skills as the seventh, so a reader is not misled.

`tc-governance-check.test.ts` matches its hook exactly. The disable escape hatch, the two user-instruction file locations, and the fail-open path when neither `HOME` nor `USERPROFILE` is set all correspond to real branches, and the test's `delete env.MOE_TC_GOVERNANCE_DISABLED` hygiene means an ambient variable cannot make the nudge test pass vacuously. The hook's `-n` test means `metadata.test.ts` passing that variable as an empty string is also correct.

`retrieving-context-contract.test.ts` asserts positional ordering (`codeGraph < sourceFallback < optionalMoedex`) rather than mere presence, which is the part that would rot silently under a reordering edit.

Both shell suites are honest. I ran `test-find-polluter.sh`: five assertions pass, all writes confined to `mktemp -d`, and the tree stayed clean. `test-render-graphs.sh` skipped its five rendering assertions on this machine because graphviz is absent, so I re-ran it with a stub `dot` on PATH that answers `-V` and emits SVG; all eight assertions pass, and `Rendered: fixture_graph.svg` matches the per-block branch of `render-graphs.mjs` rather than the `--combine` branch. The `var=$(cmd)` followed by `status=$?` idiom is correct in both files, and `set -e` exemption rules make the `&&` chains in `recover-workers.sh` safe. I checked the bash 3.2 empty-array trap that script explicitly targets: `"${arr[@]}"` under `set -u` does abort on this machine's `/bin/bash` 3.2.57, but every such expansion in the file is guarded by a `${#arr[@]}` count test first, and `A=("$@")` with no positional parameters is fine.

The tmux layer is built the right way. `packages/crew/src/core/tmux.ts` passes every argument through an argv array to `execFile`, so no tmux invocation is shell-interpreted; the injection above comes from a generated script, not from process spawning. `resolveCwd` uses `realpathSync`, and `cmdLaunch` refuses a duplicate tmux session name.

`crew/hooks/hooks.json` pointing all five events at `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/emit-event.cjs` while `plugins/moe-crew/` carries no `dist/` is a known, documented staging step, not a defect: `tsup.config.ts` emits that bundle, and `.claude/skills/moe-dogfood/SKILL.md` records both the copy (`packages/crew/dist` to `moe-crew/dist`, "`plugins/` carries no build output") and the `cjs/loader` MODULE_NOT_FOUND symptom when it is skipped. The absent `"shell": "bash"` on those entries differs from core's hooks, which assert it for Windows PowerShell reasons, but `mint/moe-crew.yaml` states this plugin "has no native-Windows story at all, because tmux does not exist there", so bash is the only shell it targets.

`cli.ts` is otherwise careful: `parseWorker` treats an empty `--worker=` as missing to preserve the bash exit-code contract, `parseReadEventsArgs` refuses to swallow a following flag as a `--type` value, `readLine` resolves with a captured line on close so a piped `echo yes` cannot lose the consent answer, and the `require.main === module` guard keeps `run()` from firing under vitest's ESM import. `context.ts` is a thin, correct discriminated-union resolver.

`proc.run` is the right shape for this tool: `execFile` with an args array, never a shell, so no amount of hostile content in a session name or prompt can become a shell token at the tmux boundary — every finding above about injection is about generated *files*, not about how tmux is invoked. `core/shell.ts` gets the harder half right too: `shellQuoteAlways` uses correct POSIX `'\''` escaping with no fast path, `codex.ts` routes every hook-command argument through it, and `tomlBasicString` escapes backslash, quote, the named control characters and the rest of U+0000–U+001F as `\uXXXX`, so a cwd with quotes or newlines survives both as a `[projects."…"]` table key and inside the shell-quoted hook `command`. The two `shellQuote` variants are documented as intentionally different and the header explains why consolidating them would be unsafe.

The three transcript parsers are genuinely defensive in the way the comments claim: `parseLines`, `parseRolloutLines` and `parsePiEntries` all skip unparseable lines, `asBlock` narrows array elements before any field access, and every string field is `typeof`-checked before use, so a torn or garbage transcript degrades to an empty or partial turn instead of throwing. `parseEvent` validates the event name against `EVENT_NAMES` before casting, and `classifyStatus`'s `never` binding makes a new event name a compile error rather than a silent `unknown`. `lastEvent`'s divergence from `readEvents` is deliberate and documented: the status path wants a torn final line to read as `unknown` rather than fall back to an older parseable event.

`read-events` handles the `--last 0` footgun explicitly (`slice(-0)` would return everything) and emits raw lines verbatim so a `--type` filter cannot reshape the payload; its tests cover the zero case, the type-then-last ordering, and extra fields. `wait-for-turn`'s default baseline of current EOF is the right choice for "wait for the *next* turn-end", and one deadline correctly governs both the file-exists and the poll phase. `converse`'s send-before-resolve ordering for a fresh derive worker is correct and well argued, and `isDeriveFirst` is shared with `cmdSend` so the two cannot drift. `diagnostics.ts` reports probe failures as text (`(ps failed: …)`) rather than an empty section, which is exactly the right instinct for a diagnostic, and it deliberately avoids GNU-only `ps -H`.

I checked `claudeTranscriptPath`'s `cwd.replace(/[/._:]/g, "-")` against the pinned snapshot in `../.moe-references/claude-session-driver` and it is byte-identical to the spec, including the `-a-my-proj` expectation for an underscore, so the narrower-than-Claude character class is inherited, not introduced here. `claudeWorkerEnv`'s pin-empty logic is careful in a way that is easy to get wrong: it pins a provider var empty only when the controller does *not* have a value, so a real provider and its credentials inherit together, and the header records the two distinct live-verified failure modes for `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` and `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION`. No credential-shaped strings appear in any of the 30 assigned files.

The harness registry, the claude and codex driver contracts, and their tests hold up: `getDriver` fails closed with a message naming the requested and available ids, `claudeWorkerEnv`'s provider-var scrubbing is pinned in both directions (pinned-empty and omitted-when-set), and codex's TOML generator is genuinely escape-safe — `tomlBasicString` covers backslash, quote and the control range, and `shellQuoteAlways` has no fast path, with tests exercising a cwd containing a space, a double quote and a backslash.

Command construction is safe by design at the process boundary: `proc.run` uses `execFile` with an argv array and never a shell, and `tmux.ts` passes every session name, pane target, key and `-e KEY=VALUE` pair as a separate argv element, so nothing in the tmux surface is shell-parsed. No credential, token or key is committed anywhere in the 30 files; the auth staging paths only copy files the operator already owns.

`runHook`'s no-op ladder is correct and well covered: bad JSON, a non-object payload, a missing or empty `session_id`, a missing meta, and an unrecognized `hook_event_name` each return `{ stdout: '' }` with nothing appended, and only `Stop` prints the approve decision. I checked the `process.stdout.write` followed by `process.exit(0)` in `main` for the classic macOS pipe-truncation hazard and measured it: writes truncate at the 64 KB pipe buffer, and the 22-byte approve payload always lands intact, so that is not a defect here.

The event vocabulary is closed and enforced — `parseEvent` rejects any name outside `EVENT_NAMES`, and `classifyStatus` uses a `never` exhaustiveness check, so adding a `WorkerEvent` variant without a status mapping is a typecheck failure. `lastEvent`'s deliberate divergence from `readEvents` (literal last line, so a torn final line yields unknown rather than a stale fallback) is both intentional and pinned by name.

The pi extension's gating is right and tested where it matters: non-interactive `input` sources are dropped, `session_shutdown` only counts as `session_end` when the reason is `quit`, `record` swallows every error so a handler can never destabilise pi, and a skipped event does not self-register a meta. I confirmed against the installed pi 0.74.0 typings that all six registered event names, the `ReadonlySessionManager` accessors the extension calls, and the payload fields it reads exist as the C1 contract block describes, and that `getSessionFile()` is defined at `session_start` whenever `--session-dir` makes the session persistent — so the "meta without a transcript_path, never repaired" shape the never-overwrite rule would otherwise expose is not reachable through the driver's own launch argv.

The three e2e flows do exercise the bundle rather than the source, and their skip is announced on stderr rather than silent, so a tmux-less CI leaves a visible trace. Within their fakes the assertions are honest: the claude flow drives the real hook to prove the meta is written before the pane starts, and the codex flow re-parses the shell-quoted baked hook args through a real shell.

Static path traversal on `/static/*` holds. I probed the running server over raw sockets, so no client-side URL parser could normalize the path first: `../server.js`, `..%2f`, `%2e%2e%2f`, `....//`, `..;/`, double-encoded `%252e%252e%252f`, a six-deep `../` chain to `/etc/passwd`, `..%5c..%5c`, and `//etc/passwd` all returned 404 with nothing leaked, while `styles.css` returned 200. WHATWG URL normalization collapses real dot-segments before `startsWith("/static/")` runs, and percent-encoded forms stay encoded in `pathname` so `join` treats them as one literal segment.

The SSE disconnect path is correctly wired despite the hand-rolled stream. `handleEvents` clears its pump interval and calls `bus.unsubscribe` only from `cancel()`, which looked like a leak, so I read `@hono/node-server` 2.1.1: `writeFromReadableStreamDefaultReader` registers `reader.cancel` on both the writable's `close` and `error` events, so an abrupt client disconnect does reach `cancel()`. Its pre-read loop also flushes headers for a stream that has emitted only the opening `": connected"` comment, which is what that comment claims to achieve. The `requestTimeout = 0` / `timeout = 0` block in `index.ts` and the `instanceof HttpServer` narrowing are both load-bearing and correct.

HTML escaping in the render path is thorough. `esc()` covers all five metacharacters in a single regex pass, and every interpolated identity, run id, cost, timestamp, title, error stage and phase word goes through it in `templates.ts` — I checked each interpolation site in `cellHtml`, `cardHtml`, `gridHtml` and `tallyHtml`. The two unescaped inlines in `layoutHtml` receive already-rendered HTML. The SSE gaps above are control-character gaps, not escaping gaps.

`renderRoot` is quadratic — `manifestCellFor` does a linear `find` over `manifest.cells` once per identity, and `headerTally` receives the same closure — so I measured it rather than assume. A synthetic 40x8x3x2 manifest (1920 cells) rendered `GET /` in 21 ms, against 11 ms for 40 cells. The constant is small enough that this is not a defect at any plausible board size, and the scanner's `cellForId` reverse lookup is bounded by the number of changed cells per tick, which is small in practice.

`scan.ts`'s authority rules read correctly: `_verdictCache` caches only present parses so a landing verdict is still seen, `readPhase` returns null on a schema miss so a pid-less phase reads as no-live-phase, `startedAtStamp` is the only positional read of a dir name, the window is the newest five by (stamp, name) with the newest live dir winning `running`, and the manifest overlay adds an empty cell for every declared cell. `DashboardVerdictSchema`'s per-field `.catch` guards do keep a malformed verdict readable as present, as documented.

`event-bus.ts` behaves as specified: drop-oldest at capacity, `drain` returning oldest-to-newest and emptying, and `publish` with no subscribers discarding silently. The drop-oldest policy is safe for the reason given, since each frame is a full-state cell swap.

On the crew side the transcript layer is the strongest thing in this shard. `transcript.test.ts` pins byte-exact output for the canonical claude fixture, covers all three harness formats, and specifically covers the malformed inputs a JSONL reader meets in the field: non-JSON lines, `null` array elements, numeric `message.content`, missing `.text` / `.name` / `.thinking` fields asserted not to render "undefined", and codex's real 0.133 `exec_command` and `custom_tool_call` shapes. `wait-for-turn.test.ts` genuinely exercises its stale-stop claim by seeding a prior-turn `stop` before the call and asserting the later one is returned. `status.test.ts`'s torn-final-line case appends a partial JSON fragment and asserts `unknown` rather than a fallback to the prior event, which is the behaviour `lastEvent` plus `classifyStatus` actually implement. `stop.test.ts` covers the self-exit-without-session_end path and the driver-grace default, and asserts the staged-credential home is removed. `shell.test.ts` does pin the behavioural difference between `shellQuote` and `shellQuoteAlways` that its docstring promises.

`core/proc.ts`'s `run` never rejects and never invokes a shell — `execFile` with an args array, as the docstring says — and every crew caller passes argv arrays, so the tmux surface has no shell-quoting exposure. The four crew config files agree with the tree: `tsconfig.json` declares no references and `package.json` declares no runtime dependencies, `tsconfig.tests.json` adds only `test/**/*` plus the two config files with `composite: false` and `noEmit`, `smol-toml` is imported only from `test/codex-driver.test.ts` so its devDependency placement is right, and `tsup.config.ts`'s shebang banner and dropped `clean` are both explained by constraints I verified against `package.json` and the gitignored `dist`.

`templates.ts` HTML escaping is complete for its own medium: every interpolated identity, verdict, cost, run id, timestamp, drift line, error stage and na-title goes through `esc()`, which covers all five metacharacters in one regex pass; the only unescaped interpolations are `f3()`-formatted numbers, integer tally counts, and the already-rendered tally and grid bodies that `layoutHtml` inlines by design. I traced every branch of `cellHtml`, `gridHtml`, `cardHtml`, `ribbonHtml` and `costBarHtml` looking for an attribute or element body reached without `esc()` and found none.

`app.js` is free of DOM injection. It builds no HTML — `hideCard` and `showCard` use `innerHTML = ""` plus `cloneNode(true)`, never assignment of markup — and `highlightColumn` runs every attribute value through `CSS.escape` before embedding it in a quoted attribute selector. I checked the quoting: `CSS.escape` escapes the double quote, backslash and control characters, and a leading digit escape stays valid inside a CSS string, so the selector cannot be broken out of. The column highlight keys on `data-agent`/`data-credential`/`data-os` rather than column index, which is what makes it survive the two-tier header and outerHTML swaps; the one branch where `data-credential` is absent is the agent-group `<th>`, which correctly takes the `[data-agent]`-only path.

`view.ts` arithmetic holds up under its edge cases. `driftFlag`'s length guard is load-bearing rather than redundant (it is what keeps `latest` from being undefined on an empty window), the strict `>` boundary matches its documented "not drift at exactly 1.5x", `costBarHeights` short-circuits a zero peak instead of dividing, `formatAge` and `latestAgeDays` clamp negatives and future timestamps, `parseDirStamp` rejects a non-matching tail rather than handing `Date.parse` a malformed string, and `cardView`'s drift branch can only be entered when at least three priced runs exist, which is exactly what its non-null assertions assume.

`htmx-ext-sse.js` matches the upstream htmx 2.x extension and is vendored verbatim per `src/static/VENDOR.md`; I confirmed `biome.json` really does disable formatter, linter and assist for `**/packages/flight/dashboard/src/static/**`, so the no-hand-edit rule is enforced rather than merely asserted. The stale listeners left behind by an outerHTML cell swap are bounded at roughly one per cell, because each cell's event name is unique and the next frame for that name removes the orphan as it adds the replacement.

The dashboard test suites are otherwise well aimed: `dashboard-scan.test.ts` names and genuinely exercises the authority rule, both abandoned-exclusion paths, the identity-less skip, the 5-run window, the `(started_at, dir-name)` ordering with a nonce tie-break, and the legacy no-os/no-credential placement; `dashboard-event-bus.test.ts` pins drop-oldest at both an explicit capacity and the 256 default and checks the exact surviving window; `dashboard-diff.test.ts` covers appeared, vanished, verdict-appeared, phase-changed and the window-length-only change while treating the reason as advisory, matching `GridChange`'s stated contract. The server suite awaits every `stop()` in `afterEach` and slices a single `<td>` before asserting so a band assertion cannot bleed into the next cell.

`docs/examples/cookies.yaml` and `passkey.yaml` carry no live secrets. The cookie values are `REPLACE_ME_WITH_REAL_SESSION_TOKEN` placeholders, and the passkey fields decode to the literal strings `TESTCREDENTIALID…`, `TESTUSERHANDLE…` and `TESTPRIVATEKEY…` under the reserved `.test` TLD, as the file claims. `examples/tutorial/.gauntlet/context/profiles/fred/cookies.yaml` is a single `session=fred` cookie scoped to `http://localhost:4444/`, which the tutorial webapp trusts by design. The tutorial webapp's plaintext passwords are fixture values for a localhost-only process and are disclosed as such.

`examples/todo/web/server.ts` handles its input correctly apart from the MIME type: the `/api/filter` route validates against the closed union before calling `setFilter`, `/api/add` rejects a missing or non-string body, and the static path guard (`resolved.startsWith(PUBLIC_DIR + "/")` after `resolve(PUBLIC_DIR, "." + reqPath)`) holds — I checked that neither WHATWG URL parsing nor `path.resolve` decodes percent-escapes, so `%2e%2e` reaches the filesystem as a literal directory name rather than a traversal. The two dashboard tsconfigs agree with the repo's two-tsconfig rule: `references: []` is correct for a package whose `dependencies` contain no workspace member, and the test program is the non-composite `noEmit` companion. `vitest.config.ts`'s separate-project rationale is sound, and its `include` of `test/**/*.test.ts` collects exactly the eight suites it claims.

`resolveInside` and `isSafePath` in `src/qa/paths.ts` are a genuine guard: absolute paths and `..` segments are rejected on both separator styles, and `canonicalize` realpaths the target so a symlink inside the context root pointing outside is caught. `install_cookies` uses it correctly and its per-step failure logging never records cookie value bytes.

Every page-side expression built in `element-selector.js`, `extraction.js`, and `capture.js` interpolates through `JSON.stringify`, so a hostile selector or attribute cannot break out of the JS string literal into the evaluated script. `getElementSelector`'s double-`JSON.stringify` for the embedded warning literal is correct. `throwIfExceptionDetails` is applied after every `Runtime.evaluate` in these modules, which is what keeps a page-side throw from surfacing as `undefined`.

The `cdp-router` sessionId dispatch is right, including the deliberate decision not to correlate root command responses (`msg.id` with no `sessionId`) so that `browser-session.js`'s `pendingRequests` stays the single correlation path; the guard `data.id !== undefined && data.sessionId === undefined` is what stops a page-session id 1 from resolving a root id 1. `unregisterSession` rejects in-flight requests rather than leaking pending promises, and `close`/`sendRaw` both re-check the `closed` flag.

`package-root.ts` resolves by walking to the nearest `package.json` rather than counting `..`, so `src/` and `dist/` agree, and the bounded loop plus the root-reached break cannot spin. `mergeEstimates` in `src/lab/tab/index.ts` handles the boundary carefully: `cache_write` maps to `total_cache_create`, approximations dedupe on a `(kind, detail)` tuple with `null` distinguished from `""`, `est_cost_usd` is null only when every model is unpriced, and the totals are consistent with moe-tab's cost model, where an unpriced model contributes zero (`crates/moe-tab-core/src/cost.rs`, "Tokens are still aggregated; cost is 0"). `TabError` is exported from a single ESM entry point, so the `instanceof` narrowing in `estimateTrajectory`/`estimateUsageSidecar` is safe. `kimiToolResultTotalBytes` validates every level of the row shape before touching `result.output` and returns 0 on unreadable or non-JSON input, as documented.

The TUI adapter's private-`-L` socket per session is the right call and the reasoning in its comment holds; session names are generated from a timestamp plus base36 nonce, so nothing user-controlled reaches the tmux argv. `close()` collects descendants before `kill-server`, honours a grace window so a well-behaved TUI can flush on `SIGHUP`, and only then `SIGKILL`s survivors. `press` validates against `KEY_MAP` before shelling out. `XtermCaptureParser` feeds each captured row with absolute cursor positioning rather than newlines, which is what keeps row 0 from scrolling off a zero-scrollback terminal, and the xterm-256 cube and grayscale ramp arithmetic is correct against the standard step table.

`cli.ts` declares and refuses `lab`/`appliance` instead of leaving them absent, re-forms `process.argv`'s shape for `parseArgs`, and routes the dashboard by module specifier rather than by path into `dist/`. No credential material is committed anywhere in the thirty files.

`lib/page-session.js` is careful in the places that matter: per-session id counters keep `{id:1, sessionId:"A"}` and `{id:1, sessionId:"B"}` from cross-resolving, `send` clears its timeout and removes the pending entry on the synchronous `sendRaw` throw, `enableDomain` memoises correctly, and `detach` is idempotent. The `unregisterSession` side in `lib/cdp-router.js` rejects in-flight requests rather than leaving awaiters hanging.

`lib/navigation.js` gets the two hard parts right. `Page.enable` plus `waitForEvent` are registered before `Page.navigate`, so a fast `data:` URL cannot fire `loadEventFired` before anyone is listening, and the `loadP.catch(() => {})` marker genuinely prevents the timer's rejection from escaping when `ps.send` throws first — `test/qa/adapters/web/lib/navigation.test.ts` pins exactly that. The selector and text arguments are `JSON.stringify`-escaped; only the timeout is not, which is the finding above.

`lib/element-selector.js` (a shard-014 file, read as a callee) escapes every interpolated selector and `:contains()` payload through `JSON.stringify`, which is the correct control for the `Runtime.evaluate` expression context these strings land in. Every consumer in my shard — `mouse.js`, `keyboard-input.js`, `screenshot.js`, `select-option.js` — goes through it rather than concatenating raw.

`passkey.ts` is the strongest security-relevant file in the shard. `resolveInside` is used for the model-supplied path, and that helper rejects absolute paths, rejects `..` split on both separators, and canonicalises through `realpathSync` so an in-root symlink pointing out is caught. `credentialContext` logs only `rpId`, resident flag, sign count, and field *lengths*, so neither `credentialId` nor `privateKey` bytes reach `run.jsonl` on either the success or the failure path — and the failure path was the easy one to get wrong. `readPasskeyFile` type-checks every field before use.

`lib/viewport.js` bounds width, height, and `deviceScaleFactor` before the CDP call and keeps the mobile UA override in lockstep with touch emulation in both directions. `lib/websocket-client.js` genuinely fixes what its comment claims — `ws` honours `perMessageDeflate: false` where undici's global `WebSocket` silently ignored the option — and `test/qa/adapters/web/lib/websocket-client-no-compression.test.ts` asserts the absence of the extension in the upgrade handshake rather than just the constructor argument, which is the right level to test it.

`lib/pick-free-port.js`, `lib/session-state.js`, `lib/package.json`, `agent/initial-message.ts`, and `tools/types.ts` are small and correct; the `"type": "commonjs"` marker is load-bearing exactly as its `//` key describes.

`tools/tabs.ts` handles focus-stack ordering correctly: `MAX_TAB_DEPTH` is checked against total depth with the user-facing message framed in side-trip terms, `close_tab` refuses the original tab, both paths call `recomputeActiveTab()` before `takeReturnScreenshot` so the capture lands on the now-active tab, and a Chrome-side close failure is surfaced as a warning rather than swallowed. `lib/tabs.js` memoises page sessions per `targetId` and detaches the cached session in `closeTab` so the sessionId-keyed router state is released.

In `agent/agent.ts`, the report-with-other-tools policy (drop the rest, log the dropped names), the bounded report re-ask followed by salvage, the criteria-consistency downgrade to `investigate`, and the stall watchdog's use of the image bytes rather than the per-call caption as the fingerprint are all coherent and match their stated specs. The `Promise.race` tool timeout attaches a handler to the tool promise, so a late rejection from an abandoned tool cannot surface as an unhandled rejection.

I confirmed no credentials are committed anywhere in the 30 files. The only secret-shaped strings are the two env-var *names* in `bash-tool.ts`.

Two things I deliberately did not file. `lib/navigation.js`'s auto-capture collects `Runtime.consoleAPICalled` into `state.consoleMessages`, waits a full `CONSOLE_LINGER_MS`, then returns a hardcoded `const consoleLog = []` while `capture.js` writes "# TODO: Console logging not yet implemented" to disk — real wasted work, but self-documented as a TODO and unreachable from Flight, since `executeNavigate` calls `navigate` with two arguments and `autoCapture` defaults to `false`. And `lib/screenshot.js`'s `execSync` interpolates the filename into a double-quoted shell word for `sips`/`identify`/`convert`; every caller builds that name internally from `path.join`, so it is defence-in-depth only, though `execFileSync` with an argv array would be the correct shape.

Defects in `lib/browser-session.js`, `lib/cdp-router.js`, and `lib/element-selector.js` are left to shard 014, which owns those files.

`prompts/generated.ts` and `prompts/loader.ts` hold together: the generated file is string
literals with no runtime fs access, `loadPromptFile` trims trailing whitespace and throws on an
unknown name as documented, and `BUNDLED_PROMPT_NAMES` matches the seven keys.

`validators.ts` is careful at the seam it claims to guard. `parseCoreFields` is applied identically
on the strict and salvage paths, so a bad verdict cannot be salvaged; `decodeArrayField`'s
single-level `JSON.parse` rescue only accepts a decoded array; `parseReportCriteria` enforces
count, order, enum and non-empty evidence; and `checkCriteriaConsistency` correctly enforces only
the one direction it documents. `validateToolArgs` is honest about being a narrow subset rather
than JSON Schema. The one nit is the `requiredKeys` set, which is populated and never read.

`WatchManager` and its two tools behave as their tests describe. The first-scan-returns-existing-
files-as-new behaviour is deliberate and pinned by "first scan with existing matching file returns
it as new_file". Clamping (`WAKE_IDLE_MS_MIN`, `WAKE_TIMEOUT_MS_MAX`) is surfaced back to the model
as `applied_idle_ms`/`applied_timeout_ms`, `maxExecutionMs` covers the internal ceiling, the
`waitInFlight` guard is set synchronously before the first `await`, and both the missing-glob-root
and raced-removal cases are handled by the `continue` branches. `buildSharedTools` mounts `read`
and `fetch_credential` conditionally and `canExecute` agrees with `definitions` and `execute`;
passing `contextRoot ?? ""` is safe because `buildFetchCredentialTool` returns null when
`contextRootIsPopulated` is false.

`shutdown.ts` and `shutdown-stub-writer.ts` are the most carefully reasoned files in the shard. The
grace → cancelAll → abortAll → patience → stub ordering matches the header comment, `abortAll` and
`cancelAll` both avoid double-counting, `ShutdownState.mark` is first-signal-wins, and the stub
writer's `existsSync` guard plus its written-out analysis of the remaining microsecond race is
accurate. `ActiveRunRegistry`'s `startedAt`-matched `unregister` and its `progressLog` cap are
correct.

`resultRoutes`' completed-run manifest gate is sound: `isSafePath` is applied to both the run
directory and the file before the manifest is consulted, the `.ansi` sibling allowance computes
the right stem, and a manifest entry that itself contains a traversal is rejected by the earlier
`isSafePath`. `parseIntParam` clamps and falls back correctly. The list endpoint's synchronous
`readdirSync` plus up-to-200 `readFileSync` per poll is a real cost, but it is bounded by the
clamp and the sort-before-load, so I did not file it.

`decideUpgrade` is a clean pure function and `parseRunId`/`parseRunSetId` are strict enough to
carry the containment burden the WebSocket path puts on them. `RunSetBroadcaster` handles empty-set
cleanup and per-client errors correctly. `scenarioRoutes`' `parseScenarioBody` is a genuine
allow-list with the create/update asymmetry enforced, and the field-by-field merge in `PUT` (rather
than a spread) is the right call under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. `buildConfigOutput`, reached
by `configEffectiveRoutes`, reduces both API keys to `"set" | "unset"` and never echoes a secret.
`mime-types.ts`'s `application/octet-stream` default is the right fallback. `reflection.ts`'s
truncation and unserializable-value handling are correct apart from the escaping gap filed above.

`read-tool.ts` is solid: every path goes through `resolveInside`, which rejects absolute inputs and `..` segments on both separators and then confirms containment against the realpath, so a symlink inside the context root that points outside is correctly refused (I confirmed this by reproduction). The binary guard, the not-a-file guard and the error-message shapes all match the pinned spec prose.

`auto-emit-html.ts` does what its docstring says — the renderer failure is logged and swallowed so a report-writing error cannot change the run's exit code — and `test/qa/cli/auto-emit.test.ts` genuinely exercises the success, `Error`, and non-`Error` throw paths through injected seams. The HTML report path it calls escapes `</script` and splices into a `type="application/json"` tag with a function replacement, so `$&` sequences in run data are not interpreted.

`config-helpers.ts` matches the precedence it documents (flag beats env beats default, empty-string env treated as unset) and the narrowed `resolveEnvOnlySetting` sibling keeps `"flag"` out of env-only source unions. `validateRunBody` is properly strict: unknown-field rejection, a targeted message for the retired `turns` field, viewport bounds, and `passes` constrained to `[1, 50]`. `parseStateDirName` correctly forbids separators and the dot forms, so the state-dir override cannot escape the project root.

`runResolver` in `credential-tool.ts` is careful where it matters: it settles on `close` rather than `exit` so stdout and stderr have drained, signals the negative pid so a shell resolver's children are reaped, caps both streams, and layers SIGKILL behind SIGTERM with a bounded fallback settle. `spawn` receives an argv array and no shell, and `validateEntity`/`validateKey` reject separators, `..`, leading dots and over-length input. `resolveCredentialResolver` checks regular-file and execute-bit at boot.

`BatchTableRenderer` is safe against the cursor arithmetic hazard I looked for, because `runRunSet` executes runs strictly serially, so there is only ever one active spinner; `pendingBlankAboveSpinner` is cleared on every commit path including `finalize`, and the spinner interval is explicitly unref'd. `format-args.ts`, `format-event.ts`, `format-timing.ts`, `colors.ts`, `format.ts`, `jsonl.ts` and `renderer.ts` each hold up on their own terms, and their tests exercise the claims they name. `writer.ts` is not exposed to filename injection through `obs.kind`: `agent/validators.ts` checks it against the `OBSERVATION_KINDS` literal before the result is ever written, and the slug is stripped to `[a-z0-9-]`. `run-one.ts`, `validate.ts`, `attach.ts` and `error-output.ts` behave as documented, including the deliberate choice to put JSON on the first line and any stack after it.

`paths.ts` holds up under adversarial probing. A scratchpad script exercised `resolveInside` against a directory symlink pointing outside the root, a file symlink pointing outside, the symlink itself, a `..` path, an empty path, a deep path whose leaf does not exist, and a sibling directory whose name is a prefix of the root. Every escape was rejected and every legitimate path allowed, including the validate-before-existence case that `canonicalize`'s walk-up exists to serve; `contextRootIsPopulated` correctly distinguishes a file, an empty directory and a populated one.

`sanitize-error.ts` does what its header claims: `sanitizeLlmError` reads only `status`, `requestID`/`request_id` and a provider error type, retains no reference to the SDK error (no `cause`, no hidden property), never throws, and `withLlmErrorSanitization` wraps the `messages.create` and `responses.create` calls in both adapters, so headers such as `anthropic-organization-id` and `set-cookie` cannot reach a transcript through this path. `resolveAnthropicAuth` and `buildAnthropicClientOptions` keep the OAuth token out of every error message, and the `apiKey: null` reasoning for Bearer-only auth is correct.

The `moe-tab` FFI seam fails loudly rather than self-skipping. A missing cdylib makes `resolveLibPath` throw a plain `Error`, not a `TabError`, so `estimateTrajectory`'s `catch` rethrows instead of degrading to `null` — the cdylib-absent case cannot masquerade as "no usage" in production, and the positive assertions in `test/lab/tab-ffi.test.ts` cannot pass without the real library. The suite is gated into its own `ffi` vitest project rather than silently skipped inside the default pass, which is the countable arrangement `vitest.config.ts` argues for. One narrow gap: "estimateTrajectory returns null when the trajectory file is absent" short-circuits on `existsSync` and never touches the FFI, so that contract lives only in a project CI does not run.

`process-tree.ts` is correct for its callers: `listDescendants` walks `ps -ax -o pid=,ppid=` breadth-first and excludes the root, and every caller passes a real detached pid (never 0), so the `process.kill(-pgid, ...)` footgun the doc comment warns about is not reachable today. The `ps` output on this machine is 10 KB for 868 processes, three orders of magnitude below `spawnSync`'s 1 MB default buffer.

`story-card.ts`'s criteria parser handles the soft-wrap case its comment claims (continuation lines joined, blank line ends a bullet, a real heading ends the section while a wrapped `#123` does not), and `serializeStoryCard` round-trips the fields it emits. `aggregate.ts`'s `deriveBucket` covers every status combination without a fall-through, and `median` guards the empty case. `snapshot.ts`'s `sourceIsPopulated` correctly narrows its swallow to `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR` so permission errors surface before the agent starts. `executeRunCore` preserves the ordering invariant its comments name — result files are written before `beforeClose`, `adapter.close()`, `detachLogger()` and `afterClose`, in both the success and the error path — and every hook failure is isolated. `parse-duration.ts` rejects the forms it says it rejects, and its only consumer compares `Date.now()` against `startTime + budgetMs` rather than arming a timer, so an absurdly large value means "no deadline" rather than an immediate one.

The `moe-tab` boundary tests hold up. `test/lab/tab.test.ts`'s fully-typed `CostEstimate` fixtures do the job their comment claims: `pricing_source` is required, so the added field cannot silently drift, and the "keeps the first TRUTHY pricing_as_of" test pins the `||` in `mergeEstimates` against a `??` regression that an empty-string date would slip past. `usage-row-contract.test.ts` is the strongest test in the shard: it asserts the literal `"moe.tab.usage"` on both sides of a boundary where both producer and consumer fail silently, then writes a real sidecar through `EvidenceLogger` and prices it through the real cdylib.

The credential-installing tools are well covered and I could not find a leak in them. `cookies.test.ts` and `passkey.test.ts` both walk every failure step (`validate_args`, `resolve_path`, `read_cookies`/`read_passkey`, `set_cookies`/`add_credential`), assert path-escape and absolute-path rejection, and check that cookie values and private-key bytes appear in neither the success nor the failure event payload. I read `cookieContext` and `credentialContext` and confirmed they emit only names, lengths and flags, and that the result text handed to the model carries names and rejection reasons but no secret bytes. `buildInstallCookiesTool`, `buildInstallPasskeyTool` and `buildReadTool` all gate on `contextRootIsPopulated`, so the "context root is empty" tests assert real behaviour even though the directory path they pass is a non-empty string.

`navigation.test.ts` earns its keep: I confirmed `navigation.js` creates `loadP` before `Page.navigate` and attaches `loadP.catch(() => {})` at creation, which is the fix the test's `unhandledRejection` listener detects, so it would genuinely fail if that line were removed. `browser-session-reconnect.test.ts` drives the PRI-1690 lazy-reconnect bug through a real mock WS server rather than a stub, and its load-bearing assertion is the positive recovery, not the rejection. `cdp-router.test.ts` covers routing, root-listener dispatch, the "sessionless command responses do not fire root listeners" boundary, unregister-rejects-pending, and unknown-session drops, all against a hand-built fake browser with no live dependency. `websocket-client-no-compression.test.ts` captures the real upgrade headers and I verified `websocket-client.js` passes `perMessageDeflate: false`.

`abort-signal.test.ts` and `empty-end-turn-safety-net.test.ts` both exercise the production paths their names claim. The three abort cases hit the two documented check points (top of the while loop, and inside the per-tool-call loop) and assert `runAgent` resolves rather than throws, which is the stated spec invariant; `executeToolCalls` counts confirm the abandoned work really was abandoned. The empty-turn tests pair the loop behaviour with direct unit coverage of both provider shapes of `synthesizeFilledAssistantMessage`.

The stall-watchdog block in `agent.test.ts` is unusually good. It covers warning at three, forced report at six, the image-result fingerprint using `image.data` rather than the per-call path text (both directions: frozen bytes with changing text, and changing bytes with identical text), chain-breaking by a text-only turn and by a mutating call, and the "exactly one reminder copy" check that catches a woven-plus-appended regression. The `_toolsPerCall` assertion proving the forced turn mounts only `report_result` is a real contract check, not a mock echo. The PRI-2140/PRI-2160 report-validation tests likewise assert against the messages actually handed back to the client, including the sibling "not executed" results and the `tool_call`/`tool_result` rows that session revival depends on.

`capture-parser.test.ts` checks wide-character cell widths and exact 256-colour hex for the cube, greyscale and base-palette arms with the arithmetic spelled out in the comment, so it is not recomputing from the module under test. `generate-html-diff.test.ts` pins the reordering case that the pre-Myers set-based implementation got wrong, which is the one assertion that would catch a regression to the old algorithm. `chrome-ws-lib-isolation.test.ts` is correctly in the `unit` project and needs no browser; `chrome-ws-lib-context-isolation.test.ts`, `side-trip-popup.test.ts`, `lib/browser-bridge.test.ts`, `lib/browser-session.test.ts`, `lib/page-session.test.ts`, `lib/tabs.test.ts` and `lib/webauthn-context.test.ts` all genuinely call `startChrome()` and are correctly gated. `webauthn-context.test.ts` in particular builds a real PKCS#8 P-256 key so `WebAuthn.addCredential` actually validates, and probes isolation in both directions.

`baseline-card.json` is a valid `StoryCard` fixture for `buildSystemPrompt`; both it and `prompt-baseline.txt` are tracked and not gitignored. Its consumer, `prompt-baseline.test.ts`, is assigned to shard 20, so I left its self-regenerating snapshot guard to that shard.

One inaccuracy I checked and decided not to raise as a defect: `vitest.config.ts`'s `ffi` project comment says "One file, run alone under `--project ffi`", but `FFI_SUITES` now holds two files (`tab-ffi.test.ts` and `usage-row-contract.test.ts`), and the comment goes on to say a second suite would need root-level `fileParallelism: false`. I read both files and neither sets `MOE_TAB_PRICING_DIR`, so the race the comment warns about is not live today — the prose is stale, not wrong about the mechanism.

`test/qa/api/active-runs.test.ts` is the strongest file in the shard: the `unregister(runId, startedAt)` guard is tested from both directions including the re-register-then-late-finally race it was written for, the 200-entry progress ring is checked at the boundary (`log[0] === "msg-50"`), and the `abortAll` trio covers count, idempotence, and a controller aborted by external code with the original reason preserved. `test/qa/agent/validators.test.ts` genuinely exercises the LLM seam rather than restating it — the PRI-2140 salvage case reproduces the real truncated-`kind` payload and asserts the verdict survives while index 4 lands in `dropped`, the double-encoded-array recovery is tested on both `observations` and `criteria`, and `checkCriteriaConsistency` is checked in both the enforced and deliberately-unenforced directions.

The traversal assertions in `test/qa/api/file-route.test.ts`, `results.test.ts`, and `run-sets.test.ts` are not vacuous. I confirmed with a minimal Hono app built from this package's own hono that `%2F` inside a path parameter is decoded before the handler sees it, so `..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd` really does arrive as `../../etc/passwd` and really does reach `isSafePath` and `RUN_SET_ID_RE`. `isSafePath` itself canonicalizes through `realpathSync` with an existing-ancestor walk, so it catches symlink escapes and still answers for not-yet-created leaves. The file route's two-layer design is properly covered: the manifest gate, the tampered-manifest case where only `isSafePath` stands between the request and `/etc/passwd`, the implicit `.json` twin of a `.ansi` capture, and — in `results.test.ts` — the live-run branch that skips the manifest, including that traversal is still blocked while a run is in flight.

`test/qa/agent/reflection-checkpoint.test.ts` drives the real `runAgent` loop rather than asserting on a mock's return value: it pins which turns fire (`extras[2]` and `extras[5]` populated, the rest `undefined`), that informational calls are excluded via the adapter's own `isMutatingTool`, that the reminder lands as one `user_message` row, and that `reflectionInterval: 0` produces no checkpoints and no events. `event-stream.test.ts` reads the actual `run.jsonl` off disk and pins row order for the first four events plus `run_end` last. `prompts-drift.test.ts` is a real guarantee, not scaffolding — it re-reads each `.md` from disk and compares against the codegen'd `PROMPT_TEXTS`, restoring the property Bun's text imports gave for free, and pins the set at seven in both directions. `watch-manager.test.ts` covers scan, append, truncation-as-activity, late-appearing directories, the idle-timer reset with a real elapsed-time assertion, and the `concurrent_call` guard.

`ErrorLog` and its route, `RunSetBroadcaster.send`/`removeClient`/`readyState` filtering, `CancelTokenRegistry` register/get/unregister, the `/api/config` and `/api/config/effective` payloads, the 429/413 cap paths with their full error envelopes, and the synchronous `inputs/{story.md,context/}` snapshot in `test/qa/api/routes/run-snapshot.test.ts` all hold up. One note on that last file: it deletes `projectRoot` in a `finally` while the detached `executeHttpRun` is still in flight, but the assertions run before the teardown and the route's `.catch(() => {})` absorbs the background failure, so it is untidy rather than flaky.

Worth recording as context for the whole shard rather than as a finding: `packages/flight/tsconfig.tests.json` deliberately excludes `test/qa/**` ("under this base its 145 suites produce 592 errors. That is a real gap, recorded as a follow-up with the triage — not a green claim"). None of my 30 files is typechecked, which is why `event-stream.test.ts` can omit the required `reflectionInterval` from `AgentOptions` and pass a bare string where a branded `RunId` is declared, and why `as unknown as Adapter` casts across the shard hide contract drift instead of surfacing it. The gap is already documented in the tree, so I am not filing it, but every coverage claim in these files rests on runtime behaviour alone.

The shutdown-drain mechanics in `src/qa/api/shutdown.ts` hold up against both suites: the grace poll, the `cancelAll`-before-`abortAll` ordering that Case 5 pins by recording call order, and the `existsSync`-before-write race guard in `writeShutdownStubs` that Case 3 verifies by pre-writing a real `result.json` for one of two stuck runs and confirming only the other is stubbed. `installShutdownHandlers` correctly keeps `process.exit` out of the testable unit, and `src/qa/index.ts` passes the results directory (not the state root) as `resultsRoot`, so stubs land where `/api/results/:runId` looks for them.

The registry-ordering test in `test/qa/api/run.test.ts` is genuinely non-vacuous: it captures `registry.has(runId)` from inside a fake socket's `send` at the moment the terminal event arrives and asserts `false`, which fails on `null` if the terminal event never fires, so it really does pin the unregister-then-broadcast order in `afterClose`. The two screencast-gate tests rest on a premise I verified — `ScreencastStreamer`'s constructor calls `mkdirSync(saveDir, { recursive: true })` before `start()` is awaited — and `mergeRunConfig` always resolves `saveScreencast` to a boolean, so the `=== false` check in `executeHttpRun` cannot be tripped by an absent value.

`decideUpgrade` and the `parseRunId`/`parseRunSetId` pair are tested at the right granularity, including the Origin allowlist in all four states (empty, matching, mismatched, absent). `test/qa/cards/store.test.ts` is the strongest file in the shard: the fast-path test proves the directory scan was skipped by planting a malformed sibling that would throw if scanned, the direct-hit-mismatch test proves the fall-through, and the error-log assertions check source and filename rather than just a count. `src/qa/api/routes/run-sets.ts` validates its `:id` with a regex before joining, so it is not exposed the way `findCard` is.

`formatTiming` is exhaustively covered at every threshold boundary (49/50/999/1000) on both the success and error paths, and matches its documented rules exactly. `formatToolArgs` is tested per tool family including the two fallback triggers (unknown tool, known tool with unrecognised shape). `formatCliError` covers both the TTY prose and piped JSON contracts, the errno passthrough, the verbose stack line, non-`Error` throws, and JSON validity under quotes, newlines and backslashes. `resolveStreamOptions`, `attachRenderer`'s silent and cleanup paths, `makePaint`'s enabled/disabled split, and `median`/`deriveBucket`'s empty-input handling all behave as their callers assume. `parseBody` in `src/qa/format/story-card.ts` handles bullet continuation, blank-line termination and the heading break correctly, and distinguishes a real heading from a wrapped `#123` reference.

The golden-fixture tests in `pretty.test.ts` are the strongest work in the shard. I re-ran the built `PrettyRenderer` over all three fixture pairs (`happy`, `failing-tool`, `fatal`) and each output matched its `.pretty.txt` byte for byte, so those goldens are current rather than stale. The narrower behavioural tests in that file — section headers, the tool-only-turn dissolve, the `pendingRewrite` invalidation guard, the `read_output` snippet scoping, the anomaly-event compaction — each assert a distinctive string the renderer only produces on the path named, and I confirmed the negative assertions (`not.toContain("valueLength")`, `not.toContain("\x1b[1A\x1b[2K")`) would genuinely fail if the corresponding branch were removed.

`credential-tool.test.ts` is otherwise thorough and honest: the overflow, stderr-overflow, spawn-failure, empty-stdout and nonzero-exit cases each drive a real shell fixture rather than a mock, and the argument-validation cases cover traversal, backslash, leading dot, empty and over-length inputs. The `entity` denylist is weaker than the `key` allowlist (shell metacharacters and a leading dash pass), but `spawn` is called with an argv array and no shell, so nothing is injectable in-process. Transcript redaction is genuinely guarded: `logger.test.ts`'s `"logToolResult prefers transcriptText over text"` asserts `JSON.stringify(row)).not.toContain("raw-secret-value")`, which is the real invariant.

`read-tool.test.ts` and `resolveInside` hold up. The traversal, absolute-path, directory and binary-sniff cases all pass through the production `resolveInside`, and I traced `isSafePath` far enough to confirm the symlink case is closed by `realpathSync` canonicalization even though no test covers it. The binary sniff stops at 8 KB, which the test comment states plainly.

`config.test.ts`, `resolve-setting.test.ts` and `source-attribution.test.ts` cover the cascade honestly, including the case that usually gets missed — a boolean flag set to `false` overriding a truthy env var, asserted as `sources.defaultSaveScreencast === "flag"`. Every case passes an explicit env bag rather than mutating `process.env`, so none of them depend on the developer's shell. `parsePortNumber` and `parseChromeEndpoint` accept trailing garbage and out-of-range ports because they only guard against `NaN`, but the failure lands as a clear `listen` error at startup.

`logger.test.ts` reads real bytes back off disk for every claim, including the event-id chaining and the oversize-spill artifact. `saveScreenshot`'s `name` parameter is unsanitized, but I checked both production callers and neither passes one. `generator.ts`'s three prompt builders and both no-op guards are tested with a stubbed client that also proves the LLM is not called, and the returned cards are re-parsed through the real `parseStoryCard` rather than compared to a recomputed expectation. `story-card.ts`'s wrapped-criteria handling — the PRI-2160 regression, the blank-line terminator, the heading terminator and the `#123` continuation case — is precise and each case is distinguishable. `credential-fixture.ts` is correct, and its comment about awaiting `fn` before `rmSync` documents a real race it avoids. `startMockWsServer`'s teardown terminates its sockets before closing; `startFetchServer` returns without awaiting readiness where its sibling awaits `listen`, which I could not reproduce as a failure and am not reporting.

`rebuild-messages.test.ts` is the strongest suite in the shard: it drives the real `rebuildMessages` over hand-built `run.jsonl` fixtures, uses the genuine `anthropicToolResultMessages` through `makeFakeAnthropicClient` rather than a stub, and pins the three recovery shapes by their distinguishing event rows, including the grace turn that must keep user-before-assistant order. The `--turn` cutoff cases, the terminal tool_use stub synthesis, and the multi-stub `report_with_other_tools_dropped` case all assert on values the production code computes.

`paths.test.ts` earns its "one and only guard" framing for the four exports it does cover: the separator-boundary case (`/a/bb` rejected under `/a/b`), the symlink-inside-base escape, and the `resolveInside` rejection set are all real, on-disk checks rather than string reasoning. `run-set-aggregate.test.ts` computes a median from three distinct sample values and would notice an off-by-one in the sample set. `run-set.test.ts` asserts card-major ordering and cancel semantics through a real executor. `render-run.test.ts`'s breakout case is well built — it checks both that the escape fired and that the JSON region between the opening tag and the legitimate closing tag holds no raw `</script`, rather than scanning the whole file. `render-run-real-template.test.ts` is the only check that the placeholder id survived the rebrand across three packages, and its skip guard prints a reason. `snapshot.test.ts` verifies that the snapshot and the seeded scratch are independent copies by mutating one and re-reading the other. `orchestrator.test.ts` pins the full hook sequence on both the success and error paths as an array equality, and its abort-signal case checks that the errored result reaches disk rather than only inspecting the return value. `answer-tool.test.ts` and `system-prompt-addendum.test.ts` are shallow but honest; `extractAnswer`'s non-string argument case matches the production narrowing.

On CI coverage: the four Chrome suites in this shard, `chrome-profile-rotation`, `web-form-post-nav`, `web-smoke` and `web-todomvc`, plus the two tmux suites, `tui-colored-alphabet` and `tui-nano`, are all excluded from the `unit` project and so never run in the pipeline. What that leaves unguarded is the whole web adapter surface — selector-based `type`, `click`, `extract`, `eval`, screenshot capture and the return_screenshot race — and the TUI capture-evidence pipeline. `tui-colored-alphabet.test.ts` is the one suite among the six whose assertions would actually catch a regression, since it reads the capture files off disk and checks that `run.jsonl` references the path instead of inlining ANSI; it is also the only guard on that behaviour, and it does not run in CI. `cli-fanout.test.ts` does run, but its `parent` and `tags` assertions read back values its own canned LLM response supplied: `generateFanout` and `generateFromObservations` only split on `---CARD---` and filter by `parseStoryCard` success, so a model that ignores the `parent:` instruction produces cards this code accepts and this test would not notice. The round-trip half of that test, writing each card to disk and reparsing, is genuine.

`parse-duration.test.ts` matches `parseDuration` case for case, including the
zero, negative, fractional and trailing-garbage rejections and the
error-message-contains-input contract. `pick-free-port.test.ts` improves on a
shape-only assertion by actually binding the returned port, and is honest about
