the TOCTOU window that `pickFreePort`'s own docstring documents.
`sanitize-error.test.ts` is the strongest file in the shard: the
`JSON.stringify(sanitized, Object.getOwnPropertyNames(sanitized))` idiom does
reach non-enumerable `message` and `stack` (an array replacer bypasses the
enumerability check), and the `util.inspect` and `.cause` assertions close the
paths an unhandled rejection would actually print, all of which line up with
`LlmError`'s allow-list.

`screencast.test.ts` holds up against `screencast.ts`: the `saveDir` gate is real
(`mkdirSync` runs only in the `if (saveDir)` branch), the stop idempotence
assertion of exactly one `Page.stopScreencast` matches the `pageSession = null`
guard, and the synchronous `readdirSync` check is valid because `writeFileSync`
precedes the first `await` in the frame handler. `spawn.test.ts` covers cwd, env
replacement, parent-env exclusion, pid, exit codes and the already-exited race
faithfully. `process-tree.test.ts`'s kill-tree test is careful in the way the
production docstring demands, snapshotting descendants while the leader is alive
and using a pid file rather than racing stderr. `serve-errors.test.ts` does
exercise its claim; I measured `stop()` returning in 0 ms after an aborted
request plus a keep-alive follow-up, so it is neither vacuous nor slow.

On the UI side, no component uses `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and every path that
turns agent-derived data into a URL goes through `api.results.fileUrl`, which
percent-encodes the runId and each path segment, so an attacker-authored
artifact path cannot become a `javascript:` href or escape the results route.
`EventLine`'s `summarize` stringifies unknown event fields into a text node,
which React escapes. `render-run.ts` escapes `</script` before splicing the
payload into the template, and the template's hydration glue is guarded by
try/catch. The `killProcessTree` pgid invariant is honoured by both callers:
`bash-tool.ts` and the CLI adapter each spawn with `detached: true`, and the
adapter tracks `pgid` separately from the pid. Both tsconfigs match AGENTS.md
rule 4, including the deliberate omission of a project reference to
`@tc/moe-flight-ui`, whose build output flight consumes by path.

The reducer in `src/lib/transcript.ts` is genuinely pure: `ensureTurn` copies the `Map` and `cloneTurn` copies the `tools` array before any mutation, so the `setModel((m) => events.reduce(applyEvent, m))` updaters in `useLiveTranscript` are safe under React 19 StrictMode's double invocation. Its `event.eventId <= model.maxEventId` idempotence guard matches the producer: `EvidenceLogger.writeEvent` increments from `eventCounter = 0`, so the first event is 1 and `maxEventId = 0` never swallows it, and `orchestrator.ts` has the only `new EvidenceLogger` call site with a fresh `outDir` per run, so no resume path can replay a lower id into the same stream. Both properties are covered by the "idempotent: applying same events twice yields the same shape" and "out-of-order events" tests.

`buildBlocks`' `SYSTEM_REMINDER_PREFIX` of `/^\s*<SYSTEM-REMINDER>/` looked case-fragile but matches the producer exactly: every injection site in `src/qa/agent/agent.ts` and `src/qa/agent/reflection.ts` writes the uppercase tag. `parseRunId` and `formatRunTimestamp` in `src/lib/runId.ts` agree with the server's `RUN_ID_RE` of `/^[a-zA-Z0-9-]+_\d{8}T\d{6}Z_[a-z0-9]{4}$/` and with `makeRunId`, including the four-character base36 nonce. The back-links in `Container` resolve against the real routes in `App.tsx`, both for `/runs/:id/transcript` and `/runs/live/:id/transcript`.

On the rendering-security lens, the shard is clean. There is no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or `innerHTML` anywhere under `ui/src`. Every piece of agent-, page- or capture-derived text reaches the DOM as a JSX child, which React escapes: `UserMessagePanel`, `SystemReminderPanel`, `ThinkingBlock`, `SystemPromptPanel`, `RunEndPanel`'s summary, reasoning and observation descriptions, `ToolPairCard`'s args and result text, and `CaptureGrid`'s per-cell `ch`. `cssColor` admits only strings starting with `#` and feeds them to React's style object, which writes through the CSSOM and cannot carry a second declaration, so a hostile capture colour cannot inject CSS. The only URL built from data is `api.results.fileUrl`, which hardcodes the `/api/results/` prefix and percent-encodes both the run id and every path segment, so `Screenshot`'s `href` and `src` cannot be steered to another origin or scheme even by a manifest path containing `..` or a colon. Its `rel="noreferrer"` is present on the `target="_blank"` link.

`useRunStream` interpolates `run=${runId}` without `encodeURIComponent`, unlike `useLiveTranscript`. I traced it and it is not exploitable: `decideUpgrade` runs `parseRunId` on `searchParams.get("run")`, and no string that survives that regex contains a character the query string would mangle, so a crafted id is rejected rather than smuggled. Worth aligning for consistency, but not a defect.

The unbounded-growth and performance lenses came back quieter than expected. `Transcript` recomputes `computePromptPairings`, `buildBlocks`, `findSoftErrors` and the anomaly `Map` on every render, and `SystemPromptPanel` re-encodes the whole prompt with `TextEncoder` plus a full `split("\n")` on every render, with no memoization anywhere and no `React.memo` on `TurnBlock` or `ToolPairCard`. I measured it rather than assuming, replaying a synthetic 300-turn run with 4kB tool results and a 200kB system prompt through the exact per-render work, at `/private/tmp/claude-503/-Users-ZKeown-Code-moe/4556b327-b63b-49d4-bbc6-78cd4f317e00/scratchpad/shard-025/perf.mts`: 81ms of JavaScript across all 1202 events, of which the `SystemPromptPanel` share is 39ms and `findSoftErrors` is 7ms. That is roughly 0.07ms per event and not worth reporting. `TuiCapture`'s roughly 4,800 DOM nodes per capture is the real cost, and its comment already states the tradeoff and names virtualization as the intended remedy.

`useActiveRuns` handles its own lifecycle correctly, setting `mountedRef.current = true` at the top of the effect so a StrictMode remount does not leave it latched false, and clearing its interval on cleanup. `useTranscript`'s three-way `TranscriptError` discrimination matches the server: `fileText` throws the sentinel `Error("not-found")` on 404, and `evidence.log` is `"run.jsonl"`, so `collectManifestPaths` does admit the transcript for a completed run and the post-hoc view is not gated out by the manifest check. `computePromptPairings` behaves as documented, including the deliberate non-reset across turn boundaries and the reset on an intervening non-consumer call, and the four `computePromptPairings` tests pin all of it. The `tsconfig.json` is a considered standalone config; its `"types": ["vite/client", "node"]` is needed by the suites that read the fixture with `fs` and `import.meta.dirname`, and I confirmed by grep that no file under `src/` reaches for a Node global, so the wider type surface is not being abused.

The five `packages/flight` configuration files hold up. `ui/turbo.json` declares both `dist/**` and `dist-static/**`, and `ui/package.json`'s `build` does run both vite builds into those two separate `outDir`s, so the cache-hit hazard its comment describes is actually closed. `ui/vite.config.ts`'s proxy target port matches `DEFAULT_PORT` in `src/qa/config.ts`. `ui/vite.static.config.ts`'s rollup input `static.html` exists, and `ui/test/` really does hold the four suites `ui/vitest.config.ts` describes. I verified all seventeen suite paths listed in `flight/vitest.config.ts`'s `CHROME_SUITES`, `FFI_SUITES` and `TMUX_SUITES` exist, and that no `*.test.ts` under `flight/test` falls outside the `unit` project's `test/qa/**` plus `test/lab/**` include — so nothing is excluded into nonexistence.

In `packages/glass`, the mint config and package manifest agree on name and version, `moe-glass` is registered in the root marketplace with the `moe` marketplace name the config sets, and the yaml's claim that the package ships no `.mcp.json` matches `plugins/moe-glass/`. The ESM shims in `src/index.ts` (`fileURLToPath`, `dirname`, `createRequire`) correctly support the runtime `require` of `chrome-ws-lib.js` from the bundled `dist/index.js`, and nothing in `src` writes to stdout, so the JSON-RPC stdio transport is not at risk — every diagnostic in the libraries I read goes to `console.error`.

On injection specifically: `element-selector.js` `JSON.stringify`s every selector it embeds (including the double-stringify in the warn line), and `extraction.js`, `mouse.js`, `keyboard-input.js` and `capture.js` all route selectors through it, so a selector cannot break out of its string literal. `file-upload.js` passes paths as CDP parameters rather than into source. `cdp-utils.js`'s `throwIfExceptionDetails` is called after essentially every `Runtime.evaluate` in these files — the `dialogs-router.js` permission send is the one omission, and that is reported above.

The transport layering is careful and correct: `cdp-router.js` keeps per-session id spaces separate and drops messages for unregistered sessions rather than misrouting them; `page-session.js` gives each session its own counter and rejects pending requests on detach; `browser-session.js` correctly correlates only untagged responses and lets sessionId-tagged ones fall through to the router. `navigation.js`'s `navigate` is the most intricate function in the shard and its hard parts hold: the `Page.loadEventFired` listener is registered before `Page.navigate` is sent, the `frameNavigated` guard correctly rejects Chrome's retrospective broadcast, `loadPromise.catch(() => {})` and `navigatePromise.catch(() => {})` prevent the orphaned-rejection process kill the comments describe, `errorText` is treated as a hard failure, and every early exit path unsubscribes and clears its timer.

`profile-lock.js` is sound — `wx` for the atomic claim, a re-test after the unlink-and-retake to catch the race it admits to, `EPERM` treated as alive so another user's lock is not stomped, and a pid comparison in `release` so a successor's lock is not removed. `chrome-launcher-helpers.js`'s port probing is right in the details that matter: the `/proc/net/tcp` field offsets and the `0A` listen-state filter are correct, `portFreeFromProbes` distinguishes an unavailable IPv6 loopback from a genuine conflict, and `findPidOnPort` validates the port as an integer in range and uses `execFileSync` argv form throughout so the port can never be shell-interpreted. I checked the `ps auxw` truncation hypothesis on this machine and it does not hold — piped output is unlimited (max line 1973 characters, with `--user-data-dir` arguments intact), so the orphan scan's problem is the substring match, not truncation. `html-diff.js`'s Myers implementation and backtrack are algorithmically correct; only its cost is a problem. `key-definitions.js`'s `charToKeyDef` mappings, shift handling and punctuation codes all check out, and `capture.js`'s process-exit handlers are registered once per module rather than once per session, with the session directory correctly rooted under `getXdgCacheHome()`.

No library or server code writes to stdout: a grep across `skills/browsing/lib`, `skills/browsing/*.js` and `src/` finds `console.log` only in the three unwired standalone scripts, and no `process.stdout` use at all, so the stdio JSON-RPC framing is intact. `installHostLifecycleWatch` and the `server.server.onclose` / `onerror` wiring in `main()` are carefully reasoned, including the distinction between a clean transport close (exit 0) and a close after an error (exit 1), and the reason for putting the handlers on the Protocol rather than the transport.

Profile-name containment holds on both entry points: `setProfileName` in `lib/chrome-process.js` and the `CHROME_WS_PROFILE` path in `session-state.js` apply the same `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$` filter, so no profile path escapes `<cache>/moe/browser-profiles/`. `getElementSelector` and `getElementSelectorAll` in `lib/element-selector.js` route every selector through `JSON.stringify` before interpolation, so selectors from tool arguments cannot break out of the evaluated expression; `select-option.js` does the same for its requested values. `src/payload.ts` is genuinely careful: the scalar/structured split is justified per action, `tryParseJsonShape`'s prefix gate keeps CSS attribute selectors away from `JSON.parse`, and the `trimBeforeParse` asymmetry between its two callers is documented as deliberate rather than accidental.

`cdp-router.unregisterSession` correctly rejects every pending request and clears listeners, so `pageSession.detach()` fails fast rather than leaving callers to time out, and per-session id counters really are independent as the comment claims. The `dialogs.smoke.test.mjs` harness is the strongest test material in the shard: it redirects `XDG_CACHE_HOME` into a per-run temp dir (which `getXdgCacheHome` honours on every platform, so the isolation is real), reserves its port with the port-0 trick, uses a unique profile name, and its tests 1, 2, 3 and 5 assert end-to-end behaviour including the negative case that `extractText` refuses rather than hangs. `bundle-drift.test.mjs` guards its own regex against bundler renames with the `calledMethods.size > 0` assertion, and the `cli-dispatch.test.mjs` fake-Chrome cases (arg building, immediate exit, live-but-unreachable port, spawn failure, headed default) each assert a distinct real outcome.

The transport layering is the strongest part of this shard and it holds up. `cdp-router.js`'s routing rules match its tests exactly: session-tagged responses correlate per session, session-tagged events fan out to that session's listeners, untagged events reach root listeners, and untagged responses deliberately fall through to `browser-session.js` — the test "does NOT route untagged responses anywhere (browser-session owns correlation)" pins the one rule a reader would most likely get wrong. `page-session.test.mjs` proves the independent per-session id counters that the module comment says are load-bearing, by attaching two sessions and showing both first messages carry `id: 1` under different session ids. `browser-session.test.mjs` covers lazy connect, single-socket behaviour under concurrent first calls, and retry after both a `chromeHttp` failure and a `connect()` rejection.

I chased the apparent no-reconnect bug in `browser-session.ensureConnected` — the resolved `connectPromise` is cached, so after a socket drop it returns without reconnecting — and it is handled a layer up: `chrome-ws-lib.js`'s `ensureBridge` checks `!state.browserSession.isConnected()` and calls `resetBridge`, which builds a fresh session from `browserSessionFactory`. `chrome-ws-lib-bridge.test.mjs` covers that stale-detection path end to end, including asserting a new WebSocket was constructed. `WebSocketClient.send` also throws when disconnected, so a stale send fails fast rather than silently dropping.

`find-pid-on-port-guard.test.mjs` is the best test in the shard. It stubs `child_process` through `require.cache`, asserts that sixteen injection-shaped and malformed port inputs are rejected *before any process is spawned*, and separately asserts that accepted inputs reach `lsof` as canonical-integer argv elements with `execFileSync` and never a shell — including the surprising-but-correct coercions (`0x23fa` becomes `-ti:9210`). The win32 branch is covered for both the matching and the near-miss port, which is the case a JS reimplementation of `netstat | findstr :PORT` would get wrong. `portFreeFromProbes` is likewise covered for all four probe combinations, and the `EADDRNOTAVAIL`/`EAFNOSUPPORT` cases carry the reasoning for why an unavailable IPv6 loopback is not a port conflict.

Selector escaping is correct everywhere I traced it. Every interpolation of a caller-supplied selector or attribute name goes through `JSON.stringify` — in `element-selector.js`, `extraction.js` (the test asserting `/getAttribute\("href"\)$/` pins it), `navigation.js`'s wait predicates, and `capture.js`'s focus path. The generated expressions are assembled in Node before being handed to CDP as an `expression` string, so a selector containing a backtick or `${` stays inert inside a double-quoted JSON literal. `element-selector.test.mjs` genuinely executes the generated code against jsdom rather than pattern-matching it, and covers visible-preferred, first-of-several-visible, all-hidden-with-warning, no-match, complex CSS, zero-width, and the XPath equivalents.

The dialog layer is well covered on both the state-machine and the routing side. `dialogs.test.mjs` pins the `PAGE_TARGET_ACTIONS`/`BROWSER_TARGET_ACTIONS` literals and their disjointness, and exercises the event handler for `Page.javascriptDialogOpening`, `javascriptDialogClosed`, main-frame versus subframe `frameNavigated`, `Fetch.authRequired` versus non-auth `Fetch.requestPaused`, `Runtime.bindingCalled`, and second-dialog suppression. `dialogs-router.test.mjs` covers every selector and kind combination in both the wsUrl and pageSession shapes, including the `clearDialog` eager-cleanup contract added for the scenario-03 regression. `dialogs-render.test.mjs` uses eleven committed golden files rather than substring matches, which is the right choice for output whose exact wording is the product.

`html-diff.test.mjs` covers the Myers property that motivated the hand-rolled implementation (reordered identical lines are a remove/add pair, not "no changes"), pure additions, pure removals, the 50-line cap with footer, and null input. `key-definitions.test.mjs` covers the shift-symbol and punctuation code maps and the `{special: 'Enter'|'Tab'}` routing. `keyboard-input.test.mjs` correctly pins the headless/headed split that the module comment calls load-bearing, including the shift+letter uppercase-text case and shift+Enter leaving `\r` alone. The page-script tests evaluate the real scripts against jsdom with `runScripts: 'dangerously'` rather than asserting on the source strings, and the markdown size-cap test carries a comment explaining why it uses one large text node instead of 100,000 elements — a considered fix to a real runner-load problem.

`capture.test.mjs`'s three named regression tests are honest about what they check. The Bug 3 pinning test really does prove that post-action captures receive `{id: ps.targetId}` rather than a re-resolved numeric index, and the Bug 4 test finds the actual `restoreFocus` expression and matches `preventScroll`. The dialog short-circuits in `capturePageArtifacts` and `captureActionWithDiff` are covered for the important property — that no `Runtime.evaluate` is issued against a suspended page. The suite also isolates `XDG_CACHE_HOME` into a temp directory, which matters because these paths do real filesystem work; `chrome-process.test.mjs` does the same at module scope with an explicit comment about not deleting the developer's live `meta.json`.

`_helpers.test.mjs` asserts only on the fakes' own behaviour, which would be a red flag anywhere else, but the fakes are the subject and the names say so. Pinning `makeFakeWs`'s single-listener replacement semantics is worthwhile, since that mirrors the real `WebSocketClient.on` and a fake that fanned out instead would hide bugs in every consumer.

Finally, the host lifecycle production code in `src/index.ts` is careful in a way worth recording: `installHostLifecycleWatch` runs before `server.connect`, handles both `end` and `close` on stdin, distinguishes an error-driven transport close (exit 1) from a clean one (exit 0) via `transportErrored`, puts the handlers on `server.server` rather than the transport with a comment explaining the SDK-version reason, and `unref`s the ppid watchdog so it cannot itself hold the process open. The four lifecycle tests cover clean stdin close, idle survival, the reparent watchdog, and the error path — real black-box tests against the built bundle, which is the right level for this behaviour.

`test/payload-normalization.test.mjs` is the strongest file in the shard: it
imports the compiled `dist/payload.js` and executes the real normalizer across
scalar-versus-structured actions, JSON-string equivalence with native objects,
malformed-JSON fallback, the deliberately-kept BOM difference between
`parsePayload` and `tryParseJsonObject`, the `numericDefaultKey` coercion, and the
`PAYLOAD_SPECS` enumeration itself, including that `switch_tab` is excluded from
numeric coercion. Its header comment correctly diagnoses why the grep-style files
in the same directory failed to catch a real bug.

`test/lib/screenshot-exec-safety.test.mjs` is a genuine CWE-78 regression gate. It
installs a recording `child_process` stub through `require.cache` before a fresh
require, drives both the macOS and Linux branches, asserts the hostile path
arrives as one verbatim argv element, asserts no string-form `execSync` is used at
all, and chdirs into a temp directory so that marker files would appear if a shell
ever ran the string. The `require.cache` builtin-injection trick is legitimate
here because `screenshot.js` requires `child_process` without the `node:` prefix,
which `Module._load` checks against the cache before falling back to the builtin.

`test/lib/tabs.test.mjs` exercises real behaviour throughout: the per-`tab.id`
attach cache, `release` detaching and evicting, `releaseAll` clearing without
detaching (correct when the socket is already dead), `prime` registering an
externally attached session and losing to an existing cache entry, the
`about:blank` default in `newTab`, and the ordering constraint that `closeTab`
detaches before issuing `/json/close`. `test/lib/viewport.test.mjs` asserts the
exact CDP method sequence and params including the touch and user-agent
side-effects, plus every validation rejection. `test/lib/profile-lock.test.mjs`
redirects `XDG_CACHE_HOME` per test and covers fresh acquire, live-holder refusal,
stale-PID reclaim, the fallback slot walk past three held names, and that
releasing a foreign-PID lock is a no-op.
`test/lib/websocket-client-no-compression.test.mjs` stands up a real capture
server and pins the load-bearing absence of `permessage-deflate` in the upgrade
headers.

`vitest.config.ts` and the package scripts agree: the three Chrome-driving suites
are quarantined in a `chrome` project, and `test` runs `--project unit` while
`test:chrome` is opt-in, so a bare `pnpm test` never launches a browser. The
`unit` project's include pattern also naturally excludes the `.js`/`.cjs` manual
files. `tsconfig.json`'s empty `references` is correct — glass's only runtime
dependencies are external npm packages, so there is no workspace edge to mirror.

`packages/memory/hooks/hooks.json` uses the two-name
`${PLUGIN_ROOT:-${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}}` fallback deliberately, and
`test/hooks.test.ts` pins both the exact command string and the absence of
`async` (unsupported by Codex plugin hooks). `packages/memory/package.json`'s
`files` list covers every directory the plugin needs (`dist`, `agents`, `hooks`,
`prompts`, `skills`, `.mcp.json`); `prompts/search-agent.md` is referenced only in
prose, so its absence from the generated plugin breaks nothing at runtime.
`mint/moe-memory.yaml` documents why this package earns a bootstrap skill and why
`marketplace.name` must be `moe`, and both claims check out against the root
`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` and the generated
`plugins/moe-memory/hooks/moe-mint/hooks.json`, which merges the bootstrap
SessionStart entry alongside the package's own rather than replacing it.

On stdio-transport hygiene in `src/cli.ts`: the `mcp-server` branch writes nothing
to stdout — the only `console.log` calls are on the help and version paths, every
diagnostic goes to `console.error`, and the top-level handler deliberately skips
`process.exit` on success so the transport keeps the event loop alive. A startup
throw is caught, reported on stderr, and turned into a non-zero exit rather than a
half-open transport.

- **Journal read containment.** `JournalSearchService.readEntry` holds up: extension check, containment in the resolved roots, `realpath`, then containment in the realpath'd roots, with `ENOENT` mapped to `null` rather than an error. The two-stage shape is necessary on macOS as its comment claims, and `isUnderRoot` uses `root + path.sep` so a sibling directory sharing a prefix cannot pass.
- **Journal cross-project isolation.** `buildFilters` constraining on `j.root IN (…)`, `journalEntryId`'s scope asymmetry, and the prune pass's `walked` set together close the three defects their comments describe. Pre-migration rows carrying `root = ''` are excluded from both retrieval and pruning, which is the safe direction.
- **`tool_calls` lifecycle.** I expected `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO tool_calls` keyed on a fresh `crypto.randomUUID()` to accumulate duplicate rows across re-indexes. It does not: the `INSERT OR REPLACE` on `exchanges` performs a delete that fires the `ON DELETE CASCADE`, clearing the old rows before the new ones are written. Verified over three re-index passes — one exchange, one tool-call row each time.
- **WAL leftovers after `--rebuild`.** I expected unlinking `db.sqlite` while `db.sqlite-wal` survived to resurrect pre-rebuild rows or corrupt the new file. Tested with an unclean `SIGKILL` to leave a 284 KB WAL, then the unlink the command performs: the reopened database is empty and `integrity_check` returns `ok`. No finding.
- **Missing `codex` binary.** I expected `detectCodexHookTrustState` to die on an unhandled `EPIPE` from `child.stdin.write` after a failed spawn. With an empty `PATH` it returns `"unknown"` and exits 0; the `child.on("error")` handler and the timeout both clean up correctly. No finding.
- **SQL injection.** Every filter in `buildSearchFilters` and `buildFilters` is a bound parameter, and the placeholder lists are generated from array length, never from input.
- **Symlink traversal of transcript trees.** `findJsonlFiles` uses `withFileTypes` and tests `entry.isFile()` / `entry.isDirectory()`, both of which are false for symlinks, so a symlink planted inside a project directory is neither read nor descended into. Only a top-level entry in the source root escapes, via `fs.statSync` in the indexer, which requires write access to `~/.claude/projects` already.
- **Thinking-block privacy.** `parseClaudeConversation` keeps only `type === "text"` blocks, so Claude thinking blocks are never indexed or embedded. Codex `reasoning` payloads are likewise skipped by `parseCodexConversation` (they surface only in `show`, from the local file).
- **Sentinel state machine.** The four-state file format in `summary-sentinel.ts` (missing / empty / `__ERRORED__` / real) is consistent across `shouldQueueForSummary`, `hasRealSummary`, the indexer's error writes, `search.ts`'s summary load and `stats.ts`'s coverage count. Read failures return `false` from `shouldQueueForSummary`, which fails closed.
- **Locking.** `file-lock.ts` delegating to `proper-lockfile` with `retries: 0` is the right call, and the error policy is explicit: only `ELOCKED` becomes `null`, everything else propagates. `runMigrationBatch` computes embeddings outside the transaction and writes one transaction per batch, so it does not hold a write lock across network or CPU work.
- **Reentrancy guard.** `MOE_MEMORY_SUMMARIZER_GUARD` is set unconditionally in `getApiEnv()`, so it is inherited by both the Claude Agent SDK subprocess and the spawned `codex app-server`, and `shouldSkipReentrantSync` reads it. `persistSession: false` keeps the summarizer's own sessions out of `~/.claude/projects`.
- **JSON-RPC request correlation.** In both `codex-hook-trust.ts` and `runCodexCommand`, `pending.set` happens synchronously inside the `new Promise` executor immediately after the write, and replies can only arrive on a later tick from a readline `line` event, so there is no lost-response race. Non-numeric and unknown ids are ignored rather than mismatched.
- **`install-check.ts`.** Resolving instead of path-probing is correct for pnpm, the required list matches `dependencies` exactly, `onnxruntime-node` and `sharp` are properly excluded, and the fallback to `<pkg>/package.json` covers packages with no CJS entry point.
- **`journal-cli.ts` argument parsing.** The single-pass positional/flag split with `VALUE_FLAGS` genuinely fixes the query-pollution defect its comment describes, including the flag-at-end-of-line and flag-followed-by-flag cases.
- **`compareSemver`.** Tolerates short and non-numeric components by coercing to 0 and compares exactly three fields, which is right for the `0.130.0` gate it serves.

The single-instance sync lock in `runSync` is correctly ordered: it is taken after the help, reentrancy and source-directory checks, released through an idempotent `releaseSyncLockOnce` from a `finally` plus exit and three signal handlers, and the `--background` re-spawn returns before the lock is taken so contention is resolved by the children rather than the parents. Re-spawning through `process.argv[1]` with an explicit `sync` subcommand is the right shape under one bin, and the fall-through when `argv[1]` is empty is handled.

`src/file-lock.ts` and `test/file-lock.test.ts` are the strongest pair in the shard. The wrapper's error policy is explicit and tested (contention returns null, I/O errors propagate), and the suite covers held locks, release and re-acquire, parent-directory creation, PID reporting including garbage content, mtime-based stale reclamation and the negative case where a fresh mutex must not be stolen. My reproduction of the underlying protocol matched the tests' expectations in every case.

`test/journal-project-isolation.test.ts` covers all three of the data-loss defects its docblock names, with a positive control (the shared user root must still be visible from the other project) alongside the two negative assertions, so the isolation tests cannot pass by returning nothing. `test/journal-search.test.ts` carries the five path-containment tests for `readEntry` intact, including the unnormalised `..` case and the symlink escape, and the two-stage resolve-then-realpath rationale is correct for macOS. `fakeEmbed` in `test/test-utils.ts` is a genuine deterministic bag-of-words encoder, unit-normalised as `l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity` requires, so the ranking assertions in the journal suites mean what they say.

`test/cosine-similarity.test.ts` pins the right formula including the clamp, and its "0.5 for distance 1" case is a real discriminator against the `d/2` mistake. `test/journal-cli-args.test.ts` covers the flag-value-leaking bug thoroughly, including a trailing flag with no value and a value-shaped positional. `test/codex-support.test.ts` and `test/codex-doctor.test.ts` exercise real behaviour against injected inputs rather than a live Codex. `test/install-check.test.ts` includes the one test that would have caught the pnpm resolution problem, running the real resolver against the real install. `test/version-consistency` is satisfied: `VERSION` is `0.0.0-tc.1` and so is `package.json`. `hooks/hooks.json` matches `test/hooks.test.ts` byte for byte, including the `PLUGIN_ROOT`/`CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` fallback and the absent `async` key.

`src/types.ts` is declarations plus `JOURNAL_SECTION_HEADINGS`, and the heading order there matches the render order asserted in `test/journal-markdown.test.ts`. The `journalEntryId` asymmetry (root in the key for `project` scope only) looked wrong against the `migrateJournalRoot` docblock until I read both comments and the project-isolation test; it is deliberate, documented at both sites, and tested from both directions.

On `copyIfNewer`: the temp-file name is scoped by pid and the rename is atomic on one filesystem, so concurrent syncs do not corrupt an archive copy. The `mtimeMs >= srcStat.mtimeMs` comparison is safe because `copyFileSync` stamps the destination at copy time rather than preserving the source mtime.

One dependency worth naming without filing: `sqlite-vec` is pinned as `^0.1.7-alpha.2`, an alpha-tagged prerelease that loads a native extension into every SQLite connection, and it is the substrate for both vector tables. The root `pnpm-lock.yaml` plus CI's `--frozen-lockfile` means installs are reproducible, which is what keeps this off the findings list, but the caret range on a prerelease is worth a deliberate decision rather than an inherited default.

The strongest suites in the shard hold up well. `test/sync-error-sentinel.test.ts` mocks only
`summarizeConversation` and then asserts real filesystem outcomes, sentinel content, mtime
backdating across the retry threshold, the environment override, and queue drainage past the
summary limit, so nothing there asserts a mock's own return value.
`test/summarizer-resume-fallback.test.ts` stubs the SDK's `query` but inspects the options and
prompt of each call, which is the contract under test rather than the stub.
`test/sync-cli-single-instance.test.ts` picks winner and loser from observed output rather
than assuming an ordering, so a broken lock fails it in both directions.
`test/tool-calls-cascade.test.ts` builds a genuine legacy schema with a deliberately
orphaned row and verifies both the orphan removal and that cascade works afterwards.
`test/model/journal-encoder.test.ts` earns its place in the encoder project: it asserts a
paraphrase match with no shared vocabulary, and separately that stored vectors are unit-norm at
the shared width, which is the undeclared precondition of `l2DistanceToCosineSimilarity`.
`test/model/search-metadata-filters.test.ts` is a good suite in the wrong project.

`fakeEmbed` in `test/test-utils.ts` is well judged: word-level hashing with L2 normalisation
means a ranking assertion carries information, and the docstring is honest that a paraphrase
scores near zero, which is why the real-encoder round trip exists separately. Both tsconfigs
are consistent with the repo rule: the package has no workspace dependencies, so empty
`references` arrays in `tsconfig.json` and `tsconfig.tests.json` are correct, the test config
is non-composite and `noEmit` as its comment states, and the two manual e2e scripts its
`exclude` names are both present on disk. The MCP tool name asserted in
`test/search-agent-template.test.ts` matches the agent frontmatter, the skill docs, the prompt
template, and the e2e harness, with no stale prefix variants anywhere in the package. The MCP
server declares `capabilities: { tools: {} }`, keeps all diagnostics on stderr so stdout stays
clean for JSON-RPC, validates every tool input with a `strict` Zod schema, and returns errors
inside the result rather than as protocol failures. Arbitrary-path reads through
`read_conversation` are bounded in practice, since the formatter's `JSON.parse` rejects any
file that is not valid JSONL carrying message content.

The shallow tier is correct on a well-formed plugin: I generated the kitchen-sink fixture into a scratchpad and every shallow check passed, including `claude plugin validate --strict`, the node and bun module imports, and the jq parse plus referenced-path sweep for all six manifest targets. The `del(.mcpServers)` exclusion in `check_manifest_harness` is justified by the fixture's own deliberately non-existent `./mcp-demo-server.js` arg, and it works. Despite `set -u` without `set -e`, every empty-array expansion in the script is guarded by a preceding count check, and the whole script ran clean under this machine's bash 3.2.

Path containment against declared config is solid: `requiredComponentPath` in `config.ts` restricts component and `release.files` paths to `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` segments and separately refuses `.` and `..`, which is what makes the raw string interpolation of `__SKILLS_DIR__` and `__BOOTSTRAP_PATH__` into the emitted OpenCode JavaScript and Pi TypeScript safe, and what keeps `replaceAll`'s `$`-substitution semantics from mattering. `PLUGIN_NAME_RE` similarly makes `toPascalCase` and the bootstrap-marker interpolation safe. `resolveHarnessSettings` validates both `harnesses.exclude` entries and per-harness block keys against `ADAPTER_NAMES`, so a typo is an error rather than a silent no-op, and `registry.test.ts` is cited as keeping that duplicated list honest.

Determinism holds for the generated tree. `generate` emits from a `Map` keyed by path with an explicit collision policy (`mergeFiles` dedupes byte-identical output across owners and throws on differing content), `saveManifest` sorts by path, the manifest is content-addressed with no timestamps, `model.ts` sorts skills, commands and agents by name, and `TOOL_VERSION` is a literal. `isSourcePath` correctly refuses to let an adapter clobber a source component. The bash escaping in `shell-hook.ts` decodes correctly through both the TypeScript and bash quoting layers: `escape_for_json` produces valid JSON string content, and `printf` with a fixed format string is not vulnerable to `%` in the bootstrap text.

`deepMerge`'s null-delete sentinel behaves as documented, including at depths where the base has no key, and `Object.entries` plus spread avoid genuine prototype pollution. `mergedClaudeHooks` uses `structuredClone` and does not mutate its input. `field-edit.ts` guards `doc.setIn`'s silent-structure-creation and raw-throw behaviour by checking existence with `getIn` first, and its `__proto__`-shaped path attack is blocked by that same existence check. `bumpVersion`'s readability preflight collects all failures before mutating anything, and `assertNoGeneratedBumpFiles` correctly refuses a `release.files` entry naming the config or a generated path. `globToRegExp` escapes every regex metacharacter the glob syntax does not claim. `injectReadme` is correctly kept outside the FileSet and manifest machinery and is inert under `pnpm mint`, since `README.md` is not among the staged `COMPONENTS`.

On the shard's explicit question of whether the checks catch a hand-edited manifest: `run-checks.sh` does not, and does not claim to. It never reads `.moe-mint/manifest.json` and never invokes `moe-mint validate`. That job belongs to `checkDrift` plus the `pnpm mint:check` git-diff gate, both of which do hold.

The collision and source-protection logic in `generate` is careful and well covered: `mergeFiles` routes adapter output and doc output through one rule set, `isSourcePath`'s `.md`-only allowance for `commands`/`agents` siblings is deliberate and tested from both directions, and the byte-identical-dedupe and differing-content-rejection paths each have a test. The prune stage's containment check on manifest paths (`isAbsolute` plus `startsWith(rootAbs + sep)`) is correct, its empty-parent cleanup terminates at `rootAbs`, and the hand-modified-stale-file warning correctly refuses to delete. The corrupt-manifest recovery is a genuinely good design call, documented in place and tested, and `saveManifest`'s path sort makes the manifest reproducible independent of adapter order.

`manifest.ts`'s `loadManifest` shape check catches both `null` and a non-object `files`, and wraps a JSON error in a `ConfigError` with a `cause`. `model.ts`'s `readJsonIfPresent` rejects `null` and arrays with a pointed message, which I confirmed by running it, and the bootstrap-skill existence check is enforced at model-build time rather than left to an adapter. `import.ts`'s round-trip through `loadConfig` after writing, with cleanup of both the config and any inline-extracted component file, is the right shape and holds: I confirmed that an escaping `skills: ../secret` path is rejected and every created file removed, and that the component-path schema's charset plus its explicit `.`/`..` segment refusal leaves no traversal that survives. `test-command.ts` builds its `docker` argv as an array rather than a shell string, interpolates only a `PLUGIN_NAME_RE`-validated name, guards double-settle between the `error` and `close` handlers, and maps the deliberately distinctive exit 3 apart from docker's own exit 1.

The test suites are unusually strong on exact content rather than shape: every adapter manifest is pinned with `toEqual` against a full literal, warning lists are asserted as complete arrays rather than with `toContain`, and the support matrix is pinned as one literal document. Several suites go past string matching into execution, which is where the real value is: the opencode plugin JS is dynamically imported and its config and transform hooks driven twice to prove idempotence and single bootstrap injection, the pi extension is type-checked under strict NodeNext against a per-event-overload stub, and a deliberately broken variant is asserted to fail compilation so the stub is shown to have teeth. `helpers.ts`'s `mustGet` turns a dropped emission into a message naming the path and listing what was emitted instead. `registry.test.ts` is the right tripwire for the `ADAPTER_NAMES` duplication that the import cycle forces. `field-edit.test.ts` covers the destructive-write cases exhaustively and asserts the file is byte-unchanged after each refusal. `config.test.ts` pins each legacy-syntax migration error as an exact string. Where a test does recompute part of its expectation from the module under test (`docs-emit.test.ts` embedding `claudeCode.installDoc!(model)` and `opencodePluginPath('kitchen-sink')`), the recomputed component is separately pinned as a literal in the owning adapter suite, so the wrapping is what is actually being asserted and the coupling is not load-bearing.

The `manifest.test.ts` suite is the strongest in the shard: `writeFileSet`'s escape rejection is genuinely atomic (validation runs as a full map pass before any write, which I confirmed against `fileset.ts`), and the `deepMerge` null-sentinel cases, the exec-bit drift cases and the corrupt-manifest cause chaining all state expectations as literals rather than recomputing them from the module under test. `model.test.ts` and `validate.test.ts` are the same shape, and the "sorts agents by their final frontmatter-overridden name" and "issue #10 v1 config" cases each pin a specific past bug with an independent expectation.

`init.test.ts` matches the implementation: every sanitization case is reachable through `sanitizePluginName`, and every output it can produce satisfies `PLUGIN_NAME_RE`, including the digit-leading `3d-tools` case. The "reports partial scaffold on generate failure" case does trip a real guard — `generate.ts` refuses to clobber a pre-existing file absent from the prior manifest whose content differs — so the test is not asserting behaviour the code lacks. `smoke.test.ts` correctly ties `TOOL_VERSION` to `package.json`. In `test-command.test.ts` the sync-throw versus promise-rejection split is right: `runTest` is a non-async function that throws synchronously for the missing manifest and returns a promise thereafter, so the two assertion styles are both correct, and the docker exit-code mapping tests cover 0, 1, 3 and 127 against the real `child.on('close')` logic. Vitest 3's default `forks` pool keeps the `process.env.PATH` mutation in that file from leaking into other suites.

The mint tsconfig pair satisfies the two-tsconfigs rule: the package has no workspace dependencies, so both `references` arrays are legitimately empty, and the test project is non-composite with `noEmit` so it cannot collide with the runtime project's `dist` output.

On the C ABI seam, the four exported symbols agree across the committed header, the Rust FFI, the Go binding's `RegisterLibFunc` names, the Python `ctypes` prototypes and both TypeScript backends; the argument and return widths line up (`int32_t` against koffi `int`, ctypes `c_int32`, purego `int32` and Bun `FFIType.i32`), and the `char**` out-parameter is modelled correctly everywhere — deliberately as `void**` in `ffi-node.ts`, with the comment explaining that `char**` would make koffi stringify and lose the pointer. I verified that pattern empirically against libSystem: koffi's `_Out_ void**` writes an external pointer into a one-element array, `koffi.decode(p, 'char', -1)` is the documented NUL-terminated decode, and a NULL `void*` decodes to `null`, so both branches of `drain` are right. Ownership matches the Rust contract in all three languages: the static `moe_tab_version` string is never freed, every `out_json` is freed exactly once through `moe_tab_string_free`, and inputs are treated as borrowed. Non-ASCII UTF-8 round-trips intact through both koffi and Bun's `CString`.

The Go `EstimatePath` and `Refresh` marshalling is correct: `append([]byte(s), 0)` always yields a non-empty slice so `&p[0]` is safe even for an empty string, `runtime.KeepAlive` covers both buffers, and `drain`'s `defer cStringFree(out)` frees on every path. `extractEmbedded`'s write itself is sound — unique temp name, chmod before rename, atomic rename, and a lost-race check that returns the winner's identical bytes. `cmd/total/main.go`'s `strconv.FormatFloat(..., 'g', -1, 64)` is the shortest round-trip form and matches what `validate-bindings.sh` normalizes against.

The Python `test_moe_tab.py` expectations are independently derived: the version comes from the workspace manifest (and `moe-tab-ffi` does inherit it via `version.workspace = true`), `pricing_as_of` comes from the fixture, and the `PricingTablesMissing` code-1 expectation matches the core's explicit-override branch rather than its bundled fallback. `setup.py`'s impure platform-tagged wheel setup is coherent, and the release tooling does stage the `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` and `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt` entries that the TypeScript `package.json` `files` array lists but git does not carry, so that is not a packaging gap. The locked network dependencies are current enough to be uninteresting: ureq 2.12.1 over rustls 0.23.43 and ring 0.17.14, with no known-vulnerable pin, though ureq 2.x is in maintenance while 3.x is current.

The C ABI contract holds across the three surfaces I could compare. The
committed `include/moe_tab.h` declares `moe_tab_version`,
`moe_tab_string_free`, `moe_tab_estimate_path` and `moe_tab_refresh_pricing`
with the same names, arities and integer widths as the `#[no_mangle]`
definitions in `crates/moe-tab-ffi/src/lib.rs`, and both TypeScript backends
bind exactly those four symbols. The `void*` for `char*` substitution in the
koffi prototype is deliberate and documented ("char** makes koffi auto-stringify
and lose the pointer, leak") and is ABI-identical; `int` for `int32_t` is
identical on every supported target. Ownership is honoured on both sides: the
Rust side NULL-initialises `*out_json` before doing anything, wraps each body in
`catch_unwind` so no panic crosses the boundary, and hands out only
`CString::into_raw` pointers; each binding's `drain` helper copies the string
out and then calls `moe_tab_string_free` exactly once on a non-NULL pointer,
and both treat `version()` as static and never free it. The Bun backend's
`?? 0n` guard against `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` correctly prevents an
`undefined` from becoming `NaN` and being passed to `free`.

`unwrap` in `src/index.ts` is a faithful decoder of the error envelope: the
`kind`, `code` and `message` defaults hold when the envelope is missing or
unparseable, and it cannot be reached with a status of 0 and a NULL payload
because `finish` in the FFI only returns `OK` after `write_out` succeeded. The
declared `pricing_source: "bundled" | "local"` matches what `PricingSource`'s
hand-written `Serialize` emits, and the adjacently tagged `Approximation`
matches the declared `{ kind, detail? }` shape. `resolveLibPath` gets the dev
fallback right for both the `src/` and `dist/` layouts, since each sits one level
under the package root, and its "never return a path that does not exist"
invariant is the one the unit test pins.

`pricing::as_of` is the most carefully written module in the shard: length,
separator, digit, calendar and clock checks are all present, the leap-year rule
handles the century cases, the sort key cannot overflow `u64`, and
`archive_file_name` cannot smuggle a path separator because the validator has
already rejected everything but the two canonical forms. The precedence logic in
`resolve_store` compares parsed stamps rather than raw strings and demotes an
unparseable local snapshot to the embedded floor, with tests pinning both. The
`utc_stamp_from_epoch` implementation in the CLI is Hinnant's civil-from-days
algorithm applied correctly, its `unreachable!` on the dialect string is
genuinely unreachable because clap's `value_parser` has already restricted the
value, and `now_stamp_passes_core_validation` closes the loop between the two
crates.

The cost engine's treatment of a provider-reported native cost is right, and
well tested: `Some(native)` short-circuits list-price math, suppresses the
`unpriced_models` entry and suppresses the tier-assumption approximation,
because none of those describe what happened. The empty-model case is
deliberately kept out of `unpriced_models` and surfaced as
`UnknownModelForTurn` instead, which preserves the distinction a consumer
needs. The ATIF cost-precedence ladder is the subtlest logic here and I could
not break it: per-step costs win when complete, `final_metrics.total_cost_usd`
wins when they are not, and the zero-token override record plus the
`Some(0.0)` suppression really does sum to the authoritative total without
double counting, with tokens still aggregated from the step records. The loss
of per-model attribution in that branch is documented in the code rather than
hidden.

The OpenAI cached-token subtraction is correct and correctly clamped with
`saturating_sub`. `normalize_litellm` and `normalize_openrouter` skip entries
they cannot price rather than defaulting them, which keeps an unpriced model
loud; the `sample_spec` pseudo-entry in the upstream LiteLLM sheet is filtered
out by the `mode != "chat"` check. Both `Cargo.toml` files inherit version,
license and repository from the workspace, `Cargo.lock` is committed and pins
ureq 2.12.1 by checksum, and the dependency set is small and maintained. The
two tsconfigs match the repo rule: the runtime program declares no references
because the cdylib is a runtime path rather than a module edge, and the
test-only program is non-composite and references the built package. The
crate-root `test_env::env_lock` and the FFI crate's own copy are the right
answer to cargo's multi-threaded test runner, and both recover from a poisoned
mutex rather than cascading; `vitest.config.ts` sets `fileParallelism: false`
for the same hazard on the TypeScript side. The `version` test derives its
expectation from the workspace manifest rather than a literal, and I confirmed
its regex selects `0.0.0-tc.1` from `[workspace.package]` rather than a
dependency's `version` key. One cosmetic redundancy, not a defect: `moe-tab-cli`
lists `moe-tab-core.workspace = true` in both `[dependencies]` and
`[dev-dependencies]`.

**The C ABI itself, verified against the shipped binaries.** `nm -gU` on both committed dylibs in `native-release/` shows exactly four exported `moe_tab_*` symbols — `estimate_path`, `refresh_pricing`, `string_free`, `version` — matching the four declarations in `crates/moe-tab-ffi/include/moe_tab.h` with nothing extra and nothing missing. A full symbol-table and strings scan for `obol` returns zero hits in both slices, so the rename landed completely in the artifacts, and the `0.0.0-tc.1` version string is present in each. Widths agree across the seam as well: `int32_t` in the header, `c_int32` in ctypes, `i32` in bun, `int` in koffi, `int32` in purego.

**`native-release/manifest.json` is fully verifiable and current.** Every claim in it checks out: both artifact `sha256` values and `bytes` counts match the committed dylibs, `licenses.payloadSha256` matches `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt`, and `cargoManifestSha256` and `cargoLockSha256` match `packages/tab/Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` in the working tree. `source.commit` is a real commit and an ancestor of HEAD, `source.cratesTree` is a real tree object equal to `packages/tab/crates` at both that commit and HEAD, and the Cargo manifests are unchanged since. This is a provenance record that actually holds.

**Memory ownership across the FFI boundary.** I traced every write path for leaks and double frees and found none. Each entry point rejects a NULL `out_json` with code 7 before doing anything, NULL-initializes `*out_json`, and runs the body under `catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(...))`. `write_out` only ever stores into a slot holding NULL: `finish` writes once and returns, and the one path where `write_out` returns false sets the slot to NULL before `fail` overwrites it. No panic can occur between `c.into_raw()` and the return, so the `ERR_PANIC` handler never clobbers a live allocation. `moe_tab_string_free` guards NULL and reconstructs with `CString::from_raw`, matching the allocator that produced the pointer. `moe_tab_version` returns a `concat!` static, correctly documented "Do NOT free". The interior-NUL branch in `write_out` is genuinely unreachable for `envelope` output, because serde_json escapes a NUL byte as the six-character sequence backslash-u-0-0-0-0. All three consumers honor the contract: `_decode_and_free` frees in a `finally`, koffi's `drain` frees whenever the pointer is non-null, and the bun path mirrors it.

**Panics and the two `unsafe` blocks.** No panic can cross the boundary: both exported functions map `Err(_)` from `catch_unwind` to code 8 with a freeable envelope. The crate-wide `#![allow(clippy::not_unsafe_ptr_arg_deref)]` is justified in the header comment and is the right call for a C-callable seam that NULL-checks internally. `parse_dialect` handles NULL, invalid UTF-8 and unknown values before `CStr::from_ptr`. The one dead edge I found is harmless: `code_and_kind` maps `TabError::UnknownDialect` to code 2, but `estimate_cost` never calls `detect`, so code 2 is unreachable through the FFI and no binding hardcodes it.

**`transcript/tab.rs` accounting.** The dispatch to `provider::{anthropic,openai}` keeps the arithmetic in one place, and `request_input_tokens` is the correct full billed input for tier selection (uncached plus cache read plus both write buckets). The hardcoded `namespace: "litellm"` is consistent with `MessageUsage`'s own comment, and the only provider tags accepted are the two that error message names. Rejecting an unknown `v` outright is the right call for a pricing tool. The test set is real, not scaffolding: `anthropic_buckets_route_through_shared_normalizer` pins the interpretation rather than the plumbing.

**Fixtures.** All three are referenced by live tests. `atif-mini.json` is internally consistent — I summed the per-step metrics and they match `final_metrics` exactly for prompt, completion and cached tokens — and its `made-up-model-zzz` step is a deliberate unpriced-model probe that the FFI test asserts on. `litellm-sample.json` and `openrouter-sample.json` both carry purposeful edge rows (`dall-e-3` with no costs and `image_generation` mode; `weird/no-pricing` with no pricing key; a `"0"` cache-write price that is distinct from absent).

**Header generation and `cbindgen` dependency risk.** `gen_header.rs` and the `header_matches_source` test build bindings the same way from the same `cbindgen.toml`, so the committed header cannot drift from source without turning `cargo test` red, and the failure message tells you to run `gen-header.sh`. `cbindgen = "0.27"` is a caret range, but `packages/tab/Cargo.lock` pins `0.27.0` with a checksum, so a formatting change in a future patch release cannot spuriously fail the test. `gen-header.sh` is a correct four-line wrapper; `cargo run --example` does get dev-dependencies.

**Shell robustness beyond the findings above.** `bash -n` passes on all five scripts. Both `mktemp -d` plus `trap ... EXIT` pairs are set immediately after assignment and only ever `rm -rf` a variable that mktemp populated. I tested two `set -e` interactions rather than reasoning about them: the trailing `command -v bun >/dev/null 2>&1 && HAVE_BUN=1` does *not* abort under `set -euo pipefail` (bash 3.2 exempts the AND-OR list), and the `$([ "$(uname)" = Darwin ] && echo dylib || echo so)` substitution yields `.dylib` and `.so` on the two branches. Assignments avoid the `local x=$(...)` trap that would mask a failure. `norm`'s `repr(float(...))` is the right canonicalizer: it erases the formatting differences between serde_json, Go's `FormatFloat('g', -1, 64)` and JavaScript's `console.log` while preserving bit-level distinctions, so the comparison is stronger than the "byte-identical" phrasing suggests. `date -u +%Y-%m-%d` is portable across BSD and GNU.

**The two `docs/history/scripts` are not defects.** `validate_against_sevals.sh` and `validate_pi.sh` reference `obol-cli`, `OBOL_PRICING_DIR`, `--dialect pi|claude|codex`, `mise exec rust@1.96.0`, and external checkouts, none of which exist here, and their `REPO` resolves to `docs/history` rather than a repo root. `docs/history/README.md` states this explicitly and correctly: "Everything under this directory is upstream `obol` material, kept byte-for-byte as received", and "neither runs against this code ... They are here as the method behind the numbers in `validation/`, not as runnable tools." Fixing or rebranding them would falsify the record, so I am reporting nothing against them. Their internal logic is otherwise sound — heredocs written to temp files to avoid tangling with subshell `cd`, and a missing-file `SKIP` guard per cell in the Pi script.

The grading state machine holds up under scrutiny. `grade_run`'s scoring rules are subtle and
correct: skipped results carry no `ok` key and are excluded from both the `unscored_failure`
scan and the outcome vote by the `if "ok" in r` filters; a check that fails without scoring
correctly suppresses a later check's score rather than letting a stale one stand in; the
`creates` promise is only enforced on a check that otherwise passed; and the grader snapshot
is written byte for byte so `grade_matches_grader` can compare parsed documents and ignore
comment-only edits. The `name` rebinding inside the `missing` comprehension does not leak,
because comprehensions have their own scope in Python 3, so the subsequent
`{"checker": name, ...}` is correct.

`normalize_check_info` genuinely closes the key-clobbering hole it claims to: `score`,
`metrics`, `tags`, and `notes` are read positively and everything else is folded into
`details`, so no checker can inject `ok`, `checker`, or `skipped` into a result. The
`{"checker": name, "ok": ok} | info` merge order is the right way round.

The traversal guard in `serve_eval` holds. `target.resolve()` plus `is_relative_to` defeats
encoded and unencoded dot segments, prefix-sibling directories, and symlinks pointing out of
the runs tree, and `test_serve_refuses_prefix_sibling_of_runs` and
`test_serve_refuses_paths_outside_runs` pin exactly the right cases. The absence of
percent-decoding is a functional defect, filed above, not a hole in this check.

`check_xml_valid` is safe against the two XML attacks worth testing here. I ran both against
the interpolated version of ElementTree: a SYSTEM entity pointing at `/etc/passwd` raises
`ParseError: undefined entity` rather than disclosing the file, and a nine-level billion-laughs
document raises `ParseError: limit on input amplification factor ... breached` in 0.04
seconds. Expat reports version 2.8.3.

Subprocess construction is correct throughout. Both `subprocess.run` calls pass a single-element
argv list with no shell, so no task, check, or model value is ever interpreted by a shell.
Runner and checker paths are resolved and then gated on `is_file() and os.access(..., os.X_OK)`
before execution. Configuration reaches the child only through prefixed environment variables,
and because every generated name carries a `MOE_PROOF_` prefix, no task or check key can
overwrite `PATH` or any other inherited variable. Both children get the parent environment,
which is how a runner reaches its API key, and no key is written into `run.yaml`, `grade.yaml`,
or the report: the recorded config holds only the config name, the resolved runner path, and
the model. `yaml.safe_load` is used for every read and `yaml.safe_dump` for every write, in
both modules, with no `yaml.load` anywhere.

`run`'s scheduling shape is right where it is tested. The repeat index is outermost, so an
interrupted session leaves balanced samples, and `test_repeat_runs_in_full_passes` pins the
`aa, bb, aa, bb` order rather than just the count. Failed runs are excluded from the target by
`count_existing_runs`, are never graded, and are excluded from `report` even when a stale grade
exists against one, and `test_failed_runs_do_not_count_toward_target` demonstrates the
shortfall is attempted once per invocation with no retry loop. The grader is validated before
any model is called, which `test_invalid_grader_fails_before_any_run` verifies by asserting no
runs directory was created. Same-second collisions get a numeric suffix under a frozen clock.

`discover_evals` stops descending at each eval, so runs trees are never scanned, and
`test_discover_evals_recurses_and_stops_at_evals` proves it with a decoy eval.yaml planted
inside a runs directory. `resolve_eval_slugs` rejects duplicate slugs in both directions.

The report arithmetic checks out. `mean_stderr` is the sample standard deviation over the
square root of n and is only reached with a non-empty list; competition ranking ties on the
displayed string rather than the raw float, which is the behaviour a reader of the output
would expect; boolean metrics are rendered as rates and numeric ones as mean plus standard
error, and `test_metrics_aggregation_numbers_and_booleans` pins both.

The 17 example YAML documents match the schema the loader actually enforces. Every eval.yaml
has the `name` that `resolve_eval_slugs` and `collect_eval` read; every config has the
`runner` and `model` keys that `run` indexes directly rather than fetching with a default;
every task has the `name` that `execute_run` requires; every grader has the `checks` list
that `grade_run` iterates. Each referenced checker path exists and is executable, `xml-valid`
is the real built-in name, and the `tags` lists in the two judge graders are read from the
`MOE_PROOF_CHECK` JSON blob rather than from an environment variable, which is correct because
`scalar_env_vars` drops list values. The one place the examples brush against that limitation
is the scalar-versus-list `creates` gap filed above.

I ran the suite with the committed virtualenv, `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` and
`-p no:cacheprovider`: 88 passed in 12.05s, and `git status --porcelain` was empty afterwards.
Dependency risk is low: `click` and `pyyaml` carry lower bounds only, but `uv.lock` pins
click 8.5.0, pyyaml 6.0.3, and pytest 9.1.1 with hashes, and the `>=3.10` floor is honest, as
the committed environment is CPython 3.10.21 and the code uses nothing newer than
`Path.is_relative_to` and dict union.

**Credentials.** `.npmrc` carries one line, an `@tc` scope registry, with no token, auth line or `_authToken` placeholder; grepping the tracked tree for `_auth`, `NPM_TOKEN` and `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` finds hits only inside the publisher. `scripts/tc-release-publish.mjs` writes its own npmrc into an `mkdtempSync` directory at mode 0600 with flag `wx`, passes it via `--userconfig` and `NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG`, and removes the directory in a `finally`. The token reaches the environment only through `ci-safe-env publish`, which rebuilds the child environment with `env -i` and forwards exactly one secret per mode; every other job runs in `safe` or `rust` mode and cannot see it. `assertPublishContext` independently re-derives the protected-default-branch-push boundary before any tar is opened, and rejects a token containing a line break. No job echoes a variable. Registry strings agree across `.npmrc`, `publishConfig.registry` and `PROGET_REGISTRY`.

**Pipeline gates.** Every gate AGENTS.md names is present and unconditional outside scheduled pipelines: `install`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `test`, `build`, `plugins` as `pnpm mint:check`, and `provenance`, with `tab` and `proof` path-scoped as described. `--frozen-lockfile` is used in the shared `.pnpm` anchor and repeated identically in the one job that needs its own `before_script` for jq. The `.not-scheduled` rules are fail-closed first with an unconditional fallback. `tc-release-pack` and `tab-native-linux` carry rule sets that match condition for condition, so the mandatory `needs` edge between them is satisfiable in every pipeline where the pack job runs; tag pipelines match no publish rule because `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is unset. `tc-release-publish` names each gate directly rather than inheriting the pack job's, and adds `environment`, `resource_group` and `interruptible: false`. The path-scoped `bin` job is redundant rather than a hole, since `pnpm test` calls `pnpm bin:test` unconditionally. jq is installed in the two jobs that reach `packages/mint/checks/run-checks.sh` and the tab version expression, and the generate-only `plugins` job needs none.

**Workspace and toolchain.** `allowBuilds` matches what pnpm applied, with nothing pending. `engines.node` and `packageManager` agree with AGENTS.md, and `pnpm --version` in this checkout reports the pinned 11.23.0. I probed `pnpm config set store-dir .pnpm-store` in a throwaway directory with `HOME` and the XDG variables redirected: it writes to the user config under `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, not the tracked `.npmrc`, and `pnpm store path` resolves the relative value against the project directory, so the GitLab `cache: paths: [.pnpm-store]` entry does receive the store and CI does not dirty a tracked file. `biome.json` parses and validates cleanly under the installed Biome.

**Release identity.** `tc-release.json` composes to `0.0.0-tc.1`, which matches the root `version`, `moeRelease.upstreamCommit`, the marketplace `metadata.version` and all five plugin entries. `EXPECTED_RELEASE_PACKAGES` really is eight entries, so the "eight artifacts" prose in the pipeline and the publisher is accurate. `MARKETPLACE.plugins` in `config/distribution.mjs` is the same set as `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` and as the directories in `plugins/`. The umbrella `files` array covers every local import the packed binaries make: the three bins and `bin/lib/probes.mjs` import only node builtins plus `./lib/probes.mjs` and `../config/distribution.mjs`, both listed.

**Privacy declaration.** `.ai-privacy.yml` declares `global_privacy_level: 3` with no per-path overrides, and its only consumer, `packages/core/hooks/tc-governance-enforce`, walks upward for the nearest declaration and denies only paths a level-1 declaration confirms. Declaration and enforcement agree, and the file is inert by design rather than by accident.

The credential path holds up under the lens that matters most here. The publish auth reaches exactly one place: a 0600 npmrc created inside a fresh mkdtemp directory with an exclusive-create flag, removed in a finally that also covers every early throw, and handed to npm both as a command-line userconfig and through an allowlisted addition that re-verifies the file is absolute, a regular file and mode 0600. No error message in the publish path interpolates a child's stdout or stderr, so a failing npm invocation cannot echo the token into a job log. The subprocess environment builder is an exact allowlist over ambient names with a second allowlist for deliberate additions, rejects non-strings and null bytes rather than coercing them, and its suite asserts that both known and novel credential-shaped names are dropped by construction. The CI wrapper reconstructs each of its four modes from nothing and its test compares the full visible key set, including that no safe directory lands inside the checkout and that a non-numeric job id is rejected.

The mutation ordering in the publisher is careful and well covered: the protected-push boundary is asserted before any command runs, every tarball is inspected and hashed before the registry is contacted, uploads happen under a candidate tag so the latest tag cannot move mid-train, an exact-integrity barrier re-queries all eight versions before any tag write, the umbrella package is promoted last, and a failed promotion rolls back in reverse with verification. The tests exercise the real behaviours they name rather than recomputing from the module: interrupted-promotion resume, mixed prior tags, a target older than the coherent prior, upload failure leaving tags untouched, rollback to a prior version and rollback by tag removal when there was none, and the npm plaintext dist-tag shape. The archive path validation rejects traversal, absolute paths, URLs, wildcards and duplicate entries, and the compose determinism claim is real: I ran the compose suite here and all eight tests pass, including byte-identical recomposition across a wall-clock gap and rejection of a genuinely repacked tarball that lost an executable bit. The tracked Apple provenance chain, the Cargo license generator's checksum verification against the lock file, and the Node-12 syntax guard on that generator all check out; I confirmed the generator uses no post-Node-12 API that the guard would miss. The shell build script is set-euo-pipefail clean under bash -n, traps its scratch directory, and its glibc ceiling check fails on an empty reading.
